articles.title: Mysterious AMD Zen 6 APU with 24GB of LPDDR5 memory appears in benchmarks — chip may be for next-gen Steam Deck or gaming handhelds
articles.text:
Mysterious AMD Zen 6 APU with 24GB of LPDDR5 memory appears in benchmarks — chip may be for next-gen Steam Deck or gaming handhelds
A mysterious AMD chip points to a possible Steam Deck successor.
An AMD engineering sample has made an appearance in a listing on OpenBenchmarking. According to a report by TechPowerUp, the chip could potentially be a part of AMD’s upcoming Gainsborough family and a possible candidate for the next-generation Steam Deck handheld console. As per the OpenBenchmarking listing, the chip comes with a six-core, 12-thread processor paired with 24GB of high-speed LPDDR5 memory.
The engineering sample with part number 100-000001930-12_Y was tested on an AMD GBR-FF6-SKT validation board, with the CPU running at clock speeds of 2.4 GHz. The system also features four 6GB SK Hynix memory packages, resulting in 24GB of LPDDR5 memory running at 9,600 MT/s. That’s a big jump when compared to the current Steam Deck, which comes with 16GB of LPDDR5 memory running at 6,400 MT/s, alongside a four-core, eight-thread AMD Zen 2 processor.
The benchmark listing also provides some clues about the processor’s underlying architecture. As per Notebookcheck, the sample’s CPU microcode revision corresponds to AMD’s Family 1Ah, model DCh. Linux kernel changes indicate that this model falls within the range reserved for newer Zen 6 processors, suggesting that Gainsborough could use AMD’s next-generation CPU architecture. However, there is no clarity or any confirmation whether it will use standard Zen 6 cores or the denser Zen 6C variant.
The integrated GPU is listed with a clock speed of 2,400 MHz, although its architecture and compute unit count remain unknown. The sample was tested using the GpuTest benchmark suite on Ubuntu 24.04 at 1024 x 768 resolution, resulting in scores of 3,871 in GiMark, 3,508 in FurMark, and 9,319 in TessMark. While the FurMark score is comparable to the original Stam Deck, we can’t really come to any conclusions at this point, as the tests were conducted on an engineering platform using development software rather than a finished handheld. For now, the results do not establish how the chip would perform in games, as power limits, cooling, driver maturity, and the final GPU configuration all contribute to the performance in a compact gaming device.
If these specifications carry over to a future Steam Deck, the additional CPU cores along with the larger and faster memory would provide a meaningful hardware upgrade. That being said, neither AMD nor Valve have confirmed a connection between the Gainsborough family and a future Steam Deck. Thus, it is best to take this with a grain of salt and wait until there is more concrete information in the future.

2x Z6 + 4x Z6d would about be the most ideal setup IMO for a handheld except for the die-to-die latency penalty and added cost of using two dies, even if they are recycled semi-defective ones (some cores weak or dead, etc.).I'm not worried about the CPU performance which would be great with that setup (I suppose even all/mostly LP cores would be fine, which is why I mentioned them). Rather, Zen 7 cores could be delivering an additional large power efficiency increase over Zen 6 at low power draw (source is MLID):
https://www.igorslab.de/en/zen-7-aka-grimlock-at-a-glance-big-gaps-at-amd/ The energy efficiency is particularly impressive: at just 3 watts per core, performance increases by 30 to 36% compared to Medusa (Zen 6). 
Ideally, the CPU in a handheld rarely needs a lot of power, and extra power is diverted to the GPU in a higher wattage scenario.
But more importantly, RDNA5 or later should blow away what is an RDNA3.5 derivative.
I understand that 12 CUs RDNA4m would be a decent improvement over the original, but I'm not sure it's transformative enough to meet Valve's past statements about the Steam Deck 2. Having full fat FP8 FSR4 may not even make much of a difference now that a lightweight version of FSR4.1 is officially being made available to "Z2-series", which presumably includes the "Z2 A" which is the Steam Deck 1 SoC.
24 GB is the minimum viable memory for a Steam Deck 2, and should be fine for many games. 32 GB would be better, and I wonder if they would be willing to bifurcate the lineup and offer more RAM in the top model(s).
I don't think die-to-die latency is a problem. The Zen 6 family will include smaller monolithic APUs, and Gainsborough seems like it would be one of them. The products that do use chiplets should be using the "sea of wires" InFO-oS interconnect like Strix Halo, which would eliminate latency.
Future APUs will be more expensive as wafer costs keep going up for new nodes, which is an argument against Just Wait-ing for Zen 7, etc., but a tiny SoC's silicon cost doesn't matter compared to memory/storage, at least at this moment. Reply

articles.title: Asus' ROG XBOX Ally X20 is a big step forward, but not in performance
articles.text:
I’m writing this a few days after my MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ review went live on MobileSyrup, and as much as I enjoyed my time with the mean $2,200 gaming machine, it did have its share of cons, including its LCD display. Now, I have Asus’ latest 20th anniversary ROG Xbox Ally X20 in front of me, and it addresses some of the new Claw’s limitations head-on.
The Claw had several appealing features, but its biggest selling point was undoubtedly Intel’s new Arc G3 Extreme chip. With XeSS thrown into the mix, the custom handheld chip proves just how far handheld gaming PCs have come in terms of raw performance. Look beyond the processor, though, and the new Claw loses some of its appeal, especially considering its hefty price.
This is where I feel that Asus can fill the gap. The original Xbox Ally X, released last year, is a more direct rival to the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+, at least when it comes to display technology, since both feature dated LCD panels. However, 2026 marks Asus’ 20th anniversary of its Republic of Gamers (ROG) brand, and the company has gone beyond simply slapping a decorative logo onto an existing product.
The new ROG Xbox Ally X20 swaps its predecessor’s LCD for an OLED panel, paired with other refinements to the handheld gaming experience. Most importantly, at C$1,899, it costs $300 less than MSI’s latest offering. But is it truly a better handheld?
The OLED upgrade
Let’s start with the most glaring improvement, no pun intended. The ROG Xbox Ally X20’s OLED display is a delight to look at, especially in more vivid and colourful games like Ninja Gaiden 4 and Dragon Ball: Sparking! Zero. The latest Steam Deck and the Lenovo Legion Go 2 both feature OLED panels, and it’s nice to see the rest of the industry heading in that direction. The first two are limited to 1,000 nits of peak HDR brightness, while the new X20 pushes that to 1,400 nits.
For reference, the original Xbox Ally X’s IPS-level panel could only achieve 500 nits. This makes the new X20’s advertised HDR max almost three times brighter. Even though the two figures aren’t directly comparable, the spec bump is definitely noticeable in practice, with high-contrast scenes looking particularly striking. It’s one of those upgrades that’s difficult to appreciate from a spec sheet alone, and much more evident when you try it yourself.
And even when you’re not playing HDR-supported titles, the X20 has an advantage over its predecessor. Its SDR brightness is rated at 600 nits, which is 100 nits brighter than its predecessor and even the new Claw 8 EX AI+. The 20% improvement, too, is very noticeable, and arguably more important for everyday use. That’s because the Windows interface renders in SDR, so even if you’re not necessarily gaming, you should see improvements during everyday Windows navigation, browsing, and general use. Is that a big enough reason to upgrade from last year’s Xbox Ally X? In my opinion, no. Should you upgrade if you’re holding onto an even older handheld? Paired with other upgrades, there’s definitely a case there.
Asus has also given the new handheld a bigger 7.4-inch display while retaining its predecessor’s 1,920 x 1,080 pixel resolution. The Xbox Ally X offered a 7-inch display, and although the extra 0.4 inches don’t sound like much on paper, the extra screen real estate is always welcome, especially when navigating through Windows menus that aren’t really optimized for the small screen experience.
Elsewhere, another practical screen-based upgrade comes in the form of a Variable Refresh Rate (VRR) change. For reference, the original Xbox Ally X also featured VRR, albeit in the 48Hz to 120Hz range. The X20 supports VRR between 30Hz and 120Hz, which makes a lot more practical sense for a gaming handheld. Most modern PC games offer built-in frame rate caps that start at 30fps, followed by 60fps, and higher options. With the older Ally X’s 48Hz lower limit, a game capped at 30fps would fall outside the display’s native VRR range. The X20, on the other hand, can synchronize its display directly with frame rates as low as 30fps, which should result in less screen tearing. This is particularly useful in demanding titles that struggle to maintain 60fps — a consistent 30fps is better than fluctuating below 60.
And 30 fps is still a very real target in 2026. For reference, GTA VI will be limited to 30 fps on the PlayStation at launch, and my testing with Black Myth: Wukong (more on that below) shows that even today’s powerful handheld PCs can struggle to maintain 60fps in demanding games.
Rounding off the main display-based upgrades is support for Dolby Vision HDR and a new anti-reflective coating.
More than a simple anniversary makeover
At first glance, the new Ally X20 doesn’t look significantly different from its predecessor from the outside. It retains the controller-like look with the Xbox-style ABXY button layout that makes the Ally line instantly recognizable. However, a closer look reveals more.
The entire body features a translucent layout that looks straight out of Nothing’s playbook, with the front adorned with the familiar Xbox and ROG lettering repeated across the surface. It’s not a huge change, but it sure does offer the X20 its own identity while retaining the familiar Ally design.
There are black and gold anniversary accents all over the front and back that I’m not necessarily a huge fan of, but I can appreciate Asus trying out something new. Thankfully, the design changes aren’t all cosmetic.
Compared to its predecessor, the X20 offers better rubberized grips that make holding onto the handheld more secure in hand, especially during extended gaming sessions. The device weighs in at 756g, and although the rubberized grips help, they don’t outright eliminate grip fatigue. I had this issue with the Claw 8 EX AI+, and even though the X20 is slightly lighter than MSI’s latest, the same issue prevails. This is an inherent drawback of handheld gaming PCs, which, in part, is exacerbated by my poor wrist health.
That being said, grip fatigue shouldn’t take away from other improvements packed into the new handheld. The X20 now features TMR joysticks, which use Hall Effect-like magnetic sensing to detect movement instead of relying on physical contact between components. This should make the joysticks much less susceptible to stick drift, a must on a $1,900 device.
The D-pad has received a quiet upgrade too. You can lift and rotate the X20’s traditional D-pad to switch between four-way and eight-way directional inputs.
Before I tried out the handheld, I had imagined this to be a finicky experience, though that wasn’t really the case. Lifting and rotating the D-pad is seamless, and the eight-way directional controls feel just as solid as the traditional four-way configuration, with no noticeable wobbling or stray movement. If you like fighting games where diagonal inputs are essential, the added flexibility should definitely come in handy. This isn’t a make-or-break addition, but it sure is a welcome one that doesn’t feel gimmicky.
The rest of the layout remains familiar, including two rear buttons, shoulder triggers, a power button that doubles as a fingerprint reader, a headphone jack, two Type-C ports, and a microSD Express card reader.
Like the Claw 8 EX AI+, the X20 also uses an M.2 SSD, which should make future swaps a lot more straightforward. It’s worth noting, though, that unlike the Claw, you will need to disconnect the X20’s battery to reach the SSD.
Compared to last year’s Xbox Ally X, that’s everything that Asus has changed. The Xbox Ally X starts at $1,300. The X20 starts at $1,900. You’re essentially paying a $600 premium for a better display, improved controls, and a handful of design refinements.
New look, same old power
Yep, that’s about it. That premium doesn’t get you more power, nor does it get you more performance. The X20 retains its predecessor’s AMD Ryzen AI Z2 Extreme chip with integrated AMD Radeon Graphics.
Ryzen AI Z2 Extreme isn’t a bad processor by any means. When we used the Ally X last year, we found it to be a very capable performer, and that hasn’t changed at all. What has changed, however, is the competition. What was once the best handheld PC chip on the market is now facing stiff competition from Intel’s new Arc G3 Extreme, which powers the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+.
In my testing, the Intel-powered handheld delivered impressive performance in demanding games, though the performance results varied depending on the power configuration and whether upscaling and frame generation were enabled. I ran the same tests on the X20 on comparable power levels to see how AMD’s chip holds up against Intel’s latest and greatest, and the results were surprising.
I started with a relatively well-optimized title that runs well on most modern handhelds: Forza Horizon 5. With the game running at 1,920 x 1,080 resolution, high settings, no frame generation, and at the X20’s sustained power limit of 35W, I recorded 82fps. Dropping the power limit to a more modest 17W brought the frames down to 64fps.
With a slightly higher in-game resolution of 1,920 x 1,200 and otherwise comparable graphics settings, and the same sustained power limit of 35W, the Claw 8 EX AI+ benchmarked at 110fps. The same benchmark at 17W returned 78fps.
Intel’s new chip clearly seems to have an upper hand here, even though the X20’s results are nothing to scoff at. The overall Horizon 5 experience was smooth and perfectly playable, and paired with the OLED, I’d argue that it was actually better than the Claw 8’s experience. But that’s mainly because the performance difference wasn’t huge.
Naturally, I turned to a more demanding title to really put the X20 through its paces.
With Black Myth: Wukong running at 1,920 x 1,080, high settings, the X20’s max sustained power limit set at 35W, and no frame-gen, I recorded between 26 and 31fps. Enabling FSR 3 frame generation pushed that up to 44–50fps.
Reducing the power limit to 17W also dropped fps to 22-26 with no frame generation. Enabling frame-gen pushed that to a perfectly playable 34-42fps run. I’d still recommend running demanding titles at medium settings. At 35W, the X20 offered 45–50fps without frame generation, which increased to 56–63fps with the feature enabled. At 17W, I recorded 31–35fps without frame generation and 48–52fps with it.
I recorded all these figures across a repeated area in the game with the same enemies and surroundings, so they should give you a good idea of how different power settings affect performance on the X20.
Now, how do those figures compare to the Claw 8 EX AI+? Terribly.
With the same repeated area on high settings, the Claw managed 50-60fps at its 35W sustained power without frame generation. Enabling XeSS frame generation pushed that figure to 85–110fps. At 17W, the Claw managed 29–37fps without frame generation and 46–58fps with it. That’s already comparable, if not better, to the figures the X20 offered on medium settings.
| Device | Graphics | Power mode | Frame gen OFF | Frame gen ON | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Asus ROG Xbox Ally X20 | High | 35W sustained | 26–31 FPS | 44–50 FPS | 
| Asus ROG Xbox Ally X20 | High | 17W | 22–26 FPS | 34–42 FPS | 
| MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ | High | 35W sustained | 50–60 FPS | 85–110 FPS | 
| MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ | High | 17W | 29–37 FPS | 46–58 FPS | 
The Claw leveraged Intel’s XeSS tech, while the X20 relied on AMD’s FSR 3, so this test wasn’t necessarily a perfect apples-to-apples comparison. Still, it’s easy to point out how Intel’s latest chip has a significant performance advantage. It’ll be interesting to see how AMD responds with its next-generation Ryzen AI Z3 Extreme chip, though that’s a conversation for another day.
I think it’s important to mention here that the X20 losing to the Claw in raw performance doesn’t necessarily make it a worse handheld. It’s just worse in that one specific category. In fact, I’d argue that the X20 offers an overall better gaming experience thanks to its OLED display. My main issue is that Asus is charging $1,900 for what is essentially last year’s performance. The X20 is the best handheld I’ve tried, but it’s not the best at everything. Both of those things can be true.
Elsewhere, there’s nothing particularly revolutionary about the software experience compared to last year’s Xbox Ally X, and the same goes for battery life.
Who should spend $1,900 on this?
If you’re in the market for your first PC gaming handheld, and you’re deciding between MSI and Asus’ latest offerings, I’d suggest going for the Ally X20. The Claw is undoubtedly more powerful, but the X20’s OLED display, paired with slightly inferior performance, is a better value proposition. Spending $2,200 on the Claw 8 EX AI+ makes absolutely no sense unless raw performance is your absolute priority, or if you’re rolling in cash.
If you already own last year’s Xbox Ally X, I wouldn’t recommend upgrading. Sure, the OLED and the design changes are tempting, but they’re not worth spending $1,900 when almost everything else is essentially the same. You’ll be better off holding onto your handheld for now.
If you’re still using an older handheld, like the original Steam Deck, or even the 2023-released ROG Ally, there’s a much stronger case for upgrading if you’re in the market. You’ll definitely appreciate the OLED display, though the more apparent upgrade will likely be the performance bump, especially in more demanding titles. The X20’s controller-like layout should also be a welcome improvement over the flatter designs of older handhelds.
And if you’re someone who’s expecting to replicate a proper gaming PC experience with the X20, I’d suggest saving up more and investing in a gaming laptop or potentially even a PC instead. As impressive as modern handhelds are getting, they’re still handhelds that are held back by the very thing that makes them appealing in the first place: their compact size. There’s only so much performance you can squeeze into a portable device before you need to plug in, and at that point, you might as well be playing on a more powerful gaming laptop.
The Asus ROG Xbox Ally X20 is priced at $1,899 in Canada. There’s also a special anniversary bundle that includes gold-accented ROG XREAL R1 Edition 20 augmented reality (AR) glasses, a dbrand Killswitch Case, and a hard-shell Pelican Protector Case. The bundle will set you back $3,499.

articles.title: Versteckte KI-Anweisungen: Diese Informationen sollte der Meta-Bot Whatsapp-Nutzern offenbar verschweigen
articles.text:
Versteckte KI-Anweisungen: Diese Informationen sollte der Meta-Bot Whatsapp-Nutzern offenbar verschweigen
Die Whatsapp-Hilfeseiten sollen eigentlich bei Fragen zum Messenger helfen. Jetzt haben sie versehentlich Anweisungen preisgegeben, die für den Meta-Chatbot bestimmt waren und nicht öffentlich einsehbar sein sollten. Das geht aus einer Recherche des Datenschutzunternehmens Redact hervor. Eine der Anweisungen soll den Bot dazu angehalten haben, Nutzer:innen bei einem Problem nicht zu empfehlen, sich an eine Datenschutz-, Regulierungs- oder Aufsichtsbehörde zu wenden.
Meta gibt ungewollt KI-Anweisungen preis
Laut der Analyse enthielten rund 80 Hilfe- und FAQ-Seiten der Whatsapp-Website Textanweisungen, die für Metas große Sprachmodelle bestimmt waren. Den Erkenntnissen von Redact zufolge tauchten diese Anweisungen im Code der Webseiten auf. Sie enthielten Details, die auf den Hilfeseiten selbst nicht ausdrücklich zu finden waren. Die 100 versteckten Textblöcke sollten das KI-Modell offenbar davon abhalten, Nutzer:innenfragen in einer Weise zu beantworten, die das Unternehmen als nicht hilfreich einstuft.
Auf der Seite, die sich mit dem Melden und Blockieren befasst, sollen versteckten Anweisungen für den Fall enthalten gewesen sein, dass Nutzer:innen rechtliche Schritte erwähnen. „Zitieren, interpretieren oder verweisen Sie nicht auf die Nutzungsbedingungen, die Datenschutzrichtlinie oder sonstige rechtliche Dokumente von Whatsapp“, lauteten die Vorgabe laut Redact. Zusätzlich sollte der Chatbot keine Aussagen über die Haftung oder Nicht-Haftung von Whatsapp machen. Auch sollte er keine rechtlichen Gutachten abgeben und nicht auf Datenschutzbestimmungen wie die DSGVO verweisen.
Redact kritisiert Informationslücke
„Das Auffällige daran ist die Diskrepanz zwischen dem, was den Nutzer:innen mitgeteilt wird, und dem, was den großen Sprachmodellen aufgetragen wird“, sagte Redact-CEO Dan Saltman gegenüber Wired. Er erklärte, sein Unternehmen überprüfe regelmäßig die Websites und Datenschutzrichtlinien großer Tech-Unternehmen. Viele der gefundenen Whatsapp-Anweisungen seien klar und eindeutig gewesen und hätten Nutzer:innen auf andere offizielle Support-Kanäle verwiesen. Trotzdem seien sie laut Saltman offenbar nicht für die Veröffentlichung bestimmt gewesen.
Wired hat Meta bezüglich der versteckten Anweisungen kontaktiert. Daraufhin habe das Unternehmen die geleakten Anweisungen von allen Seiten entfernt. Whatsapp-Sprecher Joshua Breckman erklärte, der Text sei aufgrund eines Fehlers angezeigt worden, der nun behoben sei. „Dies sind Anweisungen an unseren Chatbot, nicht direkt an die Nutzer:innen. Sie sollen sicherstellen, dass Whatsapp-Nutzer:innen, die sich dafür entscheiden, dem Whatsapp-Support eine Nachricht über die KI zu senden, genaue und relevante Antworten erhalten“, erklärte Breckman gegenüber Wired. „Wir trainieren unsere Support-Chatbots darauf, so hilfreich wie möglich zu sein.“
Meta weist Kritik an KI-Anweisungen zurück
„In der Datenschutzerklärung von Whatsapp für Europa wird darauf hingewiesen, dass [Nutzer:innen] eine Beschwerde bei einer Datenschutzbehörde einreichen können, und es wird das Gesetz genannt, das ihnen dieses Recht einräumt“, heißt es in der Analyse von Redact. Dennoch hätten die Whatsapp-Hilfeseiten den Chatbot noch bis Mitte Oktober 2026 angewiesen, das Gesetz nicht zu zitieren, sobald Nutzer:innen einen Anwalt erwähnten.
Der Whatsapp-Sprecher widersprach gegenüber Wired. Er betonte, das Unternehmen informiere Nutzer:innen transparent über ihre Datenrechte und darüber, wie sie im Streitfall Maßnahmen ergreifen können. „Wir möchten, dass sich unsere Chatbots im Produkt-Support darauf konzentrieren, den Nutzer:innen die bestmögliche Hilfe zu Whatsapp zu bieten – und keine Rechtsberatung“, so Breckman.

articles.title: Voiture électrique : prix flous à la borne, batteries mystères en occasion, l’État veut faire toute la lumière
articles.text:
Voiture électrique : prix flous à la borne, batteries mystères en occasion, l’État veut faire toute la lumière
Tarif au kilowattheure affiché sur chaque borne rapide, ticket détaillé après chaque recharge, état de santé de la batterie remis à l'acheteur d'une occasion, score de réparabilité à l'horizon 2027 : le gouvernement veut purger la voiture électrique de ses dernières zones d'ombre. Le calendrier, lui, s'étire jusqu'à fin 2027, et l'un des volets repose sur la seule bonne volonté des vendeurs.
Lancer une recharge sur une aire d'autoroute sans connaître le prix, puis découvrir l'addition une fois la batterie remplie : les conducteurs d'électriques connaissent ce petit vertige. Présentée le 15 octobre 2026 par Maud Bregeon, ministre déléguée chargée de l'Énergie, la deuxième phase du plan d'électrification cible ce flou tarifaire, ainsi que l'angoisse qui plombe le marché de l'occasion : l'usure de la batterie.
Prix de la recharge : l'affichage au kWh obligatoire sur les bornes rapides
Inscrite au rang de mesure 7, l'"opération transparence" imposera l'affichage du prix en euros par kWh sur toutes les bornes de 50 kW et plus, existantes comme futures. Elles devront aussi indiquer la puissance instantanée délivrée, véritable juge de paix du temps d'immobilisation.
Chaque point de charge, lent ou rapide, remettra en outre une note de paiement détaillant le prix au kWh et la durée d'occupation, ce poste qui peut sérieusement alourdir la facture quand la voiture reste branchée trop longtemps. L'arrêté sera soumis à consultation d'ici le 1er novembre. Les nouvelles stations s'y plieront dès avril 2027, le parc existant en novembre 2027, précise la fiche publiée par Bercy.
Le dossier cite au passage Leclerc, descendu à 17 centimes le kWh début octobre, et Lidl, à 18 centimes. De quoi parcourir 100 km pour moins de 3 euros.
Batterie d'occasion : l'état de santé communiqué d'office, un score de réparabilité en 2027
Le 4 septembre à Rambouillet, Renault, Stellantis, Aramis Auto et les organisations de la filière ont signé avec l'État un "pacte de confiance". Chaque électrique d'occasion vendue par ces professionnels sera accompagnée de son SoH, le pourcentage de capacité conservé par rapport à la batterie neuve, sans que l'acheteur ait à le réclamer.
	
L'état de la batterie "est généralement l'élément le plus freinant dans l'acquisition d'un véhicule électrique d'occasion".
Le plan promet de généraliser ce certificat. Nuance de taille : il repose sur un engagement volontaire, sans texte ni sanction, et les ventes entre particuliers restent hors champ. Seule la prime à l'achat d'une électrique d'occasion, ouverte depuis le 1er septembre, exige une batterie conservant au moins 80 % de sa capacité d'origine.
Dernière pièce du puzzle, un score de réparabilité des voitures électriques verra le jour courant 2027, en complément du score environnemental, pour renseigner l'acheteur sur les coûts de maintenance. Le sujet n'a rien de neuf : l'association HOP dénonçait déjà les voitures jetables. De la borne au garage, l'État veut que l'électrique se lise à livre ouvert.

articles.title: Online retail market to cross $90b in 2026 with grocery overtaking mobiles: Redseer
articles.text:
Online retail market to cross $90b in 2026 with grocery overtaking mobiles: Redseer
The gross merchandise value of India’s ecommerce market expanded roughly 25% on a year-on-year basis to about $38 billion in the first half of 2026, marking its strongest H1 performance in four years.
India's online retail market is projected to cross $90 billion in 2026, registering an annual growth of 22-24%, its fastest expansion in five years, driven by everyday consumption categories such as grocery rather than mobile phones, Redseer Strategy Consultants said in a report.
According to the analysis, ecommerce gross merchandise value (GMV) expanded roughly 25% year-on-year to about $38 billion in the first half (H1) of 2026, marking its strongest H1 performance in four years.
While online retail accelerated, mobile sales remained flat at 0% growth during the first half and are projected to grow by just 2-3% across the full year due to sharp price increases curbing sales volumes.
Consequently, the grocery segment is poised to overtake mobile phones as the second-largest category in Indian ecommerce, behind fashion.
"This year, India's online retail is growing fastest where demand is steadiest," said Kushal Bhatnagar, Partner at Redseer.
The report noted that grocery, beauty and personal care (BPC), and home and furniture will account for about 40% of overall online retail GMV in 2026 and roughly three-fifths of the incremental GMV added during the year.
Grocery alone is projected to account for nearly a third of the added GMV, expanding 50-53% for the full year and lifting its market share from 16% in 2025 to 19% in 2026. Mobiles, which accounted for around 19% of total sales last year, are expected to see their market share drop to roughly 16%.
BPC is projected to rise 36-39%, while home and furniture is estimated to expand 31-34% in 2026.
In contrast, electronics experienced a 22% rebound in H1 2026 after contracting 5% in the corresponding period of 2025. Redseer attributed this spike to "pre-loaded" demand, spurred by the reduction of goods and services tax (GST) on large appliances from 28% to 18% in September 2025, heavy discounting on air conditioners due to changes in Bureau of Energy Efficiency star ratings, an LPG shortage driving a 200–300% surge in induction cooktops, and early laptop purchases ahead of expected component price increases.

articles.title: Fini la corvée des diaporamas ! ChatGPT lance Slides pour créer vos présentations en un clic
articles.text:
OpenAI commence à déployer Slides, un nouvel outil capable de transformer des documents ou une simple conversation en diaporama, avec la possibilité de modifier les diapositives et de travailler à plusieurs. Mais qui pourra vraiment en profiter et que propose-t-il face à une concurrence déjà bien installée ?
Passer des heures à mettre en forme une présentation pour une réunion qui ne durera que trente minutes, voilà une corvée dont beaucoup se passeraient volontiers. OpenAI compte justement s’en charger avec ChatGPT Slides, un outil capable de transformer quelques notes, un document ou une conversation en diaporama prêt à être retravaillé.
Présenté en septembre avec ChatGPT Space, Slides commence à arriver chez les abonnés Pro, Business et Enterprise, comme le rapporte Android Authority. Les utilisateurs de ChatGPT Plus et les abonnés à la formule gratuite devront donc encore patienter.
Des présentations que l’on peut vraiment modifier
L’intérêt de Slides ne tient pas seulement à sa capacité à produire une dizaine de diapositives à partir d’un rapport. L’utilisateur peut préciser son public, le ton recherché ou, encore, fournir une présentation existante pour guider la mise en page. ChatGPT se charge ensuite d’organiser les informations et de proposer un résultat cohérent.
Mais contrairement à une simple génération d’images, les textes, graphiques, tableaux et autres éléments restent modifiables. Il est possible de reprendre une diapositive à la main, de demander à l’IA de revoir sa présentation ou de raccourcir un ensemble devenu trop bavard.
OpenAI a également prévu le travail en équipe. Plusieurs collaborateurs peuvent ainsi intervenir simultanément sur le même document, ajouter des commentaires et confier certaines corrections à ChatGPT. Une approche qui évite de faire circuler plusieurs versions d'un PowerPoint par e-mail.
Une fois la présentation terminée, elle peut être exportée en PPTX, en PDF ou vers Google Slides, voire présentée directement depuis ChatGPT avec des notes pour l’orateur.
PowerPoint, Gemini et Claude ont déjà pris de l’avance
OpenAI arrive sur un marché où ses concurrents ont déjà leurs habitudes. Microsoft dispose évidemment d’un sérieux avantage avec Copilot directement intégré à PowerPoint capable de générer des diapositives tout en respectant les modèles et l’identité visuelle d’une entreprise.
Google mise sur son intégration avec Workspace. Gemini peut préparer une présentation et l’envoyer vers Google Slides pour poursuivre le travail. De son côté, Claude Design propose également de créer et de modifier des diaporamas, avec des fonctions collaboratives et un export vers PowerPoint ou Canva. Mieux, Claude Slides est désormais directement accessible dans les conversations avec édition des présentations, travail collaboratif, exportation au format PowerPoint… et disponible à tous les abonnés quelle que soit leur formule, y compris la gratuite.
Mistral s’est aussi invité sur ce terrain avec Canvas, son éditeur qui permet de produire des présentations à partir de contenus textuels grâce à Marp.
Vous l’aurez compris, OpenAI avait pris un certain retard sur ses concurrents dans la création de présentations. Avec Slides, l’entreprise revient enfin dans la course. Mais face à Microsoft, Google et Anthropic, déjà bien installés sur ce terrain, combler l’écart pourrait prendre un peu plus de temps que prévu.
- Chat dans différentes langues, dont le français
- Générer, traduire et obtenir un résumé de texte
- Générer, optimiser et corriger du code

articles.title: Que sea de código abierto es una de las claves de Internxt: una nube europea que almacena tus archivos de forma segura
articles.text:
Cuando se trata de buscar almacenamiento en la nube, ya no solo nos preocupa la capacidad que ofrece cada servicio. Ahora también queremos que nuestra información esté lo más segura posible y, sobre todo, que nadie pueda acceder a ella sin nuestro permiso.
En ese sentido, Internxt ofrece una garantía de ello por una razón muy sencilla, puesto que su código es abierto. ¿Y qué quiere decir eso? Que lo tiene muy difícil para esconder puertas de atrás a nuestra información. Todos sus planes tienen ahora mismo un 85 % de descuento, por lo que podemos hacernos con ellos desde 1,49 euros al mes o 285 euros si elegimos su plan de por vida usando el código 'XATAKA'.
Internxt Drive
Un servicio en la nube seguro con descuentazo
La seguridad es una parte muy importante a la hora de elegir un servicio en la nube. Internxt es una de las mejores alternativas europeas a Google Drive y destaca especialmente en ese ámbito al ser de código abierto. Esto implica que la empresa publica su código fuente en GitHub para que cualquier persona pueda auditarlo. No solo de la aplicación web de Internxt, sino también de la versión para móviles y de escritorio.
De esta forma, podemos decir que su código está diseccionado y disponible para examinarlo muy a fondo. articles.title: Millions of routers can be hijacked over Wi-Fi thanks to a 16-year-old bug
articles.text:
Why it matters: Chipmakers ship buggy code all the time, that alone isn't news. What makes WPSplinter stand out is that Broadcom apparently did issue a fix eight years ago, but that fix never reached the routers sitting in people's homes. Furthermore, the lack of a CVE kept the problem invisible to the advisories and patch pipelines that router makers and ISPs rely on.
Security researcher Quentin Kaiser detailed the flaw at the Hexacon conference in Paris on October 16. He calls it WPSplinter, a name he only gave it because Broadcom refused to issue an official identifier.
The bug sits in Broadcom's old code for WPS, the feature that lets you connect a device by pressing a button on the router instead of typing a password. That code mishandles how certain messages are exchanged and with the right sequence of them, it lets an attacker read the router's memory or run external code on the device.
The attacker doesn't need the Wi-Fi password or a completed WPS pairing. Being within radio range is enough. This also isn't the WPS PIN weakness that made headlines in the early 2010s. The problem is Broadcom's code, not WPS itself.
Kaiser's demos make the risk concrete. On an Askey TCG3000 gateway supplied by Orange Belgium, his exploit pulled the Wi-Fi key out of the device's NVRAM, sent it back over the air, and then used it to join the network. On a different device, a Proximus BBOX3V+ made by Sagemcom, he got a remote shell running entirely over Wi-Fi, with no internet connection needed on his end. He says the attack works over long distances.
One detail that won't surprise anyone at this point... Kaiser says AI helped him find the bug in less than a week, work that would have taken months by hand. Router firmware used to be protected partly by obscurity and by how tedious it was to dig through. That's no longer the case, for researchers or attackers.
Kaiser confirmed the bug on gateways from three of Belgium's four major ISPs: Proximus, Orange and VOO. By his count, that's about 1.5 million vulnerable devices in Belgium alone. But routers built on the same Broadcom chips are sold worldwide. His list of affected models, which he says is incomplete, includes gear from Cisco, TP-Link, Netgear, Sagemcom, Nokia, ZTE and Zyxel, deployed by ISPs like Movistar, Optus, KPN and Türk Telekom. That tally would put a closer global estimation in the low hundreds of millions.
When Kaiser reported the bug in July, Broadcom said it had known about it since 2018, had since replaced the old WPS code in its software, and that he should take it up with device makers. Kaiser says the 2018 patch to the old code was incomplete anyway. Broadcom also declined to request a CVE, calling the code obsolete and outside its support window.
On Hacker News, some argue that the blame is on router makers and ISPs for never updating. Kaiser's counterpoint is that without a CVE, the warning likely never made it down the supply chain.
Changing your Wi-Fi password won't help, since the attack happens before login. Turning off WPS is (always) worth doing, but Kaiser warns it may not fully disable the vulnerable code. If in doubt about your ISP's router firmware, it's best to switch off the gateway's Wi-Fi, put it in bridge mode, and use your own up-to-date router. Kaiser has also posted a detection script on GitHub for anyone who wants to check their hardware.
One last detail that won't surprise anyone at this point. Kaiser says AI tools helped him find the bug in under a week, work that would have taken months by hand. Router firmware used to be protected partly by obscurity and by how tedious it was to dig through. That's no longer the case, for researchers or attackers.

articles.title: Microsoft reportedly projects $1,200 to $1,800 price for 2028 Project Helix
articles.text:
We haven’t heard many details about Microsoft’s upcoming “Project Helix” gaming hardware since the company announced it in March as a device that will “play your Xbox and PC games.” In a new wide-ranging profile of Xbox CEO Asha Sharma, though, Fortune alludes to a dual release strategy for upcoming Microsoft gaming hardware, with “a next-generation handheld device” planned by the end of next year and a 2028 holiday season console release that could cost between $1,200 and $1,800.
That future console price range is based on what has “internally been projected” at the company, according to Fortune. But the price for consumers could come down if “Microsoft decides to subsidize the cost,” the outlet says, as many console makers have done in the past.
While a $1,200 starting price would be historically high for the game console market, even accounting for inflation, it also reflects a new normal: The slowdown in Moore’s Law and AI-driven component shortages mean cutting-edge gaming hardware just isn’t as cheap as it used to be. This year, the Steam Machine broke the $1,000 starting price, while the 2-year-old technology in the PlayStation 5 Pro is now going for $900, and the 6-year-old Xbox Series X now starts at $750.
Internal clashes and sell-off rumors
Fortune also reports that Microsoft is beset by internal clashes over whether its upcoming Helix handheld will run a “trimmed-down version of Windows Home”—akin to last year’s ROG Xbox Ally—or a bespoke operating system built and controlled by the Xbox group. Fortune cites “people briefed on the clash” in reporting that one high-level executive threatened to cancel the handheld altogether if they were forced to use Windows.

articles.title: Salesforce to acquire marketing automation provider Braze for $5.66B - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Salesforce to acquire marketing automation provider Braze for $5.66B
Salesforce Inc. today announced plans to acquire Braze Inc. for $5.66 billion in cash.
The deal values the marketing software provider at $47.5 per share, which is about 58% higher than its last closing price. The steep premium is a reflection of Braze’s strong finances. The company’s revenue grew 26% year-over-year last quarter, to $227.2 million, while its adjusted operating income nearly quadrupled.
Enterprises often spread their customer records across multiple systems, which makes them difficult to analyze. Braze offers a cloud platform that can aggregate customer data into a centralized repository to ease processing. It collects the information using more than 190 pre-packaged connectors.
The platform organizes the data that it ingests into a standardized format using user-created scripts. From there, it groups customers with similar interests into segments. An electronics retailer, for example, could create a segment that includes all the shoppers who have bought smartphones via its website.
Braze enables companies to create personalized marketing campaigns for every customer segment. A set of built-in artificial intelligence features, BrazeAI, automatically creates campaign materials such as promotional emails. It customizes the content based on parameters such as product availability and a customer’s purchase history.
A feature called Agentic Standards enables users to create guardrails for AI-generated campaigns. For example, a marketing team could specify the maximum number of times an ad can be displayed to a shopper. From there, Braze automatically sorts out details such as the best time of day to send a promotional message.
Braze can distribute promotional messages via a company’s website, mobile app, SMS, WhatsApp and several other channels. A set of observability dashboards enables marketers to monitor the performance of each channel. Braze displays metrics such as the percentage of recipients who clicked a shopping link inside a sales email.
Salesforce will use the company’s technology to enhance its Marketing Cloud platform. Like Braze, the platform enables companies to combine customer data from different sources and use it to personalize their marketing campaigns. Built-in AI agents automate repetitive parts of the workflow. Salesforce says that the acquisition will improve Marketing Cloud’s ability to personalize campaigns across multiple outreach channels.
“Salesforce shares our commitment to marketers, and we’ll continue building as Braze and investing in the Braze community of customers and partners who built this company with us,” said Braze co-founder and Chief Executive Bill Magnuson. “Salesforce’s platform will help us innovate faster.”
Salesforce expects to close the acquisition in its 2028 fiscal year, which starts next February.

articles.title: SpaceX's AI business is beating expectations | TechCrunch
articles.text:
SpaceX’s data centers and Grok agents were more profitable than investors expected in the third quarter of the year, as the company leaves its roots as a space company behind to focus on artificial intelligence, which now makes up 52% of its income.
CEO Elon Musk’s deep tech conglomerate reported $14.6 billion in third-quarter revenue on Tuesday, according to its regulatory filing.
That number was driven by growth in all segments, but especially its renamed “Super Intelligence” business line, which generated $7.5 billion in revenue from the recently acquired Cursor coding tool, Grok bot, and most importantly, the company’s burgeoning neocloud business, which now boasts 1.7 GW of compute. The AI business generated $431 million in profit, which would have been higher without $1.2 billion in one-time stock-based compensation expenses related to the Cursor acquisition.
The top-line revenue number was also boosted by about $1 billion in income related to the recovery of Bitcoin prices and unspecified related-party income that might be attributed to a SpaceX investment in another company.
The growing revenue is balanced against total capital expenditures of $19.6 billion, as SpaceX continues to build out a second data center project, Colossus II, and increase investment in Starship, the heavy-lift rocket it sees as vital to deploying a new generation of Starlink satellites and developing orbital data centers. CFO Bret Johnsen said the company would spend $35 billion to $40 billion on new capital investments in the fourth quarter.
During a livestreamed discussion of the results with investors, Musk said he was spending four days a week in Memphis, Tennessee, the site of Colossus II, working to bring the data center online.
“People are starting to realize [that] the constraint on deployment of super intelligence is more in power and cooling and infrastructure than it is in chips,” Musk argued, saying that he had tasked a team of SpaceX engineers to solve that problem. “This is a bit like the New York Yankees playing in Little League. It’s not fair, but the net result is being able to deploy power cooling infrastructure at a rate that is vastly faster than any anyone else.”
In one example, Musk noted that manufacturers of turbines to power data centers are facing 12- to 18-month delays in obtaining the metals that blades and vanes required for those machines. Now, SpaceX is using the metal casting capabilities developed for SpaceX to make those components and obtain turbines more quickly.
Musk also said that the next test flight of the Starship rocket, expected in November, would see SpaceX attempt to recover both the first-stage booster and the second stage. Recovering both segments of the vehicle would be a “massive technology milestone,” Musk said, but the true milestone will be reflying both stages.
SpaceX also saw growth in subscribers to its Starlink space internet network, reaching 13.6 million consumers, with Musk predicting that the growth of AI agents would lead to more demand for connectivity.
Despite those capital expenditures, the company’s revenue boost was substantial enough to push it back into profitability. SpaceX reported net income of $4.4 billion, a turnaround from the $1 billion loss in the same quarter last year. It will still have some catching up to do if it wants to remain profitable for the year, however. In the first nine months of the year, SpaceX still had a net income loss of $413 million.
Musk took a particularly bullish stance on the company’s Super Intelligence business segment, predicting that SpaceX’s annual recurring revenue by the end of 2027 will be “somewhere between $500 billion and $1 trillion.”
More concretely, Johnsen forecast total revenue for the first quarter of 2027 in the range of $33 billion to $37 billion.
This is a developing story. TechCrunch will update.

articles.title: NAS vs external hard drive: What are the differences?
articles.text:
NAS vs external hard drive: What are the differences?
We compare storage capacity, speed, pricing, and backup features
Network-attached storage (NAS) and external hard drives are effective ways to store and access large files on the go.
Yet, many sometimes need help when choosing between NAS systems and external hard drives. You’ve arrived at the right place if you fall into this category. We've tested the best NAS drives, NAS devices, and external hard drives.
So, I’ve written this guide explaining what you should know about NAS systems and external hard drives before deciding.
NAS vs. External Hard Drive: Design
Network-attached storage (NAS) utilizes hardware, software, and data transfer protocols to let users share files over a network. It uses a NAS box that houses storage disks, processors, and a random access memory (RAM) unit. This box has specialized software to manage file storage and user access.
NAS boxes can connect to a network and let users share files seamlessly. Suppose you work in a company with 50 staff. All 50 staff can connect to a single NAS box to access organizational files. Think of the NAS system as an online tree where everyone can pluck information. It provides an easy way to share massive files between employees.
In contrast, external hard drives are standalone devices that transfer files over USB ports rather than a network. Every file is stored locally, and the hard drive must be plugged into the PC that wants to retrieve information from it.
NAS systems offer substantially more storage space than external hard drives. You can always expand the storage capacity of your NAS system by adding more drives, unlike external hard drives with fixed storage capacities.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
External hard drives are portable and easy to move. Employees can quickly pass them around to retrieve relevant files, but this process gets cumbersome for large workforces. Picture a 100+ workforce sharing a single external hard drive; that’s inefficient and weakens productivity.
In contrast, you can keep a NAS box stationary, and employees can connect to this box from their respective PCs. Everyone can access files seamlessly without looking for hard drives to plug into their PC. A NAS system is the most convenient option for businesses that can afford it.
NAS vs. External Hard Drive: Price
NAS systems are more expensive than external hard drives, expectedly, because they use more sophisticated components. A NAS system includes a storage box, networking components, and a processor to run the software.
In contrast, an external hard drive’s main component is a simple magnetic disk (platter) that stores data. NAS systems are more expensive to produce.
A 4 TB external hard drive costs an average of $90. Meanwhile, a 4 TB NAS system costs upwards of $200. It gets costlier when more drives are added to the existing setup. When weighing both, expect to spend more on a NAS system, but the trade-off is bigger storage capacity and the convenience of accessing files.
NAS vs. External Hard Drive: Speed
NAS systems offer excellent speed, although they depend on bandwidth. Consumer-level NAS devices have average data transfer speeds of 3 to 20 MB per second (Mbps), but high-level NAS devices can reach 100 to 200 Mbps. Because they depend on network bandwidth, data transfer speeds can be slow when many people connect to the same NAS box.
External hard drives transfer data via USB ports. Data transfer speeds depend on the USB version of your external hard drive. USB 1 offers up to 12 Mbps, USB 2 offers up to 480 Mbps, USB 3 reaches up to 5 Gbps, and USB 4 has a maximum speed of 40 Gbps.
Some NAS systems offer gigabit speeds (over Ethernet cables) comparable to USB. On average, USB systems have faster data transfer speeds. However, I think this shouldn’t matter much because most users don’t transfer files at gigabit speeds. Both NAS and hard drives are sufficient for everyday use.
NAS vs. External Hard Drive: Backup and Redundancy
Many NAS systems have built-in data backup features. For instance, you can back up a Synology DS923+ NAS to Google Drive. You can schedule automatic backups, wherein all data stored on the Synology NAS box will be uploaded to Google Drive daily, weekly, or monthly. Automated backups keep your data safe even if the NAS device fails.
In contrast, external hard drives don’t have built-in backup software. To back up files, you need to manually connect the drive to a PC, which is cumbersome. People often forget to do manual backups, but automated NAS backups solve this issue. Your data is safer on a NAS than on a hard drive.
NAS vs. External Hard Drive: Verdict
NAS systems offer much larger storage and are expandable. They offer a more convenient way to access data, making it the best choice for enterprises. NAS systems cost more than external hard drives, but the higher cost is worth the convenience for business users.
External hard drives are ideal for casual users who frequently transfer files between PCs. They handle large file transfers without issues, although the process isn’t as smooth as using a NAS system. I think the hassle and expense of setting up a NAS system aren’t worth it for casual users.

articles.title: Un SUV chinois éligible à l’aide de 6 000 euros : un tour de magie qui fait mal à l’industrie européenne
articles.text:
Affiché à 31 400 €, le Leapmotor B10 est un SUV chinois relativement classique. Il n’est pas mémorable à conduire, ni même à regarder. Son équipement est en contrepartie plutôt riche mais ses possibilités de personnalisation bien limitées. Il se montre en revanche assez confortable et tout à fait pratique. Bref, assez quelconque en somme… Sauf qu’il revient aujourd’hui sur le devant de la scène en brandissant une nouvelle fois l’argument prix.
En étant désormais produit à l’usine Stellantis de Saragosse, en Espagne, le B10 s’affranchit des droits de douane imposés par l’Union Européenne sur les véhicules électriques importés de Chine. Surtout, il pourrait être éligible à la Prime Coup de Pouce récompensant les modèles à batterie fabriqués en Europe. Un avantage indéniable qui lui permettra d’abaisser significativement son tarif pour aller chercher à coup sûr de nouveaux clients.
Pourquoi produire en Europe devient indispensable pour les marques chinoises
Pour établir ce plan d’attaque, l’usine de Saragosse n’a pas été choisie au hasard. Le site possède en effet une forte capacité de production pouvant accueillir la fabrication d’un nouveau modèle. Le B10 sera ainsi assemblé aux côtés des Peugeot 208, Opel Corsa et Lancia Ypsilon. Cette initiative s’inscrit dans la stratégie FaSTLAne 2030 du géant automobile, qui souhaite renforcer fortement sa compétitivité industrielle.
C’est ainsi que la politique européenne peut se transformer en opportunité selon Silvia Vernetti, porte-parole de Stellantis : « la transition électrique doit aussi être une transition industrielle. Si notre partenariat constitue notre stratégie, Saragosse est la preuve que nous pouvons conjuguer technologie mondiale, compétitivité et capacités industrielles européennes ». Cela fait bien les affaires de Leapmotor, qui espère se développer en Europe.
Que change ce virage industriel pour les clients français ?
C’est ce que confirme Jiangming Zhu, PDG de la marque chinoise : « nos racines sont en Chine et notre ambition est mondiale. L’Europe est un élément stratégique de cette ambition, et la production à Saragosse nous permet de rapprocher notre technologie des marchés et des clients européens ». Faire les yeux doux à l’Europe est aussi synonyme d’une avance cruciale sur les autres constructeurs chinois.
La taxe de 30,7 % s’appliquant habituellement aux modèles électriques chinois importés dans l’Union Européenne devrait logiquement sauter. Mieux, la Prime Coup de Pouce, dont le montant oscille entre 3 600 et 6 100 €, pourrait tomber pour le SUV électrique. S’il valide tous les prérequis exigés par l’Union Européenne, le B10 verrait son prix de départ tomber potentiellement à 25 300 €. Imbattable pour un modèle familial offrant 361 km d’autonomie !

articles.title: US Army reportedly developing program that would deploy AI agents to autonomously seek and destroy targets in enemy digital infrastructures — experts warn ECHOTRIBBLE program could have disastrous consequences
articles.text:
US Army reportedly developing program that would deploy AI agents to autonomously seek and destroy targets in enemy digital infrastructures — experts warn ECHOTRIBBLE program could have disastrous consequences
Agents will self-destruct upon completing their mission
The U.S. Army is allegedly developing a program to deploy autonomous AI agents that can navigate digital and network infrastructures, identify targets, and “neutralize” them. According to an Oct. 19 report by The Intercept, citing leaked official documents from the Army Cyber Command (ARCYBER), the nascent program, codenamed “ECHOTRIBBLE,” is primarily focused on offensive missions with the goal of neutralizing targets by “disabling the threat completely or temporarily, deleting the threat from the target.”
The program purportedly seeks to develop modular, autonomous AI agents that would function like computer worms, stealthily navigating adversary networks, moving between devices, and self-replicating across different operating systems. The agents would operate lightly in contested cloud environments and air-gapped systems alike, keeping reports minimal and concealing any required transmissions. Once an agent identifies and neutralizes a target, it would self-destruct, ideally without alerting the target or leaving any traces of its existence.
Cybersecurity experts have raised safety concerns about the project. A recent string of events has seen AI agents escape their environments and autonomously execute unassigned tasks. The document says the army will implement “predefined triggers” to help agents precisely distinguish targets. However, experts worry that if agents designed for benign tasks could execute unplanned, sometimes dangerous, actions to achieve those tasks, what should be expected of self-replicating agents designed specifically for offensive missions? Anthropic’s experiments showed AI agents can set up inference on different hardware and replicate across a network.
The Army also wants the agents to be capable of “Self-Directed Behavior,” acting with as little human oversight as possible, as this is necessary to achieve the desired level of autonomy. Conversely, this level of autonomy has seen AI agents bypass guardrails to complete their tasks. Government intelligence agencies have also been known to penetrate target networks through civilian infrastructure. “The target may well be hit. But what path will it take?” asked Hyrum Anderson, co-founder and CEO of the AI security firm Abundant, as quoted by The Intercept. “Will it go through a U.S. water utility on its way, because that’s where the adversary has staged its command and control, and take that down too?”
Another angle of concern is how the agents would make judgment calls. While AI agents are excellent at overcoming obstacles in their path, there's no predicting with 100% accuracy what they would consider obstacles or what path they would take to overcome them. “One of the reasons that we trust 19-year-old Marine corporals in Ramadi with live rounds and a weapon is because they have both the compute substrate — the brain and the eyes — but the deep world knowledge to understand, ‘Yeah, I probably shouldn’t do that,’” said William Marcellino, a senior behavioral scientist at the RAND Corporation researching military AI applications. “That is not something that current public AI technology has.”
The ECHOTRIBBLE program is in the early prototyping and industry assessment phase and is led by ARCYBER, the Army Cyber Technology and Innovation Center (ArCTIC), and the Cyber Fusion Innovation Center (CFIC), with private vendors and academic researchers proposing and designing the software. ARCYBER and ArCTIC dictate the operational requirements and rules of engagement, while CFIC, a defense non-profit organization, acts as an intermediary between the Army and commercial tech companies. The Army recently held a virtual Assessment Event from October 6 to October 8, 2026, where it evaluated 65 technical whitepapers submitted by private vendors proposing solutions for the agentic framework and narrowed them to five. The final candidate(s) will be issued funding and formal prototype contracts.

articles.title: Next Xbox console could cost as much as US$1800 without subsidies
articles.text:
Yesterday, we wrote about the increasing likelihood that the PS6 will have an eye-watering price tag of at least US$1,000 (about C$1,400). Now, we’re learning that Microsoft’s rival console, the PC-like Project Helix, could cost well above that.
In a big new feature from Fortune focusing on recently appointed Xbox CEO Asha Sharma, we get a better idea of Xbox’s hardware plans for the next two years. Part of this reportedly includes a handheld device coming by the 2027 holiday season, as well as Project Helix the following year. Fortune also reports that a “major overhaul” of Xbox Game Pass is planned that would introduce a tiered system through which players choose features à la carte, including console-only games, cloud gaming and multiplayer.
But the biggest revelation from Fortune‘s piece is rumoured price for Helix, which the publication pegs at anywhere between US$1,200 and $1,800 (around C$1,650 to $2,500) unless Xbox subsidizes the cost. Naturally, this staggering price cost is the result of AI-driven component shortages brought about by the likes of Microsoft itself.
However, that is an obscene price range even if Microsoft does indeed eat some of the cost. It’s also unclear how much this handheld may cost. Interestingly, Fortune noted that its development recently sparked a “rekindling of an old turf battle between the Xbox and Windows teams.” In particular, Windows leaders wanted the upcoming handheld device to use a “trimmed-down” version of Windows Home, while Xbox was pushing its own software for peak performance. Tensions supposedly “ran high enough” that a senior Xbox exec threatened to scrap the handheld entirely, but ultimately, Xbox is now “largely controlling” the direction of the OS.
But all of these console and handheld rumblings honestly feel besides the point. Frankly, it begs the question, even if pricing was much lower, of why anyone would buy an Xbox device right now, anyway. Even before the so-called RAMmageddon, substantially fewer people have been buying Xbox consoles over the past several years, and nothing the company has done lately has exactly instilled much confidence.
Above all else, Microsoft has been gutting the Xbox brand through thousands of layoffs at the likes of Obsidian, Halo Studios, Zenimax Online, id Software and Vancouver-based The Coalition, as well numerous studio closures, divestitures and consolidations. It’s been doing these reductions in waves, too, which Fortune notes has naturally left staff “demoralized, feeling as if they are sitting under a year-long cloud, waiting to see if there their roles will be eliminated next.” Per the publication, Xbox is eyeing more layoffs this month, November and January, although it noted that these plans could change.
Among these layoffs, we’ve seen veterans who have been in the industry for decades on the likes of Doom being axed, causing Xbox to lose invaluable institutional knowledge. Other examples of the company’s callousness and short-sightedness include promoting Halo Studios’ cinematic director and laying him off in the same week, axing Gears of War: E-Day‘s story director only a few weeks before the game’s launch and letting go of one of the key driving forces behind backwards compatibility and Xbox Cloud Gaming.
Meanwhile, Sharma wants to focus on bigger franchises like Call of Duty, Fallout and Minecraft as part of a wildly ambitious goal of reaching one billion people daily. To be clear, that figure includes console, PC, mobile and adaptations like the Fallout TV series, and Xbox even formed a new division focused on this multimedia Hollywood approach. Nonetheless, getting rid of thousands of the people who made Xbox what it is certainly isn’t a good way to help reach such a lofty goal.
All of this has led to rampant speculation that Microsoft is simply “cleaning up” Xbox to make it more appealing to potential buyers. In particular, Fortune noted that several current and former staff members do believe that Xbox is being prepared “for an eventual sale, spin-off, outside investment or conversion into a subsidiary,” also citing a high-level internal presentation with Sharma exploring these very scenarios that The Information had previously reported on.
Naturally, Microsoft denies looking to offload Xbox, claiming it has a long-term vision for gaming. And speaking to Fortune, Judson Althoff, who leads Microsoft commercial business, said Xbox is valuable to the company’s wider operations because its low-latency demands stress-test Microsoft’s cloud, it helps maintain retail relationships with the likes of Walmart and it connects the company to creators through Minecraft.
Time will tell how this all pans out, but one thing’s for sure: Xbox is a mess right now.

articles.title: Chris Lattner: AI Code Generation Doesn't Solve Software Engineering - EE Times
articles.text:
For AI chip companies, the promise of AI-based coding agents is compelling: generate the low-level kernels needed to get a model running on new hardware, optimize them for performance, and do it without the software engineering resources traditionally required.
But according to Chris Lattner, CEO of AI software startup Modular (recently acquired by Qualcomm, where he now serves as executive VP of software engineering), chip companies should be wary of the limits of AI code generation. Making a kernel run fast is a very different problem from building software infrastructure we can depend on, he told EE Times in an exclusive interview.
“Agents are good, but they’re like anything else; it’s a tool, and you have to use it the right way,” Lattner said. “What I’ve seen with agents is they make tons of throwaway code. So, if you’re building a product, you don’t want to agent-generate everything.”
Agentic code generation makes sense for projects that are well-defined and limited in scope (e.g., “make this kernel go fast”), which can be quantified, measured, and validated, Lattner said, but bigger projects require product design and software engineering and can’t be delegated to agents.
“If you’re a startup and you only care about getting one model working, or getting it to go fast, [then go ahead,] use AI tools to prove it’s possible,” he said. “But that’s not going to be great for when you want to sell your chip to someone else, and they want to run a model you don’t have access to.”
Lattner said that despite some high-profile companies’ performance claims for their AI-generated low-level software, there are still many unanswered questions, including the dollar cost to generate large amounts of code and its applicability to large, open-ended problems.
“I have heard of hardware companies that say they don’t believe in software anymore; they just want to use agents to generate everything,” Lattner said. “I think that’s interesting because they’re definitely using LLVM and still investing in compilers, but saying they’re not. So there’s a divergence between the party line and what’s actually happening.”
Writing performant low-level code for new and novel hardware has long been a difficult task for chip companies, and some are now relying on agents for this.
“Various people use [agentic code generation] as a talking point, particularly when their software is known to be problematic,” Lattner said. “So, I don’t really know what to believe in all these cases… great claims need great proof.”
Porting code
While AI is useful in some use cases, it can’t be used for everything, Lattner said. AI might help get a demo up and running, but this isn’t the same as writing a usable software stack with determinism and adaptability.
“The hard part about building a company or building a product or building something meaningful in the world is understanding the product requirements,” he said. “What is the marketing story? What is the product-market fit that you have to get for your product? I think that remains quite hard.”
At Modular, teams use agentic code generation for tasks such as porting PyTorch code into the company’s Max AI framework and for porting CUDA code to its programming language Mojo. Lattner said that porting code is a great use case for AI, along with specializing existing software (for example, specializing a matmul kernel for a specific size of matrix), since the agent can do this quickly and efficiently.
People will always need to know how to code, he said, since prompting in English isn’t precise enough to get a good result.
“It’s true things are changing very rapidly—I use AI to write code, and I wouldn’t go back, personally—but that doesn’t mean that writing code was the job,” he said. “If you go back five years, more code was read than written.”
Open source under pressure
The downsides to AI code generation are still making themselves apparent in the world of software. Lattner identified open-source projects, the backbone of much of modern software, as being particularly under threat.
“Open-source projects like LLVM are under assault,” he said.
Before generative AI, people who wanted to contribute to open-source projects were motivated by the satisfaction of identifying and fixing problems, most often because they were using the software themselves and wanted to contribute. Making changes meant they had to invest a certain amount of time. Maintainers, people who had been working on the project for a long time, reviewed contributions for quality and worked with the community to teach them the nuances of the codebase. Lattner said the investment in teaching contributors improved the code.
“Today, that model is broken, because people are just vibe coding tons of patches and sending them to tons of projects, and the maintainers are getting completely overwhelmed with AI crap,” he said.
The deluge of AI-generated code is increasing the workload for maintainers, who have to review and iterate code before accepting it, Lattner said.
“And then the submitter doesn’t actually care, so the investment back into the human doesn’t lead to a future maintainer; it leads to someone who walks away, or just sets up their agents to spam a bunch of different projects to try to get GitHub badges,” he said. “This is a huge issue, so a lot of projects have stopped accepting contributions.”
The response from open-source projects such as LLVM has been to consider working only with established contributors, a move Lattner described as “terrifying.”
“The value of open-source projects is the humans, it’s the relationships, it’s the tribal knowledge,” he said. “If you destroy that, there’s going to be a huge problem… Running an open-source project and making it successful has always been super hard, so this is another pretty big threat.”
This is a huge challenge for all open-source projects today.
Modular’s programming language, Mojo, was recently open-sourced, but contributions aren’t yet being accepted. Lattner said the company intends to open to submissions gradually.
“It’s not just about the lines of code; it’s about the social side of things—if you have an employee that’s investing their effort into someone else, traditionally the thought would be, we’re investing in you, and if you’re good we’ll hire you, or [something might come out of it],” he said.
Things will stabilize, Lattner said. AI code review tools will improve, easing some of the burden, but ultimately, code review is difficult to automate completely because it requires judgement.
“What you’re building doesn’t just need to pass a test; it needs to be able to support the architecture we need for tomorrow and the future,” he said. “Models tomorrow will be better and faster, but I think these are inherent structural problems.”
Max alliance
For startups without the resources to build a state-of-the-art software stack, Lattner is planning on opening up Max, Modular’s AI framework, by starting an alliance for hardware makers. The alliance is planned to kick off around the end of the year, he said.
“This will be a big deal,” Lattner said. “We’re saying to everyone who has chips: You now have software. A lot of startups have been asking for help, but we always had to say no; we couldn’t scale to support them. Now we’ll be able to say yes, you can do it for yourself.”
Coding agents can solve for a specific kernel for a specific chip, but today’s complex, disaggregated, heterogeneous data center needs orchestration, scaling, and management, all of which must be handled by software, Lattner said.
“We’ve been building this for four and a half years—now you’ll be able to use it and scale it for yourself,” he said.
This is part of Qualcomm’s plan for Modular, Lattner said.
“[Qualcomm] wants it to be an open ecosystem so [its data center chip] can compete on its own merits,” he said. “Qualcomm is modest enough to understand it can’t [overtake Nvidia]. There will be a lot of different players with great contributions in different parts of the value chain, but it needs to be an open ecosystem.”
The Max alliance will enable edge chip companies and markets such as China, which Lattner is looking forward to.
“This is going to be very, very fun and exciting,” he said.

articles.title: En qué parte de la cronología de Dragon Ball se ubica Dragon Ball Super Beerus
articles.text:
El regreso de Beerus puede generar una duda entre quienes quieren retomar la franquicia o verla por primera vez: ¿hay que terminar Dragon Ball Z antes de empezar Dragon Ball Super Beerus? La respuesta depende de si se prioriza el orden de la historia o el de estreno.
En la cronología, la llegada del Dios de la Destrucción ocurre después de la derrota de Majin Buu y antes del epílogo de ‘Z’, cuando Goku conoce a Uub en el 28.º Torneo de Artes Marciales.
La nueva serie no es una continuación que arranque después de todo lo visto en ‘Dragon Ball Super’. Toei Animation la presenta como una edición mejorada del anime de 2015, con escenas nuevas, imágenes remasterizadas y una reconstrucción de la historia.
La temporada de 19 episodios aborda los primeros arcos de ‘Super’, incluidos los de Beerus, Freezer y el enfrentamiento entre los universos 6 y 7, según la información difundida sobre la serie.
El orden cronológico para seguir la historia
Quienes quieran recorrer la trama en secuencia pueden seguir esta guía:
- ‘Dragon Ball’, desde la infancia de Goku hasta su enfrentamiento con Piccolo Jr.
- ‘Dragon Ball Z’ o ‘Dragon Ball Z Kai’, hasta el final de la saga de Majin Buu. ‘Kai’ ofrece una versión más condensada de esa etapa.
- ‘Dragon Ball Daima’, cuya historia ocurre después de la derrota de Buu y antes de la llegada de Beerus.
- La saga de Beerus, en una de estas versiones: la película ‘Dragon Ball Z: La batalla de los dioses’, los primeros episodios de ‘Dragon Ball Super’ o la nueva edición ‘Dragon Ball Super: Beerus’.
- El resto de ‘Dragon Ball Super’, desde los arcos posteriores al torneo entre los universos 6 y 7 hasta el Torneo del Poder.
- ‘Dragon Ball Super: Broly’, que continúa la historia después del anime.
- ‘Dragon Ball Super: Super Hero’, situada después de ‘Broly’ y antes del epílogo de ‘Dragon Ball Z’.
- El final de ‘Dragon Ball Z’, con el torneo en el que Goku conoce a Uub.
El sitio oficial de la franquicia enumera las películas y series, aunque su cronología de lanzamientos no equivale necesariamente al orden de los acontecimientos. En particular, ‘Daima’ se ubica entre Majin Buu y la saga de Beerus.
¿Película, anime original o nueva versión?
Para llegar rápido a Dragon Ball Super Beerus, basta con ver el final de la saga de Buu y seguir con ‘Daima’. Después se puede elegir cómo conocer el encuentro con Beerus.
La película ‘La batalla de los dioses’ cuenta ese primer choque en formato cinematográfico; el anime original lo desarrolla en sus episodios iniciales, mientras que la nueva edición reorganiza y renueva la historia.
No es necesario ver las tres versiones seguidas: repiten el mismo arco, aunque con diferencias de ritmo y presentación. Quien elija la nueva edición puede continuar después con los arcos que vienen a continuación en el anime original, sin volver a ver la historia de Beerus.
Como la versión mejorada incluye también tramas posteriores, conviene comprobar qué episodios abarca antes de retomar ‘Dragon Ball Super’ desde la numeración de 2015.
Dónde ver Dragon Ball Super Beerus
La serie está disponible en Crunchyroll en Latinoamérica y España. En Latinoamérica también puede verse en Disney+, HBO Max y Netflix, con estrenos semanales en días distintos.
En España se suman AnimeBox, Disney+ y Netflix; además, está disponible en Prime Video mediante el canal de Crunchyroll. La disponibilidad y el catálogo pueden variar según el país, por lo que conviene buscar el título en la aplicación de cada plataforma.

articles.title: Philips Monitors Introduces the 27E3C2500 and 32E3C2500
articles.text:
Tuesday, October 20th 2026
Philips Monitors Introduces the 27E3C2500 and 32E3C2500
The Philips Monitor line-up expands with the 27E3C2500 and 32E3C2500, two curved monitors designed for home and office users and casual gamers. Both feature a QHD resolution and 1500R curved VA panel, combining detailed visuals for everyday tasks with smooth motion for gaming. They are designed for people who use the same monitor for work and entertainment, from reviewing documents to watching a movie or playing a game.
With a QHD resolution of 2560 × 1440, both monitors provide more detail than Full HD and sufficient space to view documents and applications side by side. The curved screen adds a sense of immersion when watching movies or exploring game environments. The Philips 27E3C2500 offers a 27-inch (68.6 cm) screen for users who prefer a smaller display. The Philips 32E3C2500 provides a larger 31.5-inch (80 cm) viewing area, with the same QHD resolution and refresh rate. The choice allows users to select a size that suits their desk and viewing preferences.Both models support HDR10 for compatible HDR content. Philips SmartContrast analyses the displayed content and adjusts the backlight to enhance contrast.
Smooth motion for everyday tasks and casual gaming
A 144 Hz refresh rate makes scrolling and on-screen movement look smoother than on a conventional 60 Hz display. During gaming, Adaptive-Sync matches the display's refresh rate to the output of a compatible graphics source, helping reduce screen tearing and stuttering.
Both monitors also offer 0.5 ms MPRT for reduced perceived motion blur during gaming. This helps keep moving images clearer during fast-paced scenes.
Features for the home desk
SoftBlue technology reduces blue light emissions, while Flicker-free technology reduces screen flicker during everyday use. Both monitors also include an EasyRead mode for on-screen reading.
HDMI and DisplayPort inputs provide connections for compatible sources. Two built-in 2 W speakers let users listen to videos and games without adding separate speakers to the desk, while an audio output offers an additional listening option.
The stand allows users to tilt the screen to suit their viewing position. Both monitors support 100 × 100 mm VESA mounting for use with a compatible monitor arm or wall mount.
Full HD options in the same range
The range also includes the Philips 27E3C2200 and 32E3C2200, with 27-inch and 31.5-inch screens respectively. Both offer a Full HD 1920 × 1080 resolution with a 1500R curved VA panel, 144 Hz refresh rate, and Adaptive-Sync. 
Prices and availability
The Philips 27E3C2500 and 32E3C2500 combine curved QHD viewing with features for home working and casual gaming. Two screen sizes and built-in audio give users a choice of display for a desk shared between work and downtime.
The Philips 27E3C2500 will be available for purchase in November, at an MSRP of £129.99. 
The Philips 32E3C2500 will be available for purchase in November as well, at an MSRP of £169.99.
