articles.title: Inside Gabon’s first angel investor network
articles.text:
20 octobre 2026
Hello 👋,
Welcome back to Francophone Weekly by TechCabal, your weekly deep dive into the tech ecosystem across French-speaking Africa. For readers who want to understand Francophone Africa beyond headlines—through markets, startups, and systems. New editions of the newsletter will land directly in your inbox every Tuesday at 12 PM WAT.
By default, this newsletter is in French. If you’re reading this in your email inbox, click the “Read in English” button below to switch to the English version. If you’re reading on our website, you can either click the button below or toggle the language selector at the top right-hand side of the page to view the English edition.
Le premier réseau structuré d’investisseurs providentiels du Gabon a déployé 67,3 millions de FCFA (118 000 dollars) dans quatre entreprises. La façon dont il y est parvenu en dit plus long sur les écosystèmes naissants que le chiffre lui-même.
En 2025, le Gabon a enregistré une seule opération de capital-risque, d’une valeur d’environ 1 million de dollars, selon l’Association africaine du capital-investissement et du capital-risque (AVCA). Le Cameroun, son voisin au sein du même bloc économique, a comptabilisé huit opérations pour 26 millions de dollars. L’Afrique centrale dans son ensemble n’a concentré que 10 opérations et 27 millions de dollars, faisant de cette région le plus petit marché de capital-risque du continent.
C’est dans ce contexte qu’est né le Gabon Angel Investor Network (GAIN), premier réseau structuré de business angels du pays. Cinq fondateurs l’ont lancé en 2021. Le réseau a réalisé son premier investissement en 2022. Depuis, il a injecté 67 345 000 FCFA (118 000 dollars) dans quatre entreprises, et son ticket moyen est passé de 11,5 millions de FCFA (19 000 dollars) à 25 millions de FCFA (43 000 dollars).
Ces chiffres paraissent modestes au regard des standards du marché du capital-risque nigérian — et c’est précisément là l’enjeu. Le GAIN construit simultanément une base d’investisseurs et un pipeline de startups, dans un marché où moins de 10 % des startups accèdent au crédit bancaire à un stade précoce.
Selon des données de la Banque des États de l’Afrique Centrale (BEAC) citées par le GAIN, le Gabon a capté 18,25 % des nouveaux crédits de la Communauté Économique et Monétaire de l’Afrique Centrale (CEMAC) au quatrième trimestre 2025, contre 63,93 % pour le Cameroun.
Des échanges avec Fabrice Nze Bekale, président du réseau, et Vanessa Adande, membre fondatrice et trésorière, en marge du sommet Africa’s Early Stage Investor Summit (AESIS) 2026 organisé par le GAIN à Libreville, la capitale gabonaise, ce mois-ci, révèlent que construire depuis zéro exige une flexibilité sur presque toutes les variables qu’un investisseur tient ordinairement pour fixes.
1. Recruter des investisseurs, une affaire de confiance
            Les participants au Libreville AESIS 2026 Investor MeetUp, la dernière rencontre du GAIN consacrée aux échanges entre investisseurs et entrepreneurs au Gabon. Source de l’image : GAIN.
       
        
    
Le GAIN a d’abord recruté dans l’entourage de ses fondateurs. Des cinq membres fondateurs, seuls Fabrice Nze Bekale et Vanessa Adande sont restés. Le déclic est venu en 2024, avec une première sortie (le remboursement intégral d’une facilité accordée à un entrepreneur) et la première édition de l’AESIS au Gabon. Cette visibilité a presque doublé le nombre de membres en 18 mois. Le GAIN en compte aujourd’hui 36.
La moitié sont des femmes, et ce résultat n’a rien d’un hasard. Adande a constaté que le rôle d’investisseur paraissait trop risqué aux femmes, vu de l’extérieur. Elle a donc appelé celles qu’elle connaissait pour leur expliquer le fonctionnement du GAIN au quotidien, et les a rassurées : investir dans un dossier identifié n’est jamais obligatoire.
Elle a aussi avancé un argument de pipeline : une entrepreneure a plus de chances d’être financée si d’autres femmes font partie du groupe d’investisseurs.
« Les hommes de l’association étaient d’ailleurs étonnés que ça demande autant d’effort. Pas moi », confie-t-elle. « Tout ce qui concerne l’argent demande de la confiance. On a confiance dans ce qu’on connaît. »
Le point dépasse largement le cas gabonais. L’AVCA classe l’Afrique centrale parmi les régions où les fondatrices ont levé la plus faible part du capital en 2025 : 8 %.
Dit Adande, l’intérêt des membres féminines s’est ravivé depuis la masterclass d’octobre, plusieurs d’entre elles ayant demandé comment fonctionnent les opérations en pratique. Le GAIN prévoit également un événement plus large dédié à l’investissement providentiel en 2027, afin d’élargir son vivier de cibles d’investissement.
La sortie de 2024 était un remboursement de prêt. Pour un réseau jeune, démontrer que les investisseurs ont récupéré leur mise fait davantage pour attirer de nouveaux membres qu’une valorisation sur le papier.
La spécialisation sectorielle est un luxe
Les réseaux d’angels matures se spécialisent. Le GAIN ne le peut pas encore.
« Dans nos pays, c’est toujours très nouveau, en particulier au Gabon, explique Fabrice Nze Bekale. On est encore à un stade où on fait des réseaux de business angels multisectoriels. On ne peut pas trop se spécialiser, un peu comme DNA [le Dakar Network of Angels] l’a fait au Sénégal, parce que ça reflète l’état de développement et de sophistication de l’écosystème entrepreneurial. »
Au Sénégal, le DNA se concentre sur les startups technologiques. Les quatre investissements du GAIN couvrent l’import-export, une marketplace, la santé et l’agro-industrie, et un dossier dans la santé est en due diligence.
Avec environ 150 startups actives au Gabon, selon la société d’incubation numérique SING, un mandat limité à la tech laisserait les membres avec presque rien à examiner. Le GAIN investit dans des startups tech et non-tech, et peut également considérer des petites et moyennes entreprises (PME) à fort potentiel de croissance. Chaque candidat doit être légalement constitué, avoir au moins un an d’existence, démontrer une traction réelle et présenter un plan d’affaires structuré.
Attendre des entreprises logicielles à l’échelle du capital-risque dans un marché de 150 startups, c’est s’exposer à des années de réunions sans jamais sortir un seul chèque. Le revers de la médaille, c’est qu’un petit groupe doit alors évaluer des profils de risque très hétérogènes — ce qui renvoie directement au problème de due diligence du GAIN.
La newsletter continue après cette publicité.
Fondateurs. Investisseurs. Décideurs politiques. Leaders d’entreprise. Moonshot 2026 rassemble les personnes qui façonnent l’écosystème technologique africain en matière d’IA, de commerce, de climat, d’entreprise et de culture. Mettez votre marque en avant dès aujourd’hui.
2. Moins de fonds propres, plus de dette
            Le Gabon Angel Investor Network (GAIN) s’emploie à connecter les entrepreneurs locaux avec des investisseurs capables d’apporter des financements, une expertise et des contacts d’affaires. Source de l’image : GAIN/LinkedIn.
       
        
    
« L’idéal, c’est toujours de faire des investissements en equity,” Nze Bekale dit. « Mais on est souvent contraints de prendre un peu d’equity pour mettre beaucoup de dette, ou bien de faire de la dette convertible dès le départ, parce que les entrepreneurs ne veulent pas ouvrir leur capital. »
La réticence à la dilution est profonde en Afrique francophone, où beaucoup d’entreprises sont familiales. Le GAIN calibre chaque opération selon la maturité de l’entreprise et sa capacité de remboursement : fonds propres, dette ou financement hybride.
Le continent évolue dans le même sens : la dette a représenté 41 % des 4,1 milliards de dollars levés par les startups africaines en 2025, un record, selon le rapport Partech 2025 Africa Tech Venture Capital.
Cette flexibilité exige une rédaction rigoureuse, car les obligations convertibles échouent en silence. Dans un cas anonymisé présenté lors de la masterclass de l’AESIS, un BSA AIR — l’équivalent français du SAFE (Simple Agreement for Future Equity) — est arrivé à échéance sans avoir converti, et la cession de l’entreprise s’est transformée en une longue négociation sur les droits des investisseurs.
Un convertible doit prévoir dès la signature son échéance, son taux, ses déclencheurs de conversion et le cas de cession. Des angels qui détiennent surtout de la dette doivent aussi évaluer la capacité de remboursement réelle d’aujourd’hui, pas celle des projections.
Expliquer ce qu’est un business angel
Un autre front se situe hors de la salle de négociation.
« On doit faire de la sensibilisation auprès des investisseurs potentiels, auprès des entrepreneurs, et surtout faire de l’advocacy auprès des autorités pour leur expliquer notre rôle, qui n’est pas celui d’une banque et qui n’est pas celui d’un incubateur, » insiste Nze Bekale.
Les autorités ont encore tendance à assimiler les business angels à des financeurs d’activités génératrices de revenus : un plombier ou un chauffeur de taxi qui s’installe à son compte, avec des budgets de 500 000 à 1 million de FCFA (900 à 1 750 dollars).
« On se regroupe pour financer des projets pour lesquels on a besoin de se regrouper, et pas des projets à 500 000 ou un million de francs CFA », précise-t-il.
Si l’État classe l’investissement providentiel dans l’appui à la micro-entreprise, il concevra ses incitations pour le mauvais segment. Le GAIN, qui travaille déjà avec le Centre gabonais de l’innovation (CGI) et le ministère des PME et des PMI, a besoin que l’investissement providentiel soit reconnu comme une catégorie à part entière.
La due diligence, goulot d’étranglement caché
Le GAIN veut augmenter ses financements cette année. C’est la due diligence qui le freine. Pour son premier deal, le réseau a rémunéré un consultant externe à hauteur de 1 à 2 % du montant levé. Pour les suivants, Nze Bekale a mené les DD lui-même.
« Comme ça a commencé à trop peser sur moi, cette année on a décidé de tester un autre modèle », raconte-t-il. Des volontaires parmi les investisseurs potentiels forment désormais une équipe et conduisent le processus.
Pourtant, cela n’a pas bien fonctionné.
« Tout le monde a des activités professionnelles principales, et donc ils ont très peu de temps à consacrer aux DD. Ce n’est même pas secondaire, c’est peut-être tertiaire ou quaternaire, » Nze Bekale dit.
Sur le dossier en cours dans la santé, l’équipe travaille depuis six ou sept mois. Un processus early-stage classique prend deux à quatre mois entre le premier rendez-vous et le décaissement.
Le GAIN envisage de revenir au consultant rémunéré. En attendant, les analystes d’ACT Afrique, le cabinet de conseil de Nze Bekale, portent une grande partie du travail.
« Je n’ai pas de problème à le faire parce que je suis le président, mais si je n’étais pas le président, la question se poserait autrement. »
Il a raison de s’inquiéter. Une due diligence qui repose sur le cabinet d’un seul membre crée un point de défaillance unique et un conflit d’intérêts latent. Le modèle de frais a son propre défaut : 2 % d’une levée de 25 millions de FCFA (43 000 dollars), c’est 500 000 FCFA (860 dollars), tout au plus quelques jours de travail d’analyste.
Deux correctifs seraient utiles. D’abord, standardiser les modèles et les listes de vérification pour réduire le nombre d’heures par opération. Ensuite, traiter la due diligence comme une infrastructure d’écosystème : les institutions de financement du développement financent déjà l’incubation, et un pool d’analystes mutualisé entre les réseaux de business angels de la CEMAC ne coûterait pas grand-chose.
L’épreuve de 2027
Le GAIN a démontré sa capacité à recruter des investisseurs, et la moitié de ses membres sont des femmes. Son prochain défi est de professionnaliser la due diligence sans s’appuyer sur le cabinet de son président. S’il y parvient, ses 36 membres pourront commencer à signer des chèques de 50 millions de FCFA (86 000 dollars) — le plafond que leur mandat autorise.
La newsletter se termine ici.
Touchez les acteurs qui font bouger l’écosystème technologique et commercial francophone. Faites de la publicité dans la newsletter hebdomadaire francophone de TechCabal et présentez votre marque aux décideurs, opérateurs, fondateurs et chefs d’entreprise qui comptent le plus pour votre croissance. Prêt à vous lancer ? Envoyez un e-mail à [email protected].

articles.title: Asus pique la technique de fabrication des MacBook d'Apple, mais sacrifie les performances de son ExpertBook A7
articles.text:
Un châssis de MacBook et un écran de Pro pour l’ExpertBook A7 d'Asus
Asus annonce l'ExpertBook A7, un ultraportable alliant un châssis en aluminium usiné couplé à un écran Oled. Mais derrière cette esthétique haut de gamme, le choix des composants internes soulève certaines interrogations.
Le fabricant taïwanais Asus vient d'annoncer l'intégration d'une nouvelle référence au sein de sa gamme professionnelle : l'ExpertBook A7. Présenté comme un ordinateur orienté vers la mobilité et prévu pour le quatrième trimestre 2026, ce portable de 14 pouces tente de conjuguer un design très soigné et des fonctionnalités adaptées aux utilisateurs nomades.
Design de l'ExpertBook A7 : un châssis monobloc en aluminium ultra-fin
Pour ce nouveau modèle, Asus a opté pour une conception entièrement en aluminium. Le châssis de l'ExpertBook A7 est usiné dans un bloc d’aluminium et non formé à partir de plaques embouties. Ce procédé de fabrication, similaire à celui employé par Apple pour ses MacBook, confère à l'appareil une meilleure rigidité et un rendu visuel de grande qualité avec une épaisseur particulièrement faible.
Nous avons pu prendre en main l'ordinateur lors du salon de l’IFA 2026 de Berlin, et sa finesse de 1 cm ainsi que son poids contenu démarrant à 1,23 kg en font un appareil esthétiquement réussi. De par ses mensurations, l’ExpertBook A7 semble dense et renvoie une impression de qualité semblable aux MacBook.
Écran Oled 3K et dalle mate : l'atout maître de l'Asus
Ce ressenti se prolonge à l’ouverture du PC grâce à une dalle Oled de 14 pouces affichant une définition 3K (2880 x 1800 pixels). Cet écran, qui occupe 90 % de la surface avec un taux de rafraîchissement de 120 Hz, offre ce qui se fait de mieux en la matière. Le point d'intérêt de cette configuration réside dans la possibilité de choisir, en option, une finition mate antireflet. Il s'agit du même traitement de surface que nous avons déjà pu éprouver lors de notre test de l'ExpertBook Ultra, qui accomplit des merveilles pour un travail confortable dans des environnements très lumineux.
Fiche technique et performances : un processeur Intel en retrait face au design
Si l’esthétique est convaincante, les caractéristiques techniques suscitent en revanche une certaine déception. L'ExpertBook A7 est propulsé par un processeur de la gamme Intel Wildcat (six cœurs), dont les capacités se rapprochent de celles d'un MacBook Neo, puisqu’il a été calibré par Intel pour proposer des PC portables à même de concurrencer le MacBook Neo d’Apple aux alentours des 800 €.
On le retrouve ainsi dans le Dell XPS 13, l'Acer Swift Air 14 ou le Samsung Galaxy Book 6, tous passés par notre labo et n'ayant pas brillé par leurs performances.
L'ensemble crée un déséquilibre technique : l'utilisateur dispose d'un châssis digne d'un MacBook Air et d'un écran rivalisant avec un MacBook Pro, mais doit se contenter d'un processeur modeste. Ce compromis s'explique en partie par le contexte industriel actuel, les fabricants de PC subissant les conséquences de la pénurie de composants et des prix élevés de la mémoire vive.
Concernant la tarification, l'ExpertBook A7 est d’ores et déjà en précommande outre-Atlantique au tarif de 1300 $ pour une configuration comprenant 16 Go de RAM, un SSD de 512 Go et le processeur Intel Core 5 320. Le constructeur propose également des déclinaisons équipées de seulement 8 Go de mémoire vive, une option que nous déconseillons pour un usage confortable sous Windows 11. Les prix définitifs pour le marché français n'ont pas encore été officialisés par la marque, mais ils devraient se situer dans la même tranche tarifaire qu’aux États-Unis une fois la conversion monétaire et la TVA appliquées.

articles.title: Nvidia's RTX 6060 probably won't arrive until 2029, will be slower than the PS6
articles.text:
Rumor mill: Rumors had already suggested that the AI business and related memory shortages would significantly widen the traditional gap between generations of Nvidia graphics cards. Now, the latest information suggests the situation could be even worse for upcoming mainstream GPUs, which probably won't match the performance of next-generation consoles.
Prominent leaker Kepler_L2 recently suggested that Nvidia's next-generation mainstream graphics card, tentatively called the RTX 6060, could be delayed until as late as 2029. Memory supply shortages are the obvious cause.
DRAM and NAND supply constraints amid the AI data center buildout have already made currently available GPUs more expensive and harder to find. As some RTX 5090 listings march dangerously close to the $10,000 mark, Nvidia had to deny reports that it is discontinuing the flagship card.
Also see: Real Stagnation: Six Years of GeForce RTX 60 Class GPUs Tested
Meanwhile, the shortages may have already forced Nvidia to delay the previously rumored RTX 50 Super series, originally expected to debut in mid-2026. They might still arrive late this year or sometime next year to compete with a single high-end AMD RDNA 5 GPU.
The RTX 60 series is not expected until 2028, possibly extending the generational release gap to nearly four years, compared to the average gap of just over two years. A 2029 debut for the RTX 6060 would separate it from the 5060 by at least 3 years and 9 months. For comparison, the 5060 launched 4 years and 2 months after the 3060.
As for estimating the RTX 6060's relationship to the PlayStation 6, it's obviously too soon for precise predictions, but Kepler believes that Sony's upcoming console will launch sooner and with a performance advantage. The comparison roughly mirrors the relationships between prior PlayStation consoles and mainstream PC GPUs.
For example, the RTX 3060 launched about two months after the PlayStation 5, and the console's performance is comparable to that of slightly more powerful graphics cards, as per TechSpot's latest trivia question.
Assuming the 6060's performance gains follow the pattern suggested by our analysis of the last several years of mainstream GPUs, it might land somewhere near the 5060 Ti or 4070. Meanwhile, many have speculated that the PS6's 40 to 48 RDNA 5 compute units could bring it closer to the 5070 Ti.
However, price will be the main difference compared to 2020 and 2021. Kepler recently pegged the bill of materials for the PS6's memory and storage alone at $680, likely pushing the console's final price well past $1,000. It remains unclear how memory shortages will impact the RTX 6060's price. The 5060 launched with a $300 MSRP but now goes for around $470.

articles.title: Ukraine’s drone rescue of wounded soldier puts much touted idea into practice
articles.text:
Ukraine’s unprecedented drone rescue of a wounded soldier from the battlefield has shown once again how battlefield necessity can spur innovation. The operation was revealed just days after separate Ukrainian drones designed for casualty evacuation were deployed for frontline testing—taking a step beyond the US military’s decades of experimentation with similar concepts.
The drone evacuation of the injured soldier took place at an undisclosed time and place on the frontline where the presence of Russian drones and landmines made it impractical to send in a wheeled ground robot, according to The Kyiv Independent. On October 19, Ukraine’s Army shared a video of the drone evacuation, showing the wounded soldier securing himself in a harness suspended beneath a heavy hexacopter drone with six rotors before being flown to safety.
“This is a historic event, the next stage of evacuating the wounded, which we will all come to,” said Napalm, a programmer of the 92nd separate assault brigade’s unmanned ground systems company, who went by his callsign per Ukrainian military practice, in a statement. “Now the serious systematic work begins, so that such missions are carried out constantly.”
Flying out the wounded
To perform the improvised aerial evacuation, the 92nd brigade prepared and tested a heavy hexacopter drone—the Heavy Shot AYUDAG 6 model—provided for free by the Ukrainian manufacturer Gurzuf Defence. Special carabiners were first delivered to the wounded soldier so he could attach himself to the drone that was equipped with a winch, according to a blog post by Gurzuf Defence.
The wounded soldier, who serves with Ukraine’s 30th separate mechanized brigade, had already spent nearly 500 days at a frontline position while under threat of Russian fire, according to Gurzuf Defence. Like many soldiers at frontline positions, he had been relying on friendly drone deliveries for ammunition and other supplies.
The drone evacuation flight took 1 hour and 14 minutes from start to finish while covering a distance of nearly 39 miles (62 kilometers). This particular hexacopter can reportedly carry up to 200 pounds (90 kilograms).

articles.title: Scaled Cognition targets customer service with low-cost voice model - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Scaled Cognition targets customer service with low-cost voice model
Scaled Cognition Inc., an artificial intelligence lab building models for enterprise customer service agents, is introducing a text-to-speech model today that it says provides more accurate pronunciation of account numbers, addresses and other details at a lower cost than competing services.
The product, called Voice, is available through an application programming interface or for self-hosted deployment. It supports more than 25 languages, voice cloning and can work with existing artificial intelligence agents, contact center platforms and older telephone systems. Voice cloning creates a digital replica of a given person’s voice.
The launch targets a gap between natural-sounding speech and AI that reliably communicates information customers need to complete transactions.
“Modern generative TTS models can sound fantastic, but they often stumble over the details that matter most in customer service, like reading back an alphanumeric confirmation code, a dollar amount or a street address,” Akshay Kannan, vice president of product management at Scaled Cognition, said in e-mailed comments.
Those difficulties become more pronounced in languages other than English, Kannan said. Scaled Cognition said Voice enables enterprises to get natural-sounding speech and accurate readings without paying premium prices.
Voice costs $9 per million characters through the hosted API or $1 per million characters for self-hosting. The latter figure excludes the infrastructure needed to operate it.
Kannan explained how the math works out to lower costs than competing providers. One graphics processing unit can handle about 32 simultaneous conversations using Voice. A redundant setup using two GPUs on standard cloud hardware costs roughly $6,000 a month and supports about 500 million characters, he said.
Including infrastructure, Kannan estimated costs at about $13 per million characters at that 500 million-character rate and less than $7 at 1.5 billion. He compared that to between $35 and $100 per million characters charged by other hosted voices, which he declined to name.
“Self-hosting gets economical faster than people expect,” he said.
Cloud option
At low usage, the self-hosting cost can exceed Scaled Cognition’s hosted API price. “Most of the enterprises we work with already run their own infrastructure, so Voice just drops in,” Kannan said. “For teams that don’t want to manage it, we host it for them.”
The company also claims 70 milliseconds of speech-generation latency, the time from receiving text to starting speech, rather than the total time an AI system takes to understand a caller and formulate an answer.
“Even with 16 live conversations sharing a single GPU slice, typical response time stays around 80 milliseconds,” he said. “The biggest factor customers control is distance.” Running Voice in the same cloud region as the rest of a call stack adds only a millisecond or two of latency. “That’s a big reason we let enterprises self-host it right next to their agents and telephony,” Kannan said.
One of the distinctive features of Voice is its ability to interpret meaning before generating audio, the company said. For example, its Smart Pronunciation capability determines whether abbreviations refer to titles, street names or other information and how numbers should be spoken. For example, it reads “Pay 1/2 by 1/2” as “pay half by January second.”
“Voice doesn’t just read text left to right,” Kannan said. “Before it says a word, Smart Pronunciation works out what the sentence actually means, powered by the same customer-experience-tuned intelligence behind our APT model.”
APT is the company’s model for customer-service conversations and actions in enterprise systems. When the products are paired, APT supplies conversation context that can help Voice resolve ambiguities beyond an individual sentence.
Voice doesn’t require APT or another large language model to operate. “It streams audio through a standard API and is tuned for phone audio, so anything that can send text and play back speech can use it, from modern AI agents and contact center platforms to legacy [interactive voice response systems],” Kannan said.
That compatibility could give enterprises a way to update interactive voice response systems without replacing the underlying applications.
Scaled Cognition is also offering a blind listening test that compares Voice with other models across price ranges. Kannan said early feedback favored Voice, although the supplied materials did not provide sample sizes or detailed results.
The company, which raised $100 million in Series A funding led by Khosla Ventures LLC, is positioning speech as another component of its enterprise AI platform.

Smart Sampa: vazamento de dados permite acesso indevido a 58 mil câmeras em SP
A Prefeitura de São Paulo está investigando o vazamento de dados sigilosos do Smart Sampa. Uma falha no sistema de vigilância permitiu o acesso indevido a mais de 58 mil câmeras após dados sigilosos ficarem expostos na internet por cerca de 11 meses. Essas informações permitiam, por exemplo, visualizar imagens de pessoas e veículos nas ruas da capital paulista, além de câmeras instaladas em creches, hospitais e centros de atendimento a dependentes químicos.
Comitê da Meta aponta falhas na moderação durante eleições no Brasil
A atuação das redes sociais durante as eleições brasileiras continua dando o que falar. O Comitê de Supervisão da Meta criticou falhas recorrentes na moderação de conteúdos políticos durante o pleito brasileiro. Em comunicado divulgado nesta terça-feira (20), o órgão cobrou mais transparência e consistência nas decisões da empresa, que podem restringir manifestações políticas legítimas ou deixar de proteger a integridade eleitoral.
IA calcula chances de sobrevivência de pacientes com câncer a partir de selfie
Uma inteligência artificial desenvolvida por pesquisadores dos Estados Unidos foi capaz de estimar a idade biológica e prever as chances de sobrevivência de pacientes com câncer a partir de uma simples selfie. articles.title: Accenture, Dragos, SANS Launch $10M Initiative to Defend Small US Utilities
articles.text:
Accenture, Dragos and the SANS Institute on Tuesday announced the Community Cyber Resilience Foundation, which aims to help under-resourced US water, electric and natural gas utilities protect their operational technology (OT) environments.
They are putting up roughly $10 million to start, a mix of funding and services. The first phase will cover up to 500 utilities, which will get free security tools, equipment, deployment help and training.
To qualify, a water, wastewater, electric or natural gas utility must be based in the US and bring in under $100 million a year. The companies estimate that this bar covers more than 50,000 organizations, or over 97% of US utilities.
Each participant gets the Dragos Platform and related services, with Accenture handling setup, integration and continued support. SANS will train utility staff in ICS/OT security so they can run their defenses internally.
The foundation will also fund the hardware needed to deploy and run the Dragos Platform. It will connect participants to a peer network of utilities that share operational experience.
The companies say many small utilities struggle with limited funding, workforce shortages and aging technology, especially those serving rural or underserved communities. They also cited recent attacks on more than 100 US water systems across over a dozen states.
“Adversaries are aggressively targeting utilities, attacking the operational environments that provide life-sustaining services to millions of Americans. Yet many small operators lack the capacity to defend against these threats,” said Dragos CEO Robert M. Lee.
The foundation builds on the Dragos Community Defense Program, which gives more than 100 utilities free access to the Dragos Platform. Dragos launched that program in December 2023 for US utilities with less than $100 million in annual revenue.
The announcement comes four months after Accenture agreed to acquire a majority stake in Dragos. The deal was part of an OT cybersecurity push valued at roughly $4.1 billion.

articles.title: The cash cost of a 60-day customer (Sponsored) | EU-Startups
articles.text:
A bigger UK contract can consume runway before it creates cash. Put the payment terms into the funding plan before signing.
A large UK customer offers a scale-up a contract with 60-day payment terms. The revenue looks attractive. The less visible question is how much cash the startup must find before the customer pays.
Before signing, put the collection date into the cash forecast and compare it with when wages, suppliers and taxes must be paid. Then test what happens if payment takes longer. A profitable contract can still need funding, and a revenue target does not supply it.
This matters particularly for founders selling services or software to larger organizations. The customer may have enough money to pay. It may also have a procurement process that requires a purchase order, an approved invoice and a particular payment run. Winning the account and financing the account are different jobs.
Thirty more days can tie up nearly £400,000
Start with a simple illustration, not an actual company. Assume annual UK credit sales of £4.8 million, spread evenly through the year, with invoices issued as sales occur. Ignore VAT, seasonality, bad debt and other changes for now.
At 30 days from invoicing to cash, average receivables would be roughly £395,000. At 60 days, they would be about £789,000. The extra 30 days ties up approximately £395,000 in invoices, without adding a pound of annual revenue.
The calculation is annual credit sales divided by 365, multiplied by the extra days to payment. Here that is £4.8 million ÷ 365 × 30, or £394,521 rounded to the nearest pound. If only part of the customer base changes terms, use that part’s sales, not the whole company’s turnover.
This is an estimate of additional receivables, not a precise funding requirement. Cash already held, supplier terms, deposits and the timing of delivery costs affect the amount the company must finance. Fast growth can also make a steady annual average misleading. Model the actual expected invoices and receipts month by month before deciding how much liquidity is needed.
The distinction is important: the £395,000 has not necessarily been lost. It is unavailable for payroll or the next product release while the business waits. The British Business Bank makes the same underlying distinction in its cash-flow guidance: rising profit does not prevent a shortage of cash when growth requires working capital.
Price the timing as well as the product
Payment terms are part of a commercial offer, not a minor line for finance to discover after the sale. If winning a contract requires financing the customer for longer, make that cost visible alongside gross margin and acquisition cost.
Using the illustration, an assumed annual funding cost of 10% on the additional £395,000 would be about £39,500 a year. That rate is a modeling assumption, not a financing quote. Fees, eligibility, concentration limits and the available facility could change the actual cost substantially.
The answer need not be a higher headline price. A setup fee payable before work starts, milestone billing or a deposit may reduce the amount financed. These are commercial options to negotiate, not terms every enterprise buyer will accept. They must fit the product and the customer’s purchasing process.
An early-payment discount also has a cost. Compare that cost against the cash released and the number of days gained, rather than assuming that faster payment is always worth any discount. The aim is to win a contract that the company can afford to deliver.
Check the customer’s record, not just its policy
Sixty-day terms and late payment are not the same thing. A customer paying exactly on day 60 has used the agreed credit period. A customer paying on day 75 has introduced another 15 days of uncertainty.
For many large UK companies, founders can check published payment-practices reports through the government’s reporting service. The reports show measures including average time to pay and the proportion of payments not made on time. Check the contracting legal entity, not merely the group’s familiar brand name.
Those reports are evidence to question, not a guarantee about one invoice. A company-wide average may not describe the startup’s business unit or contract. Use the information to ask concrete questions before signing: when does the clock start, which purchase-order details are mandatory, who accepts delivery and what happens if an invoice is rejected?
Ask the sales team to resolve those questions while the customer still wants the contract signed. Otherwise, an apparent 60-day deal may include weeks of avoidable administration before the agreed period even begins.
Do not fund growth with an assumed recovery
Keep a distinction between invoices expected to pay normally and overdue balances whose timing is uncertain. Repeated promises should not become fresh, certain cash dates in the board forecast.
For a UK receivable that has genuinely become overdue, establish whether the issue is administrative, a dispute or an inability to pay. Reconcile the balance and set a decision point for seeking local collection or legal advice, whether directly or through a platform such as Debitura. That is a recovery decision, not a substitute for funding the next month’s operating costs. Neither an instruction to collect nor a legal claim makes the money immediately available.
The useful board conversation comes before a cash crisis: how much growth can current liquidity support if customers take the time already allowed in their contracts? Run a second version with plausible delays and identify the point at which hiring or delivery commitments would need to change.
A prestigious customer can be a good investment. But its logo does not pay wages. The payment terms belong in the funding plan on the day the contract is evaluated, not on the day the first invoice goes overdue.

articles.title: Amazon wants you to wear an AI that remembers your conversations — but do you really want it knowing that much about you?
articles.text:
Amazon's new Bee AI device can turn every conversation into a shopping opportunity — and that's deeply unsettling
Turning private conversations into product recommendations makes convenience feel like surveillance
Amazon has found another way to make itself part of our everyday lives with its new Bee AI devices. The Bees can record conversations and are pitched as a way to remember important details and translate plans into actions. Naturally, those actions can include buying things from Amazon, making every casual conversation a potential shopping cart. You can pay $75 or $100 for the privilege, depending on whether you choose the Bee Frontier, which clips to a wrist strap or clothes, or the Bee Eclipse, a magnetic smartphone attachment.
There are practical applications for something that remembers conversation details you might otherwise forget. An assistant that recalls an appointment, prepares a follow-up email, or reminds you about a promise could save considerable time. But Amazon's announcement also promises personalized shopping recommendations based on what Bee learns about you, which strikes me as a depressing, if inevitable destination for AI tools.
Of course, you might argue plenty of people have invited Amazon into their homes through Alexa devices. Plus, Amazon already has a potentially huge amount of customer data from shopping histories, which lets it recommend products so well that it's a cliché joke to feel like you only have to mention a topic out loud for related items to show up in your recommendations.
That joke is an explicit feature of the new Bees. Turning spoken conversations into another source of personalized assistance is supposed to appeal to potential customers. The question is whether this is a bridge too far when it comes to allowing Amazon to eavesdrop on our lives to shape our shopping.
Idle chat becomes a shopping list
The idea of an AI assistant remembering what you say and not letting anything important slip through the cracks is enticing for the convenience it promises. But imagine casually mentioning that your back hurts, your car is making a strange noise, or your child has developed an interest in dinosaurs. Those aren't just setups for a reminder to make a doctor's appointment, bring in your car, and buy tickets to the museum you'll get. They're also data points for potential purchasing interests that might otherwise never have reached a retailer.
Amazon hasn't said Bee will automatically turn every overheard complaint into a product recommendation, yet the shopping integration creates an obvious path to do so. But it might be too much personalization. Adding information from spoken conversations to what Amazon already knows could paint a much more intimate picture of someone's life, good and bad, regardless of Amazon's promises to keep data under the user's control.
And there are real privacy protections in the system, according to the company. Bee's AI processes audio in real time and deletes it rather than retaining recordings, while conversation transcripts are encrypted and users can delete them. The devices also include physical controls and lights that indicate when they're listening. Plus, the Amazon shopping connection is optional and opt-in.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
But deleting the original audio doesn't eliminate every privacy concern when a device is specifically designed to remember and interpret what people say. The information extracted from a conversation can be just as revealing as the recording itself.
Eavesdropping Bees
The privacy problem becomes even more complicated when other people enter the conversation. Someone wearing a Bee device might be perfectly comfortable having their conversations analyzed, but their friends and colleagues haven't necessarily agreed to participate. A small recording indicator is hardly a substitute for meaningful consent, especially when people may not recognize the device or understand what it does.
We've already seen this controversy unfold with Meta's Ray-Ban smart glasses. People have reported unexpected recordings, and even filming. Bee doesn't have the same camera-related concerns, but recording conversations introduces its own problems. A friend discussing a medical diagnosis or workplace dispute in confidence might not feel so open if they know you're wearing a Bee. They haven't necessarily agreed to have an AI system connected to the world's largest online retailer convert their comments into searchable data.
There are also practical questions about where recording is appropriate. Private conversations can involve confidential information, and recording laws can be wildly different depending on location and circumstances. Anyone using Bee needs to consider the consent of the people talking around them, regardless of whether Amazon deletes the original audio.
The fact that personalized shopping is part of the product's ambitions says something revealing about how the company imagines the future of personal AI. Amazon and Meta seem convinced that the future involves devices observing more of our lives so they can anticipate what we need next. And it's easy to think of reasons to develop these capabilities. People with memory difficulties, busy professionals, and anyone struggling to manage complicated schedules could benefit from reliable reminders and searchable conversations. But making recording devices an ordinary accessory could have far-reaching consequences, not all pleasant.
For me, the shopping integration is where Amazon's vision becomes particularly unappealing. I can appreciate an assistant remembering that I promised to call someone or reminding me about an appointment. I have considerably less enthusiasm for a device that might turn a casual remark about needing new shoes into another opportunity for Amazon to suggest something I should purchase.
We've spent years teaching technology companies about our interests through searches, purchases, clicks, and browsing histories. Wearable AI assistants like the Bee could extend that relationship into our conversations with other people. I don't particularly want my conversations becoming another source of shopping recommendations, though. If it's that important, maybe just write it down.

articles.title: Meta's Muse hits 10M US downloads in 40 days, a milestone reached by only 11 other apps | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Meta’s AI companion, Muse, is now one of only a dozen mobile apps to have reached 10 million U.S. downloads in its first 40 days on the market. According to new data from market intelligence provider Sensor Tower, Muse has seen 10.9 million downloads since its September debut, 10.2 million of which were in the United States.
Only 11 other apps to date have reached this type of post-launch milestone, said Sensor Tower’s senior insights analyst Kara Lee. The most recent of these was Meta’s Threads, back in July 2023.
Other apps that saw this kind of scale were largely mobile games, Lee noted, like Fortnite, PUBG Mobile, Pokémon GO, and others. Besides Threads, Disney+ was the only other nongame app to make it into the exclusive club.
Meta’s success is tied to the company’s ability to scale its new apps by marketing them across its other services, which it has done with both Threads and Muse. Threads was built on top of Instagram’s social graph, and its content has been integrated into both Facebook and Instagram. However, Muse isn’t only benefiting from Meta’s ability to market the AI agent across its family of apps, which today includes 3.6 billion daily active users; the company is also heavily investing in advertising to drive new users to Muse.
Per Sensor Tower’s data, Meta has allocated 39% of its total advertising spend to market Muse in October, up from 23% last month. In addition, Muse now ranks as the 21st largest brand in the U.S. by advertising impressions this month, up from 73rd in September.
Still, marketing an app and retaining users after the initial shine wears off are two different things. In this case, Muse is seeing better retention rates than its AI competitors like ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok.
In the U.S., the app had a 30% retention rate after 7 days and a 23% retention rate after 14 days. By comparison, its rivals saw an average of a 19% 7-day retention rate and a 16% 14-day retention rate, according to the firm’s data.
Muse also hit another milestone that demonstrates active engagement with the AI app. Its daily active users reached 2.5 million for the first time on October 16, a 15% week-over-week increase.
Meta’s latest AI app, which can handle various tasks on users’ behalf, has seen breakout success since its debut. It shot up to No. 1 on the App Store and at one point even outpaced some of the metrics ChatGPT saw following its launch. Its latest milestone sees it topping its rivals again, as ChatGPT saw 3.7 million U.S. downloads in its first 40 days on the market. Grok and Claude saw only 500,000 and 200,000 U.S. downloads, respectively, in their first 40 days.
Globally, ChatGPT beat out Muse, having scaled to around 15 million global downloads in its first 40 days. But this isn’t a fair comparison, as ChatGPT benefited from a wider reach. Muse is only available in the U.S. and Canada for now, while ChatGPT’s app attracted attention from markets like Japan, Brazil, and Germany, too. (Japan, for instance, accounted for 25% of its global installs during its first 40 days.)
Since launching, Muse has retained its No. 1 rank on the U.S. App Store for all days except October 19, when streaming app Kick briefly beat it out. It has since reclaimed the top spot as of Tuesday. Muse has also been No. 1 on Google Play over the past 30 days.

articles.title: Intel asks FCC for waiver to buy foreign robots — chipmaker’s automated guided vehicles could run afoul of agency’s sweeping robot ban
articles.text:
Intel asks FCC for waiver to buy foreign robots — chipmaker’s automated guided vehicles could run afoul of agency’s sweeping robot ban
These robots move chips between tools and sections of the fab.
Intel has asked the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to make an exception for the automated guided vehicles (AGVs) that the company uses to transport the sensitive silicon wafers and other materials, containers, and supplies needed to make the most advanced chips in its fabs. According to Bloomberg, the American chipmaker fears that its AGVs would fall under the blanket prohibition against foreign-made robots after they were added to the FCC’s Covered List.
AGVs are niche machines that chip fabs use to transport materials and supplies between tools and sections of the fab, helping ensure that the cleanroom conditions required for each manufacturing process are maintained. This makes them critical equipment for U.S. semiconductor manufacturing, but, apparently, there are no suitable domestic alternatives for these devices at the moment. Intel’s current fleet of AGVs requires continuous maintenance, including software and firmware updates, and if it’s forced to find a local supplier for its AGVs, the company says that it would take years, crippling the United States’ chipmaking efforts.
The biggest AGV suppliers are Japanese companies like Murata Machinery and Daifuku Co., while a few smaller businesses from South Korea and Taiwan are also trying to break into the market. It’s unclear why these companies haven’t applied for a conditional approval yet, which would allow them to continue selling these products in the U.S. while also promising Washington that they’ll set up a manufacturing base in the country. This is something that Netgear has already done, allowing it to continue selling its foreign-made routers despite being an American company.
Intel says that it remains unclear if updates to its AGVs would break compliance with the FCC, and that it’s asking the agency to issue a conditional waiver “out of an abundance of caution to ensure the ongoing operation of these specific AGV units.” While Team Blue is the only company concerned about AGVs at the moment, other chip manufacturers would likely need a similar waiver in the near future, especially as they build more fabs in the U.S. This includes TSMC, which is planning to build 12 more fabs and four packaging facilities in Arizona, Samsung, with its new Taylor, Texas, fab, and even Elon Musk’s Terafab, which has already begun construction.
Washington has been using the FCC to force companies to invest in American manufacturing. Its blanket bans on foreign-made products like drones and routers have affected some of the biggest brands in the U.S., including DJI and TP-Link. While these bans do not outright ban the sale of all products made by these companies, especially those that have already been approved before, they make it impossible for them to introduce new products and even release software updates to their existing product line. The FCC eventually walked back on the software update ban, but they still would not be able to register new products unless they build them in the U.S.

articles.title: Final Fantasy Resonance is comfort food at its most delicious
articles.text:
Final Fantasy Resonance feels like a long-lost SNES Final Fantasy game in the best way. Smartly, it takes the grand sense of adventure and purposeful structure of those 16-bit era JRPGs and introduces some welcome modernizations. It might not do anything wholly new, but when it’s all so slickly crafted, you can’t help but love it all the same.
The savviest thing Square Enix did with its first proper turn-based FF in years, ironically enough, was to look to none other than mobile gaming. Indeed, Resonance is an extensive remake of Brave Exvius, a now-discontinued FF Android and iOS title. Similar to how last year’s Octopath Traveler 0 adapted Champions of the Continent, Resonance takes Exvius‘ core story and world and dramatically expands it with significantly more narrative material, overhauled gameplay mechanics and other additional content.
What’s more, Resonance is the first-ever HD-2D Final Fantasy, meaning it benefits from the arrestingly beautiful blend of retro-inspired pixel art and sprites with 3D environments and modern rendering effects like dynamic lighting that was introduced with Octopath Traveler. Given that the 2018 JRPG was itself so inspired by Final Fantasy, it’s so wonderfully fitting for Final Fantasy to at long last be given the same treatment. And boy, is it something.
A fondly familiar fantasy
Beyond the aesthetic, Resonance feels like a proper SNES-era FF through and through. For one, the premise is an unabashed throwback to the FFs of old, focusing on a plucky band of warriors, mages, and mechanics who set out on a journey to stop a villainous cohort from destroying the Crystals that serve as the world’s life force. It’s a very basic FF plot, but that’s a feature, not a bug. It allows Resonance to play the hits, paying tribute to everything from legendary composer Nobuo Uematsu’s original iconic melodies to the Rebel Army from FFII, Golbez from FFIV, the Steampunk world of FFVI and, of course, people named Cid.
The narrative itself, meanwhile, is admittedly fairly standard. None of the cast has all that much depth, with main character Rain, in particular, being an archetypal “pure-hearted knight” who doesn’t ever really change. Meanwhile, big twists revealing the secret identities of certain villains can be seen a mile away. But in keeping with the loving homage to FF history, Resonance on the whole has an endearing playfulness and sense of humour that, when paired with exceptional voice acting, keeps it consistently enjoyable. In fact, it reminded me a lot of FFV, a very whimsical and humorous romp that was sandwiched between two decidedly darker SNES numbered entries. This lightheartedness is honestly refreshing, especially after Final Fantasy XVI went for a Game of Thrones-inspired dourness.
Resonance also harkens back to FF‘s roots with its fully turn-based combat system. Not Active Time Battle where metres slowly fill, not some action-menu hybrid like the FFVII Remake series — pure “nothing-happens-until-you-act” battles. It’s glorious, and it’s something that has sorely been missing from FF pretty much this entire millennium. In these four-character skirmishes, you select from your regular attacks, character-specific skills, magic abilities and other commands like you would in the FFs of old. You’ll use these moves to exploit enemy weaknesses and, eventually, fill a Stagger bar to make them significantly more susceptible to damage for a brief period.
But Resonance‘s unique gimmick, which is also lovingly rooted in nostalgia, is the Vision system. As you explore the world of Lapis, you’ll come across caves containing Visions, which are spirits of characters from all 16 FF mainline games, plus some folks who were created for Brave Exvius/Resonance. Each of these encounters are accompanied by short cutscenes featuring music and montages from their original game, which is a sweet bit of fan service. From there, they’ll join you as a sort of equippable gear that imbues your party members with special abilities and attributes.
It’s a brilliant mechanic, allowing you to combine predefined character archetypes with the unique strengths of fan-favourite heroes. On his own, Rain only has Fire-based sword moves, but with FFVII‘s Cloud, he gets powerful Lightning and Water attacks to bolster his offensive prowess. Conversely, Fina the mage is better served as a healer and buffer, so FFXIV‘s Y’shtola provides some welcome boosts on that front. But of course, you can mix-and-match for wilder combinations that play against type but might still help chip away at elemental weaknesses and more quickly Stagger enemies.
Turn orders, which you can see in the top left, are also essential to maximizing effectiveness. Upon Staggering every enemy, you’ll enter a period in which the party can launch a series of attacks that culminates in a special Resonance move of your choice from one of your Visions. These flashy pre-rendered cinematics unleash devastating assaults that can also sometimes have bonus effects like Regen, so it’s always immensely satisfying to successfully execute them after Staggering an enemy to deal extra damage.
Resonance‘s gameplay as a whole is so pleasant outside of combat, too, thanks to how tight it all feels. Dungeons never overstay their welcome due to little navigational gimmicks, multiple save points and the ability to return to the entrance before the boss. Fast travel is available throughout the entire world. You can change the party at any time. Altogether, it’s a splendid line-up improvements from some classic FF games where you could sometimes soft-lock yourself in a particularly tough dungeon.
But perhaps best of all are the sidequests. This collection of short stories actually fleshes out the characters in ways that the main quest often doesn’t, especially once the world opens up via airship. Take Rain’s Knight companion Lasswell, a similarly morally virtuous man and pretty standard “best friend” archetype. One sidequest has him dealing with a Robin Hood-type figure in his past, revealing shades of grey we hadn’t previously seen. Another sidequest, meanwhile, sees Nichol, the stoic strategist of a city of monks, having to grapple with his people’s prosperity has come at the cost of another tribue. In keeping with the FFV comparisons, though, my favourite sidequest chain by far is one I won’t dare say much about but can tease that it involves Gilgamesh, everyone’s lovably goofy multi-armed antihero from that very same 1992 SNES classic.
My only gripe with the otherwise ample quality side content is that some of it can drag. On the whole, Resonance is a fairly easy game on Normal difficulty, but some of these endgame challenges feel exponentially harder and even artificially padded due to enemies’ extremely large health bars coupled with a maddening tendency to heal themselves. (Also: not necessarily a flaw, per se, but the game features a mechanic that lets you see when your next random encounter will occur. It’s novel in concept, but because it always happens after a set period and there’s no way to prevent it, the strategic value here is pretty much non-existent.)
A crystalline comeback
Final Fantasy Resonance is a game that doesn’t reinvent the wheel at all, but that’s absolutely not a bad thing. If anything, it serves as the perfect celebration of Final Fantasy, right on time for the series’ 40th anniversary next year. With its excellent mix of stunning aesthetics, fanciful charm, satisfying combat system that makes classic FF characters an actual part of character progression and numerous quality-of-life features, Resonance is a thoroughly enjoyable ride that rarely lulls.
As I reflect on my time with Resonance, I’m reminded of one of the standout songs from FFV, “Home, Sweet Home.” It’s sweet, tender melody that, as the name suggests, brings to mind many nostalgic memories of childhood — of simpler, more comforting times. That’s Final Fantasy Resonance in a nutshell, and really, what’s more resonant than that?
Final Fantasy Resonance launches on PS5, Xbox Series X/S, Nintendo Switch 2, Nintendo Switch and PC on Oct. 20.

articles.title: It’s a bird, it’s a plane … it’s a robo-puffin?
articles.text:
It’s a bird, it’s a plane … it’s a robo-puffin?
MIT engineers’ design for a robot that both swims and flies could lead to a new class of vehicles for ocean exploration.
Given that water is 1,000 times denser than air, moving through those two mediums requires very different mechanics—or so one might assume. Yet birds like gulls and puffins can plunge into the sea, swim underwater, and leap back into the air to fly away. And now engineers at MIT and EPFL in Lausanne, Switzerland, have designed a robot that can do likewise.
The “flapping-wing aerial-aquatic vehicle,” or FAAV, weighs less than 300 grams (about half a pound) and is equipped with a central fuselage, two flexible wings, and a steerable tail. The body contains a battery and a waterproof electric motor that drives a crankshaft, which pumps the wings up and down at preset frequencies. The wings are made of thin membranes that are coated with hydrophobic nanoparticles to help wick away water. And the tail is motorized, enabling it to change its angle to help the robot fly up or dive down.
In experiments carried out in a water tank and at Lake Geneva, a team led by Raphael Zufferey, an assistant professor of mechanical engineering at MIT, identified combinations of wing size, flapping frequency, and tail angle that enable the robot to smoothly transition from swimming to flying.
The best results came with medium-size wings that were flexible enough to minimize flapping amplitude in water and also firm enough to keep the robot aloft in the air. The speeds and flapping frequencies were similar to those used by actual birds, and a pitch of 70 degrees—a relatively steep angle—allowed the robot to make the leap from water to air. Interestingly, although many diving birds paddle their feet to help them take off from the water’s surface, the team found that the bot didn’t need feet at all.
The engineers’ results could help pave the way for a new class of drones and vehicles that could fly to and sample from aquatic regions too dangerous for traditional vessels to access.
“Our dream vision is for oceanographers, marine biologists, and members of coastal communities to launch this robot from a boat, or from shore, and it would fly close to the area of interest, such as an iceberg or a port facility, or over a pod of whales,” says Zufferey. “It would dive into the water to take a measurement or collect a sample, and fly back to deliver the data at a fraction of the cost of traditional methods. Then it could go back out to dive for more.”
The researchers are now trying to design wings that can turn as well as flap. They will also test the robot’s performance under turbulent conditions, such as swimming in choppy waters and flying through wind. Then they hope to deploy the vehicle to help answer questions in ocean science.
“One of the major challenges in ocean science is collecting data both frequently and across many locations, which is something this robot could do in the future,” Zufferey says. “You could send this out not just every week, but every hour. It could fly out at high speeds, dive in, fly back, deliver its data, and go back out, multiple times.”

articles.title: ChatGPT ya programa en COBOL, un lenguaje más viejo que muchos de sus usuarios
articles.text:
Cuando pensamos en la IA y vibe coding, lo primero que nos viene a la mente es la programación con lenguajes modernos como Python o JavaScript. Si bien esto es útil, una parte importante de la infraestructura tecnológica mundial sigue ligada a tecnologías mucho más antiguas. Sistemas bancarios o aplicaciones gubernamentales se crearon con lenguajes que ya no se usan, por lo que OpenAI ha entrenado a ChatGPT para que pueda trabajar con ellos.
En una publicación de su blog, la compañía anunció que sus modelos de IA mejoraron notablemente en tareas relacionadas con tecnología antigua. Lenguajes como COBOL, Fortran, OCaml y Visual Basic, que hoy reciben menos atención que JavaScript y otros lenguajes modernos, siguen siendo fundamentales para el funcionamiento de empresas y gobiernos. Debido a ello, OpenAI entrenó a sus modelos para programar y migrar código en estos lenguajes.
Para medir los avances, la empresa desarrolló una herramienta conocida como MultiLangBench, en donde la IA debe construir un motor compatible con SQLite en 20 lenguajes de programación distintos. A eso se suma un benchmark de migración de COBOL, que mide si el modelo puede trasladar aplicaciones heredadas a otros lenguajes manteniendo su comportamiento.
Según los primeros datos, GPT-6 Astra logró una tasa media de éxito del 87,4% en MultiLangBench, que representa un salto notable si comparamos el 26,8% que lograba GPT‑5.6 Sol. En COBOL, Astra pasó del 10,9% al 72,1%, mientras que en Fortran aumentó del 21,4% al 83,5%. En el caso de Visual Basic, la IA registró una tasa de éxito cercana al 90%, lo que significa que el modelo más reciente de ChatGPT puede comprender este lenguaje que en su momento fue muy utilizado.
ChatGPT ya es capaz de migrar aplicaciones de COBOL a otro lenguaje
Lejos de los números, la verdadera prueba de fuego fue la de modernizar las aplicaciones antiguas. Este es uno de los principales cuellos de botella para muchas empresas y organizaciones, que tienen que mantener programas desarrollados hace décadas. En algunos casos, los empleados que los implementaron ya no laboran ahí o la documentación se perdió, lo que incrementa el coste de manutención.
Al intentar migrar una aplicación de COBOL a lenguajes como C++, Java, Kotlin, Python o Rust manteniendo la misma funcionalidad, GPT-6.1 Sol consiguió una tasa de éxito del 86,6% con bajo esfuerzo de razonamiento. Cuando se le permitió emplear un proceso más exhaustivo, la IA logró una precisión del 97,9%.
“Para comprobar si estos comportamientos se conservan, evaluamos nuestros modelos en pruebas ocultas que requieren paridad byte por byte en salidas observables”, mencionó la compañía. “Una migración solo se considera exitosa si todas las pruebas pasan”.
Según OpenAI, estos resultados sugieren que ChatGPT podría convertirse en una herramienta para actualizar infraestructuras tecnológicas heredadas. Lejos de limitarse a resolver errores o generar fragmentos de código, la IA ya es capaz de comprender sistemas construidos sobre lenguajes antiguos. Esto ayudaría a que los nuevos programadores que no crecieron con COBOL o Visual Basic puedan modernizar las viejas aplicaciones.
La compañía ha liberado MultiLangBench en GitHub para que los desarrolladores puedan revisar la metodología y analizar el rendimiento por lenguaje.

articles.title: Building Physical AI Systems That Can Work in the Real World - EE Times
articles.text:
Physical AI brings AI into machines that must sense their surroundings, make decisions, and act in the physical world. The market opportunity is substantial: McKinsey estimates that AI-powered agents and robots could unlock about $2.9 trillion in annual economic value in the U.S. by 2030. However, realizing this opportunity depends on moving from working prototypes to products that can operate reliably, safely, and economically at scale.
That exposes a different engineering problem. In a prototype, teams can often add more compute, sensors, cooling, or power to prove that a capability works. In deployment, every added capability must fit within the size, weight, power, and cost budget, often abbreviated to SWaP-C, of the system.
Those constraints shape how a robot performs: How long it can operate between charges, how much productive payload it can carry, and how reliably it operates over time. The challenge is not simply adding more intelligence but integrating it effectively into deployable products.
A robot must continuously interpret its surroundings, decide how to respond, and translate those decisions into physical action. Doing that requires capabilities from perception and AI inference to planning and motion control to work together, while meeting different compute and timing requirements.
System constraints shape intelligence
Every physical AI system has a finite design envelope. Processors, batteries, cooling, sensors, actuators, and mechanical components all compete for space, power, thermal headroom, and cost.
In a deployable robot, every gram matters. A larger battery may extend operating time but adds weight and takes up space. More compute can enable more advanced AI models, but places greater demands on cooling and energy.
Consider a quadruped robot navigating challenging terrain. Much of its onboard energy and weight budget must support the basic demands of locomotion, while the same system needs sensing, perception, navigation, and control to operate autonomously. More sophisticated reasoning cannot be added in isolation. It has to fit alongside motors, batteries, sensors, and other components within the same finite system envelope.
This makes physical AI a capability integration exercise. As Arm’s Federico Pecora explains in a recent paper titled The Missing Science of Robotic Systems: Capability Integration in the Model-Centric Era, robot intelligence depends on how perception, planning, control, safety, and orchestration work together across different timing, compute, and memory requirements. The “robot brain” is not only the largest model that runs on an accelerator, but the system architecture that enables these capabilities to work together at the right rates and with the right level of assurance.
The tradeoffs also vary significantly by machine. A quadruped navigating rough terrain, a humanoid manipulating objects, and a stationary industrial robot may all be described as robots, but they require different combinations of capabilities—and different levels of compute performance, energy efficiency, responsiveness, and safety.
As robotic systems become more capable, the industry needs more consistent ways to describe those capabilities and connect them to the underlying system requirements. That is why we are working with the ecosystem to establish a Robotics Capability Framework, which seeks to establish a common language to define and compare intelligent robotic systems.
AI changes the design equation
AI is changing how robotic and autonomous systems are designed. These machines increasingly need to interpret changing environments, respond to live data, and operate predictably as conditions change.
Doing that efficiently requires compute, software, memory, sensors, and safety functions to be planned together. Multiple workloads operate simultaneously with different timing requirements and priorities.
Heterogeneous compute gives engineering teams flexibility to match each workload to the right processing resource. Demanding AI workloads may run on dedicated accelerators, for example, while CPUs coordinate the wider system and microcontrollers handle low-latency control close to the hardware.
The value comes from designing these components as one coordinated system, with workloads running in the right place at the right time, with the right level of priority and isolation.
Deployment makes compute architecture a competitive advantage
Scaling physical AI is about more than raw performance. Every new model, sensor, reasoning layer, or safety function must fit within the available size, weight, power, thermal, memory, and cost envelope.
The systems that scale will extract more intelligence from every watt, coordinate diverse workloads efficiently, and keep safety-critical behavior predictable as AI demands increase. Managing these constraints can extend operating time, preserve productive payload, and make fleets more practical and economical to deploy.
Physical AI will be defined by products that are capable enough to be useful, efficient enough to scale, and predictable enough to trust.
Read also:
Physical AI Needs An Ecosystem
What Robots Show Us: Display and Data in Physical AI
Physical AI Isn’t Just Bigger AI; It’s a Systems Architecture Challenge
Dear Dermot,
At UNER AI (https://uner.ai/), our approach aligns closely with the article’s conclusion: physical AI requires coordinated hardware and software within real-world power, timing and cost constraints. We provide and deploy Autoware-based AI solutions across Renesas R-Car V4M, NVIDIA Orin and AMD Xilinx FPGA platforms, combining AI acceleration, MCU orchestration and Digital Twin validation to address these requirements.
I would conclude that successful physical AI depends on the entire system working together within real-world constraints.
Regards
CEO
Sergey Christ

articles.title: Mit deutschen Sensoren zum Mars: Was Technik aus Jena zur japanischen Mission beiträgt
articles.text:
Japans Marsmission: So sollen Sensoren aus Deutschland zum Erfolg beitragen
Eine japanische Raumsonde mit dem deutsch-französischen Rover „Idefix“ ist Richtung Mars aufgebrochen – und Sensoren aus Jena helfen ihr beim Navigieren im All. Zwei Stern-Sensoren des Thüringer Raumfahrtunternehmens Jena-Optronik sollen die Raumsonde zu den Marsmonden Phobos und Deimos geleiten. Sie tragen nach Unternehmensangaben zur exakten Ausrichtung und Navigation des Raumschiffs bei.
Jena-Optronik war nach eigenen Angaben ein wichtiger Zulieferer für die Mitsubishi Electric Corporation bei dem Projekt. Die Stern-Sensoren seien Teil des Lage- und Bahnsteuerungssystems. Die Rakete mit der Sonde und den Sensoren aus Jena war in der Nacht erfolgreich von Japans Weltraumbahnhof Tanegashima abgehoben.
Sensoren als „Auge“ beim Navigieren
Die Stern-Sensoren von Jena-Optronik, die Optik mit Bildverarbeitung kombinieren und Sterne zur Orientierung nutzen, gehören zu den grundlegenden optischen Navigationssystemen in der Raumfahrt. Sie dienten quasi als Auges des Lageregulierungssystems der Raumsonde, so das Unternehmen.
Auf dem Marsmond Phobos soll ein vom Deutschen Zentrum für Luft- und Raumfahrt (DLR) und der französischen Raumfahrtbehörde CNES entworfener Rover im Jahr 2029 aufsetzen. 2031 sollen dann mit einem Rückkehrmodul erstmals Proben von Phobos zur Erde gebracht werden.
Die Sensoren, die nur wenig Strom verbrauchten, erfassen nach Angaben von Jena-Optronik das die Sonde umgebende Sternenfeld und vergleichen es augenblicklich mit einem integrierten Sternenkatalog, um die exakte Ausrichtung des Flugkörpers im Raum zu bestimmen. Auch wissenschaftliche Instrumente seien auf eine sehr präzise Ausrichtung angewiesen, um genaue Daten von den Oberflächen der Marsmonde zu erfassen.
Jenaer Technik bei vielen Weltraummissionen dabei
Stern-Sensoren aus Jena hatten in diesem Jahr bereits bei der in den USA gestarteten Artemis-Mission zum Mond eine Rolle gespielt.
Jena-Optronik hat eine lange Tradition bei der Produktion von Systemen zur Lageregulierung von Satelliten, aber auch Raumschiffen. Diese geht bis in die DDR-Zeit zurück. Stern- sowie Rendezvous- und Dockingsensoren aus Jena waren bereits bei einer Vielzahl von Weltraummissionen dabei. Das Unternehmen hat nach eigenen Angaben bisher mehr als 450 Lageregelungssensoren verkauft, die weltweit in nationalen und internationalen Projekten eingesetzt werden. Jena-Optronik ist eine Tochter von Airbus Defence and Space.
