articles.title: How a blockchain marketplace is unlocking clean gas production in Kenya - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
African technologists and entrepreneurs are applying blockchain in innovative ways, creating a new financial infrastructure for the continent with wide-ranging benefits, including for the humanitarian sector.
Through its Blockchain Ventures investment programme, supported by the Ethereum Foundation and GSR Foundation, UNICEF Office of Innovation provides funding and technical assistance to emerging market startups building innovative blockchain-based solutions.
Kenya-based Autonomous Systems Research (ASR) began by exploring how drones could support disaster response, wildlife and environmental conservation. Working in remote areas led founder Moses Gichanga to investigate another challenge: generating electricity without transporting fuel into the field. ASR is developing ways to turn waste plant material into gas and electricity, and using blockchain to track traceability of biomass, payments to suppliers as well as applications in mobile money and disaster response.
How did a hobby building drones turn into Autonomous Systems Research?
Back in 2011, my daughter was two and a half and needed amusing, so I made her a kite. When the kite got boring, I built a small aeroplane out of paper bags. One early version had an eight-foot wingspan, with a laptop strapped to it and car wiper motors working the controls. Then I asked myself what would happen if I strapped a camera to one and flew it in a national reserve. That was when I started flying drones in Tsavo National Park.
I began asking how we could use this technology to help elephants and other wildlife, and to conserve ecological areas. That grew into Autonomous Systems Research. Later, ASR received its first grant from UNICEF Office of Innovation. We used it to explore whether drones could be useful for disaster response planning, ecological conservation, wildlife and agriculture, and what data would come out of that work. Since then, we have flown missions with government agencies, including Kenya Wildlife Service.
How did conservation work lead you from drones to producing energy from plant material?
Some of the places where we work are very remote and have no electricity. Our drones need charging, so we used a generator. But it became unsustainable to keep carrying fuel into the wilderness. We looked at solar panels, but they took up space and time. So we thought about modifying a generator to run on gas made from biomass. Later, people in communities saw that we had electricity in places without a supply and asked where we got it. We began thinking about making gas and electricity available to them too.
Where would the biomass come from, and what could the gas and electricity be used for?
We still use drones to look for potential sources of biomass. Once we identify some, we send someone to find out whether we can purchase it or otherwise acquire it. We want waste biomass. We do not want to cut down trees, and we do not want people planting biomass to sell to us instead of growing food. Coffee bushes, for example, produce material when they are pruned. We can turn that into gas.
We have developed equipment that converts biomass into gas, which we can use to run an engine. Gas is the primary thing we produce, but we can generate electricity as well. We have a site near our rural office where we are working with people who provide biomass and receive gas. We are also in the process of bringing local primary schools into the project. We are also in the process of brining local primary schools into the project. We want to see whether – with the right safety checks, ventilation and supervision – the gas could be used to cook meals and heat water, as an alternative to open fires.
You began using blockchain to track biomass. What does it record, and where else might you use it?
We wanted an audit trail that someone else could inspect. For the biomass, we record where it comes from, what type it is, the quantity, who gave permission to clear it, what they were paid, if anything, and how much gas we produced from it. We also have a payment mechanism for people who provide biomass, connected to mobile money platforms, M-Pesa and Airtel Money. We are interested in carbon credits in the future, and for that we would need a record people can trace.
We are looking at other applications too. Through our work on payments, we have engaged a local bank and are building a platform intended to offer mobile money services using blockchain. We also do volunteer work in emergencies, and we have developed a ledger system that can record where survivors are and what help they need after a disaster, though we have not applied that in a real-world setting yet.
What is holding the gas project back from operating at a larger scale?
We can produce the gas, but we have not reached the point of liquefying it efficiently. At the moment, we store it without liquefying it, which takes up more space. If we could liquefy it, we could fit more into a cylinder and look at selling it on a larger scale. We have tried some basic methods, but they use too much energy to work commercially. Finding a better way to do it would require substantial investment.
ASR began with drones, but you are now developing energy and other technologies. Is the idea to test solutions at ASR, then build separate businesses around the ones that work?
Yes. ASR does research into systems that can run themselves. That includes the drones and, eventually, the gas plant. When we develop a project, we intend to incorporate it as its own company, with its own governance structure, while ASR continues doing research.
We do not plan for ASR itself to become the gas supplier. The gas business could sell the product and make money as its own company, although we would still expect to have a role in its governance. We want to take an idea through the research and testing stage and then allow it to become something that can stand on its own.
ASR is a for-profit company, but you describe social good as central to its work. How do those aims fit together?
Social good is front and centre in what we do. Our tagline is “tools for transformative change”. We are structured as a limited liability company and we intend to make a profit, but we engage in projects that have a social good component.
We hope to make a lot of money. We want to do it in a way that helps our neighbours make money too. The more money they make, the less they need from us or from donors. There is a limit to how long someone can keep holding your hand. At some point, you need to become self-sustaining.
Take the gas project. We intend to sell the gas, but I also think about children collecting twigs for firewood. If we can make gas affordable to their households, they would not have to do that. I do not see a conflict between the social purpose and the business: we want to produce the gas cheaply enough that we can sell it at a price people can afford. As we see it, it is easier to get a shilling each from a million people than a million shillings from one person.
UNICEF was ASR’s first backer. Beyond the grant, what did its support make possible?
The first grant let us explore whether drones could be used for disaster response planning, conservation, wildlife and agriculture. Later, when we approached other organizations, we could show them what we had done and what we had learned. We have since received grants from other organizations, including Kenya’s National Commission for Science, Technology and Innovation, and done business with local government organizations.
We have also remained part of UNICEF’s alumni community since its investment. UNICEF organized a session for us with Google for Startups, and we later graduated from that programme. They organized seminars and workshops and supported our attendance at the World Economic Forum’s Annual Meeting of the New Champions. Those opportunities helped us think differently about what we could do.

articles.title: Hacker gets 8 years for stealing $3.3 million from taxpayers
articles.text:
A Nigerian national was sentenced to eight years in prison for his involvement in a series of spearphishing attacks targeting US tax preparation businesses since 2019.
40-year-old Chukwuemeka Victor Amachukwu (also known as Chukwuemeka Victor Eletuo and So Kwan Leung) has pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit computer intrusions and wire fraud after being extradited from France to the United States in August 2025.
"Chukwuemeka Amachukwu believed he was operating safely offshore when he targeted his victims, but he has now been held to account and now faces a serious sentence for his crimes," said US Attorney Jamie McDonald in a Monday press release.
"Amachukwu took part in sophisticated schemes to hack into US businesses, steal and use stolen identity information of victims, and commit fraud. These crimes imposed significant harm on the victims and the public, and so it is only appropriate that the crimes also come with a significant sentence for the defendant."
According to court documents, Amachukwu and his accomplices stole more than $3 million after filing fraudulent tax and loan applications with the Internal Revenue Service and state tax authorities using their victims' stolen personal data.
Together with co-defendant Kingsley Uchelue Utulu and other Nigerian co-conspirators, Amachukwu launched spearphishing attacks against tax preparation businesses in New York, Texas, and other US states between 2019 and 2021, gaining unauthorized access to their targets' computers and stealing the tax and personally identifiable information (PII) of at least 800 customers.
In total, he allegedly obtained about $2.5 million in fraudulent tax refunds (after filing for $8.4 million in refunds) and another $819,000 through fraudulent loan applications with the Small Business Administration's Economic Injury Disaster Loan program.
Amachukwu was also involved in a fake investment scheme that offered potential US victims investments in what the scammers described as valuable standby letters of credit. However, these investments did not exist, and the fraudsters stole more than $7 million from multiple victims.
In addition to the prison term, the court sentenced Amachukwu to one year of supervised release and ordered him to pay $3.6 million in restitution and forfeit nearly $11 million.
Once attackers have valid credentials, only 37% of their actions are blocked

articles.title: El Fire TV se vuelve mucho más útil en España: ahora también permite jugar a Amazon Luna a través de Prime Video
articles.text:
Poco a poco, Amazon va integrando más funciones útiles a sus dispositivos Fire TV Stick, sobre todo a los de las generaciones más actuales. Más allá de ser un reproductor de contenido de cine y series, ahora también lo es para gaming gracias al paso que ha dado: integrar Amazon Luna en sus Fire TV Stick a través de Prime Video.
Fire TV Stick 4K Plus
Todo desde una sola app
Amazon Luna es el servicio de videojuegos de Amazon, similar a Game Pass, aunque salvando las grandes distancias. Lo que ofrece Amazon es un catálogo de títulos en la nube a los que ahora podemos acceder a través de la plataforma Prime Video, uniendo así este catálogo al de películas, series y documentales a través de su correspondiente sección de "juegos".
Esto ofrece una utilidad mucho más grande a estos pequeños dispositivos, permitiendo que podamos acceder a ellos a través de Internet, sin necesidad de tener a mano una consola o un PC gaming. Y lo bueno es que Amazon suele renovar los títulos con frecuencia.
Ahora mismo, por ejemplo, hay bastantes títulos como 'Star Wars Outlaws', el videojuego de la saga desarrollado por Ubisoft. También podemos encontrar 'Hogwarts Legacy', 'Marvel's Guardianes de la Galaxia', 'Indiana Jones y el Gran Círculo', 'Death Stranding Director's Cut' o 'Alan Wake II' y 'Assassin's Creed Valhalla'. También hay títulos para los más peques como 'Bluey'.
La diferencia con lo que teníamos antes es que, hasta ahora, teníamos que abrir la app de Luna para poder acceder al catálogo de videojuegos. Ahora lo tenemos todo mucho más unificado a través de Prime Video.
Amazon Luna ya está disponible a través de Prime Video. Para poder acceder a los videojuegos, hay que utilizar un smartphone o directamente un mando compatible, no necesariamente el de Luna (yo utilizo el 8Bitdo Pro 3). Además, es necesario tener una suscripción activa a Amazon Prime, que actualmente tiene un precio de 4,99 euros al mes o 49,90 euros al año.
También te puede interesar
Amazon Fire TV Stick 4K (última generación): streaming 4K sencillo con nuevo mando Fire TV; ten todas tus apps en un solo lugar, TV gratuita y en directo, y encuentra series más rápido con Alexa+
Amazon Fire TV Stick 4K Select: comienza a reproducir contenido 4K en streaming, ve cientos de miles de películas y episodios de series, encuentra series más rápido con Alexa+

articles.title: Tesla Roadster moins cher : la marque annonce un 4e bolide plus « abordable »
articles.text:
Le 15 octobre dernier, Elon Musk a dévoilé le Tesla Roadster. Pour rappel, le modèle est décliné en trois versions : le Roadster Performance (une version routière classique, deux places, avec aérodynamique active et système d’aspiration sous la voiture), le Roadster Thrust (une version deux places ajoutant des propulseurs à gaz froid à l’arrière pour améliorer l’accélération) et le Roadster Rocket (une version monoplace, avec des propulseurs répartis autour du véhicule et des capacités de décollage). La présentation du 15 octobre était centrée sur ce dernier modèle, particulièrement impressionnant, il faut le dire. Ces trois modèles sont présents sur le site de Tesla, et une quatrième version pourrait prochainement les rejoindre.
Une Tesla Roadster standard
Franz von Holzhausen, designer en chef de Tesla, a confirmé l’information auprès du magazine MotorTrend : un quatrième modèle de Tesla Roadster rejoindra prochainement les trois autres. Concrètement, il est question d’une version standard, placée juste en dessous de la Roadster Performance, et donc moins performante, mais aussi plus « abordable ».
Selon Top Gear, ce modèle Standard atteindrait 1 090 ch, contre 1 360 ch pour la Performance. Il serait dépourvu du système d’aspiration multimode et pourrait également faire l’impasse sur l’aérodynamique active. Le véhicule pourrait donc être moins performant sur les accélérations, tout en offrant une meilleure autonomie. Les matériaux haut de gamme au sein de l’habitacle et le revêtement doré sur les vitres teintées pourraient aussi être remplacés par d’autres matériaux afin de faire baisser le prix. En revanche, ce modèle standard devrait bel et bien intégrer une propulsion, avec deux moteurs installés à l’arrière.
Quel prix pour ce modèle standard ?
Pour l’instant, Tesla ne présente pas ce modèle standard sur son site. Étant donné que nous ne disposons pas de fiches techniques, toutes ces informations devront être confirmées. En revanche, l’existence de ce modèle « plus accessible » semble actée. À ce titre, il reste aussi à connaître son prix. Ce modèle standard devrait afficher un prix plus bas que celui de la Roadster Performance, mais il devrait tout de même coûter un bras.
Pour rappel, Tesla demande un acompte de 50 000 € pour la Roadster Performance. En ce qui concerne le modèle Roadster Thrust, l’acompte s’élève à 250 000 €. Les prix de ces deux modèles sont toujours inconnus à l’heure où nous écrivons ces lignes, et il n’y a aucune garantie de livraison.

Le set LEGO Pokémon Poké Ball Moments culte de Dresseur (72154) est à 189,99 € (-27 %)
Le set LEGO Pokémon 72154 réunit 2 386 pièces pour construire une Poké Ball ouvrante, avec deux décors intérieurs et cinq personnages de l’univers Pokémon.
Amazon propose le set LEGO Pokémon Poké Ball Moments culte de Dresseur (72154) à 189,99 €, contre un prix conseillé de 259,99 €. L’économie atteint 70 €, soit environ 27 %. Ce modèle destiné aux adultes est expédié par Amazon.
Une Poké Ball ouvrante avec deux décors intérieurs
Le set de construction LEGO Pokémon 72154 compte 2 386 pièces. Une fois assemblée, la Poké Ball peut rester fermée pour présenter sa silhouette rouge et blanche, ou s’ouvrir pour dévoiler deux scènes. La partie inférieure accueille un espace de combat, tandis que la moitié supérieure reproduit le laboratoire du Professeur Chen.
L’intérieur comprend notamment une bibliothèque, des ordinateurs, trois petites Poké Balls moulées et deux tuiles représentant des Pokédex. Le support habillé de végétation complète la présentation en donnant l’impression que la grande Poké Ball vient d’être lancée sur le sol.
Trois minifigurines et deux Pokémon pour accompagner la maquette
La boîte contient les minifigurines de Red, de Pique-Nique et du Professeur Chen, ainsi que les figurines de Pikachu et d’Évoli. Ces cinq personnages permettent de peupler les décors et de varier la présentation du modèle. Le set est recommandé à partir de 18 ans.

articles.title: Après les violents pillages, pourquoi l’état d’urgence ne permettrait pas de bloquer les réseaux sociaux
articles.text:
Après les pillages du 17 octobre, certains, comme Bruno Retailleau, réclame l’état d’urgence et le gouvernement le garde en réserve. Ce régime d’exception issu d’une loi de 1955 permettrait surtout des mesures individuelles, mais pas de couper librement les réseaux sociaux.
Depuis les pillages qui ont suivi les manifestations du 17 octobre, l'état d'urgence s'est invité dans de nombreuses conversations, des plateaux télé aux fils d'actualité, aussi bien c'est ceux qui réclament son instauration que ceux qui le vilipendent. Le gouvernement de Sébastien Lecornu a préféré miser lundi soir des couvre-feux localisés à Paris, Lyon ou Lille, tout en gardant le régime d'exception sous le coude « si c'est nécessaire ». Entre la loi de 1955, la jurisprudence du Conseil d’État sur TikTok et le règlement européen DSA sur le services numériques, les marges de manœuvre de l’exécutif sont pourtant plus étroites qu’il n’y paraît.
L'état d’urgence, un pouvoir d’exception, pas un chèque en blanc
Cette fameuse loi de 1955, justement, mérite qu'on s'y arrête. Votée le 3 avril 1955, en pleine guerre d'Algérie, elle a donné naissance à un régime d'exception que la Constitution ne mentionne même pas, et qui ne peut être déclenché qu'en cas de péril imminent lié à des atteintes graves à l'ordre public. Le président le décrète en conseil des ministres, pour douze jours maximum. Au-delà, seul le Parlement peut le prolonger par une loi, qui devient caduque quinze jours après une démission du gouvernement ou une dissolution de l'Assemblée. Dimanche soir, dans son allocution, Emmanuel Macron s'est bien gardé de franchir le pas, pour le moment.
Les couvre-feux instaurés lundi soir, eux, s'en passent très bien. À Paris, la place de la République et une partie des Halles étaient concernées de 23 heures à 6 heures. Un hélicoptère rodait d'ailleurs dans le ciel de la Capitale. À Lyon, c'était une partie de la Presqu'île dès 21 heures. Dans le Nord, l'arrêté préfectoral vise les mineurs non accompagnés, même si Denain a étendu la mesure aux adultes. Les préfets et maires disposent déjà de ce levier, à condition qu'il reste limité dans le temps et l'espace. Pour Antoine Fouret, avocat associé au cabinet Nausica Avocats, l'apport de l'état d'urgence se joue ailleurs, à savoir dans les mesures qui visent des personnes précises. Il s'agit de l'assignation à résidence, de l'interdiction de séjour dans un périmètre et, si le décret ou la loi le prévoit, des perquisitions administratives sans feu vert préalable d'un juge. Le changement est bien réel, car en temps normal, le droit commun ne prévoit même pas d'interdiction administrative de manifester visant un individu.
Les sanctions, elles aussi, changent d'échelle. Braver un couvre-feu décrété sous état d'urgence peut coûter jusqu'à six mois de prison et 7 500 euros d'amende, contre une simple contravention en temps normal. Il permet en outre de dissoudre des groupements impliqués dans les violences, et ces dissolutions survivent à la fin du dispositif. Chaque décision reste toutefois contestable devant le juge administratif, souvent en 48 heures. Elle doit reposer sur le comportement de la personne visée, pas sur ses convictions. La France a d'ailleurs été condamnée en 2024 par la Cour européenne des droits de l'homme pour une assignation à résidence prononcée en 2015. « Régime d'exception, l'état d'urgence n'en demeure pas moins un régime de droit », rappelle maître Antoine Fouret. Mais qu'en est-il des réseaux sociaux ?
Le précédent calédonien plane sur le blocage des réseaux sociaux
Couper ou brider les réseaux sociaux est presque un vieux serpent de mer de notre ère moderne, comme la remise en cause du chiffrement des communications d'ailleurs. Sur la radio RTL, Gabriel Attal, candidat Renaissance à la présidentielle, a plaidé pour un blocage « temporaire, ciblé » des réseaux sociaux, limité aux territoires touchés par les émeutes, comme nous le racontions ce matin. Il reproche à ces plateformes de rassembler les casseurs et d'entretenir un effet de meute. L'ancien Premier ministre connaît le sujet, puisque c'est lui qui avait fait couper TikTok en Nouvelle-Calédonie en 2024. Mais l'état d'urgence ne lui offrirait pas ce pouvoir, souligne Antoine Fouret. La loi de 1955 autorise bien le ministre de l'Intérieur à suspendre un site ou un réseau social, mais dans un seul cas : lorsqu'il pousse à commettre des actes terroristes ou en fait l'apologie. Un appel au pillage, aussi choquant soit-il, ne relève pas du terrorisme et n'entre donc a priori pas dans cette case.
Il y a toutefois le cas des circonstances exceptionnelles. Le Conseil d'État l'a balisée en avril 2025, en jugeant le blocage de TikTok décidé en Nouvelle-Calédonie en mai 2024. Une coupure n'est admise que si elle est indispensable face à des événements d'une particulière gravité, sans alternative technique moins intrusive, et pour une durée limitée. Décidée sans échéance, celle de l'archipel a été jugée illégale. La plupart des géants visés relèvent en outre du règlement européen DSA, dont l'application revient à la Commission européenne. Le gouvernement prévoit, lui, une visioconférence avec les plateformes, invitées à modérer les contenus.
Juridiquement, rien n'interdit de dégainer l'état d'urgence face à des violences urbaines. La France l'a fait en 2005, puis en Nouvelle-Calédonie en 2024, mais pas pendant les Gilets jaunes. Encore faut-il démontrer un risque sérieux que les violences se répètent, insiste l'avocat. Bruno Retailleau, lui, réclame « l'état d'urgence maintenant, sans attendre le couvre-feu ».
En attendant, la traque des pilleurs se poursuit surtout devant des écrans. Les enquêteurs épluchent les images de vidéosurveillance, mais aussi les vidéos publiées sur les réseaux sociaux, où certains se sont eux-mêmes filmés en plein pillage, comme nous l'expliquions. L'autre dossier, c'est celui des objets volés ont été remis en vente sur Vinted ou Leboncoin dans les heures qui ont suivi. Le gouvernement a réuni ces plateformes, qui viennent de s'engager à « transmettre régulièrement aux autorités un bilan chiffré des actions de retrait des annonces problématiques, des mesures mises en œuvre, ainsi que des signalements transmis aux autorités, avec un premier retour attendu sous 48 heures », comme l'a déclaré le gouvernement ce mardi 20 octobre.

articles.title: Sam Altman confiesa su mayor temor con ChatGPT: “No he dormido bien ni una sola noche”
articles.text:
Sam Altman, director ejecutivo de OpenAI, reconoció que la responsabilidad de decidir cómo debe responder ChatGPT le ha impedido descansar con tranquilidad desde el lanzamiento del servicio. “No he dormido bien ni una sola noche”, afirmó al describir el peso de definir límites, criterios y respuestas para una herramienta que utilizan cientos de millones de personas. El ejecutivo situó así el debate sobre inteligencia artificial en un terreno cotidiano y decisivo.
Sus palabras importan porque el funcionamiento de un modelo de lenguaje no depende solo de su capacidad técnica para generar textos o resolver consultas. También está condicionado por reglas humanas sobre aquello que puede explicar, negar, advertir o matizar.
Altman sostuvo que OpenAI consultó a cientos de expertos, pero admitió que la decisión final recae en la empresa y, de cara al público, en él. Ese margen de decisión abre preguntas sobre moral, seguridad y libertad.
El comportamiento del modelo nace de decisiones humanas
En una entrevista con The Tucker Carlson Show, Altman explicó que la compañía recurre a filósofos morales y especialistas en ética tecnológica para evaluar las pautas de ChatGPT. El objetivo es construir un marco que permita responder a peticiones diversas sin convertir la plataforma en un mecanismo para causar daño.
Aun así, señaló que ninguna consulta externa elimina la responsabilidad de OpenAI sobre los criterios adoptados. La empresa cuenta con un equipo dedicado al comportamiento del modelo, aunque Altman aceptó que sus decisiones pueden no acertar siempre.
La dificultad aumenta porque millones de conversaciones plantean circunstancias distintas. Una misma regla puede resultar adecuada para evitar un perjuicio y, al mismo tiempo, limitar una consulta legítima en educación, salud o investigación.
Para Altman, los dilemas más visibles no son los únicos que requieren atención. Le inquietan especialmente las decisiones pequeñas: el tono de una respuesta, la cantidad de información que se entrega, el modo de rechazar un pedido o la advertencia que acompaña una explicación.
La libertad de los usuarios tiene límites de seguridad
El director ejecutivo defendió que ChatGPT debe tratar a los adultos como adultos y ofrecer una herramienta flexible, con garantías de protección. Sin embargo, afirmó que esa libertad entra en conflicto con la seguridad cuando una solicitud puede facilitar daños graves.
Mencionó como ejemplo las instrucciones para fabricar un arma biológica o desarrollar síntesis virales. Aunque alguien presente esos pedidos como investigación, OpenAI considera que ChatGPT no debe contribuir a actividades sin interés social legítimo y con potencial de daño.
El caso de las armas biológicas parece más claro que otros asuntos, pero Altman señaló que muchos límites carecen de una respuesta inmediata. Las fronteras se vuelven menos precisas cuando el modelo aborda controversias políticas, asuntos culturales o preguntas relacionadas con valores personales.
En esas situaciones, la inteligencia artificial puede influir en la forma en que una persona ordena sus opciones, aunque no decida por ella. Por eso, el diseño de cada respuesta exige revisar sus consecuencias y admitir que el criterio puede cambiar con el tiempo.
OpenAI busca reflejar normas sin imponer una moral individual
Altman afirmó que OpenAI procura respetar las leyes de cada sociedad y representar un promedio de las preferencias morales de sus usuarios. Según su planteamiento, la compañía actúa como facilitadora de una tecnología que debe admitir posturas distintas, en lugar de trasladar al sistema la visión personal de sus directivos.
Esa aspiración enfrenta un límite evidente: las normas cambian entre países y las demandas sociales también se transforman. El modelo debe adaptarse a esas diferencias sin abandonar sus protecciones.
La inquietud de Altman resume ese desafío: cada ajuste aplicado a ChatGPT puede parecer menor dentro de una conversación, pero adquiere otra escala cuando afecta a millones de intercambios. La discusión sobre su conducta seguirá abierta mientras la tecnología amplíe su presencia en la vida.

articles.title: Presque trois fois mieux que ChatGPT à ses débuts : l'agent IA Muse de Meta cartonne aux États-Unis — Frandroid
articles.text:
Meta tient enfin un succès dans l’IA grand public. Ce mardi 20 octobre, TechCrunch a publié des chiffres du cabinet Sensor Tower, qui mesure les téléchargements sur les boutiques d’applications.
L’application Muse en compte 10,9 millions depuis son lancement le 8 septembre, dont 10,2 millions aux États-Unis. C’est presque trois fois ce que ChatGPT avait fait sur le sol américain dans le même délai. Par contre, les Français ne peuvent pas l’installer : Muse n’est disponible qu’aux États-Unis et au Canada.
    Pour aller plus loin
L’agent IA Muse de Meta peut gérer vos mails, votre agenda et votre compte en banque pour vous
            
Muse est un agent IA personnel, c’est-à-dire une IA qui fait les choses à votre place au lieu de seulement répondre. Dans son article de lancement, Meta explique qu’elle peut envoyer un mail, réserver un voyage, remplir des formulaires ou négocier une facture. Elle demande votre accord avant d’envoyer un message ou de payer. Pour y arriver, elle se branche sur vos mails, votre agenda et même votre compte en banque.
Pour Mark Zuckerberg, CEO de Meta, le succès tombe à pic. Le groupe courait derrière OpenAI et Google depuis l’accueil tiède de Llama 4, son modèle ouvert sorti en avril 2025. Muse est le premier gros produit grand public piloté par Alexandr Wang, recruté en 2025 pour diriger l’IA de Meta.
Un club de douze applications, dont deux de Meta
Seules onze autres applications avaient dépassé les 10 millions de téléchargements américains en 40 jours, selon Kara Lee, analyste chez Sensor Tower. Il s’agit surtout de jeux mobiles, et la dernière en date venait déjà de Meta : Threads, en juillet 2023. Sur ses 40 premiers jours aux États-Unis, ChatGPT avait fait 3,7 millions de téléchargements. Grok en avait fait 500 000 et Claude 200 000.
Dans le monde, ChatGPT reste devant, avec 15 millions de téléchargements sur ses 40 premiers jours. Pourtant, il est injuste de comparer : l’application d’OpenAI était disponible dans bien plus de pays, et le Japon représentait à lui seul 25 % de ses installations.
Meta a aussi les moyens de pousser son application. Le groupe peut la mettre en avant auprès des 3,6 milliards de personnes qui utilisent chaque jour Facebook, Instagram ou WhatsApp. Et il a sorti le chéquier : d’après Sensor Tower, Muse a reçu 39 % du budget publicitaire total de Meta en octobre, contre 23 % en septembre. Muse est ainsi passée du 73e au 21e rang des marques américaines en nombre d’impressions publicitaires (le nombre de fois où une publicité s’affiche).
La publicité n’explique pas tout pour autant. Muse est devenue l’application gratuite la plus téléchargée sur l’App Store américain dès le 18 septembre, avec 730 000 téléchargements sur ses cinq premiers jours. Surtout, les gens la gardent. Aux États-Unis, 30 % des utilisateurs ouvrent encore Muse sept jours après l’avoir installée, et 23 % au bout de quatorze jours. Pour ChatGPT, Claude et Grok, la moyenne tombe à 19 % et 16 %.
L’application a passé les 2,5 millions d’utilisateurs actifs par jour, le 16 octobre, 15 % de plus qu’une semaine plus tôt. Meta en profite pour avancer ses pions, avec un nouveau modèle, Muse Wonder, présenté comme au niveau des meilleurs, et un modèle ouvert qui tourne en local sur deux Mac Studio.
Et en France, c’est pour quand ?
Aucune date n’est annoncée. Le billet de Meta ne cite que les États-Unis, sans calendrier ni explication pour les autres pays.
Meta ne donne pas de raison, mais il y a un précédent. En 2024, le groupe avait suspendu ses projets d’IA dans l’Union européenne à la demande du régulateur irlandais des données personnelles, et Meta AI n’y est arrivé qu’en mars 2025.
Un agent qui lit vos mails et accède à votre banque pose des questions encore plus lourdes au regard du RGPD (le règlement européen sur les données personnelles). Meta prévoit aussi Muse sur ses lunettes connectées et sur le Muse Charm, un porte-clés dédié.
Pour essayer quand même, il faut passer par un VPN. Clubic détaille la méthode : se connecter à un serveur américain, puis créer un compte réservé à Muse plutôt que d’utiliser son compte principal. Réfléchissez bien avant de confier vos e-mails ou votre banque à un service qui n’est pas officiellement proposé en France.
Utilisez-vous Google News (Actualités en France) ? Vous pouvez suivre vos médias favoris. Suivez Frandroid sur Google.

articles.title: Data centre vs Cloud platform: Is there a difference?
articles.text:
You have probably seen the words “data centre” and “cloud” used interchangeably. They don’t mean the same thing, and the difference matters. It shapes how businesses buy technology, how regulators write rules and where investors see opportunity.
A data centre is a building. It is a secure, purpose-built facility with reliable power, cooling, security and internet connections, so that computers can run around the clock. A cloud platform is a service. It is software that lets customers rent computing power, storage, and networking on demand, switch them on or off themselves, and pay only for what they use.
Think of an airport and an airline. The airport provides the runway, fuel, and terminal; the airline provides the service you actually book. Every cloud platform runs inside a data centre, but most data centres do not offer a cloud platform. Owning an airport does not make you an airline.
Data centre grading and cloud computing standards
Companies that rent space for their own servers in someone else’s facility are buying what the industry calls “colocation”. A facility’s reliability is rated on a four-level scale from the Uptime Institute.
Tier I has no backup equipment, so any fault results in downtime. Tier II adds spares but has a single path for power and cooling.
Tier III has more than one path, so any part can be serviced without switching anything off; it is the level most serious operators aim for. Tier IV survives any single failure.
Be careful, though: “built to Tier III standards” is not the same as certified, so ask which certificate a provider actually holds.
The US National Institute of Standards and Technology defines cloud computing by five features: customers can provision resources themselves, access them over the internet, share the provider’s pool of equipment, scale capacity up or down quickly, and pay only for what they use.
A bank that runs virtualised software in a rented cage has a more efficient setup, but it only becomes a cloud when self-service, automation, and metering are added.
Why this matters for Nigeria
Customers spent US$143.4 billion on cloud infrastructure in the second quarter of 2026 alone, with Amazon, Microsoft, and Google capturing about 63 per cent of that spending. None of them runs a full cloud region in Nigeria.
Amazon has a smaller facility called a Local Zone in Lagos, but for Microsoft, Google, and Oracle, the nearest full regions are in South Africa. So when a Nigerian bank says its data is “in the cloud”, that data is often outside the country.
That is why the Central Bank of Nigeria’s order to keep payment data on local infrastructure by 1 January 2027 puts this distinction at the centre of the debate. Moving data home requires local data centres and local cloud platforms that offer the ease, scale, and reliability banks expect. Operators such as MTN, which launched cloud services alongside a new Tier III data centre in Lagos in 2025, are starting to fill that gap.
Power and progress in Nigerian infrastructure
A Tier III data centre is built on the assumption that the public grid will fail. Rack Centre in Lagos runs entirely off-grid on its own 13.5 MW gas-powered system and reports 100 per cent uptime since 2013. Where electricity does matter is cost: generating your own power is expensive, and that shows up in prices. That is a real competitiveness issue, but a different story from “Nigerian data centres keep going down because of NEPA.”
When I chose a data centre for a bank’s workloads in 2012, there was only one commercial option worth serious consideration. Rack Centre in Ikeja opened in 2013 and later became the first facility in Nigeria and West Africa to win Uptime Institute Tier III design certification.
Today, industry counts put Nigeria at around 26 operational data centres, about 28 including those being built, with 210 to 300 MW of capacity expected by 2030. In my experience, the leading operators have not lost a minute of service to a power failure.
A data centre is the foundation; a cloud platform is what you build on it. Nigeria now has a strong, professionally run foundation. The next challenge, made urgent by data localisation and demand for AI, is building cloud platforms on top of it.
Policymakers, journalists, and business leaders should ask not only “Do we have enough data centres?” but “Do we have cloud platforms to make them useful?”
Remi Adejumo is a Cloud and Infrastructure Architect with over 20 years’ experience in cloud computing, data centres, virtualisation, and enterprise IT transformation across the UK, the US, and Africa.

articles.title: How to review AI code without reading the code
articles.text:
How to review AI code without reading the code
The argument over whether engineers should stop reading code is over, because we already have.
Faros AI’s new report shows a 76.3% increase in pull requests merged without review since their last report in April. Many companies now run AI reviews on 50% to 80% of their PRs. AI review took over bug-finding. But it didn’t take over the conversation where a team debates what it decided and why, and that is the part I missed too.
The part AI review doesn’t solve
Most teams are stuck in one of two modes. They review every line and become the bottleneck, or they rubber-stamp and lose track of what changed and why. There is no middle ground yet.
“The argument over whether engineers should stop reading code is over, because we already have.”
AI review is good at the mechanical half of the job. It never gets tired, it reads every line, and it holds the same standard on every PR. But it never saw what was decided. It won’t tell you not to build something, and it can’t be accountable for the result. A better model won’t fix that, because the tool reads the wrong artifact at the wrong time.
As I wrote in “Kill the code review theater, keep the review,” code review is how a team builds a mental model of its system. That has been the only scheduled moment for engineers to talk to each other about that system. Teams that hand code reviews to AI tools rarely notice they’ve also given up that moment.
I didn’t notice either. The five layers of trust I proposed in March for replacing code review all checked the code. Four asked, “Is it right?” One asked, “Is that what we meant?” None asked, “Are we building the right thing?”
Debating decisions replaces reading the code
A decision is any point where the change could have gone another way: a token bucket or a sliding window, fail open or fail closed, one limit for every customer or one each. An AI-written PR is full of them, and almost none of them show up in the diff.
My new framework for the review bottleneck also has five layers.
- Challenge. Before the PR exists, a second agent on a different model pushes back on the coding agent’s approach. The output records what was proposed, what was rejected and why, and which agent gave ground. Settled points stay on the record too, because two agents can also agree to look the other way.
- Capture. The intent (why we’re making the change) and the acceptance criteria (how it should behave) get captured from coding with the agent and go onto the PR. You need both: intent without criteria can’t be checked, and criteria without intent can’t be judged.
- Codify. Review comments your team keeps repeating, like “use the Money type, not float,” go into an AI slop registry, and become invariants, standing rules checked on every change.
- Debate. People discuss the decisions the agents surfaced and couldn’t settle, and leave the line-by-line checking to the machines. It’s the only layer that asks whether we’re building the right thing.
- Own. A model has no reputation and can’t be asked why, so a named team owns the invariants and the mental model behind them, and signs off on the change.
The first three are work for machines, and tools for them exist today. Debate and Own are work for people, and Debate is the layer that was missing.
“The principle we designed around is simple: agents verify, people decide.”
The principle we designed around is simple: agents verify, people decide. People are better at judging whether a change is right, weighing trade-offs and risks, and owning the decision. Invariants are rules for agents. Decisions are judgment calls for people, and the calls that keep coming back become rules.
Debate also ends the argument over whether engineers should read AI-generated code.
I recently spoke to Robert ‘Uncle Bob’ Martin, the author of “Clean Code,” who recently said that he doesn’t read the code anymore. But he did say that humans should take responsibility for the systems, just above the code. Decisions sit at that level.
A reviewer who has debated the decisions doesn’t have to read code line by line to explain a change.
Should we just review specs?
The obvious objection is that this just moves the reading somewhere else, and at some point that place was specs. My issue with reviewing specs is that it seems backward. A spec takes time to write, gets written before the work teaches you anything, and drifts the moment implementation starts.
Decisions come out of the work itself. They are generated live, they are short, and each one exists because the change could have gone another way. That is also why Capture pulls the intent and acceptance criteria out of the coding session after the work, instead of asking anyone to write them up front.
How I see decision review working
Here is how I see it working, based on what we’ve been building at Aviator.
Where decisions come from
Most decisions already happen on the author’s machine, and today we throw them away.
- A capture skill pulls intent, acceptance criteria, and decisions out of the coding agent session. Every time the agent stops to ask and the engineer makes a call, it records that call.
- A review skill runs an adversarial review agent that argues with the coding agent before the PR is submitted. It records what they disagreed about and how they settled it. What they couldn’t settle is what the team debates.
What a decision looks like
This example uses a PR that adds a per-installation rate limit to webhook ingest.
The intent is one sentence: throttle webhook bursts per GitHub installation so one noisy customer can’t starve the broker, without dropping events or breaking their order.
The PR carries six decisions. The one still open is a product call, not a code one: the burst limit is one value for every customer. Two are accepted risks: a Redis outage fails open, and deferred events hold their payload in the broker. Exposing limiter metrics on the on-prem Grafana board became a follow-up with a linked ticket. The other two were argued out between the author, the reviewer, and the agents and settled.
Take one of the settled ones, “token bucket, not a sliding window.” The author’s agent explains it in the thread: one Lua call per event instead of a sorted-set scan, chosen after profiling a replay of a webhook storm. A reviewer who disagrees can push back in the same thread or ask the agent directly.
None of that is visible in the diff.
What the reviewer does
The reviewer’s part comes down to three steps:
- Read the intent and what’s changing.
- Go through the decisions and argue where you disagree.
- Check what isn’t passing, then approve.
That is enough to understand the change, build a mental model, and argue about what matters, without reading line by line.
Each decision is its own thread, with humans and agents labeled separately, so you know who made which call. A reviewer can agree, challenge, override, or turn a decision into a tracked follow-up. The code is still there. You open it where a decision sends you, and comments on the code join the same record.
What happens after the merge
The decisions outlive the review.
- Your team’s week. You see the key decisions made in your part of the codebase over the last day or week, without reading the PRs. That is what knowledge-sharing code review was always for.
- Memory for agents. Coding and review agents pull past decisions for the code they touch, so they don’t re-argue settled trade-offs.
- Follow-ups that stick. “Do it later” becomes a linked ticket, not a line in a PR description nobody reads again.
- Rules from patterns. When a decision keeps recurring, propose it as an invariant; it becomes a rule only after someone approves it.
Someone still has to sign. A model has no reputation and can’t be asked why, so every debated decision ends with a named person who agreed to it. That is where Debate hands off to the last layer, Own.
“If AI already reviews most of your PRs, try one question on your team: what did we decide last week, and who agreed to it?”
If AI already reviews most of your PRs, try one question on your team: what did we decide last week, and who agreed to it?

articles.title: Beyond the KV cache: Training and serving i14’s Laplace 3B linear attention model on AWS Trainium2 with native PyTorch | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Beyond the KV cache: Training and serving i14’s Laplace 3B linear attention model on AWS Trainium2 with native PyTorch
Most large language models (LLMs) use transformer architectures with softmax attention. During inference, their key-value (KV) cache grows with the conversation or document context. This can reduce concurrency, increase serving cost, and force agentic applications to discard useful history.
i14 designed Laplace 3B as a linear attention alternative. Its recurrent state stays at 29.5 MB per sequence, independent of context length. Working with AWS, i14 used native PyTorch support through TorchNeuron Native to bring this custom architecture to AWS Trainium2. This preserved its Gated Linear Attention (GLA) design and Muon optimizer.
On one trn2.48xlarge instance, Laplace 3B trained at about 120,000 tokens per second. The model served 11,544 output tokens per second across 1,280 concurrent sequences. This post explains the model design, the changes i14 made for Trainium2, and the training and inference results.
About i14
i14 is an AI research and technology company that develops model architectures, components, and runtimes. Its work draws on AI, computational cognitive science, and research into how biological systems learn over time. i14 applies these ideas to models that can retain long-range context without allowing serving state to grow with every token.
Why linear attention models?
Transformer softmax attention compares tokens across the context. During training, this computation grows quadratically with sequence length. During inference, the KV cache grows as the model processes more tokens.
Linear attention reorganizes the computation around a recurrent state that is updated for each token. Laplace 3B uses GLA to compress prior context into a fixed-size matrix state. This changes training attention from O(T2) to O(T) and keeps inference state fixed at 29.5 MB per sequence.
| Consideration | Transformer softmax attention | Laplace 3B with GLA | 
| Training attention | Builds pairwise token scores with O(T2) scaling | Updates chunked recurrent state with O(T) scaling | 
| Inference memory | KV cache grows with context | Recurrent state remains fixed in size | 
| Longer contexts | Each sequence consumes more accelerator memory | Context length does not increase recurrent-state allocation | 
| Implementation | Uses widely optimized attention kernels | Requires architecture-specific kernels and compiler tuning | 
Linear attention compresses history rather than retaining every key and value. You must therefore evaluate retrieval quality for your workloads. The fixed state can benefit long-running agents, large-document analysis, and applications that need persistent memory with predictable serving requirements.
How i14 adapted Laplace 3B for AWS Trainium2
The original implementation of Laplace 3B used GPU-optimized Triton kernels. The AWS Generative AI Innovation Center (GenAIIC) team first rewrote the GLA kernel with standard PyTorch operators for Trainium2. After comparing both approaches, the team chose the beta version of TorchNeuron Native, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium, because it performed better.
The implementation required three changes:
- Using native PyTorch for the GLA attention kernel. The team replaced the GPU-specific fused_chunk_simple_gla Triton kernel with standard PyTorch operators, using 16 chunks of 128 tokens to match the 128 partitions of the NeuronCore on-chip buffer.
- Redesigning how Muon communicates. Two all_to_all collectives in MuonFSDP2 cut per-rank traffic by 24 times and raised throughput by 1.63 times.
- Compiling the sequential backward pass. The team statically unrolled the 16 chunk steps of the GLA recurrence to fit the graph-size and on-chip memory limits of the compiler.
The engineering challenges section describes each change in detail.
Why AWS Trainium accelerators?
AWS Trainium is a family of AWS machine learning (ML) accelerators designed for model training and inference. A trn2.48xlarge instance combines 16 Trainium2 chips, 64 logical NeuronCores, high-bandwidth memory, and NeuronLink-v3 connectivity. These resources support the distributed training and inference configurations described in this post.
Three properties of Trainium2 shaped the implementation: software-managed on-chip memory (Challenge 1), a fast chip-to-chip interconnect (Challenge 2), and a static compiler (Challenge 3). The compiler traces the GLA recurrence as a fixed graph.
Software-managed on-chip memory. Each NeuronCore has a 28 MiB State Buffer (SBUF) with 128 partitions and a 2 MiB partial-sum buffer (PSUM). The PSUM is wired to a 128×128 systolic Tensor Engine, alongside separate vector and scalar units. The SBUF is not a cache: the compiler schedules every HBM-to-SBUF transfer ahead of time, so the data is in place with no evictions or misses (Figure 1).
i14 and the Laplace 3B architecture
Laplace 3B is the 24-layer i14 decoder, where every layer replaces softmax attention with Simple GLA. Figure 2 follows one layer from the input xt at the top to the output xt + 1 at the bottom. This section explains each module: normalization and convolution, the QKVG projection, the GLA mixer, and the feed-forward channel mixer.
Normalization and convolution. Each token’s residual-stream vector xt ∈ ℝD (D = 3, 072) passes through a LayerNorm and a depth-wise causal Conv1d of width k = 4 with SiLU. This gives every position a 4-gram summary before the mixer. The GLA mixer then does content-based retrieval over the whole history through its decaying state.
QKVG projection. The post-conv output goes through one fused matrix Wqkvg ∈ ℝ9, 216 × 3, 072, where 9, 216 = H × (2dk + 2dv). It splits into four per-token streams: queries qt, keys kt, values vt, and a gate gt (H = 16, dk = 96, dv = 192). The gate is used after the mixer.
GLA mixer. Each head h keeps a matrix state St(h) of size dk × dv (96 × 192), a compressed, decaying record of past key-value pairs. At each token, it updates as:
Here λh is the fixed per-head decay, and ktvt⊤ is the rank-1 outer product that writes the current key-value pair into the state. The readout queries the state:
Next, a self-augmentation step adds a gated copy of the value to each head’s output:
Here σ is the sigmoid and ⊙ is the element-wise product. The gate is the query dotted with a learned per-channel rescaling of the key, where a is the learned scale (aug_balance). At initialization, a = 0, which gives a half-strength skip of the value. The per-head outputs pass through a Head RMSNorm within each decay tier, are concatenated, gated by SiLU(gt), and projected by Wout ∈ ℝD × D back to the residual stream.
Decay schedule. The per-head decay rate λh controls how fast a head forgets past tokens. It is fixed at initialization (not learned) and set by a geometric schedule. The schedule gives the 16 heads a spread of memory lengths and defines each head’s log-decay rate γh:
Decay schedule’s reach. For this model, Tmin = 1 and Tmax = 2, 048. Head 0 therefore has λ0 = 0.5 (half-life of one token), and head 15 has λ15 ≈ 0.9997 (half-life of 2,048 tokens). Heads are grouped into tiers, each sharing a Head RMSNorm.
Channel mixer (FFN). After the attention block and its residual, a second LayerNorm feeds a GLU (SiLU) FFN with inner dimension 8,192. Its three matrices are two up-projections W1, W2 ∈ ℝ8, 192 × D and one down-projection W3 ∈ ℝD × 8, 192. A second residual follows.
The state S(h) is fixed at dk × dv = 96 × 192 per head regardless of sequence length. As a result, inference is O(1) per token, and training is O(T) rather than O(T2).
| Parameter | Value | 
| Parameters | 3.028B total (2.718B Muon + 309.6M AdamW) | 
| Layers | 24 decoder layers, D = 3, 072 hidden dim | 
| Heads | 16 heads, dk = 96 (half-width Q/K), dv = 192 (full-width V) | 
| Mixer | Simple GLA with fixed geometric decay (Tmin = 1, Tmax = 2, 048) | 
| Conv | Depth-wise causal Conv1d, kernel width 4, SiLU | 
| FFN | GLU (SiLU), inner dim 8,192 | 
| Norm | LayerNorm pre-attn + Head RMSNorm (per tier) + LayerNorm pre-FFN | 
| Vocab | 50,304 (padded to multiple of 64) | 
| Sequence | 2,048 | 
| Training data | 100B tokens, FineWeb-Edu | 
| Optimizer | Muon for 2D weight matrices; AdamW for embeddings, norms | 
| Batch size | 524,288 tokens/step, cosine LR, 3,815-step warmup | 
Engineering challenges
Each of the three changes raised its own engineering challenge.
Challenge 1: Using native PyTorch on Trainium for GLA
On GPU, GLA runs as the fused Triton kernel fused_chunk_simple_gla from the flash-linear-attention library. The GenAIIC team re-expressed it with standard PyTorch operators running through TorchNeuron Native, as explicit loops over fixed-size chunks. The chunk count is fixed at compile time and sets the backward-unroll depth. The team uses fla_num_chunks = 16, so each chunk holds C = 128 tokens.
Within each chunk c, the intra-chunk output is masked linear attention, and the running state S adds earlier context:
The state then advances to the next chunk:
Here λC is the per-head decay compounded over the chunk. The 16 intra-chunk computations run in parallel, and only the state update is sequential (Figure 3).
Because the SBUF has 128 partitions, each 128-token chunk maps one token per partition, with no padding or cross-partition movement. This alignment increased measured throughput by 14 percent (Figure 4).
Challenge 2: Distributed Muon orthogonalization under FSDP2
Muon orthogonalizes each gradient before the update. For each of the 96 two-dimensional weight matrices (2.718 billion parameters), it runs five Newton–Schulz iterations (Algorithm 1).
The distributed problem. The Gram matrix A = XX⊤ correlates every row of the weight with every other row. Under Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP2), each of the 64 ranks holds only 1/64 of the rows. A shard-local XX⊤ therefore yields only a diagonal block and drops every cross-shard term (Figure 5).
Naive approach: Gather and broadcast. Every rank gathers the full gradient (5.44 GB), one rank runs Newton–Schulz, and it broadcasts the result. This moves 10.87 GB per step while the other 63 ranks wait.
Production approach: all_to_all transposition. In MuonFSDP2, one all_to_all gives each rank a few complete matrices, all 64 ranks run Newton–Schulz in parallel, and a second all_to_all returns the results. Per-rank traffic drops to 0.45 GB, 24 times less. Throughput rises from 73,378 to 119,934 tokens per second, 1.63 times higher, with a bit-identical loss curve (Figure 6).
Communication cost. Newton–Schulz is only about 2 percent of the FLOPs in a training step (1.95 × 1014 of 9.53 × 1015), so communication was the bottleneck. Over NeuronLink-v3 at 1.28 TB/s, the 0.45 GB exchange takes under 0.4 ms of the roughly 4.4-second step.
Challenge 3: Backward-pass unrolling for a sequential recurrence
The backward pass differentiates through all 16 sequential state updates. On GPU, autograd builds this graph at runtime. On Trainium2, the compiler must see the whole unrolled 16-step graph in advance, which creates three constraints.
Graph depth grows with chunk count: at 32 chunks (C = 64), the graph overflowed the scheduler. Per-chunk memory grows with chunk size: at 8 chunks (C = 256), intermediates spilled into HBM. Every shape is fixed at trace time, so each loop intermediate needs its own static allocation.
Sixteen chunks (C = 128) satisfy all three: the unroll fits the scheduler, intermediates stay on chip, and tiles align with the 128 SBUF partitions.
Training results
The GenAIIC team trained Laplace 3B on one trn2.48xlarge instance using all 64 logical NeuronCores and the all_to_all Muon path. The full recipe is 190,735 steps (100 billion FineWeb-Edu tokens). The following results are through step 84,210, about 44 billion tokens.
Throughput. After compilation warmup, throughput settles at roughly 120,000 tokens per second and holds there through step 84,210.
Loss and gradient stability. The loss (Figure 7a) drops smoothly from about 11.4 to 2.3729 at step 84,210. The gradient norm (Figure 7b) shows the expected early spike then a steady decline to about 0.05, with no post-warmup spikes, divergence, or NaN/Inf values.
Inference optimization on Trainium2
Through an unmodified vLLM engine, the GenAIIC team served 11,544 output tokens per second at 1,280 concurrent sequences on one trn2.48xlarge instance.
Constant serving state. The 29.5 MB recurrent state per sequence is roughly 82 times smaller than a comparable KV cache at 8,192 tokens. Increasing the prompt from 2,048 to 8,192 tokens added only 0.5% to the cost per output token.
Unmodified vLLM. A wrapper replaces one attribute per decoder layer, the token mixer, to read and write the recurrent state in the vLLM pool. Because the model declares itself attention-free, vLLM allocates one fixed page per sequence. Outputs matched the i14 reference token for token (48/48 steps on 3/3 prompts in BF16).
Finding the bottleneck. A linear fit of decode time against the number of decoder layers L gives:
At L = 24, that is 168.1 ms per step, 96.9 percent of it inside the decoder layers. The large projections cost 13.27 ms, near the 12 ms HBM-streaming floor. Most time went to small operators dispatched one at a time under eager PyTorch.
Scaling to a full instance. Without tensor parallelism, throughput scales through replicas, with one engine and 20 sequences per logical NeuronCore. Eager throughput grew from 133 output tokens per second on one replica to 6,772 on 64, where host CPU usage reached 82 percent. Compiling the decode step removed per-operator dispatch and raised throughput 1.7 times, to 11,544 (Figure 8).
What fixed-batch benchmarks hide. Under real traffic, each new decode batch width is a separately compiled shape whose first use costs about 11 seconds. These steps were only 1.1 percent of the total but consumed 47.5 percent of decode time. Padding to fixed widths removed this cost with bit-exact results. Compiled decode then improved per-replica throughput 3.52 times under staggered arrivals, compared with 1.46 times on fixed batches. Because BF16 reassociation makes compiled output differ slightly from eager, use eager decode when exact reproducibility matters.
Key takeaways
The project produced lessons across both training and inference:
- Native PyTorch can support custom architectures on Trainium2. i14 retained the GLA architecture and used TorchNeuron Native for the final implementation.
- Communication design matters for custom optimizers. The Muon all_to_all design reduced per-rank traffic by 24 times and increased training throughput by 1.63 times.
- Fixed state keeps inference memory predictable. Each sequence uses 29.5 MB regardless of context length.
- Profile before compiling. Operator dispatch, rather than arithmetic or HBM bandwidth, accounted for most decode time.
- Benchmark realistic arrival patterns. Fixed batches hid the cost of compiling new shapes for changing batch widths.
Conclusion
Laplace 3B shows that AWS Trainium2 can support model architectures beyond standard transformers. Using native PyTorch through TorchNeuron Native and the AWS Neuron SDK, i14 trained and served its GLA-based model while preserving a fixed recurrent state.
For agentic systems, this changes a basic serving constraint. Longer histories don’t require a larger per-sequence state, which can help teams retain more context while keeping memory use predictable.
If growing context is increasing serving cost, reducing concurrency, or limiting agent memory, try i14 or contact your AWS account team to evaluate Laplace 3B on AWS Trainium2.

articles.title: "I have to stop this": Retired professor arrested for blocking delivery robots she says are taking human jobs
articles.text:
A hot potato: A lot of people are angry at the sight of robots carrying out deliveries, seeing it as another sign that machines are making more human jobs obsolete. One such person, a 78-year-old retired professor, made her displeasure known last week by repeatedly standing in front of a delivery robot, blocking its path. The situation ended with her being handcuffed and arrested, but it hasn't deterred her from staging more protests.
Carolyn Marvin, a professor emeritus at the University of Pennsylvania's Annenberg School of Communication, decided to take a literal stand against an oncoming Avride delivery robot from Uber Eats in Philadelphia's Center City. She repeatedly stood in its path so it couldn't move.
Marvin's actions drew a small crowd, and Philadelphia police eventually responded after witnesses reported a disturbance near Reading Terminal Market.
ABC13 reports that Marvin repeatedly ignored officers' requests to allow the robot to pass. She was arrested and charged with disorderly conduct.
Marvin later said she was protesting the use of delivery robots because she believes they are replacing human workers.
"I know they're taking the jobs of human delivery workers and so, I have been protesting them whenever I saw them by standing in front of them and preventing them from going forward," Marvin said, adding that she considers her action as protected speech.
She also confirmed that she had confronted delivery robots on multiple occasions. One witness to a previous encounter thought the machine had hit Marvin. When asked if she was okay, Marvin replied, "No, I have to stop this. They're taking over the world."
When asked if she plans to continue her protests following her arrest, Marvin said, "I do. Why not? I think it's my First Amendment right to publicly demonstrate on a sidewalk to protest against delivery robots."
In a different interview with KYW Newsradio, Marvin went into more detail about why she was interfering with the robots. She called it a protest against the "ruthless way that rich corporations are casting aside human workers – and here, we're talking about the humble delivery folks – in order to enrich their bottom lines."
Marvin added that she hopes the attention her protests receive will encourage more discussion about delivery robots, artificial intelligence and their growing role in everyday life.
Earlier this year, it was reported that as the number of delivery robots on the streets increases, so too does the number of social media clips showing people kicking, grabbing, and even attempting to destroy the machines. While some incidents involve attempted theft, many appear to be expressions of anger at the bots, which symbolize the automation of a job once performed exclusively by humans.

articles.title: Quantum error correction goes well beyond breakeven
articles.text:
Running complicated algorithms on quantum computing hardware is going to require the use of logical qubits, where collections of hardware qubits are linked together in ways that allow errors to be detected and corrected. In general, the more hardware qubits you dedicate to each logical qubit, the better the chances are of identifying errors. But, given that the hardware qubits are prone to errors, adding more of them also increases the probability that errors will occur. If the hardware error rate is too high, then growing the logical qubit will only make matters worse.
Fortunately, several companies have demonstrated hardware where the error rate is not too high. Several demonstrations show logical qubits are beyond the breakeven point, where adding more qubits improves performance. The problem is that the improvement isn’t very dramatic. To lower error rates to levels we’ll need to run complex algorithms, we’d have to add a completely impractical number of qubits to each logical qubit.
On Monday, Quantinuum announced that its current generation of hardware is capable of scaling well beyond the breakeven point. Each step up in the size of logical qubits improved some measures of their performance by a factor of over 10.
Error correction codes and scaling
To understand the results, we must take a little detour through the ideas behind error correction. A logical qubit consists of a set of qubits that hold data, and another set that is used for measurements, all of them entangled to others. There are various error correction “codes,” each of which has a different geometry of entangled connections among its constituent qubits. During operations, measurements of the appropriate qubits produce what’s called “syndrome data,” which can be interpreted to provide an indication of whether an error has occurred within the logical qubit, as well as where and its nature.
Depending on their geometry, error codes have a number of key properties: how many hardware qubits are needed for it to work, how many individual logical qubits it hosts, and something called the distance, which is a rough measure of how many errors can occur simultaneously before the logical qubit fails.
Members of some families of error correction codes differ in a fairly simple way: Each step up in size (which may require multiple hardware qubits) means a greater distance. So by adding more hardware qubits, you can create a similar geometry while providing a greater distance.
These sorts of codes can be used to measure how well a given quantum processor’s error correction scales. You start by measuring the error rate of the logical qubit with a small distance, say three. Then you can devote more hardware qubits to the text and measure it at a distance of five, repeat the process for a distance of seven, and so on until you run out of hardware qubits to add.
If the hardware is past the breakeven point, then the error rate will be lower with each step up in distance. And the scaling factor—how much better the error rate gets at each step—gives you a sense of how far beyond breakeven it is. This matters a great deal for practical reasons. If each step up in size cuts the error rate by a factor of 10, then you only have to step up in distance a few times to get the error rate down by a considerable amount. If, by contrast, the scaling factor is closer to two, then you have to go up in distance many, many times to get the same effect.
So far, most demonstrations of scaling beyond the breakeven point have seen the error rate drop by something much closer to two than 10. Which may mean that we’d need to add many thousands of hardware qubits to the logical qubit just to get the error rate down to what we’d need to run a complex algorithm.
Meet Helios
Quantinuum builds what are called trapped ion quantum computers. As their name implies, each qubit is stored in an ion, an atom that has lost one or more of its electrons. Because they are charged, it’s possible to manipulate these using electrical fields generated by electronics, moving them around and rearranging them. The company’s latest hardware, called Helios, rotates the ions around a ring, selectively shifting the appropriate ones into one of two arms where measurements and operations of the ions’ quantum states can be performed using lasers. Because any two ions can be brought into these arms at the same time, it’s possible to entangle any ion with any other, providing Helios the ability to host essentially any error code.
In general, the company’s hardware has relatively low error rates. But previous iterations didn’t have enough qubits to increase the distance of logical qubits very much. But with Helios, the company finally had the ability to use versions of an error correction code (called a color code) with distances of three, five, and seven (though it only has enough hardware qubits to host a single distance of seven logical qubits at a time).
In addition, Quantinuum has made a key change in how its processor operates. A significant number of errors in earlier Quantinuum processors occurred through what’s called “leakage.” This occurs when a qubit, instead of occupying one of the two energy states used for calculations, ends up in a nearby energy state that’s not normally used. Now, the company is using a scheme that uses laser light to selectively manipulate those qubits that have leaked into other energy states and bring them back to one of the two used for computation. This suppresses leakage errors by a factor of 6.5 and can be done at the same time the system is using lasers to cool the ions.
It has also developed a software-based system that can take any leaked data-holding qubits and swap them out for measurement qubits, which can then be reset and reused.
Color coding
For one of the two experiments the company is announcing today, the company was able to use 13 hardware qubits to build a distance three color code, 37 for distance five, and 73 hardware qubits to get a distance seven logical qubit. These were then used to estimate the error rate that occurs when the logical qubits are simply used to hold onto the same state, essentially acting as a form of quantum memory. The performance of the hardware is good enough now, however, that just doing one round of error correction and measuring can’t provide an accurate measure of how often problems occur—errors are too rare. So instead, the team did 20 rounds of error correction before measuring to determine whether the memory had been maintained.
To get this to work, the system had to take the syndrome data obtained from querying the measurement qubits and figure out the nature of any errors that were detected. As the distance of the error correction code goes up, it gets increasingly challenging to perform this analysis rapidly enough to keep it from becoming a bottleneck. The Quantinuum team showed that they had three different pieces of software, each able to operate in real time: a standard algorithm, a convolutional neural network, and a transformer-based neural network.
For the distance three color code, the logical error rate was about 5 x 10-4. Stepping up to the distance five code brought that down to about 4 x 10-5, and the distance seven code saw another order-of-magnitude drop, down to 5 x 10-6. Overall, each step up in distance reduced the logical error rate by roughly a factor of 12. That is, to my knowledge, the best scaling seen yet.
Another important step that was done here is showing that the syndrome data from one round only correlates with the data from the one immediately before and immediately after. This indicates that there are no systemic sources of error that are biasing the error-detection process.
Of course, performing actual operations involves doing considerably more to the logical qubits than allowing them to just sit still and hold their state. So, the researchers also looked at the logical error rate associated with performing a relatively simple two-qubit gate operation. Unfortunately, this requires using two logical qubits, and the Helios processor isn’t able to hold more than one distance seven error code at a time. So instead, the researchers compared using hardware qubits directly and using distance three and five color codes.
Running these two-qubit gates directly on the hardware produced an error rate of about 10-3, and the distance three code didn’t improve things dramatically. But the distance five code dropped the logical error rate to about 7 x 10-5. So, the hardware seems to be well beyond breakeven, even when it’s being asked to perform relatively complicated tasks.
That other scaling
These results can be viewed a couple of different ways. From the “no big deal” perspective, even the best logical error rate is still too high to perform complicated algorithms, and getting there had some major drawbacks: it was only seen when operations weren’t being performed on the qubit, and the system is only big enough to host one of these. We still have a long way to go before we’re ready to perform lots of error-corrected operations at a potentially useful error rate.
From a more optimistic perspective, this is the best scaling I’m aware of, and the performance suggests that getting the hardware error rate down a bit further could have significant payoffs. The logical error rate depends on the hardware error rate in a way that means that, once things get good enough, then small improvements can have very large impacts on the logical error rate. The scaling seen here doesn’t tell us that we’re at that point, but it is suggestive that we’re getting close.
The main question for Quantinuum is whether it can scale its qubit counts as effectively as its roadmap suggests it will. If so, it may not need to drop its hardware error rate much to start being able to generate useful logical qubits. That may mean solving somewhat different problems than some of its competitors, who will need to do different combinations of dropping the hardware error rate, boosting qubit counts, or figuring out how to integrate multiple functional units into a single computer.
John is Ars Technica's science editor. He has a Bachelor of Arts in Biochemistry from Columbia University, and a Ph.D. in Molecular and Cell Biology from the University of California, Berkeley. When physically separated from his keyboard, he tends to seek out a bicycle, or a scenic location for communing with his hiking boots.

articles.title: US Agencies Detail Incident Response Practices for Rogue AI Agents
articles.text:
Effective and efficient use of complex agentic systems is important for all organizations, but recognizing, preventing and recovering from them going rogue could be an existential necessity.
NIST, the NSA, and CISA recognize the increasing potential for AI agents to behave in an unexpected and potentially harmful manner, and has responded with a list of key practices for both preparing for and responding to such behavior. The report (Key Practices for Incident Readiness and Response in Super Intelligence Training and Evaluation) uses the term super intelligence (SI) rather than artificial intelligence (AI) in line with presidential executive order 14434.
In the report, the ten key practices are grouped into five stages: prepare, detect, respond, recover, and report. For clarity, the report also includes three useful terminology definitions covering AI agents, AI control incident, and AI control near-miss.
“The practices are intended to help the frontier SI industry prevent, prepare for, and respond rapidly to incidents in which SI systems do not act as intended or authorized,” the agencies explain.
Preparation includes activities such as asset and risk inventories, defense-in-depth, least privilege, zero-trust controls, credential management, supply chain risk management and more.
Detection requires continuous monitoring for correct behavior, and anomalous activity and indications of compromise.
Response entails isolating affected systems, revoking credentials, rebuilding compromised environments, determining the blast radius, and conducting root-cause analysis that looks past the specific vulnerability exploited.
Recovery requires testing restoration procedures in advance and documenting recovery decisions along with any residual risk accepted.
Reporting requirements are three-fold: report incidents to all affected parties, wherever required by law, and publicly and widely.
None of the stages or practices is given any greater weight over the others. Instead, the five stages should be treated as a single target. Complex agents all have the potential for misbehavior bordering on rogue and dangerous. These ten practices combine to help organizations develop a stable and effective environment for complex agentic systems, where problems can be detected early and effective operation maintained.
Only the final two practices (#9 and #10 in the Report stage) go beyond the more technical steps of incident readiness and response.
The first of these, ‘Notify Government’, may be a legal requirement, including: “Adhere to any applicable legal reporting requirements, including cybersecurity incident reporting obligations to CISA, law enforcement, and/or cyber-defense organizations.”
The last, Share Information Publicly, is mainstream good behavior throughout cybersecurity that will benefit everyone: “Share details with the public, where appropriate, as early as feasible,” and “Identify and publicly report key practices, takeaways, or improvements adopted in response to the incident or that could benefit other actors in the ecosystem.”
The value of this document is not in providing any new or unrecognized information for AI agent governance, but in providing a very clear and thorough checklist for use by security professionals to maximize the use of agents while minimizing or recovering from agentic incidents.
