articles.title: EIF commits €20 million to Swedish VC BackingMinds to support underrepresented entrepreneurs | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Swedish VC firm BackingMinds has received around €20 million from the European Investment Fund (EIF) for BackingMinds Invest III in order to seek out promising entrepreneurs and businesses often overlooked by traditional investors.
The EIF, which is part of the Luxembourg-based European Investment Bank (EIB) Group, will be the first institutional investor in the fund – backed by the EU’s InvestEU programme. This follows their €50 million fund close in 2022 and its investment in Swedish entrepreneurship platform Techarena in 2025.
“The future is never where you expect it, and neither are the founders building it,” says BackingMinds Founding Partner Sara Wimmercranz. “Some of the most innovative companies in the Nordics are being built where venture capital rarely reaches. A network is a filter. It lets through what already looks like the network and repeats the patterns of the past. As investors, we need to be more open and seek founders out. The EIF’s commitment lets us do that on a larger scale.”
BackingMinds’ EIF commitment comes amid further institutional backing for specialised European venture funds in 2026.
In Sweden, Norrsken Evolve closed a €62 million pre-Seed fund, while Turbine Capital reached a €54 million final close for Nordic DeepTech investments, both with EIF backing.
Elsewhere, Berlin-based Auxxo closed its €33.3 million Female Catalyst Fund II, Copenhagen’s Climentum Capital secured a €60 million first close for climate HardTech, including €40 million from the EIF, and Munich-based Ananda Impact Ventures raised €73 million at first close for impact investments.
Together, these fund closings represent approximately €282.3 million, excluding BackingMinds’ separate €20 million EIF commitment.
“Europe cannot afford to leave talented entrepreneurs undiscovered simply because they are outside the traditional venture capital networks,” adds EIF Deputy Chief Executive Merete Clausen. “BackingMinds has shown that promising businesses can be found in places and among founders that investors too often miss. By supporting this fund, we are helping to unlock that potential and bring more capital to companies tackling some of Europe’s most pressing challenges.”
Founded in 2016, BackingMinds is a Stockholm-based VC firm, founded by Sara Wimmercranz and Susanne Najafi to address the gaps in capital distribution. Through its two earlier funds, BackingMinds has invested in 23 companies.
Of these, 46% have had at least one female founder, 43% have had founders with immigrant backgrounds and 71% were established outside a capital city.
The new fund will finance early-stage companies primarily in Sweden and across the Nordic region, aiming to find entrepreneurial talent beyond established venture capital networks. It will seek out businesses founded by women as well as by people with immigrant backgrounds and based outside capital cities.
The focus will also be on commercially promising companies that address environmental or social challenges ranging from reducing carbon emissions and upgrading energy efficiency to improving healthcare and bolstering education.
According to the EIF, their support is aimed at helping BackingMinds Invest III attract other institutional investors.

articles.title: AI startup Firefly secures $20M to make the physical world a safer place - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
AI startup Firefly secures $20M to make the physical world a safer place
The digital world has already become much smarter thanks to the rise of artificial intelligence, and now a startup called Firefly Technology Inc. wants to do the same for the physical world, beginning with workplace safety.
It has just raised $20 million in funding via a Series A round to make that happen. Today’s round was led by Definition Capital, which previously funded Ramp Business Corp. and Cognition Inc., developer of the AI coding assistant Devin. It was joined by BoxGroup, making its third investment in Firefly, and Susa Ventures, which led the startup’s seed round earlier this year.
Firefly’s goal is to make the world a safer place, and it believes it can do that by extending AI into the physical world to make safety systems more intelligent. Though devices such as security cameras, radios and sensors have helped make locations such as schools, hospitals and other venues safer than they used to be, there’s still a lot of disconnect between these systems. Cameras can see what’s happening, radios can facilitate communication between security personnel and sensors can trigger alarms, but these devices all work in isolation.
What this means is that when something happens, humans still need to waste valuable time understanding the situation before they can put together a response.
Firefly co-founder and Chief Executive James Batt Buckley believes AI can help to close this gap. He says the next frontier for AI is the physical world, which he wants to become as intelligent, connected and programmable as the digital one already is. His idea is to build a single, intelligent system that spans security cameras, sensors and communications, so that AI will immediately understand what’s happening and coordinate a response the moment the alarm registers within the brains of the humans tasked with executing that response.
The startup has developed a combination of purpose-built safety hardware and emergency response management software that’s designed to plug into existing hardware such as cameras and radios. The Ember Safety Management platform works by extracting intelligence from those devices and sensors to build up a clear picture of what the situation is, so it can immediately detect an incident, provide the right context and then organize the response. Firefly has also developed specialized hardware such as wearable panic buttons and AI beacons that enable panic button triangulation and detect gunshots, as well as a network gateway to ensure those systems are always connected.
Buckley said the safety technology industry has seemingly accepted a very strange contradiction. “The more important the job, the more complicated the tools seem to become,” he said. “But we now have the technology to build something fundamentally different. We’re starting with safety because it’s a problem we know deeply, but what we’re building has the potential to transform how people interact with the physical world.”
Constellation Research analyst Holger Mueller said startups such as Firefly are a reminder that AI is going to impact a lot more than just our digital experiences. “Ultimately, AI is going to have a dramatic impact on the physical world too, with one of the first being to improve physical safety in places like schools, hospitals and other large venues,” he said.
The analyst believes AI has obvious advantages over humans when it comes to monitoring a physical area for signs of danger, because it’s always on, always focused and therefore much more vigilant than any human security guard could be. “It will provide more timely and reliable alerts to any malfeasance,” Mueller said. “As with any AI innovation, a degree of cautiousness is still needed to make sure Firefly’s systems work as intended, but any teething problems can probably be ironed out. It’s good to see the innovation helping to keep schools and the kids inside them safe.”
Firefly’s platform has already been deployed by Colorado’s largest community college, Front Range Community College, where it provides unified intelligence across three expansive campuses, helping safety teams to quickly understand emergencies and take action. The startup now wants to expand its deployments, targeting educational centers, hospitals, enterprise campuses and other locations.
Definition Capital’s Teddy Citrin said the intersection of AI and hardware means organizations now have better ways to protect their people. “Firefly is building the central nervous system for physical safety, bringing together specialized hardware, existing data and coordinated action into a single platform,” he said.

articles.title: Ex-Nvidia-turned-VC Amulya Vishwanath: 'Physical AI is in its LEGO era' | TechCrunch
articles.text:
It’s the moment everyone is waiting for — the ChatGPT moment for robotics, Amulya Vishwanath explained to TechCrunch’s Equity.
She is the founder and managing partner of Techable Ventures, a VC firm focused on physical AI, which she started after spending nearly seven years as a product marketer at Nvidia. Before that, she held the same role at a company that was later bought by Intel and was a digital signal processing engineer at Interconnect Systems, which was later bought by the electronics manufacturer Molex.
She stopped by Equity to talk about the future of physical AI — one of the industry’s latest buzzwords.
“A lot of companies and experts have been talking about the ChatGPT moment for robotics,” she said, adding that right now the industry was more in a “LEGO era.”
“There are a lot of foundational software and building blocks for robotics that are being rethought right now as we speak, and it’s super important in order for innovation to scale,” she continued.
Right now, people are building the basics — the robotic hands or the actuators — that can one day come together and build that big-ticket-item, like a bunch of LEGOs coming together. There’s general- and special-purpose robots being built right now, too, and eventually, as people continue building them, they will get better and more advanced.
“We’ve done this during the internet era,” she said. “We’ve done this long, long time ago with the Industrial Revolution. I think it’s just a matter of time before things fall into place.”
“Talent is also going to be very critical,” she continued, adding elsewhere in the convo that talent is still a key definer of the U.S. market. This is one of the “moats” of her firm, she said, helping connect founders to top talent so they can stay competitive right now, as so much talent is going to big companies like Anthropic and Nvidia. She pointed out that she’s built up a strong network to help founders from her years of working in this space.
“This just makes it a lot easier for me to be the strength or the first call for founders,” she said.

articles.title: Chinese hacker hits over 100 company websites using AI agents — Deere and SharkNinja among top brands affected in attack
articles.text:
Chinese hacker hits over 100 company websites using AI agents — Deere and SharkNinja among top brands affected in attack
It seems the goal was to establish persistence
- A hacker used AI agents to target more than 1,200 websites, compromising over 100 in under a month
- Autonomous agents tested vulnerabilities, adapted tactics, and established access with minimal human input
- Researchers warn AI-powered attacks are making large-scale website compromise faster and cheaper
In less than a month, a single Chinese hacker managed to break into more than 100 company websites, while doing almost none of the work himself. Instead, he tasked AI agents to do it for him and paid them around $5,000 in tokens for the job.
The campaign was spotted by cybersecurity researcher Snorre Fagerland from NorForge, who was looking for exposed Cairn installations when he found approximately two dozen being used for malicious purposes. These gave him first-hand insight into an active cybercriminal operation.
Cairn is described as an open source, general-purpose AI problem-solving engine, designed to help autonomous agents find solutions to complex tasks. Instead of focusing on a single application, Cairn provides a framework that defines goals, explores different approaches, and then executes actions to try and solve the problem. According to numerous media outlets, Cairn is quite popular in the cybercriminal community (although it’s not malicious by design).
When security becomes a problem needing solving
In this case, the “problem” Cairn was trying to solve for the attacker was how to run code on a website without signing in. They were trying out SQL injection, file uploads, as well as unsafe handling of stored objects. The goal, according to the researcher, was to establish persistent access to shopping and payment systems which could later be used to steal money.
Fagerland said the attacker used a combination of models, likely Claude Code with a DeepSeek model, although it is very difficult to determine. The instructions themselves were very brief, generally fewer than 100 Chinese characters, and in less than a month, the agents tried to break into more than 1,200 sites.
On average, the agents poke around a website for a day (23 hours), before either breaking in or moving on. With some 100 successful break-ins, Fagerland says the hacker paid $50 for tokens on average, per breach. This, however, is an estimate and not a confirmed billing.
The analyst did not name the victims. In its report, Cybersecurity News said the victims were mainly online stores in the United States, Canada, Australia and Japan, and Reuters managed to confirm some targets by “independently reviewing the hacker's Cairn activity”: including Deere (farm equipment maker), SharkNinja (home appliance company), and Cummins (engine manufacturer). It added that two “smaller businesses” also acknowledged being compromised but did not reply to the agency’s inquiries.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Impressive technique
Deere told Reuters it took “necessary remediation actions” and added that there was “no indication that sensitive information was accessed.” SharkNinja said the breach hit a standalone site carrying product support information only, and that the threat had been remediated. Cummins just said it was looking into reports.
So far, no one knows if the attacker managed to steal any sensitive data from his victims, and if so - how many. The researcher apparently found “hundreds” of exposed secrets in the open panels and was working with Reuters to let the victims know.
Fageraland told Reuters he was “impressed” by some of the techniques the agents used while compromising their victims. Apparently, after hitting a dead end against one of the targets, the AI agents scanned digital records in search of associated infrastructure. When they found a public-facing control panel, they discovered a “subtle weakness” in how it processed data. It took “hours of trial and error” before finally being able to execute a malicious command on the website’s server.
"It's not straightforward to come up with solutions like that," Fagerland said. "It's not script kiddie stuff."
AI attackers are the new normal, it seems. Business owners are advised to patch public-facing applications, restrict access to admin panels, and keep an eye on unexpected files in web directories.

articles.title: Netflix lucra R$ 19,8 bi no trimestre, mas admite dificuldade para prender atenção do público
articles.text:
A Netflix registrou lucro líquido de US$ 3,66 bilhões (cerca de R$ 19,8 bilhões) no terceiro trimestre de 2026, alta de 43,9% em relação ao mesmo período do ano passado. A receita da plataforma de streaming também avançou, chegando a US$ 12,87 bilhões (cerca de R$ 69,5 bilhões), crescimento de 11,8% na comparação anual.
Apesar dos resultados positivos, a empresa enfrenta dificuldades para acelerar o crescimento da audiência, especialmente nos Estados Unidos e no Canadá. O reconhecimento do problema, somado à previsão mais fraca para o próximo trimestre e à redução da expectativa de receita com publicidade, pressionou as ações da companhia, que caíram mais de 5% nas negociações após o fechamento do mercado na terça-feira (20).
O crescimento da receita no terceiro trimestre foi o menor em quase três anos. Em carta aos investidores, a Netflix reconheceu a preocupação do mercado com a evolução do tempo de visualização na plataforma, particularmente na América do Norte. “Sabemos que há alguma preocupação dos investidores com o crescimento das nossas horas de visualização”, afirmou a companhia no documento.
Ted Sarandos, co-CEO da Netflix, reconheceu que a empresa precisa melhorar sua execução no mercado estadunidense, embora tenha descartado a necessidade de mudança fundamental na estratégia. “Não há necessidade de uma mudança fundamental na estratégia. Precisamos de uma execução melhor nos Estados Unidos”, declarou durante a teleconferência sobre os resultados.
Lucro operacional cresce 37%
- Além do avanço do lucro líquido, a Netflix registrou crescimento de 37,3% no lucro operacional, que chegou a US$ 4,46 bilhões (cerca de R$ 24,1 bilhões). A margem operacional subiu de 28,2% no terceiro trimestre de 2025 para 34,6% no mesmo período deste ano;
- Segundo a companhia, o desempenho foi impulsionado principalmente pelo aumento da receita com assinaturas, reajustes de preços e expansão da publicidade, além de efeitos cambiais favoráveis. A empresa também atribuiu parte da melhora na margem ao calendário de despesas, que ficou abaixo do previsto no período;
- O fluxo de caixa livre alcançou US$ 2,88 bilhões (cerca de R$ 15,6 bilhões), ante US$ 2,66 bilhões (cerca de R$ 14,4 bilhões) um ano antes;
- Para 2026, a Netflix manteve a expectativa de receita de US$ 51,1 bilhões (cerca de R$ 276 bilhões), equivalente a crescimento anual de 13%. A projeção de margem operacional para o ano é de 31,5%;
- A perspectiva para o quarto trimestre, entretanto, indica continuidade da desaceleração. A empresa espera receita de US$ 13,44 bilhões (cerca de R$ 72,6 bilhões), com crescimento anual de aproximadamente 11,5%.
Publicidade fica abaixo das expectativas
A Netflix também reduziu sua previsão de receita publicitária para 2026. A empresa agora espera arrecadar aproximadamente US$ 2,7 bilhões (cerca de R$ 14,6 bilhões) com anúncios, ante a estimativa anterior de US$ 3 bilhões (cerca de R$ 16,2 bilhões).
De acordo com a companhia, o ajuste reflete atrasos um pouco maiores que o esperado na implementação de determinados recursos e produtos publicitários.
A revisão representa desafio para uma das frentes de expansão do negócio. A Netflix busca aumentar a monetização de seu plano com anúncios por meio de novas ferramentas, ampliação da demanda de anunciantes e melhorias na tecnologia publicitária.
Mesmo com o corte na previsão, a empresa afirmou que espera continuar ampliando a receita com publicidade nos próximos anos. A estratégia envolve aumentar tanto o número de assinantes do plano com anúncios quanto a capacidade de gerar receita com cada usuário.
Leia mais:
- Netflix compra direitos da Copa do Mundo de 2030
- Netflix aumenta preços no Brasil: plano mais caro chega a R$ 71,90 por mês
- Netflix: lançamentos da semana (19 a 25 de outubro)
Netflix admite que precisa de novos sucessos
A preocupação com o crescimento da audiência também está relacionada à dificuldade de manter uma sequência de grandes sucessos. A plataforma ainda conta com produções de alcance global, mas enfrenta o desafio de substituir títulos, como Stranger Things e Round 6, por novos fenômenos capazes de mobilizar o público.
Segundo as métricas divulgadas pela própria Netflix, temporadas recentes de produções, como Treta, O Agente Noturno e Avatar: O Último Mestre do Ar, registraram quedas significativas de audiência em relação às temporadas anteriores.
No cinema, nenhum lançamento do verão estadunidense se destacou como grande fenômeno comparável aos sucessos do ano passado, como Guerreiras do K-pop e Um Maluco no Golfe 2. O principal filme da empresa no trimestre, The Last House, acumulou 91 milhões de visualizações, mas teve avaliações ruins tanto da crítica quanto do público.
A concorrência também pressiona o tempo que os usuários dedicam à plataforma. Serviços gratuitos e redes sociais, como YouTube e TikTok, disputam a atenção dos espectadores, enquanto a Netflix busca manter seus conteúdos entre as principais opções de entretenimento.
Jesse Cohen, analista sênior do Investing.com, avaliou ao The New York Times que a empresa enfrenta problema de engajamento e precisa de novos sucessos para recuperar o ritmo de crescimento.
Executivos defendem estratégia atual
Apesar das dificuldades, os dirigentes da Netflix afirmaram que a estratégia central da empresa permanece inalterada. O co-CEO Greg Peters disse que a retenção de assinantes continua saudável em todas as regiões e que a taxa de cancelamentos melhorou na comparação anual, tanto globalmente quanto nos Estados Unidos.
Peters também destacou resultados positivos em mercados internacionais, incluindo Índia, Coreia do Sul e Japão. Segundo ele, produções desses países continuam contribuindo para o engajamento, o crescimento de assinantes e a receita da companhia.
A empresa pretende manter o foco em séries, filmes e eventos ao vivo, ao mesmo tempo em que amplia a oferta de conteúdos licenciados de terceiros. Entre as iniciativas previstas estão novas temporadas de produções conhecidas, lançamentos cinematográficos e transmissões esportivas.
O desempenho do mercado estadunidense, contudo, continuará no centro das atenções. A Netflix considera que a região tem potencial para crescer mais rapidamente e espera melhorar a capacidade de produzir conteúdos capazes de conquistar grandes audiências e repercutir internacionalmente.
A pressão sobre os resultados ocorre em meio à reorganização interna. Na semana passada, a empresa anunciou o corte de aproximadamente mil postos de trabalho, cerca de 6% de sua força de trabalho, e substituiu Bela Bajaria no comando de conteúdo por Peter Rice, ex-executivo de Disney e Fox. O chefe da divisão cinematográfica, Dan Lin, também deixou a companhia.
As mudanças refletem a tentativa de melhorar a execução e aumentar a eficiência dos investimentos em conteúdo. Para os investidores, porém, o desafio vai além de controlar custos: a Netflix precisa transformar seus gastos com produções em mais audiência, retenção e crescimento sustentável da receita.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Here’s the tea
articles.text:
Here’s the tea
An MIT historian uncovers the true origins of an artifact once thought to be a relic of the Boston Tea Party.
When Tristan Brown, an associate professor of history at MIT, first examined a Chinese tea chest label displayed at Old South Meeting House, he had no reason to doubt its story. Descendants of the Boston blacksmith Thomas Wells had donated the label in 1987, saying it had been recovered after colonial protesters threw tea into Boston Harbor in 1773.
But after a year of research, Brown reached a different conclusion: The label was made nearly a century later. The decisive clue came when he read the Chinese text in Cantonese rather than Mandarin, as previous scholars had done. He found that the characters had been used phonetically, in slightly variant forms across contemporary sources, to represent the name of Smith, Archer & Co., a US firm that acquired Asian tea for shipment to American markets during the 1860s and 1870s.
Working with the Wells family, he traced the label to a relative who traveled from Michigan to California during the Gold Rush era before returning and operating a business known as the California Tea Store. Brown argues that claims for its revolutionary pedigree probably developed later, amid the centennial commemorations of the 1870s.
The discovery does not make the label historically insignificant, he says. Instead, what began as an inquiry into a supposed artifact of the Boston Tea Party became a study of how ordinary objects acquire historical authority, and how historical memory itself is made.
“History is never finished,” he says. “Even objects that have sat in museums for decades can reveal entirely new stories when we ask new questions.”

articles.title: YouTube might be testing hiding the dislike button
articles.text:
YouTube appears to be testing hiding the dislike button on videos, as reported by 9to5Google. At least two users on X have recently shared screenshots of the dislike button now being placed in the three-dots submenu, and a user on Reddit also shared an image of the dislike button being absent for them.
YouTube might be testing hiding the dislike button
Some users have reported that their YouTube dislike button has been moved to the three-dots menu.
Right now, for me, the dislike button sits right next to the like button under a video. Moving it to a submenu would make it considerably more of an effort to access, meaning that fewer people would likely use it.
It’s unclear how widely this apparent test may be rolled out, and Google didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment.
YouTube has shown a willingness to make changes to the dislike button. In 2021, it hid the public dislike count on videos to help “protect creators from harassment,” though creators can still see dislike counts. Earlier this year, YouTube removed the dislike button from YouTube Shorts, suggesting instead that users take advantage of options in the three-dots menu.

articles.title: El Galaxy S27 traería pésimas noticias: Samsung recortaría la RAM de su próximo tope de gama
articles.text:
Los Samsung Galaxy S27 podrían llegar con una sorpresa desagradable. Según recoge 9to5Google, nuevas filtraciones apuntan a que la firma coreana podría disminuir la cantidad de memoria RAM a implementar en las variantes de entrada de su próxima línea de topes de gama.
Puntualmente, se indica que el Galaxy S27 y el S27+ tendrían 8 GB de RAM, y no solo los 12 GB que han sido el estándar en los S25 y S26. Si esto se confirma será una pésima noticia para los compradores, pues la reducción en la cantidad de memoria instalada no necesariamente implicaría salvarse de pagar precios más altos que en la actualidad.
La información es para tomar con pinzas, por supuesto. Pero la crisis de la RAM ha dejado señales bastante evidentes de su impacto en toda la electrónica de consumo, y en el pasado analistas han barajado la posibilidad de que los móviles de alta gama comiencen a recular en su elección de hardware para mitigar la escasez y el encarecimiento de este componente.
De acuerdo con la nueva filtración, el Galaxy S27 podría volver a una configuración segmentada como la que Samsung usó por última vez en el S24. Si esto se confirma, tanto el S27 estándar como la variante Plus llegarían con 8 GB en sus opciones de 256 GB de espacio interno y mantendrían los 12 GB para las versiones de 512 GB.
Samsung podría volver a los 8 GB de RAM con el Galaxy S27
El citado reporte indica que Samsung no habría tomado una decisión final sobre qué configuraciones ofrecería con el nuevo S27 Pro. Dicho modelo llegaría seguro con 12 GB de RAM, pero también estaría "en consideración" la posibilidad de ofrecer alguna opción con 16 GB.
En el caso del Galaxy S27 Ultra, Samsung mantendría la estrategia ya existente de equipar sus versiones de 256 y 512 GB con 12 GB de RAM, mientras que la de 1 TB seguiría siendo la única con 16 GB de memoria. Ya veremos si esto realmente es así o si se trata de meros supuestos relacionados con la actualidad de la industria.
Que el mercado de la electrónica de consumo transita uno de sus períodos más complejos por la escasez y el encarecimiento de componentes cruciales, es verdad. Aunque también hay mucha especulación que se debe tomar con cautela.
Pocos días atrás se conoció el rumor de que Samsung supuestamente analizaría no lanzar los Galaxy S27 con el chip Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 de Qualcomm, por presuntos problemas de sobrecalentamiento. Claro que la compañía coreana no ha revelado nada oficialmente en tal sentido, así que por ahora hay que tomarlo como un rumor y no mucho más.

articles.title: Windows 98 SE users get a Thunderbolt 4 driver, thanks to AI assistance — vibe-coded xHCI98 driver works in Microsoft OSes up to Windows 7
articles.text:
Windows 98 SE users get a Thunderbolt 4 driver, thanks to AI assistance — vibe-coded xHCI98 driver works in Microsoft OSes up to Windows 7
If you've ever wanted to run Windows 98 SE on your mid-2010s or newer PC with fast USB hub support, here's your chance.
Windows 98 SE devotees can now enjoy (experimental) support for USB4 and Thunderbolt 3/4. Developer and maker Yeo Kheng Meng, who also enjoys retrocomputing, recently released the vibe-coded xHCI98 v3.0.0.0, enabling the practical use of generic USB 3.x, USB4, and Thunderbolt 3/4 host controllers on systems running Windows 98 SE, ME, 2000, XP, Vista, and 7. An extensive blog post by the dev provides further reading about the driver, compatibility, its creation, and usage.
Demo video “shows many different USB devices being hotplugged to a modern 2020 ThinkPad P14s Gen 1 with only xHCI controller.”
Some of you will be wondering why a project to bring USB4 (Thunderbolt 3 and 4) to PCs running Windows 98 SE exists. Retro computing fan Meng explains on his GitHub that this project should appeal directly to users of PCs from the mid-2010s that have xHCI-only (USB 3.x) chipsets and no legacy EHCI controller. However, older OSes don’t have xHCI drivers, and that’s where xHCI98 steps in. “Without xHCI support, even keyboards, mice, and flash drives need the BIOS's legacy support, cannot be hotplugged, and devices such as Ethernet and audio do not work at all,” explains Meng, revealing his motivation. “This project fills that gap.”
Impressively, xHCI98 drives a lot more than USB storage. It replaces Windows’ own USB port and hub drivers to facilitate the connection and use of USB 1.1 and 2.0 and SuperSpeed (USB 3.x) devices and hubs, UAS (USB Attached SCSI) storage through a second driver (xhciuas.sys), and Thunderbolt 3 and USB4 docks and NVMe enclosures through a third driver (xhcicm.sys).
Meng has developed and tested xHCI98 mostly on Intel hardware, as that is what he owns. Candidly, he admits “this is a solo human's project with AI assistance, so bugs are not unexpected,” even if you do have the same hardware as the dev - a 2020 ThinkPad P14s Gen 1 (Comet Lake xHCI, no EHCI). It stands up pretty well during the plug/unplug video demo above, though the test rig used is not quite the USB cart of death.
As a solo developer, Meng isn't shy to admit he leaned heavily on AI assistance to prepare the xHCI98 release. His vibe coding adventure was supported by Claude Fable 5.1 for planning, Claude Opus 5.5 for coding, and Codex GPT 6 Astra as an adversarial reviewer.
In addition to a few bug warnings, there are some other things to know about using this driver with the various older versions of Windows it supports, standby and hibernation, and more. The dev helpfully sketches out a process for checking your hardware, outlines various install methods, discusses updating, and talks about tuning the driver for those who will be jumping in at the deep end with this project.

articles.title: SA’s Injini launches EdTech for Employment incubation programme - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
South African ed-tech incubator Injini has launched a new two-year programme that will support 10 early-stage South African edtech startups building solutions that create or support employment pathways for young people.
Founded in 2017, Injini, which is a member of the UVU Africa Group, is a registered non-profit company that exists for the sole purpose of improving educational outcomes in Sub-Saharan Africa. Its programmes and research via the Injini Think Tank contribute towards its mission to increase the quality, accessibility, and relevance of education in the region. It announced its latest cohort earlier this year.
The EdTech for Employment Incubation Programme, which is financed by Zurich-based Leopold Bachmann Foundation, will run from October 2026 to September 2028, and targets startups whose solutions serve youth aged between 15 and 30.
The programme comes against the backdrop of a South African youth unemployment rate that stood at 46.1 per cent in the first quarter of this year, according to Stats SA, which is among the highest in the world. Injini said the figure reflects a structural shortage of quality vocational and work-readiness pathways connecting young people to the economy.
A growing number of edtech startups are building solutions in this space, including teacher training platforms, tutoring and mentorship tools, and technologies that prepare young people for economic participation. However, Injini said these companies often lack the structured support, market access and proof-of-concept evidence they need to scale.
“South Africa’s youth aren’t short on ambition or ability. What they need are structured pathways into work,” said Krista Davidson, executive director at Injini. “We’ve spent years watching talented edtech founders build real solutions to this problem, without the support to test what works, prove it, and scale it. This programme is designed to close that gap.
The programme will run two cohorts of five startups each. Each cycle begins with a recruitment and selection process, followed by a six-month incubation period built around four pillars: product foundations, business sustainability, market access, and impact measurement.
Participating startups will receive hands-on support from Injini’s team, as well as access to a network of specialist consultants matched to their needs. Founders will also have opportunities to network and engage with the wider ecosystem and potential users.
Over its two-year run, the programme aims to reach 20,000 underserved youth, help up to 2,000 of them access work or income-generating opportunities, and create 20 direct jobs within the cohort companies.
“We’re looking for ed-tech companies that are already doing the hard work of connecting young people to skills and income,” Davidson said. “Over the next two years, we want to give ten of them the structural support, proof points and market access they need to grow.”
Both non-profit and for-profit edtech startups with a clear social impact mandate are eligible, with priority given to those working in work-readiness and digital skills, teacher training and professional development, and tutoring or peer-learning models that generate income and employment opportunities for young people.
Interested startups can apply here.

articles.title: Foxconn's latest EV push is a $727 million bet for half of Mitsubishi Electric's car parts business
articles.text:
What just happened? Foxconn has agreed to pay $727 million for a 50% stake in Mitsubishi Electric's automotive equipment business, gaining access to vehicle-control technology and software expertise for its push to develop electric vehicles for other manufacturers. The deal gives Foxconn a broader engineering base, but much of the business it is buying still serves conventional vehicles. Its success will depend on turning that expertise into products automakers want to buy.
The companies plan to combine Mitsubishi Electric's powertrain, autonomous-driving and in-car computing technology with Foxconn's manufacturing operations. They want to build EV platforms in Japan, sell them first to Japanese automakers and then seek customers overseas.
"What attracted us most was the electronic-control technology – and the substantial software resources behind them," Jun Seki, Foxconn's chief strategy officer for EVs, said at a news conference in Tokyo.
Mitsubishi Electric Mobility's products include alternators, starters, ignition coils, radar sensors and electric powertrain equipment. Its established automaker relationships also give Foxconn a route to potential customers.
But Foxconn is not buying into all of Mitsubishi Electric's EV technology. The Japanese company's power-semiconductor business is outside the agreement. That includes silicon-carbide and insulated-gate bipolar transistor power modules used in EV inverters.
The automotive deal instead covers the equipment business that Mitsubishi Electric spun off into Mitsubishi Electric Mobility in April 2024. Before closing, Mitsubishi Electric will move its remaining automotive operations, including those held by overseas subsidiaries, into that company.
Foxconn's investment arm, Lin Yin International Investment, will acquire half of the combined business. The partners expect the deal to close in October 2027, following antitrust reviews and other required approvals.
Mitsubishi Electric has been reshaping its portfolio, exiting car multimedia and fuel injectors and transferring its lighting business to Stanley Electric.
An earlier electric-powertrain partnership changed course. In May 2024, Mitsubishi Electric Mobility and Aisin agreed to establish a joint venture for traction motors, inverters and control software. Five months later, they dropped the joint-venture plan and opted for a business alliance.
The purchase gives Foxconn another way into the car industry after several years of prototypes, partnerships and setbacks.
Foxconn had planned to build Fisker's Pear EV at its Lordstown, Ohio, factory, but the vehicle never reached production. Fisker went bankrupt in 2024, and Foxconn sold the factory last year.
Foxconn has made progress elsewhere. Mitsubishi Motors, which is separate from Mitsubishi Electric, is putting its badge on the Foxtron-developed ASX VR-e for Australia and New Zealand. Foxconn also has a bus joint venture with Mitsubishi Fuso and is a partner in Saudi Arabia's Ceer EV brand.
The Mitsubishi Electric agreement adds an established automotive supplier to Foxconn's network, alongside its existing vehicle-development and manufacturing partnerships.

articles.title: Work management context for AI agents with Smartsheet MCP on AWS | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Work management context for AI agents with Smartsheet MCP on AWS
AI agents are most useful when they can act on the real work happening across your organization. Work management involves complex, cross-functional tasks such as updating project timelines, reassigning tasks, and surfacing status. AI agents can support you with these without anyone switching tools. Smartsheet, the work management platform for managing projects, portfolios, and operations, has launched a generally available Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server.
With the Smartsheet MCP Server, AI assistants can read, write, and manage Smartsheet data through a standardized protocol. The protocol spans more than 40 tools for exploring, creating, and managing sheets, rows, columns, and automations. You can update task statuses, create rows, and modify project structure directly through natural language.
In this post, we walk through two ways you can connect it to your existing workflows. Amazon Quick is an agentic AI workspace built for business users, project managers, and operations teams. They can ask questions, update sheets, and build dashboards through natural language without writing code. Kiro is an agentic IDE where developers connect to Smartsheet through MCP to reference project specs, update task status, and track dependencies without leaving their coding workflow.
Architecture overview
The following diagram shows how the Smartsheet MCP Server sits as the central integration layer connecting to AWS services. Amazon Quick and Kiro connect directly as MCP clients.
Amazon Quick serves knowledge workers, project managers, and operations teams who want to query, update, and automate Smartsheet through natural language. With Kiro, developers can reference project specs, update task status, and track dependencies without leaving their coding workflow.
The following architecture diagram illustrates these integration paths: the Smartsheet MCP Server in the center, with Amazon Quick and Kiro as MCP clients on the left, and Smartsheet’s API and data layer on the right.
Sprint management with Amazon Quick and Kiro
Consider a software engineering team that tracks their sprint in Smartsheet. Tasks, owners, statuses, and blockers all live in a project sheet. Here’s what each path looks like for the same team:
When a user such as a project manager wants to check which sprint tasks are blocked this week, they can ask Amazon Quick through natural language. The Amazon Quick chat agent queries the Smartsheet MCP Server, pulls the relevant rows, and surfaces a summary with owner names and due dates. The response is generated from live Smartsheet data without building a report or dashboard.
For developers who are fixing bugs or working through features, they can ask Kiro to pull the current sprint sheet and show them the open backend tasks assigned to them. Kiro queries Smartsheet through MCP and surfaces the list inline. When the fix is committed, a Kiro hook automatically updates the corresponding row status to Complete.
Prerequisites
Smartsheet MCP Server delivers precisely structured context, including row relationships, column types, cell history, and comments. This produces token-efficient payload sizes rather than returning raw API payloads. This engineering decision compounds into reduced cost and improved latency at scale when running hundreds of AI-assisted queries across a project portfolio. To learn how Smartsheet built their remote MCP server on AWS, see How Smartsheet built a remote MCP server on AWS.
Before connecting the Smartsheet MCP Server to Amazon Quick and Kiro, verify that you have the following in place:
- An active AWS account with appropriate AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions for the service you’re connecting (Amazon Quick, or Kiro)
- A Smartsheet account on a Business, Enterprise, or AWM plan.
- A Smartsheet Personal Access Token, or OAuth credentials if your client supports the OAuth flow.
- For Amazon Quick: Author or higher permissions in your Amazon Quick account.
- For Kiro: Kiro IDE installed from kiro.dev with Node.js available in your environment.
The Smartsheet MCP Server is available at three regional endpoints. It uses Streamable HTTP transport (MCP spec versions 2025-06-18 and 2025-03-26) and is authenticated with either OAuth 2.0 or a Personal Access Token.
- Commercial US: https://mcp.smartsheet.com.
- EU: https://mcp.smartsheet.eu.
- AU: https://mcp.smartsheet.au.
Both options expose the same Smartsheet toolset. The right choice depends on where your work gets done:
Choose Amazon Quick if you need a fully managed, organization-wide solution your whole team can use: no app registration, only pre-built OAuth, and it scales across knowledge workers in your enterprise.
Choose Kiro if you’re a developer who wants something lightweight: no infrastructure, only a config file and a personal access token, scoped to your own workflow.
Amazon Quick integration
Amazon Quick includes Smartsheet as a pre-built connector in its directory. That means reading project status, updating rows, creating discussions, and surfacing risks, all in the same interface your business users already work in.
Amazon Quick makes that integration available across the organization, from project managers and operations teams to business users who manage work in Smartsheet.
To add the Quick integration:
- In the Amazon Quick console, navigate to Connectors and find Smartsheet in the directory.
- Select the Smartsheet connector tile.
- Enter the following integration details: 
         
  - Name – Descriptive name for your Smartsheet integration.
  - Keep the Connection type and Auth configuration settings as is.
  - Base URL – https://mcp.smartsheet.com.
  - Client ID – App client ID from your Smartsheet Developer Tools app registration.
  - Client Secret – App secret from your Smartsheet Developer Tools app registration.
  - Token URL – https://api.smartsheet.com/2.0/token.
  - Auth URL – https://app.smartsheet.com/b/authorize.
- Choose Next.
- On the Manage Tools & Permissions page, you see a list of available tools. Choose Next.
- On the Publish page, choose who can access this connection, and then choose Publish.
- Choose Next.
After you’re connected, your Amazon Quick chat agent can work with Smartsheet data through natural language:
- “What projects in our portfolio are currently At Risk?”
- “Update the status of the authentication task in the Backend API sheet to Complete.”
- “Create a summary of all overdue items across the Q3 Roadmap and send it to the team.”
Kiro integration
Kiro is the right path when developers want Smartsheet project context available directly in their development environment, alongside their code, without context-switching.
Kiro is built around spec-driven development. It turns high-level prompts into structured specs, then into working code, docs, and tests. MCP servers are how Kiro gets real-world context by connecting to documentation, databases, APIs, and enterprise systems to ground its agent in live data rather than training-time knowledge.
A Kiro feature called powers is a one-click installable bundle that packages a curated MCP server with steering files and hooks. It gives the Kiro coding agent a new capability out of the box. For Smartsheet, configuring the connection takes a single JSON configuration block and from that point, the Kiro agent can reference live project data as part of a development workflow.
To connect the Smartsheet MCP Server to Kiro, add it to your Kiro MCP configuration (.kiro/settings/mcp.json for workspace scope). For a full walkthrough, see Getting Started with Kiro and MCP Servers:
This configuration uses the Personal Access Token (API key) approach. For production deployments, OAuth is recommended.
Set SMARTSHEET_API_TOKEN to your Smartsheet Personal Access Token in your environment. Kiro loads MCP servers as background processes on startup. After it’s initialized, Smartsheet tools are available to the Kiro agent across all modes: chat, spec planning, and hooks-based automation. Full details in the Smartsheet MCP Server Documentation.
From there, Kiro can reference Smartsheet data as part of development workflows:
- “Check the Backend API project sheet for any open bugs and generate a prioritized fix list.”
- “Pull the Q3 Roadmap sheet and create a spec for the features marked In Progress.”
Enterprise governance
For builders deploying in regulated or enterprise environments, the Smartsheet MCP Server security model is built on the same infrastructure and permissions layer as the Smartsheet REST API. It’s not a new trust boundary:
- OAuth 2.0 and Personal Access Token authentication: choose the auth method supported by your MCP client.
- User-level permission enforcement: agents can only access data the authenticated user has permission to see. No privilege escalation through natural language prompts.
- Organization-level AI controls: system administrators can turn on or off AI features globally. Write-tool access is configurable by user group.
- Streamable HTTP transport: firewall allowlisting is done by fully qualified domain name (FQDN) (mcp.smartsheet.com), not IP address.
For compliance architects, the MCP Server doesn’t store prompts, and prompt content stays between the AI client and the model. Smartsheet sees only the structured tool calls and their results.
Clean up
If you followed this walkthrough and want to remove the integration afterward, here’s how to undo each path:
Amazon Quick
- In the Amazon Quick console, navigate to Connectors.
- Select your Smartsheet connector.
- Choose Delete to remove the connection. This revokes the OAuth token and stops agent access to Smartsheet data.
Kiro
- Open your MCP configuration file (.kiro/settings/mcp.json).
- Remove the smartsheet-us entry from the mcpServers object.
- Restart Kiro to unload the server.
Next steps
For background on how the server works, see How Smartsheet built a remote MCP server on AWS. After you’ve connected the Smartsheet MCP Server to your system of choice, here are four actions we recommend trying:
You can ask the chat agent to monitor your active project sheets, identify rows marked Blocked or At Risk. You can also ask to annotate projects with a discussion comment, and deliver a structured summary to your team through your preferred channel. This would be an example workflow that chains get_sheet_summary, search, and create_discussion_on_row.
The agent can also retrieve data through the Smartsheet MCP Server to reconcile task statuses between your issue tracker and your Smartsheet project plan. It can flag drift between the two, and update the affected rows, using get_sheet_summary, get_columns, update_rows, and create_discussion_on_row in sequence.
You can also try to aggregate project health signals across your reports and dashboards. You can use it to produce a structured briefing without manual data gathering, drawing on list_reports, get_report, list_dashboards, get_dashboard, and search.
Lastly, you can use the agent to follow every write with a discussion comment explaining what changed and why. This creates a human-readable audit trail inside Smartsheet through the combination of update_rows and create_discussion_on_row.
All four patterns work across the preceding paths: Amazon Quick for business-user-facing workflows, and Kiro for developer-initiated actions.
Building something with Smartsheet MCP and AWS? Share what you’re working on in the comments, or connect with us in the Smartsheet Developer Community.

articles.title: AOMEI Backupper Compromised in Short-Burst Supply Chain Campaign
articles.text:
Between April and July, AOMEI Backupper served malware to its users multiple times in short-burst supply chain compromises, security researchers warn.
AOMEI Backupper is Windows backup, sync, and disk cloning software, available in free and paid editions for home users, businesses, and Windows Server environments. AOMEI says its products are used by more than 186 million people worldwide.
Unlike typical supply chain attacks, this campaign relied on short-lived tampering windows to serve the CrossRoad downloader and the ShinyRoad backdoor.
“Each tampering window remained active for only five to ten minutes before reverting to authentic versions,” report Google Cloud’s Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant, which investigated the attack alongside ManageEngine Threat Analysis Lab (METAL).
The attacks hit all systems that fetched the modified AOMEI Backupper packages during the attack windows, suggesting an opportunistic campaign rather than a targeted one.
However, throughout the investigation, Google Cloud identified higher education, IT services, and telecommunications entities in Australia, Brazil, India, Pakistan, Portugal, Singapore, South Africa, Spain, Switzerland, Türkiye, and the United States that have been compromised.
“We confirmed several tampering windows in 2026, alongside related malware samples observed in the wild starting in late April. However, given the short duration of these windows, it is probable that additional tampering occurred throughout the campaign that remained outside our visibility,” Google Cloud notes.
During the very short attack windows, the threat actor, tracked as UNC7017, tampered with the update server’s update settings file to redirect to a malicious ZIP archive and modified the server’s automatic notification service to force systems into automatically executing the malware.
METAL’s analysis of the incident shows that the hackers abused AOMEI Backupper’s promotional content channel for malware distribution. The channel runs background services that poll AOMEI’s servers for content and includes two configuration paths that deliver content to a directory and execute it.
“The two paths converge on the same location. One controls what lands in html\; the other controls what can be executed from it. Neither configuration file is cryptographically authenticated by the client, and the checksum used to validate the archive is declared inside the same unauthenticated file that names it,” METAL explains.
ManageEngine’s threat analysts caught a glimpse of the potential attack path on May 28, and observed in real time the change in payloads served by AOMEI on July 16. On July 20, the short-burst tampering was also caught by Mandiant.
Analysis of the payload showed the delivery of a legitimate version of the Radmin Server remote administration tool alongside a malicious DLL loaded through it that would establish a reverse TCP connection to the attackers’ command-and-control (C&C) server.
Google Cloud’s researchers also observed UNC7017 introducing a secondary exploitation vector, replacing a legitimate banner with a 1×1 pixel window assigned maximum execution priority that forced the AOMEI client to request a remote resource via WebDAV, thus sending NetNTLMv2 authentication hashes to the attackers.
Throughout the various stages of the campaign, the threat actor delivered multiple payloads, including the CrossRoad dropper, a modified version of Radmin Server, and the Adaptix C&C framework.
CrossRoad was seen performing system validation, cleanup, and payload staging, establishing persistence for the late-stage backdoor, and deleting itself from the disk. The final payload was the ShinyRoad modular backdoor framework.
In July, after the successful deployment of ShinyRoad, UNC7017 was seen dropping AdaptAgent, which is part of the Adaptix C2 post-exploitation framework.
“This campaign highlights a broader evolution in software supply chain attack methodologies. Supply chain intrusions have historically focused on inserting backdoors into software source code or tampering with developer build pipelines. UNC7017’s use of ephemeral configuration tampering represents a lower-overhead, higher-stealth alternative,” Google Cloud notes.
METAL says it initially notified AOMEI Technology of the potential tampering in early June, but the vendor dismissed the report, claiming the content was likely intercepted and modified in transit. Google Cloud notified it again in mid-July, and the company said in late July that it had taken corrective actions.

articles.title: Meta tries to scapegoat staff who downloaded torrents to spare execs
articles.text:
In copyright lawsuits over AI training, Meta has spent weeks blaming staff for downloading torrents. The company has now been ordered to name executives who authorized decisions to pirate books from shadow libraries like Anna’s Archive and LibGen, TorrentFreak reported.
In a discovery order impacting a class action raised by book authors—including Richard Kadrey and Sarah Silverman—as well as a lawsuit from publisher Entrepreneur Media, Magistrate Judge Thomas Hixon largely agreed that Meta must clearly identify key decision-makers. Following testimony from Meta staff who downloaded torrents, the order could expose a wider range of supervisors, managers, and executives whom staffers said greenlit the piracy.
Meta had been hoping to avoid detailing the chain of command, particularly for leadership involved in early AI training. According to a Meta court filing, its initial efforts to compile massive AI datasets were managed through an “informal approach” where supposedly nobody with authority made any decisions. Instead, Meta insisted that a “decision” was “made only in the sense” that some staffers “technically” downloaded torrents.
Zuckerberg could be roped in
Authors and publishers have argued that Meta made a willful choice to induce infringement by downloading and illegally distributing their copyrighted works. Since torrenting depends on a swarm of users, Meta could not have quickly downloaded 80.6 terabytes of data from LibGen or 35.7 terabytes through Anna’s Archive if the company wasn’t also seeding, authors have argued. (Meta has argued that it relied on “mitigations” to prevent seeding.)
Meta’s efforts to scapegoat staff seem to ignore that staff expressed discomfort in being directed to pirate work. In the past year, authors’ lawsuits have exposed internal messages in which staff pushed back or rejected directions on torrenting, including one worker who commented that “torrenting from a corporate laptop doesn’t feel right.” Another staffer testified that he initiated downloads that “required some director or VP level approval to use for training,” a joint letter from Entrepreneur Media and Meta noted. There was also a time when leadership halted, then resumed, downloading torrents sourced from Anna’s Archive, another staffer testified. And while Meta has argued that communications that might identify who specifically authorized certain torrenting instances are privileged, at least one string of unredacted messages unsealed early last year allegedly showed that the decision to download from LibGen, for example, occurred after “a prior escalation to MZ” (Mark Zuckerberg).

articles.title: University of Alberta partners with Silicon Valley VC firm to help commercialize research | BetaKit
articles.text:
The University of Alberta (U of A) is enlisting the help of a US venture capital firm to guide its staff in moving deep tech research from the lab to the marketplace.
The news: The U of A announced a partnership with Celesta Capital on Oct. 14. The aim is to bring Celesta’s expertise to the U of A’s students and staff with training on entrepreneurship, patents, commercialization, intellectual property, and more. The partnership will also include industry and venture capital summit events held at the university.
From the source: “The U of A produces research with global reach, and our job is to move that work into the world where it creates companies, jobs, and impact,” associate vice-president of innovation, knowledge, mobilization, and partnerships Darren Fast said in a statement. “Partnering with Celesta gives our researchers and founders direct access to investors and operators who have built deep tech companies at a global scale.”
The context: Celesta’s partnership with the U of A comes at a time when Edmonton’s startup ecosystem is betting on deep tech as the city’s next flashpoint. The news comes on the heels of an announcement by Edmonton Unlimited that it will launch a Deep Tech Foundry program early next year with the specific goal of meeting the unique demands of commercializing deep tech.
Programming under the Celesta-U of A partnership will launch later this month with Scientific Entrepreneurship Day. Coordinated between Edmonton Unlimited, Celesta, the Alberta Machine Intelligence Institute, and the U of A, the day will feature a curriculum designed to cover fundraising, intellectual property strategy, market validation, team building, and more.
Final thought: Celesta partner Charles Lespérance said Alberta broadly has the ingredients needed to develop a world-class deep tech ecosystem, including research expertise, technical prowess, and ambitious founders. But deep tech has historically faced unique hurdles to commercialization, including greater technical risk, high capital costs, and long research and development cycles.
That has created trepidation for some investors. Speaking at the NACO Summit this past summer, Émilie Boutros of TandemLaunch said deep tech companies often fail not on their technology, but due to a lack of business coaching. Celesta’s partnership with the U of A brings that coaching together with the resources Edmonton’s deep tech community already has.

articles.title: Thought Industries' Lens checks product knowledge for conflicts before customers see it - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Thought Industries’ Lens checks product knowledge for conflicts before customers see it
Customer learning software company Thought Industries Inc. today launched Lens, an artificial intelligence product that checks a business’ product knowledge for conflicts before it reaches customers.
Thought Industries Academy, its existing course software, joins Lens in a new Customer Knowledge AI Platform.
The launch is seeking to take on the problem of knowledge silos. At many companies, customer and product knowledge lives wherever the team that produced it happens to work. Because AI tools now answer queries from customers from many of those separate sources, the same question can draw two different answers. Customers who get stuck between those answers adopt less of the product, the company said.
Lens connects to the places where business already keeps that material, the help center and product documentation among them. None of it has to move. On top sits what the company calls a governed knowledge layer, where agents inside Lens look for sources that disagree. The business sets the trust rules in plain language. When a product changes, the agents work to bring the affected guidance up to date.
Customers can get answers from Lens inside the product itself or through whatever AI assistant they prefer. The agents can also complete workflows. Logged questions show businesses which parts of a product keep tripping customers up.
Checking for conflicts between sources is what Thought Industries says existing tools lack. It sees Model Context Protocol connectors and the AI built into individual systems as mostly finding information. Chief Executive Irana Wasti said search and retrieval alone do not settle which source is right.
“When every agent is working from a different version of product knowledge, they can simply spread wrong answers faster,” she said. Customers who do get what they need “use more, buy more and stay longer,” according to Wasti.
The Linux Foundation, which runs training and certification programs for open-source software, plans to use Lens. Clyde Seepersad, senior vice president and general manager of education there, said the information its users search for often sits in systems beyond the courseware. The foundation keeps control over what gets surfaced, he said, and the questions coming in should give it “a much clearer picture of what customers need.”
Thought Industries is also changing how it describes its own business. Customer and product leaders are now the stated audience, and the pitch centers on turning scattered knowledge into a competitive advantage. Academy remains the piece that runs courses, learning paths and certifications, with AI recommending what a learner should take next.
Lens is available now in beta. Thought Industries is a private equity-backed company that has sold customer training software since 2013, and Luminate Capital Partners made a strategic growth investment in it in 2019.

articles.title: I sunk 15 hours into Nintendo Switch Sports Resort, and it's even better than the first game — it's filled with multiplayer fun and bolstered replayability
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
Nintendo Switch Sports Resort is a considerable improvement over its predecessor, with more events, more single-player depth, and more ways to play. While it would’ve been good to have seen sports such as Football and Chambara at launch, and the visual style still feels a bit lacking, responsive controls and chaotic multiplayer gameplay make this title well worth adding to your library.
Reasons to buy
- + Full of chaotic multiplayer fun
- + Incredibly responsive motion and mouse controls
- + Island Crown adds much needed single-player depth
Reasons to avoid
- - Some key sports have been cut
- - Visual style slightly lacking in character
- - Exploration-based modes could be better
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Nintendo Switch Sports Resort is here, and this new first-party Nintendo Switch 2 exclusive has big shoes to fill.
You see, when Wii Sports entered the scene 20 years ago, it was a total phenomenon. It was a smash hit thanks to its simplistic yet addictive gameplay, enticing players of all ages…even your grandparents could get involved.
Platform reviewed: Nintendo Switch 2
Available on: Nintendo Switch 2 only
Release date: October 22, 2026
Its successor, Wii Sports Resort, expanded on the formula, adding more sports, more depth, and more precise controls. And Nintendo Switch Sports Resort is attempting to do the very same for a new generation — to refine the relatively basic Nintendo Switch Sports and create a more fleshed-out experience, all while retaining that sense of widespread appeal for players of all ages.
But can Nintendo Switch Sports Resort pull off this seemingly daunting task? I’ve spent about 15 hours playing the game solo, with friends, and with fellow gaming journalists online, and this is my verdict.
Getting sporty on Switch 2
The original Nintendo Switch Sports was a decent overall experience. It was a bit thin at launch and lacked single-player replayability, but the version we know today has a solid lineup of events, with fairly responsive controls, and is a good party game to enjoy with friends. And luckily, it feels like Nintendo Switch Sports Resort has fixed a lot of the issues I had with its predecessor.
Let’s start off by talking about the sporting variety on offer. There are 12 core sports available here. You’ve got some classic options like Basketball, Bowling, Boxing, and Tennis, as well as some Leisure Sports, such as Power Cruising and Prop Plane. What’s more, there are two sports that have never been seen in previous entries — namely Skateboarding and Thumb Wrestling.
I found that all 12 of the included sports were great fun to play. Let’s start with the returning events. Sports such as Basketball and Tennis are much unchanged, but feel incredibly tight and enjoyable, with accurate motion controls and multiple modes, such as Three-Point Contest for the former and a slower-paced Laid-Back Match for the latter. Bowling, Golf, and Volleyball are similarly unchanged, and continue to be a favorite for my pals and me, with plenty of laughs and tense moments.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Some of the returning sports feel far more refined, though. The biggest example of this is Boxing. Gone are the days of randomly flailing your disconnected gloves to down your opponent. Now, Boxing feels far more tactical. You have a stamina bar; it's far easier to land uppercuts and hooks, and picking the right moment to land your knockout punch is crucial.
My highlight was definitely conquering the island champion in Table Tennis. This was my favorite sport by quite a margin, and landing a crushing power shot to snag the number one ranking felt incredible. Take that, Yunsu. I’m the champion now.
It’s a similar story with Table Tennis, which, in my view, is the most fun sport in the game. At higher levels, you’ll need to be incredibly strategic with your slice shots to recover back to the centre and perfect your timing to hit shots right onto the table edge. The Return Challenge mode is also a whole lot of fun, and honing your accuracy to beat your high score feels super rewarding.
Archery is another highlight, with the Joy-Con 2 controllers providing pinpoint precision when aiming for the target. There are also some hidden targets to discover, adding plenty of replay value to the sport. Other sports, like Power Cruising and Prop Plane, translate nicely onto Switch 2 as well, and although the latter asks you to hold the Joy-Con 2 in a slightly bizarre way, it’s fairly comfortable and effective after you get used to it.
Out with the old, in with the new
We’ll get onto the new events in just a moment, but before we do that, let’s talk about something that irked me a little. Some of the events from the original Nintendo Switch Sports have been cut.
Yes, it’s out with the old and in with the new, as three events — Badminton, Chambara, and Football (or soccer) — are no more. This is a shame, as these were all among my favorite sports last time out. Football in particular is a big miss — it provided a chaotic, all-action multi-player experience with tense last-minute theatrics. Will these sports return in some kind of update or DLC? Quite possibly. But I would’ve loved to have seen them here at launch.
Anyway, no point in crying over spilt milk, eh? After all, the newly added sports are a blast. Thumb wrestling is a truly bizarre addition, and I can’t believe that Nintendo managed to make this feel fun. You have to hold your thumb against your opponent's hand to enlarge it, and then pin them down to attain victory. I feel like they missed a trick by leaving out ‘one, two, three, four, I declare a thumb war’ as the countdown, but otherwise, no complaints here.
I can see skateboarding dividing opinion, but I had good fun with it. This mode makes use of the Switch 2’s mouse mode capabilities, and this works surprisingly well. Whether I was lifting the Joy-Con 2 to jump or trick, tilting to steer, or pushing back to accelerate, movement always seemed to be accurate. The Skate Sprint mode is definitely the highlight here; tricking to gain speed, sneaking up behind your opponents, and grinding on railings is a whole lot of fun.
What I would say, however, is that the Free Play mode could’ve been better. The world that you skate around isn’t empty or anything, but I wish there was more to do and explore. The Sightseeing Tour is also a little lacking; you’re tasked with collecting photos, which isn’t the most thrilling experience — I would’ve preferred the option to collect customization parts for my board or character instead. This also applies to the Prop Plane and Power Cruising modes, which have Free Play options as well.
Oh, and a quick note on online play, which was very enjoyable in my experience. Here, you can expect highly responsive, smooth controls. Even though my home Wi-Fi is far from great, I ran into no performance issues whatsoever when linking up with a couple of other gaming journalists online — vital when playing reaction-based sports like Table Tennis and Volleyball.
A more replayable sporting experience
Nintendo Switch Sports Resort has made one other key addition that helps it to totally surpass its predecessor, that being Island Crown.
Island Crown is a primarily single-player experience, where you have to rise up the ranks in a particular sport and challenge the island champion. Initially, your foes will seem laughably weak, but as you climb up the table, some highly skilled challengers will stand before you. If you manage to beat the island champion, you’ll have the opportunity to face a legendary Mii from the Wii era…I won’t spoil the identity of these, though; I’ll let you discover them for yourself.
This mode has kept me coming back to Nintendo Switch Sports Resort time after time. You get new customization options as you improve your rank; the challenge of beating tough opponents is highly compelling, and the mode serves as an excellent way to develop your sporting prowess. This is the sort of single-player replayability that the original Switch Sports was crying out for, and I absolutely loved it.
I’ve mentioned customization options a few times in this review, so let’s talk about them. By playing sports, you’ll earn points which you can spend at the item center to get a random title, hairstyle, costume, or such things. Previously, you could only earn points online to customize your character — meaning you’d need a Nintendo Switch Online subscription, but no longer. Now, you can earn points offline too, and I loved a lot of the straight-up weird customization options available. I mean, come on, just look at my character.
You can either customize your standard character or a Mii that’s saved on your Switch 2 console. But I never deviated from the standard option. I’m afraid that the Miis just look so out of place in this game, with this visual style...and I feel like it’s time to let them go. Maybe they should simply remain as a relic of a bygone era.
More generally, I would say that the visual style of Nintendo Switch Sports is a bit lackluster. It misses the personality and sauce of the Wii era titles, and goes for a more ‘streamlined,’ modern look which ends up feeling a tad soulless. Even the menus are a touch dull, and given that this is a Nintendo game, I expected more flair, and perhaps a few nods to the company’s most beloved IPs to add even more charm.
The quality of the visuals is generally strong, though, and frame rates are consistent in docked or tabletop mode. I did notice a few texture loading issues in tabletop when playing Prop Plane, but this was fairly minor.
Otherwise, though, I’m coming away from my experience with Nintendo Switch Sports Resort feeling largely positive. The bolstered single-player replayability, enjoyable new sports, refined classics, and brilliantly responsive controls ensure it's a hit that’s especially great for multiplayer mayhem.
It’s a shame that some sports were cut, and I’m still not sold on this series’ visual direction, but just like Wii Sports Resort, this entry succeeds in building on its predecessor with additional depth and versatility. So, if you’re looking for a fun sporting experience to add to your Switch 2 library, this is well worth picking up.
Should you play Nintendo Switch Sports Resort?
Play it if…
You want to enjoy more multiplayer mayhem on Switch 2
The Nintendo Switch 2 already has an excellent lineup of multiplayer experiences, and Nintendo Switch Sports only adds more variety into the mix. I enjoyed playing all 12 of the sports here with friends and family, and had no end of chaotic showdowns. This one’s definitely going to remain in my party game rotation alongside Mario Party Jamboree and Mario Kart World.
You’re looking for more single-player goodness
The inclusion of Island Crown means that there’s so much single player replayability on offer in Nintendo Switch Sports Resort. Fighting to rise up the ranks and defeat the island champion is an absolute blast, and keeps the experience feeling fresh, even without friends or online rivals.
Don't play it if...
You’re not a big fan of motion controls
If you don’t enjoy motion controls, this is one to be avoided. All of the sports here highly rely on motion, with no other control schemes available, other than the mouse mode-enabled Skateboarding.
You didn’t vibe with the previous game’s visuals
The visual style from the original Nintendo Switch Sports has been retained here, and again, it doesn’t feel very inspired or charismatic. If that ended up being a major turn off for you last time, don’t expect much in the way of change here.
Accessibility features
You can change the dominant hand for each individual sport, alter camera controls for Prop Plane and Skateboarding, and turn on Shot Assist for Golf, which makes it easier to hit the ball accurately. Otherwise, there aren’t many ways to customize your experience in Nintendo Switch Sports Resort, with no colorblind modes or alternate control schemes available.
How I reviewed Nintendo Switch Sports Resort
I spent 15 hours playing Nintendo Switch Sports Resort, trying out Island Crown mode in single-player, as well as a number of core and Leisure Sports via local and online multiplayer.
For the most part, I played in docked mode, with my console connected to the Sky Glass Gen 2 TV and the Marshall Heston 120 soundbar. However, I did dabble in some tabletop mode gameplay, and used the JBL Live Beam 4 to enjoy in-game audio.
More generally, I’ve spent years reviewing gaming software and hardware here at TechRadar. I’ve reviewed a number of Nintendo Switch 2 exclusives, including Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave, Yoshi and the Mysterious Book, and Kirby Air Riders. I've also logged more than 50 hours on the original Nintendo Switch Sports, which I directly compared against its newly released successor.
First reviewed October 2026
Harry is a Senior Reviews Writer for TechRadar. He reviews everything from party speakers to wall chargers and has a particular interest in the worlds of audio and gaming. Harry has a background in business tech journalism, particularly around the telecoms industry.

articles.title: Melt it, spin it, use it again
articles.text:
Melt it, spin it, use it again
A plastic-based recyclable yarn is as strong and stretchy as spandex.
The average American throws out around 81 pounds of clothing each year, and there are few options for recycling it. MIT engineers hope to cut down on that textile waste with a new type of yarn.
The thermoplastic yarn mimics the properties of conventional elastic yarns, which typically combine spandex with polyester or nylon. Those fibers would have to be separated for recycling—a process that isn’t practical. But the MIT team found a way to create a similarly stretchy yarn from two variations of polyethylene, a material commonly used in milk jugs and grocery bags. Because they come from the same chemical family, the yarn can be melted as is. Svetlana Boriskina, who led the work as a research scientist in the Department of Mechanical Engineering, says a garment made from this material could then be spun into new yarn for a next generation of clothing. Even after 10 cycles of melting and respinning, the yarn stays as strong and flexible as conventional thread.
“Now we have something that can be knitted and woven,” Boriskina says. “That is the next stage.” Someday, the researchers hope, a polyethylene garment could be dropped in a collection bin and sent to a recycling facility, promoting a more sustainable, circular textile economy.
