articles.title: Can a Simple App Really Fix PC Game Stutters?
articles.text:
Shader compilation stutter has plagued PC gaming for years, and a new application called Shader Compilation Stutter Killer, or SCSKiller for short, promises to do something about it. The idea is simple enough: compile shaders before launching a game rather than waiting for them to be compiled during gameplay. But does it actually work?
That's what we set out to find out, testing the application across several notoriously stutter-prone games. Along the way, we also discovered something rather interesting about shader compilation on Radeon GPUs. Something that could be a pretty big deal, and that we hadn't heard about before.
What's SCSKiller?
SCSKiller is a free and open-source application, so if you're interested, we recommend downloading it and giving it a shot for yourself. For those unfamiliar with shader compilation stutter, it's a common issue in modern PC gaming where a game briefly freezes or hitches the first time a new visual effect appears.
Some games attempt to address this by precompiling shaders before gameplay begins. The Last of Us Part I, for example, is famous for its lengthy shader compilation process.
Unfortunately, even games that precompile shaders can still suffer from horrific shader compilation stutter, while others don't bother precompiling much of anything, which can also lead to a poor experience.
Rather than relying on a game to compile shaders, either beforehand or on the fly, SCSKiller attempts to do the work before you launch it. The application scans game files, extracts the necessary shader code, and compiles as many shader pipelines as possible into the GPU driver's cache. The idea is that when you launch the game, those shaders are already compiled, so the driver doesn't have to interrupt gameplay to process new visual effects.
SCSKiller doesn't rely on a whitelist of specific games. Instead, it works at the engine level, with support for games built using Unreal Engine 4 and 5, Unity, RE Engine, and FromSoftware's engines, alongside a more generic approach for other DirectX 12 titles. It also supports DirectX 11 games on Nvidia GPUs.
For games where shader pipelines can't easily be extracted from the game files, SCSKiller includes an optional recorder. This allows you to play for a few minutes with recording enabled, after which the application can use the collected data to compile additional shaders.
It's important to understand that SCSKiller doesn't solve all forms of stuttering, because not every stutter you encounter is related to shader compilation. One of the biggest issues, particularly with Unreal Engine 5 games, has been traversal stutter, and SCSKiller can't address that.
In our opinion, traversal stuttering is generally more disruptive, as it can result in longer pauses when new environmental assets are loaded from local storage. This typically happens as you cross an invisible boundary within the game world, triggering the loading of additional assets. Perhaps we'll get a Shader Traversal Stutter Killer, or STSKiller, in the future. Fingers crossed.
The Drawbacks: Compilation Time, Storage, and Memory
There are some drawbacks to SCSKiller, though they're largely unavoidable consequences of how the application works. For starters, brute-forcing thousands of shader pipelines can take considerable time, depending on how many shaders need compiling and the performance of your CPU.
Of course, the advantage is that you can run the compilation process when you're not actively using your PC. Just be aware that it can pin CPU usage at 100% for extended periods, though with a properly configured system, that shouldn't be an issue.
SCSKiller also consumes additional storage space, and with SSDs at a premium right now, that's something worth considering. Compiling thousands of shaders increases the size of the GPU driver's shader cache. As a result, you may need to increase the cache size to prevent older compiled shaders from being removed.
Nvidia users can adjust this through the driver settings. The standard limit is typically 10 GB, but you can increase it to 100 GB or even set it to unlimited, preventing older shaders from being deleted as new ones are added.
Unfortunately, things are more restrictive for Radeon users. According to SCSKiller, AMD's driver has a fixed shader cache limit of 16 GB. We haven't independently confirmed that limit with AMD, but if accurate, it means Radeon owners can't simply increase the cache size. Once the cache reaches its limit, older entries are removed to make room for new ones. SCSKiller will then identify previously optimized games as needing to be compiled again.
This potentially limits the usefulness of SCSKiller on Radeon GPUs, particularly if you're trying to optimize a large library of games. That said, there's no need to panic. As we discovered during testing, AMD has some pretty interesting shader compilation behavior of its own, and we'll explore that shortly.
Test System and Methodology
For all of this initial testing, we used our Ryzen 7 9800X3D test system with 32 GB of RAM, initially paired with the GeForce RTX 5090. Later, we also tested the Radeon RX 9070 XT and GeForce RTX 5070 to investigate some interesting differences in shader compilation behavior.
We may explore additional hardware configurations in the future, particularly slower CPUs. For now, though, the goal was simply to determine whether SCSKiller actually works. As it turns out, we were able to demonstrate that quite clearly using the 9800X3D. So, let's get into the results.
Test System Specs
| CPU | AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D | 
| Motherboard | MSI MPG X870E Carbon WiFi [BIOS 7E49v1AA7] | 
| Memory | G.Skill Trident Z5 RGB DDR5-6000 32GB CL30 [CL30-38-38-96] | 
| Graphics Card | GeForce RTX 5090, GeForce RTX 5070, Radeon RX 9070 XT | 
| ATX Case | MSI Prospect 700R | 
| Power Supply | Kolink Regulator Gold ATX 3.0 1200W | 
| Storage | TeamGroup T-Force Cardea A440 M.2 PCIe Gen4 NVMe SSD 4TB | 
| Operating System | Windows 11 25H2 | 
| Display Driver | AMD Radeon Adrenalin 26.9.2 Nvidia GeForce Game Ready Driver 617.42 | 
Gaming Benchmarks
Star Wars Jedi: Survivor
We'll start with Star Wars Jedi: Survivor, a game famous for its numerous stuttering issues. Jedi: Survivor precompiles shaders when loading for the first time. For this initial test, both configurations were running the game for the first time immediately after completing that initial shader compilation process.
There are quite a few interesting things to note here. First, performance was substantially better with SCSKiller enabled, boosting the average frame rate by 25%, with a similar improvement to the 1% lows. However, you might have also noticed that the standard configuration was consuming around 60% more GPU power, at least at the beginning of the test. That difference gradually decreased to just under 40% by the end of our run.
Despite the game precompiling shaders when initially loading, there appears to be considerable additional shader compilation work taking place during gameplay, particularly in the early stages. This can reduce frame rates and increase the processing overhead associated with rendering new effects.
Something else worth noting is that SCSKiller increased system memory usage. We're looking at around 7% more RAM consumption in this example, apparently due to the additional precompiled shader data being buffered into system memory.
For our second Jedi: Survivor test, we loaded an earlier section of the game immediately after completing the first run. By this point, the game had already been running for quite some time. In terms of performance, the SCSKiller configuration was around 14% faster, though neither configuration suffered from what we'd consider shader compilation stutter.
Interestingly, SCSKiller was now consuming around 30% more system memory, representing almost 7 GB of additional RAM usage. That wasn't a problem for our 32 GB configuration, but it's certainly something to consider if you have less than 32 GB of system memory.
GPU power consumption also increased with SCSKiller this time, which makes sense given that we were rendering more frames. It also suggests the RTX 5090 was spending less time dealing with shader compilation work during gameplay. Although SCSKiller wasn't solving any noticeable shader compilation stutter in this particular example, since the standard configuration wasn't stuttering to begin with, it still managed to improve performance substantially.
It's possible that slower hardware would have exhibited more obvious stuttering with the standard configuration, but that's something we'll need to explore in future testing. It's also worth noting that despite consuming more system memory, SCSKiller didn't always improve frame rates. In another section of the game, performance was much the same between the two configurations. And as we mentioned earlier, SCSKiller can't fix traversal stutter, which remained clearly visible at several points throughout our testing.
Grounded 2
Another game reportedly affected by shader compilation stutter is Grounded 2, so we decided to take a look. However, with the hardware configuration we were testing, we didn't encounter any significant stuttering issues, at least in the sections of the game we examined.
Despite SCSKiller increasing system memory usage by around 5 to 6 GB, there were no measurable performance improvements. In this case, the application simply didn't provide any meaningful benefit.
Hogwarts Legacy
Another game we were particularly keen to investigate was Hogwarts Legacy, especially since the developer of SCSKiller specifically highlights performance improvements in this title. Unfortunately, we couldn't reproduce those improvements in our testing. Initially, we tested using the Ultra quality preset at 4K with Performance upscaling and ray tracing enabled.
Performance remained pretty poor even after running SCSKiller, particularly the 1% lows, and we couldn't identify any meaningful improvements to frame times. What we did see, however, was a substantial increase in system memory usage of over 20%, effectively maxing out our 32 GB capacity.
Concerned that the additional memory consumption might be preventing SCSKiller from delivering an improvement, we decided to retest with ray tracing disabled, which reduced overall memory usage. Unfortunately, that didn't change much. Performance was virtually identical between the two configurations. If anything, the standard configuration was slightly faster, while SCSKiller was now consuming over 50% more system memory without providing any measurable advantage.
Frame pacing was also largely unchanged. In a final attempt to reduce system memory usage, we dropped to the Medium quality preset, again with ray tracing disabled. But once again, frame rates and frame pacing were essentially identical between the two configurations. This time, SCSKiller increased system memory usage by around 25%, still without delivering any meaningful improvement.
So, what's going on here?
It's possible that our hardware configuration was influencing the results, though the SCSKiller developer also reported improvements using an RTX 5090. Alternatively, it could simply be that the section of the game we tested wasn't particularly affected by shader compilation stutter. Either way, we weren't able to reproduce the improvements claimed by the developer, despite testing several graphics configurations.
The Blood of Dawnwalker
The Blood of Dawnwalker is another game we've heard suffers from shader compilation stutter, though in our testing, the issue didn't seem particularly problematic. That said, SCSKiller did manage to deliver a reasonable performance improvement, presumably by making additional compiled shader data available in system memory.
By the end of our test, the 1% lows had improved by 15%, accompanied by a 6% increase in the average frame rate. That's a pretty decent improvement considering the application is free, assuming you have enough storage space and system memory available.
In this example, system memory usage increased by 33%, with SCSKiller consuming approximately 5 GB of additional RAM.
Silent Hill: Townfall
Another relatively new game we decided to examine was Silent Hill: Townfall. Unfortunately, performance was much the same between the two configurations, and SCSKiller wasn't able to eliminate the stuttering we encountered.
In fact, we observed more stuttering with SCSKiller enabled, though it's important to note that this was based on a single pass through the game. That's one limitation of this type of side-by-side testing, as stuttering behavior can vary between runs, so we wouldn't read too much into that particular result. Still, there was no evidence of a meaningful improvement in the section we tested.
Tiny Tina's Wonderlands: A Dramatic Improvement
Now, here's a game we know stutters like absolute buggery. Tiny Tina's Wonderlands is an Unreal Engine 4 title with so much shader compilation stutter that it's almost unplayable at times. And keep in mind, we're testing with a Ryzen 7 9800X3D and GeForce RTX 5090 here. The average frame rate looks pretty impressive, but the 1% lows tell a very different story. They're absolutely horrid.
The game does precompile shaders before you start playing, and while things improve as you spend more time in the same area, moving somewhere new often means it's Stutter City all over again. For example, we left our initial test area for a few minutes before returning. Despite having already explored that section of the game, it didn't take long for the shader compilation stutters to return.
Admittedly, they weren't quite as severe as before, but they remained pretty annoying, especially considering the hardware we were using. This is where SCSKiller really comes into its own. It transformed Tiny Tina's Wonderlands from a stuttery mess into an exceptionally smooth experience, eliminating the constant hitching we had been experiencing.
By the end of our test, the 1% lows had improved from just 45 fps to an incredible 147 fps. More importantly, the constant stuttering and hitching were completely gone in the section we tested. This was one of the most impressive results we'd seen so far, demonstrating SCSKiller can be effective when shader compilation is responsible for poor performance.
However, what happened next was arguably even more interesting.
AMD's Background Shader Compilation: An Unexpected Discovery
Having seen how dramatically SCSKiller improved performance on the RTX 5090 in Tiny Tina's Wonderlands, we decided to swap out the GeForce GPU for a Radeon RX 9070 XT. And we're glad we did, because the results were rather puzzling, but in a good way. What we observed was the first few seconds of gameplay after freshly installing the RX 9070 XT along with AMD's latest display driver. SCSKiller hadn't been used at all.
We simply allowed the game to perform its usual shader precompilation process before loading our save file. Yet, despite everything we'd just seen with the RTX 5090, the game ran perfectly smoothly. There was no noticeable stuttering whatsoever. We couldn't quite believe what we were seeing, especially after spending so much time testing the GeForce GPU, where the experience had been a complete mess.
We continued playing, exploring several new areas, but at no point did the game exhibit the same stuttering problems. This left us looking for answers. That's when we came across an extremely brief article on AMD's website titled AMD Software: Adrenalin Edition 26.9.2 Background Shader Compilation. This was the exact driver we were using for our testing. The article explains that AMD has expanded its DirectX 12 background shader processing support to Unreal Engine 5 games.
According to AMD, the functionality was already enabled for Unreal Engine 4 titles, along with several specifically named games, including Borderlands 3, Dirt 5, Cyberpunk 2077, Guardians of the Galaxy, Halo Infinite, and Tiny Tina's Wonderlands. AMD also notes that background shader compilation can reduce initial game loading times, though performance may be temporarily reduced while compilation is taking place. Because shader compilation is CPU-intensive, the time required to complete the process depends on the processor and overall system load.
For benchmarking purposes, AMD recommends allowing approximately 15 minutes of gameplay for background compilation to finish before recording performance measurements. The company also recommends excluding the first run of each new session when using an in-game benchmark. Based on that explanation, AMD appears to be saying that background shader compilation has already been supported in Unreal Engine 4 titles for some time, with Unreal Engine 5 support arriving more recently.
So the bigger news for Radeon owners is that AMD has been working on background shader compilation at the driver level, and its latest update expands that functionality to Unreal Engine 5 games. This was news to us. Admittedly, shader compilation performance isn't something we've investigated in detail for quite some time. There didn't appear to be much progress on the issue, so it had become one of those unfortunate realities of PC gaming that we'd more or less accepted.
But based on what we're seeing in Tiny Tina's Wonderlands, AMD appears to have effectively solved shader compilation stutter in this particular game. And what's particularly impressive is how quickly it happens. After a brief shader preparation process, we could simply load into the game and start playing without encountering any noticeable stutters. Meanwhile, the same game remained a complete mess on our GeForce GPUs without SCSKiller.
Tiny Tina's Wonderlands: Radeon vs. GeForce
Despite Tiny Tina's Wonderlands already running perfectly smoothly on the RX 9070 XT, we still wanted to see what would happen if we used SCSKiller. This was also when we discovered the apparent 16 GB shader cache limitation on Radeon GPUs. After precompiling the game's shaders using SCSKiller, we ran the test again and found virtually identical performance. SCSKiller increased system memory usage by approximately 2 GB, but this had no measurable effect on frame rates or frame pacing. In other words, AMD's standard driver configuration was already doing everything we needed.
For a better representation of image quality comparisons, check out the HUB video below:
For comparison, we also tested the GeForce RTX 5070 under identical conditions, both with the standard driver configuration and after using SCSKiller. As expected, the RTX 5070 suffered from severe shader compilation stutter when running the game normally. However, after using SCSKiller, those issues were completely eliminated in our test. The application also increased VRAM usage by around 4 GB, bringing it roughly in line with what we observed on the Radeon RX 9070 XT.
Comparing the two GPUs with their standard driver configurations reveals how significant AMD's advantage was in this particular game. Although average frame rates were similar, the 1% and 0.1% lows were substantially better on the Radeon GPU, with AMD's background shader compilation apparently doing an excellent job of preventing the constant interruptions we encountered on GeForce.
For a better representation of image quality comparisons, check out the HUB video below:
Now, compare the standard RX 9070 XT configuration against the RTX 5070 after using SCSKiller. Both GPUs delivered exceptionally smooth performance at roughly the same frame rates, with the GeForce GPU actually coming out ever so slightly ahead. That's a good result for SCSKiller, but it's also a demonstration of what AMD's driver is already doing.
What makes this particularly interesting is the amount of preparation required. For the RX 9070 XT, we literally installed the driver, restarted the system, loaded into Windows, and immediately launched Tiny Tina's Wonderlands. After the game's brief initial shader preparation process, we were playing without any issues.
For the RTX 5070 to deliver the same kind of smooth performance, we first had to install SCSKiller and then spend around 30 minutes precompiling shaders. Only after completing that process were we able to achieve the results shown here. So, at least in Tiny Tina's Wonderlands, AMD's driver implementation appears considerably more efficient at preparing shaders and avoiding compilation stutter. Very impressive stuff.
Final Fantasy VII Rebirth: Another Stutter-Filled Experience
Finally, we wanted to compare the RTX 5070 and RX 9070 XT in Final Fantasy VII Rebirth, another game we've heard suffers from severe shader compilation stutter. And unfortunately, those reports appear to be accurate. Starting with the RX 9070 XT, we compared the standard driver configuration against SCSKiller. Neither configuration was flawless.
It's worth noting that Final Fantasy VII Rebirth has a hard 120 fps frame rate cap, which is a little annoying for this type of testing. However, we're primarily interested in the 1% and 0.1% lows anyway, so the cap isn't a major concern. With the standard Radeon driver configuration, 1% lows remained above 60 fps, but there were still noticeable stutters, reflected in the 0.1% low results. SCSKiller certainly helped, though it wasn't able to eliminate every stuttering issue in this particular title.
While the RX 9070 XT wasn't perfect, its performance was considerably better than what we observed with the RTX 5070. In fact, the situation was remarkably similar to Tiny Tina's Wonderlands. With the standard GeForce driver configuration, Final Fantasy VII Rebirth was a stuttery mess. Whereas the Radeon GPU managed to keep its 1% lows above 60 fps, the RTX 5070 suffered from severe performance drops, with its 1% lows falling into single digits. Average frame rates were very similar between the two GPUs, but the 1% and 0.1% lows on the GeForce GPU were terrible.
Then we enabled SCSKiller. After precompiling shaders, the RTX 5070's performance problems were essentially eliminated. The jarring stutters disappeared, 1% lows remained well above 60 fps throughout our testing, and even the 0.1% lows were very good. Frame pacing was excellent, resulting in a completely transformed gaming experience.
We initially captured several minutes of gameplay, but continued playing beyond that and didn't encounter any further issues in the areas we explored. Comparing the RX 9070 XT and RTX 5070 with SCSKiller enabled on both GPUs produced very similar results. Interestingly, SCSKiller consumed more system memory with the RTX 5070 than with the RX 9070 XT. It's possible that this relates to the Radeon driver's more restrictive on-disk shader cache capacity.
Overall, SCSKiller helped improve performance on both GPUs, though the most dramatic improvement was clearly seen on the GeForce side.
Conclusion: Does SCSKiller Actually Work?
SCSKiller certainly took us down a rabbit hole we weren't expecting. At some point, we might conduct a more extensive investigation comparing Radeon and GeForce GPUs across a broader range of hardware configurations and games. For now, though, we can conclude that SCSKiller is genuinely useful and it can improve performance in games affected by shader compilation stutter.
That doesn't mean it's a universal solution. It doesn't address traversal stutter, and even in games where shader compilation is an issue, the benefits can vary significantly depending on the hardware and the sections being tested. In some titles, such as Hogwarts Legacy, we couldn't reproduce the developer's claimed improvements at all. In others, such as Star Wars Jedi: Survivor and The Blood of Dawnwalker, we observed respectable performance gains, even when the standard configuration wasn't exhibiting particularly severe stuttering.
Then there are games like Tiny Tina's Wonderlands and Final Fantasy VII Rebirth, where SCSKiller completely transformed the experience on our GeForce GPUs.
Of course, there are some practical considerations. Compiling shaders can take considerable time, particularly when dealing with thousands of pipelines. You may also need to repeat the process after driver or game updates, and the resulting shader cache can consume a substantial amount of local storage. SCSKiller can also increase system memory consumption considerably, which may or may not be a problem depending on your PC's configuration.
But the good news is that the application itself is free, and there's little downside to trying it in a game you're already having trouble with, provided you're mindful of storage requirements and anti-cheat compatibility. It's straightforward to download and use, and based on our results, certainly worth experimenting with if you're experiencing shader-related stutters.
The Radeon results, however, are a different story, and potentially the more interesting discovery to come out of this testing. Initially, the inability to increase AMD's on-disk shader cache size seemed like a bit of a Radeon fail. And while we'd still like to see AMD provide more control over that limit, if the company continues improving background shader compilation, perhaps it won't be such a significant limitation after all.
We actually spoke with AMD about this, and the company said that while it appreciates third-party applications such as SCSKiller, it also considers itself an industry leader in supporting DirectX 12 Advanced Shader Delivery, which aims to address the same underlying problems through an officially supported approach.
Advanced Shader Delivery is a separate technology developed by Microsoft for Windows 11 and DirectX 12. It allows supported games to download precompiled shaders, reducing the need for compilation on the player's PC and helping prevent stuttering. AMD has been an early supporter of this technology, though its benefits depend on game and platform support.
In any case, there's clearly more testing to be done. We're particularly interested in seeing how AMD's background shader compilation performs across more games, different CPU configurations, and older Radeon hardware. Likewise, SCSKiller deserves a closer look with slower processors, where shader compilation stutter may be even more disruptive. For now, though, we've learned two things: SCSKiller really can work, and AMD's shader compilation improvements might be a bigger deal than we initially realized.

articles.title: Meta Muse exposes users' personal and business secrets when they share conversations
articles.text:
Muse, the new general-purpose AI agent from Meta, can expose sensitive information when users share conversations through web links, researchers reported Monday. In response to questions from Ars about the behavior, Meta said it’s suspending the sharing feature while the company reviews it and considers making changes.
Like many online services, Muse has allowed users to share searches, conversations, images, and similar content with other people. Such share features usually involve clicking an option to create a unique URL that anyone can use to load a page hosting the content. To keep potentially sensitive information from being accessible to unintended people, the URLs typically contain a long sequence of text that can’t be easily guessed.
A single query is all that’s required
Muse, which Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said last month was “built from the ground up for privacy and security,” seems to take the same precautions. But a central design decision for constructing URLs has made the links easy to discover. As a result, researchers from security firm Claroc said they were able to enumerate 6,800 links Muse users created for sharing conversations with others. After opening a few hundred of them, the researchers found information that was clearly not intended to be publicly available, including:
- a candidate’s notes preparing for a confidential executive-search call with a frontier AI lab, naming the lab’s internal contact and the meeting time
- a national marketing company’s internal revenue review, marked for its CEO
- a small-business owner’s loan application, with the amount requested
- a to-do list that included a bank fraud alert, with a partial account number and a transaction amount and time
- a real-estate investor’s internal performance report, with two property addresses and exact return, income, and mortgage figures
- a workplace’s full-year staff vacation calendar, listing dozens of employees against the week each one would be away
“If you had asked us beforehand, we would have guessed that gathering these would take real effort,” the researchers wrote. “It took one query.”
In an emailed statement responding to questions from Ars, Meta said:
We opened the Muse bug bounty program so researchers could raise different scenarios and help us continue improving the product. People have the ability to share specific Muse artifacts, which creates a page that can be accessed by those with the link. However, we’ve paused this functionality while we review this report and consider changes to how these links can be discovered.
Asaf Aprozper, the co-founder and CTO of Claroc, said he reported the findings through Meta’s bug bounty program on October 8 and also tried reaching people at Meta on LinkedIn, but got no reply either way.
The easiest way to discover the URLs is to perform a passive DNS search through one of many available commercial services. Passive DNS records store the historical resolution of domain names to IP addresses, as well as nameserver, and mail-server records over time. Passive DNS systems typically collect DNS responses from sensors positioned at recursive DNS resolvers or other infrastructure. A passive DNS record is generally created when a monitoring system observes a DNS response. In the case here, once the intended party clicks on the share link, the DNS information is recorded in a searchable database.
And look! They call it superintelligence on that page, just like Trump.
Oh boy…

articles.title: Germany’s NEURA Robotics shows no signs of slowing down as it teams up with Austria’s NXAI for physical AI | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Following last week’s announcement that Germany’s NEURA Robotics would be launching its multimodal foundation for physical AI, today the company confirmed that it would be working with Austria’s NXAI on a building block for the memory of cognitive robots.
To this end, the partners are combining NEURA’s Physical AI stack with xLSTM, a recurrent architecture from NXAI that can efficiently maintain and update state over long sequences. Furthermore, NXAI plans to make its own model, based on the xLSTM architecture, available on the Neuraverse platform.
It is set to be available alongside NEURA’s own foundation model, Neuron AI, in future.
“A robot that truly helps in everyday life and in industry must be able to remember,” says David Reger, founder and CEO of NEURA Robotics. “With Neuron AI, we have the foundation. With Neuraverse, we are creating the platform on which other powerful AI approaches can also find their way into robots. Together with Sepp Hochreiter and NXAI, we are expanding this memory capability. Two European strengths, one goal: Physical AI from Europe, together for the world.”
This follows a period of sustained growth for the Metzingen-based robotics unicorn.
As previously reported by EU-Startups, NEURA secured €15 million from InterAlpen Partners in 2023, following a €52 million round earlier that year. By September 2024, the company had reportedly raised €148.67 million in total, before securing a further €120 million Series B in January 2025. At the time, NEURA reported having doubled its workforce to more than 300 employees and increased its revenue tenfold over the preceding year.
This was followed by the announcement of a Series C of up to €1.2 billion in June 2026, and subsequently by acquisitions involving mobile logistics and autonomous cleaning robotics compamy Adlatus Robotics, extending its capabilities and the potential applications of its Neuraverse ecosystem.
“Memory and experience are essential for robots to reliably solve tasks involving many steps,” says Prof. Dr Sepp Hochreiter, founder of NXAI. “xLSTM is built for this; it is fast, memory-efficient and can maintain its state over long sequences. Together with NEURA, we are bringing this strength to Physical AI – from Europe for the world.”
Today’s news brings two companies that already share many touch-points even closer together.
Founded in 2019, Neura develops the technologies that enable intelligent machines to learn, adapt and work side by side with humans in the real world. The company develops cognitive robots that can see, hear, feel and learn, as well as the software, AI and data infrastructure required for their large-scale deployment.
Founded in 2023, NXAI is an Austrian DeepTech company based in Linz that develops solutions for industrial applications. The company’s mission is to translate its own AI research into market-ready products and to bridge the gap between research and industry. Its research focuses on xLSTM models in the fields of time series and robotics.
The planned integration between the two is intended to enable companies to tailor the NXAI model to their own tasks using the Neuraverse toolchain, test it in the NEURA Gyms and deploy it on suitable robots. This will allow customers to utilise different model approaches within the same training and application environment.
Neuron AI remains NEURA’s own multimodal foundation model and will continue to be developed independently. The partnership brings an additional model option to the platform and includes joint research. Companies retain control over their process knowledge and decide for themselves whether to share data and capabilities.
NEURA contributes the Physical AI Stack: its own multimodal foundation models, robotics, sensor technology, real-world training data from the NEURA Gyms, and the platform for industrial deployment. NXAI brings decades of AI research and a fundamentally different approach to recurrent intelligence and memory. Together, the two aim to make capabilities available more quickly.
In the long term, the aim is for robots not only to perform individual tasks, but to build on their experience over time. This aligns with the vision of the Neuraverse and the Robot Skill Economy: skills that robots learn from interacting with the real world, improve upon, and transfer to other machines and environments.
Editor’s Note: Albert Ortig, CEO of NXAI, will be speaking at the MeOut Summit (November 25-26) – co-organised by EU-Startups.

articles.title: Repeat tech entrepreneur Ryan St. Germaine joins Raven as partner | BetaKit
articles.text:
Vancouver’s Raven Indigenous Capital Partners has bolstered its investment team as it prepares to raise its next fund.
The news: Ryan St. Germaine has joined the impact-driven venture capital (VC) firm as a general partner (GP). He and Raven announced the news on LinkedIn last week, when he officially assumed the role. Raven, which claims to be North America’s only Indigenous-led and owned VC firm, backs Indigenous-led tech businesses across the continent, from seed to Series A rounds. Its portfolio includes AdvancedAg, Animikii, CruxOCM, and PLATO Testing, among others.
From the source: “We talk about wanting more Indigenous folks in venture, and if we want to do that, we’ve got to take bets on the people that we believe can get it done,” St. Germaine told BetaKit in an interview. “I think people recognize my abilities. I’ve founded and led and exited companies on the other side, and it’s not that different.”
The context: In VC, moving straight to GP is rare, as most people gradually work their way up the ranks. But St. Germaine and Raven are confident that he has the chops to excel in this position. The Métis serial technology entrepreneur behind BCjobs.ca, Jobcast, and Indigenous Tech Circle had sat on Raven’s investment committee for its $100-million CAD second fund and served as an entrepreneur-in-residence since early 2024, where the firm said he has played “an important part” in its work.
St. Germaine joins existing Raven GPs Althea Wishloff and Sean McCormick under managing partner Stephen Nairne. He said there are no other immediate changes to Raven’s leadership. Raven plans to begin raising its next fund in late 2025 or early 2026. For now, he’s supporting existing Raven companies from Fund II and its $25-million predecessor. The firm is also deploying a $32-million Indigenous Outcomes Fund that’s geared toward supporting climate and health initiatives that improve outcomes for Indigenous communities.
Final thought: The new Raven GP said Indigenous companies don’t receive enough early-stage risk capital. St. Germaine is excited by the chance to help create “more equitable outcomes” for the community. He is also looking forward to working more closely with the startups he previously pitched on participating in Indigenous Tech Circle, where he plans to transition out of the CEO role but stay involved on the board.
Feature image courtesy Raven Indigenous Capital Partners.

articles.title: “Nothing has to be”: New York mayor Zohran Mamdani tells citizens to fight back against the AI doom and gloom
articles.text:
“Nothing has to be”: New York mayor Zohran Mamdani tells citizens to fight back against the AI doom and gloom
Not enough is being done to regulate AI, Mamdani says
- Mayor Zohran Mamdani has urged New Yorkers to push back against AI
- He says there has been a 'complete abdication of federal law' when it comes to regulating the technology
- Mamdani has banned AI use in some schools in New York and has banned AI from being used to generate images on property listings
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani has urged city residents to push back against the doom and gloom feelings around AI, telling them that “Nothing has to be.”
Speaking at The People’s AI Assembly, hosted by the AI Now Institute in Webster Hall, Manhattan, Mamdani noted there has been a “reckless adoption of technology without any kind of a reckoning with the limitations of that technology.”
“There’s a creep that comes with this, and there’s an intent to overwhelm that leaves people feeling as if there is simply no option,” Mamdani said.
“Reckless adoption of technology”
Federal regulations on AI are few and far between, and are failing to keep pace with the technology, prompting widespread worry that AI will replace jobs and harm education for both New Yorkers and people around the world.
Mamdani’s comment centers around how AI technology is being relentlessly pushed into products, services, education, and elsewhere with people having very little say in how it is used.
Schools were a particular sticking point for the conversation on AI. Mamdani recently introduced a ban on AI use in elementary and middle schools after the technology began creeping its way into classrooms. Actress and activist Ilana Glazer, interviewing Mamdani, said, “It just makes me nervous. It feels so non-consensual, as though…this has to be in schools. It wasn’t two years ago. Why does it have to be in schools?”
AI is also having an impact on schools in other ways. Speaking on the reckless adoption of AI, Mamdani referenced the US military’s use of an AI targeting tool that was involved in a strike on a school in Iran earlier this year that killed over 150 people including at least 123 children. A subsequent Pentagon investigation found that overreliance on AI tools was a factor in the deadly strike.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
President Trump has pushed forward with an AI at any cost rhetoric framed as an arms race against China, with the President arguing that any attempts to regulate AI could cost the US its lead. “There is this desire to speak about [AI] as if it is infallible, as if it cannot be questioned, as if the only people who can regulate it are the ones who are currently developing it,” Mamdani said.
“What it really is, is an attempt to escape any kind of accountability at any level, without also jeopardizing the potential valuation from an IPO.”
Anthropic is set to enter the public markets before the end of 2026, with OpenAI looking to make the same move in 2027. Both companies have been involved in hacking incidents where AI agents undergoing testing have escaped sandboxes and breached other companies. These incidents have been labelled as ‘rogue’ behavior, despite evidence from investigations suggesting the AI agents were behaving exactly as intended.
The use of the word ‘rogue’ has also been questioned by experts, with Tenable Field CTO Bernard Montel saying the use of the word “muddies the public policy debate by distracting regulators from enforcing strict legal liability for flawed software deployments.”
Despite these events, little movement has been made to introduce regulations, which Mamdani labelled as a “complete abdication of federal law.”
“As we are looking at what comes after this federal administration, there has to be a very different kind of framework in how we think about AI, talk about AI, the accountability we’re willing to bring forward when it comes to that,” he said.

articles.title: Spotify se sube al modelo Patreon con sus nuevas membresías para podcasts
articles.text:
Spotify acaba de incorporar una nueva vía de monetización para podcasts, de la mano de membresías. En adelante, los usuarios podrán comprar suscripciones de pago para apoyar a sus creadores de contenido favoritos, recibiendo contenidos exclusivos y otros beneficios a cambio.
A través de las membresías, los realizadores de podcasts contarán con una nueva opción para generar dinero a través de Spotify. De esta manera, ya no dependerán de la publicidad como fuente de ingresos y podrán fortalecer la conexión con su público y forjar una comunidad más estrecha.
Los requisitos de Spotify para ofrecer membresías a través de los podcasts son bastante accesibles. La plataforma exige que las producciones estén alojadas en Megaphone o Spotify for Creators, y que tengan al menos 3 episodios publicados, 100 oyentes/espectadores y 100 horas de consumo en Spotify en los 30 días previos.
Otro detalle interesante es que los creadores podrán quedarse con el 90 % de los ingresos que sus podcasts generen a través de las nuevas membresías de Spotify. Sin dudas, una opción muy atractiva para ampliar la monetización del material y fidelizar todavía más a su audiencia.
Los podcasts de Spotify adoptan el modelo Patreon a través de membresías
A través de las membresías de Spotify, los creadores de podcasts podrán ofrecer contenidos exclusivos y otros beneficios a quienes les apoyan económicamente. La plataforma de streaming se ha inspirado en el modelo de Patreon, aunque no es la primera en hacerlo. Otros servicios de distribución de contenidos llevan tiempo brindando soluciones similares, como YouTube.
Es importante mencionar que para comprar la membresía de un podcast no será necesario pagar por Spotify Premium. Esta nueva función estará disponible tanto para los usuarios de pago como para quienes tienen una cuenta gratuita en el servicio.
Respecto de los beneficios que se pueden brindar a través de las membresías, Spotify indica que los podcasts podrán dar acceso temprano a nuevos episodios, entregas exclusivas o menos anuncios, por citar algunos ejemplos. También será posible implementar distintos niveles de apoyo, con precios y perks diferentes para cada uno. La nueva vía de monetización incluso admite pruebas gratis por 7 días.
Quienes compren las membresías para los podcasts de Spotify recibirán insignias que se podrán mostrar junto a su perfil al momento de comentar publicaciones. Una iniciativa interesante y que ya se está poniendo en marcha con títulos seleccionados (y bastante populares) como The Shawn Ryan Show, Two Hot Takes y The Adam Friedland Show.
Eso sí, las nuevas membresías no llegarán a todos los países de inmediato. Spotify está ofreciendo esta herramienta para podcasts en 34 mercados, entre los que se encuentra España. Por lo pronto, Latinoamérica no aparece entre los territorios contemplados. Seguramente se expandirá a más lugares con el correr del tiempo, aunque no hay precisiones en tal sentido.

articles.title: Google’s more personalized Gemini AI is heading to your car
articles.text:
Google is bringing Personal Intelligence to Gemini AI in your car. With this update, Gemini in Android Auto and cars with Google built-in can tap into your information across Google apps, including Gmail, Calendar, Maps, Photos, YouTube, and Search.
Google’s more personalized Gemini AI is heading to your car
Gemini AI can now draw from Gmail, Calendar, Maps, Photos, and other apps while you drive.
As an example, Google says you can ask Gemini about your flight status if you’re driving to the airport. The AI assistant can pull your flight details from a confirmation message in Gmail and then use that information to look up the status. You can also ask Gemini to “take me to my doctor’s appointment” instead of pulling up directions manually, or ask it to “find the car wash from the photo I took last week and navigate there.”
Google brought its Gemini assistant to Android Auto last year before rolling it out to cars with Google built-in in April. Several carmakers—including Ford, GM, Honda, Nissan, Volvo, and Polestar—have shipped newer cars with Google built-in, which adds support for native Android apps.
Google says it will connect your apps to Gemini only if you enable its Personal Intelligence setting. It will also share personalized responses only if you have your phone connected to your car. “If you don’t use Personal Intelligence, everything in the car still works: You can use navigation, listen to music, make calls, and ask questions, but the answers won’t be tailored to you,” Google says.
Personal Intelligence is rolling out to Android Auto today, with support coming to cars with Google built-in in the coming months.

articles.title: Forscher entdecken ersten grünen Stern: Ist das Universum doch bunter, als bisher angenommen?
articles.text:
Bunter als gedacht: Warum tote Sterne rosa, blau und sogar grün leuchten können
Forscher:innen haben den ersten grünen Stern entdeckt. Dabei handelt es sich um einen Weißen Zwerg, also einen kleinen, alten Stern. Bisher galt die Temperatur als farbbestimmend: Kühle Sterne erscheinen orange, Sterne wie die Sonne weiß und die heißesten blassblau. Laut einer aktuellen Studie spielen allerdings auch andere Faktoren eine Rolle. Die Ergebnisse wurden in der Fachzeitschrift RAS Techniques and Instruments veröffentlicht.
Universum könnte bunter sein als vermutet
Weiße Zwerge erhielten ihren Namen, weil sie bei ihrer Entdeckung weiß oder blassblau leuchteten. Laut der neuen Studie könnte das aber mit ihrer Entfernung zusammenhängen, weshalb Forscher:innen ihre wahre Farbe von der Erde aus schlicht nicht erkennen konnten. „Niemand hatte sich wirklich damit beschäftigt, was bei Weißen Zwergen sonst noch möglich sein könnte“, sagte Teamleiter Mark Hollands von der University of Warwick gegenüber Space. „Es stellt sich heraus, dass diese unglaublich dichten Sterne Farben erzeugen können, die niemand erwartet hätte, und einige davon haben mich wirklich überrascht.“
Der Schlüssel zur regenbogenartigen Farbpalette der Himmelskörper ist ihre Dichte. Weiße Zwerge entstehen, wenn Sterne mit etwa der Masse der Sonne der Brennstoff ausgeht und ihre Kerne unter der Schwerkraft kollabieren. Die Materie ist danach millionenfach dichter als die Photosphäre der Sonne. Unter diesen Bedingungen wechselwirken Elemente wie Kohlenstoff, Kalzium und Natrium mit dem dichten Heliumplasma und absorbieren Licht über einen breiteren Farbbereich. So verschieben sich die Farben weg vom bekannten Weiß-Blau.
WD J1330+6435 ist der erste grüne Stern
Weiße Zwerge mit hohem Kohlenstoffgehalt schimmern rosa oder violett. Solche, die mit Trümmern verschlungener Asteroiden oder Kometen angereichert sind, wirken laut den Forscher:innen eher gelblich. Kühlere Weiße Zwerge mit gemischten Wasserstoff- und Heliumatmosphären leuchten oft cyanfarben oder blassblau, da Wasserstoffmoleküle mit Heliumatomen kollidieren. Besonders auffällig wird die Färbung allerdings, wenn einer dieser „lebenden Toten” beginnt, sich von Planeten in seiner Umgebung zu ernähren. Manche erscheinen dadurch sogar ein wenig grün.
Ein Beispiel dafür ist WD J1330+6435, der etwa 326 Lichtjahre entfernt ist. Er hat laut den Forscher:innen gesteiniges Material von einem planetarischen Begleiter aufgenommen, wodurch seine Atmosphäre mit Kalzium, Lithium und Natrium angereichert wurde – und dadurch entstand der grüne Farbton. „Die Natriumspuren in der Atmosphäre dieses Weißen Zwergs absorbieren den orangefarbenen Teil des Spektrums und hinterlassen ein gespenstisches grünes Leuchten”, so Holland gegenüber Space. Da bisher noch von keinem anderen Stern glaubwürdig berichtet wurde, dass er grün ist, gilt WD J1330+6435 als der erste bekannte grüne Stern.
Die meisten Weißen Zwerge sind weiß
Trotz dieser Vielfalt bleibt Weiß nach Einschätzung des Teams die häufigste Farbe der Weißen Zwerge. Nur fünf der 151 toten Sterne im Umkreis von etwa 65 Lichtjahren um die Erde zeigen eine außergewöhnliche Färbung. „Einer von dreißig klingt vielleicht nicht nach einem großen Anteil, aber bezogen auf die gesamte Anzahl der Weißen Zwerge im Universum sind das immer noch sehr viele seltsam gefärbte Sterne da draußen“, kommentierte Boris Gänsicke vom Fachbereich Physik der Universität Warwick. „Betrachtet man aber den Median einer repräsentativen Population von Weißen Zwergen, stellt man fest, dass der durchschnittliche Weiße Zwerg tatsächlich weiß ist.“

articles.title: OVHcloud CLI releases backdoored on GitHub to steal developer secrets
articles.text:
French cloud and hosting provider OVHcloud is warning users that attackers compromised its open-source command-line interface (CLI) tool to distribute information-stealing malware.
The attacker hijacked a developer’s GitHub account to gain access to the OVHcloud CLI repository and modify versions 0.11.0 through 0.15.0 of the tool.
OVHcloud offers the CLI tool as an alternative for system administrators and developers to manage cloud and hosting services directly from a terminal, including for automating tasks.
OVHcloud CEO Octave Klaba disclosed that the company’s CLI repository on GitHub had been compromised, urging users who downloaded the latest version yesterday to update or remove the tool.
Klaba said that the compromised release appeared at 14:47 on October 19 and was detected and blocked at 16:21 after a customer reported it.
"The compromised versions are v0.11.0 v0.12.0 v0.13.0 v0.14.0 v0.15.0," the CEO said, adding that older version 0.10.0 and the latest release 0.16.0 were clean.
Despite the poor quality of the malware, its purpose was to "retrieve secrets from the disk," Klaba explained.
In a later update, Klaba shared that GitHub’s release immutability setting was disabled, allowing a sufficiently privileged account to modify existing releases without passing CI/CD checks.
"The entire set of CI/CD pipelines with unit tests, functional tests, CVE detection, etc., were not impacted."
OVHcloud has enabled GitHub’s release immutability feature and considers the incident resolved.
However, Klaba urges users who downloaded a compromised CLI package to perform a system cleanup and revoke all secrets.
"The quality of the binary is poor but it can go all the way. If you are affected, please change all the secrets on your disk."
GlassWorm connection
According to OpenSourceMalware, a community-driven threat intelligence platform, the attack was likely part of a new GlassWorm operation, known for campaigns since late 2025 that impacted the VSCode, OpenVSX, GitHub, and npm software development ecosystems.
The researchers confirmed that the attacker did not tamper with the CI/CD pipelines and uploaded malware-infected packages built locally.
The researchers note that the GitHub account used in the attack had been compromised for more than half a year.
"Its public repositories show a scripted history rewrite on 5 March 2026 and a hidden preinstall.js loader that decodes to a second stage using a Solana memo dead drop," OpenSourceMalware researchers found.
Although the associated wallet is a known GlassWorm indicator, the researchers did not analyze the malicious payload delivered through a trojanized version of the OVHcloud CLI.
According to OpenSourceMalware's report, affected platforms are macOS (Intel and ARM), Linux (x86_64 and ARM64), and Windows x86-64. Source builds and Docker images remained unaffected.
Anyone who ran an affected binary should treat all secrets on the machine as compromised.

articles.title: Elon Musk et Anthropic s'engagent à redistribuer les richesses générées par l’IA
articles.text:
« Il est courant que les entreprises technologiques offrent des rémunérations progressives à leurs dirigeants. Nous, au contraire, orientons ces capitaux vers le bien public » : Anthropic a annoncé la création de l’Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, une entité dédiée à la redistribution d’une partie des bénéfices générés par l’intelligence artificielle. Elon Musk a réagi à cette annonce en présentant sa vision des choses et en faisant une promesse à tous les enfants américains.
Anthropic crée un fonds pour redistribuer les bénéfices générés par l’IA
Anthropic a annoncé le lancement de l’Anthropic Public Benefit Fund. Pour être plus précis, il s’agit d’une LLC (Limited Liability Company), c’est-à-dire une entité juridique américaine entièrement détenue par Anthropic. Son principe est relativement simple : redistribuer une partie des bénéfices de l’entreprise à des personnes dans le besoin ou à des entités d’intérêt public. Anthropic explique : « nous pourrions envisager des dons importants à des organisations à but non lucratif traditionnelles ou des distributions directes à des populations spécifiques », tout en précisant ensuite que « L’impact sur le marché du travail en est un exemple ».
L’intelligence artificielle risquant d’entraîner d’importantes pertes d’emploi dans certains secteurs, Anthropic voudrait donc aider financièrement les personnes concernées. Il ne s’agit pas ici d’un revenu universel, mais de fonds attribués dans le cadre de situations spécifiques. Anthropic précise au passage que cette entité ne sera « en aucun cas utilisée à des fins de lobbying ou de financement politique, que ce soit aux États-Unis ou à l’étranger ». Avec cette annonce, près de 20 % des actions d’Anthropic seront consacrées à l’intérêt général. Sous réserve de l’approbation des actionnaires, 5 % des actions seront attribués au nouveau fonds, dont la part pourrait encore augmenter en fonction de la valorisation de l’entreprise.
Elon Musk promet de donner une action de SpaceX à chaque enfant américain
Pour Elon Musk, il n’est pas question de financer des ONG, dont certaines, selon lui, défendent des intérêts politiques ou financiers. En réponse au post X d’Anthropic annonçant la création de l’Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, Elon Musk a donné sa vision de la répartition des bénéfices générés par les grands fournisseurs d’IA et fait une promesse pour le moins surprenante.
Le dirigeant de SpaceX recommande ainsi aux grands fournisseurs d’IA « de donner les actions directement au public », sans passer par des ONG ou toute autre entité se présentant comme d’intérêt général. Il effectue ensuite une annonce en grande pompe : « L’année prochaine, je donnerai une de mes actions SpaceX à chaque enfant en Amérique. Ce sera la première d’une longue série ». Comme le souligne l’Associated Press, cette promesse représenterait un don d’une valeur estimée à 10,66 milliards de dollars, sur la base du cours de clôture de l’action SpaceX et du nombre d’enfants vivant aux États-Unis.
Elon Musk et Anthropic affichent donc une vision résolument philanthrope de la redistribution des richesses générées par l’IA, tout en divergeant sur un point : les modalités de cette redistribution, directe ou indirecte, à la population. Il reste maintenant à voir comment ces belles promesses pourraient être appliquées dans les faits.

articles.title: Aspiration de 8 000 Pa et vidage automatique : le robot Roborock Q7 L5+ est à 179,99 €
articles.text:
Le robot aspirateur laveur Roborock Q7 L5+ avec station est à 179,99 € (-54 %)
Le robot aspirateur laveur Roborock Q7 L5+ combine navigation LiDAR, aspiration de 8 000 Pa et station de vidage automatique pour l’entretien quotidien des sols.
Amazon propose le robot aspirateur laveur Roborock Q7 L5+ blanc à 179,99 €, contre un prix conseillé de 389,99 €, soit une réduction de 54 %. Par rapport au prix le plus bas des 30 derniers jours, indiqué à 189,99 €, l’économie atteint 10 €, soit environ 5 %. L’appareil est vendu par Roborock Official EU et expédié par Amazon.
Une aspiration de 8 000 Pa et un parcours guidé par LiDAR
Le robot aspirateur laveur Roborock Q7 L5+ annonce une puissance d’aspiration maximale de 8 000 Pa. Ses brosses principale et latérale sont conçues pour limiter l’enroulement des cheveux et des poils. Cela ne dispense pas de leur entretien, mais vise à réduire les interventions nécessaires.
La navigation LiDAR PreciSense cartographie le logement pour organiser les déplacements. Depuis l’application Roborock, il est possible de programmer les séances, de sélectionner les pièces et de définir des zones interdites. Le fabricant annonce jusqu’à 150 minutes d’autonomie, une durée qui varie selon les réglages et les conditions d’utilisation.
Une station de vidage et une serpillière plate
La station RockDock Plus récupère automatiquement la poussière dans un sac de 2,7 litres. Roborock annonce jusqu’à sept semaines avant son remplacement, selon la fréquence des nettoyages et la quantité de saletés collectées. Elle réduit ainsi le besoin de vider manuellement le bac du robot après chaque passage.
Pour les sols durs, le robot peut aspirer et passer une serpillière avec trois niveaux de débit d’eau. Le lavage repose sur une lingette plate entraînée par les déplacements de l’appareil, sans rotation ni vibration. Le remplissage du réservoir et le nettoyage de la serpillière restent manuels : la station assure le vidage de la poussière et la recharge.

articles.title: Spotify : ce nouveau QR code pourrait sérieusement compliquer le partage de votre abonnement
articles.text:
Spotify renforce la vérification des abonnements Premium Famille avec un QR code à scanner en présence du gestionnaire. Une procédure qui pourrait compliquer le partage entre plusieurs foyers, avec des conséquences importantes pour ceux qui ne respectent pas le délai imposé.
Partager son abonnement Spotify avec cinq proches, c’est pratique pour réduire la facture. Encore faut-il vivre sous le même toit, une condition que la plateforme impose depuis longtemps, mais dont la vérification reposait principalement sur une adresse postale. Spotify semble désormais décidé à aller plus loin. Certains utilisateurs doivent confirmer leur présence physique auprès du titulaire de l’abonnement en scannant un QR code sur son téléphone. Une manipulation assez simple en apparence, mais qui pourrait compliquer les arrangements entre amis ou membres d’une famille vivant à plusieurs adresses.
Un QR code à scanner en personne pour conserver son abonnement
Comme le rapporte 9to5Google, Spotify déploie une nouvelle procédure destinée à vérifier que les membres d’un abonnement Premium Famille résident bien avec le propriétaire du compte.
Le fonctionnement est détaillé dans la documentation officielle française de Spotify. Lorsqu’un membre reçoit une demande de vérification, le gestionnaire doit ouvrir l’application Spotify sur son téléphone, accéder à la rubrique « Votre abonnement Premium », puis sélectionner « Gérer » pour afficher un QR code.
Le membre invité doit ensuite scanner ce code avec son propre smartphone. Les deux personnes sont censées se trouver au même endroit pour effectuer la manipulation.
Spotify précise que le QR code change toutes les quelques secondes, ce qui complique l’utilisation d’une simple capture d’écran envoyée à distance. La vérification s’effectue exclusivement depuis l'application mobile.
Et mieux vaut ne pas laisser traîner la notification. Les membres disposent de sept jours pour effectuer le contrôle. En cas d’échec, ils risquent de perdre leur accès Premium et de revenir à l’offre gratuite. Ils ne pourront pas non plus rejoindre un autre abonnement Famille ou Duo pendant douze mois. Spotify permet toutefois de retrouver le même abonnement partagé, sous réserve de remplir les conditions requises, ou de souscrire une offre individuelle.
Spotify serre la vis sur une règle qui existe depuis longtemps
Cette nouvelle vérification ne change pas les conditions de Premium Famille. L’offre reste réservée à six personnes maximum vivant à la même adresse, chacune disposant de son propre compte.
Jusqu'ici, Spotify vérifiait principalement le domicile déclaré lors de l’inscription ou lorsqu’une nouvelle confirmation était nécessaire. Une procédure que nous évoquions déjà dans notre guide consacré au partage des abonnements, et qui reposait largement sur la bonne foi des utilisateurs.
Avec le QR code dynamique, la plateforme cherche désormais à rendre les contrôles plus contraignants. Cela ne garantit pas pour autant qu’elle puisse établir durablement que deux personnes vivent ensemble : une vérification ponctuelle confirme surtout leur présence au même endroit à un instant donné.
Se pose enfin la question de la disponibilité. La procédure figure déjà dans l’assistance française de Spotify, mais le service ne précise ni les pays concernés par son déploiement actuel, ni le nombre d’abonnés qui recevront cette demande. Rien ne permet donc d’affirmer que tous les comptes Premium Famille français sont déjà soumis à ce contrôle.
Pour les familles qui partagent réellement le même logement, la nouveauté devrait se résumer à quelques manipulations supplémentaires. Pour ceux qui ont pris l’habitude de répartir le prix de l’abonnement entre plusieurs adresses, en revanche, il pourrait devenir plus difficile de conserver leurs habitudes.

articles.title: Orange éteint définitivement sa 2G : 1,7 million de SIM concernées, SFR et Bouygues suivront en décembre
articles.text:
Trente-quatre ans après le lancement d’Itinéris par France Télécom, Orange a éteint ce mardi 20 octobre son réseau 2G dans l’Hexagone, là où il fonctionnait encore. Quarante-trois départements de l’Hexagone étaient concernés, de la Normandie à la Gironde.
Cette coupure, annoncée dans un communiqué, boucle presque l’extinction de la 2G d’Orange, déjà terminée à La Réunion en octobre 2025. La fin de cette génération de téléphonie mobile s’était ensuite faite par vagues en métropole depuis le 31 mars, de Bayonne, Anglet et Biarritz jusqu’à 44 départements d’un coup le 6 octobre.
Un téléphone qui ne capte que la 2G ne peut plus appeler ni envoyer de SMS sur le réseau d’Orange. C’est aussi le cas chez Free Mobile, qui passe par ce réseau.
Pour Orange, la 2G, déployée dans les années 1990, « ne répond plus aux exigences actuelles en matière de connectivité ». Les fréquences occupées par cette norme vont être recyclées pour servir aux nouvelles générations que sont la 4G et la 5G. Orange avance aussi un argument énergétique en citant la Fédération française des télécoms : un gigaoctet transmis en 2G consomme jusqu’à 500 fois plus d’énergie qu’en 5G.
Quelques endroits garderont la 2G d’Orange un peu plus longtemps. À Mayotte, l’opérateur la coupera le 31 décembre. Quant aux zones blanches réglementaires, ces communes rurales où les opérateurs partagent les mêmes antennes, elles la perdront entre le 1er et le 15 décembre.
Plus d’un million de téléphones 2G encore actifs cet été
Fin juin 2026, 1,06 million de cartes SIM tournaient encore dans des téléphones et des tablettes qui ne fonctionnent qu’en 2G. Le chiffre vient de l’observatoire publié le 24 septembre par l’Arcep, le régulateur des télécoms. S’y ajoutaient 620 000 cartes glissées dans des alarmes, des téléassistances ou des systèmes de télésurveillance, soit près de 1,7 million au total.
Le régulateur pressait depuis des mois les opérateurs d’accélérer la migration de leurs abonnés vers la 4G. De son côté, le gouvernement avait prévenu les derniers utilisateurs dès mai 2025.
Chez SFR, la 2G s’arrête le 15 novembre 2026. Bouygues Telecom la coupe le même jour à Brest, Guipavas, Nancy et Vandœuvre-lès-Nancy, puis partout ailleurs entre le 1er et le 15 décembre. D’ici là, vérifiez que le vieux mobile ou la téléalarme que vous utilisez fonctionne bien en 4G.
