articles.title: Beam pulls single app windows off the Mac Mini running your agents
articles.text:
Beam pulls single app windows off the Mac Mini running your agents
Beam is a new Mac app that takes a window running on one Mac and puts it on another, where it behaves like a locally installed app. Why? Agents.
Serial founder Hiten Shah, who co-founded Crazy Egg and KISSmetrics, built it with Sam Asante under a company called Noats. It launched on Product Hunt on Tuesday and is aimed at the headless Mac Mini sitting in a closet running AI agents.
The pitch is great: Instead of opening Screen Sharing and steering a full remote desktop, a user picks a single window on the other machine, say a Terminal session or a browser window an agent is working in, and it opens alongside everything else on the Mac in front of them. It gets its own Dock icon and can be called using the Command+Tab switcher. Resizing the window resizes the window on the other Mac. Keyboard shortcuts work, files can be dragged across, and the app’s audio can play locally. The app itself never leaves the original machine. When one window isn’t enough, Beam can pull over a full display or the whole Mac.
Shah frames it around his own setup in his Product Hunt launch post, describing Macs running agents and local models “with work continuing even when nobody’s sitting in front of them.” Getting to one of those machines usually means Screen Sharing and a second desktop to navigate. Beam is meant to cut that down to the one window that matters.
Beam plays into the exploding ecosystem of Macs powering AI systems, so the app runs only on macOS. And both Macs need Apple Silicon, macOS Sonoma or later, and Beam installed. The machines find each other on the same Wi-Fi network, or anywhere through Tailscale.
The company says windows, keystrokes, clipboard, and audio travel directly between Macs, encrypted, and never pass through its servers. It also says hidden windows and password managers never show up in the window picker.
For devices without Beam, a share link opens a single window in any browser, view-only unless control is granted, and expires after anywhere from an hour to a week.
Asante said on Product Hunt that native iOS and Android apps are on the way.
Pricing depends on the setup. Hosting a Mac and joining a share link are free. Using your own Mac is free for 20 minutes a day, then $12 a month, $84 a year, or $199 for a lifetime license.
Beam follows where agents’ hardware is growing. The Mac Mini is becoming the default home for always-on agents, driven initially by OpenClaw, but others like Perplexity followed. Apple credited agentic workloads on its April earnings call.
The New Stack‘s Janakiram MSV caught the trend early and covered the shift in May, writing, “the Mac mini just became infrastructure.”
Beam isn’t the first to this problem. I used Astropad’s Workbench for a few weeks, and it let me remotely access agents on my desktop and through iOS apps. Workbench bets on mobile devices, while Beam bets that the unit of remote access should be the window, not the screen. Jump Desktop, Screens and Apple’s own Screen Sharing all cover the basics too.
Still, the problem is real and growing. The Mac stashed in a closet or on a rack is becoming a normal part of a developer’s setup. Beam’s answer is to stop treating it like a second desktop at all.

articles.title: Fine-tuning GPT-OSS-20B for multilingual reasoning on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Fine-tuning GPT-OSS-20B for multilingual reasoning on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod
GPT-OSS-20B is an open-weight reasoning model that thinks in English. Ask it to reason in French, German, Spanish, or Italian and it acknowledges the instruction, then produces its chain-of-thought in English anyway. On a 50-example multilingual reasoning test, the base model reasoned in the correct target language only 22 percent of the time. That 22 percent was almost entirely the English examples (English 100 percent, French 0 percent, German 10 percent, Spanish 0 percent, Italian 0 percent).
For teams deploying reasoning models for non-English users, that gap matters. A user who asks a question in French expects the model to reason and answer in French, not to switch to English mid-thought. Closing that gap is a fine-tuning problem. It raises a question every team faces once they start customizing open-weight models: supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reinforcement learning with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), or both?
In this post, we walk through how we fine-tuned GPT-OSS-20B for multilingual reasoning on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod. We show when SFT alone was sufficient and when GRPO added measurable value on top. To understand more broadly when GRPO helps, we also ran a controlled Qwen2.5-7B experiment across two tasks with different capability gaps. The short answer: SFT does most of the work, GRPO refines when there is headroom to refine, and matching the technique to the capability gap is what decides the outcome.
Solution overview
This section covers the multilingual reasoning task and dataset, how SFT and GRPO complement each other, and the training stack we ran on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod.
The task and dataset
The dataset is HuggingFaceH4/Multilingual-Thinking — a chain-of-thought reasoning dataset translated into French, Spanish, German, and Italian alongside English, roughly 949 training and 50 validation examples. The model receives a reasoning language: system-prompt instruction and must both reason and answer in that target language, overriding its strong English prior. The evaluation is 50 test cases: 10 math/logic problems across 5 languages (EN/FR/DE/ES/IT).
Two metrics matter:
- Reasoning-language correct – is the chain-of-thought in the requested language?
- Answer-language correct – is the final answer in the requested language?
How SFT and GRPO fit together
The clearest way to think about the two techniques: SFT teaches a behavior the model doesn’t have. GRPO optimizes a behavior the model can already sometimes produce. GRPO works by sampling a group of responses per prompt and pushing the policy toward the above-average ones. If the desired behavior has zero probability in the base distribution, there is very little for GRPO to reinforce. That single idea explains almost every result in this post.
The training stack
We ran on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod with Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) orchestration. For the initial SFT and GRPO runs on GPT-OSS-20B, we used the PyTorch TRL library. For the Qwen control experiment, we switched to veRL as the trainer, with Ray and KubeRay for distributed orchestration and vLLM for fast rollout generation. Checkpoints and datasets lived on Amazon FSx for Lustre, and the inter-node fabric used Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA). All fine-tuning used Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), which is parameter-efficient and well-suited to both SFT and GRPO.
The following diagram shows the training data path end-to-end. A submission from the user lands on the Amazon EKS control plane of the Amazon SageMaker HyperPod cluster. Amazon EKS schedules a Ray head pod plus worker pods that run the veRL trainer and vLLM rollout workers. Both sets of pods mount Amazon FSx for Lustre for the base model, training data, and checkpoints. Inter-node collectives use EFA. Rollouts stream from vLLM back to the veRL trainer, and the trainer writes checkpoints back to Amazon FSx for Lustre.
The following describes each hop in more detail. The submitter starts the run from Amazon SageMaker Studio or the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI). The Amazon EKS control plane on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod places pods on GPU nodes and starts a Ray head with worker pods for the veRL trainer and the vLLM rollout workers. Amazon FSx for Lustre provides shared, high-throughput storage for the base model, the training data, and the checkpoints. When training completes, the trainer writes the LoRA adapter back to Amazon FSx for Lustre for downstream evaluation or serving.
Prerequisites
To follow along, you need:
- An Amazon SageMaker HyperPod cluster with Amazon EKS orchestration. GPT-OSS SFT used 4× ml.g6e.12xlarge (16× L40S 48GB). The Qwen control used 2× g6e.48xlarge (16× L40S).
- An Amazon FSx for Lustre file system mounted on the cluster with a PersistentVolumeClaim named fsx-claim at /fsx.
- EFA-enabled instances and a working NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) and aws-ofi-nccl stack for multi-node SFT.
- A container registry such as Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) to hold the training image built from the reference repository.
- A HuggingFace access token for openai/gpt-oss-20b and the HuggingFaceH4/Multilingual-Thinking dataset.
- The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), kubectl, docker, and envsubst available on your workstation.
Set up the training environment
All of the commands, manifests, and scripts referenced below live in the awsome-distributed-ai GitHub repository under 3.test_cases/pytorch/trl/gpt-oss-lora-grpo/. Clone the repository and change into the test case directory:
Copy the environment template, then edit env_vars to set your ECR registry, image name, tag, and HuggingFace token:
Build the training image and push it to your registry. The image bundles PyTorch, TRL, HuggingFace Transformers, PEFT, and the training and inference scripts:
Point kubectl at your cluster and apply the FSx storage manager pod. The storage manager gives you a shell into the shared file system for checkpoint conversion and eval-log inspection:
Fine-tune GPT-OSS-20B with SFT and LoRA
We begin by measuring the base model, then configure the SFT run and examine the results.
The base-model gap
Base GPT-OSS-20B on the 50-case eval scored 22 percent reasoning-language correct (11/50). Per-language: English 100 percent, French 0 percent, German 10 percent, Spanish 0 percent, Italian 0 percent. The model defaults to English reasoning regardless of the instruction.
SFT configuration
The SFT setup used LoRA r=8, α=16, trained for 1,000 steps on 4× ml.g6e.12xlarge (16× L40S 48GB) with Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) full-shard, bf16 precision, and gradient checkpointing. The job runs as an elastic HyperPodPyTorchJob managed by Kueue, launched with hyperpodrun.
Apply the SFT manifest:
Watch training progress:
Loss and gradient norm print each step. A healthy run looks like this:
When training completes, convert the FSDP checkpoint to the Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) format that TRL’s GRPO trainer and the inference scripts expect:
SFT results and the staged learning curve
After SFT, the model reasons in the correct language 100 percent of the time (50/50) across all five languages. SFT learned this in two stages:
- Around step 200, the model learned to reason in the target language (reasoning-language metric hits 100 percent).
- Around step 1000, the model additionally learned to give the answer in the target language.
Final SFT eval (step 1000):
- Reasoning-language correct: 100 percent (50/50).
- Answer-language correct: 62 percent (31/50).
- Both correct: 62 percent (31/50).
- Per-language answer accuracy: FR 60 percent, DE 60 percent, ES 30 percent, IT 60 percent, EN 100 percent.
Takeaway: SFT is not optional here. The base model can’t follow the reasoning-language instruction at all, and SFT takes reasoning-language from 22 percent to 100 percent. The remaining gap is answer-language at 62 percent. That’s the harder half, because the final answer is short and the English prior is strongest there.
Refine answer-language with GRPO
Answer-language was the obvious target for GRPO. SFT already produced correct reasoning 100 percent of the time, and the model sometimes produced the answer in the right language, so there was a signal to reinforce.
Run GRPO on top of the SFT checkpoint
We ran GRPO with TRL’s GRPOTrainer, starting from the SFT checkpoint. The setup: load the SFT LoRA, call merge_and_unload, and add a new LoRA (r=8, α=16, about 0.068 percent trainable parameters, 13.6M of 20B). Training used K=8 generations per prompt, device_map=auto, learning rate 1e-6, and 10 epochs. The reward function scored answer-language (±5.0), reasoning-language (±1.5), and brevity (+0.5 or −1.0), for a combined range of −7.5 to +7.0.
Launch GRPO from the converted SFT checkpoint:
GRPO writes checkpoints to /fsx/checkpoints/grpo-singlenode/. Pick the best checkpoint against your held-out eval (the answer-language metric peaked early in this run) and convert it to PEFT format for inference and evaluation.
Result (from the SFT checkpoint):
- Reasoning-language correct: 100 percent (held: GRPO didn’t break what SFT taught).
- Answer-language correct: 62 to 70 percent (+8 points, 35/50).
- Both correct: 70 percent.
- Per-language answer: FR 70 percent, DE 80 percent, ES 60 percent, IT 40 percent, EN 100 percent.
GRPO delivered a real +8 point gain on the answer-language metric while holding reasoning at 100 percent. The gain came where there was headroom to gain. Answer-language was the sometimes-correct behavior that SFT had not fully converged on, and GRPO reinforced it.
Compare base, SFT, and GRPO inference side by side
To see the qualitative difference, deploy three inference pods that share the same base model but load different adapters:
Run the same French-reasoning prompt through each variant:
The base pod reasons in English despite the instruction. The SFT pod reasons in French but often answers in English. The GRPO pod reasons and answers in French. To reproduce the full 50-case eval that generated the numbers earlier, run the evaluation manifest and read the result file from the FSx storage manager:
To understand more broadly when GRPO adds value, we ran a controlled experiment on Qwen2.5-7B across two tasks with different capability gaps.
Test the pattern with a Qwen2.5-7B control
To test the “match technique to capability gap” thesis on a different model and different tasks, we ran controlled experiments on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. The first task is the same multilingual reasoning task (where headroom exists). The second task is GSM8K, where the model is already at peak accuracy. This is an internal experiment, and the public repo has not yet been released.
Infrastructure: 2× g6e.48xlarge (16× L40S), EFA 100Gbps, FSx Lustre, Ray 2.44 + KubeRay 1.4.2, veRL v0.6.1, vLLM 0.8.4.
Arms: A = base, B = SFT-only, C = SFT+GRPO.
Multilingual reasoning (50 cases)
| Metric | A base | B SFT | C SFT+GRPO | Δ GRPO | 
| Structured format | 0% | 92% | 98% | +6 | 
| Reasoning language | 0% | 96% | 98% | +2 | 
| Answer language | 0% | 38% | 44% | +6 | 
| Both correct | 0% | 38% | 44% | +6 | 
GSM8K, a task with no headroom
On GSM8K, base Qwen2.5-7B already scores 90.5 percent (181/200). GRPO at step 30 also scores 90.5 percent. When most sampled groups are all-correct, the group-relative advantage collapses to zero, so there is no learning signal. This is the other half of the thesis: GRPO needs headroom (pass@k >> pass@1) to have anything to optimize. No headroom means no gain.
Best practices
- Start with SFT. GRPO cannot teach a behavior with zero base probability. It can only reinforce responses the model already sometimes produces. SFT took reasoning-language from 22 percent to 100 percent, and every GRPO win in this work was built on that SFT checkpoint.
- Use LoRA for both SFT and GRPO. LoRA r=8/α=16 was parameter-efficient (0.068 percent trainable), and on the Qwen control it stayed numerically stable through GRPO (grad norm 0.23, about 11.7 GB per GPU). It’s a strong default when you want SFT and GRPO to share the same adapter shape.
- Match the technique to the gap. Use SFT for missing behavior. Use GRPO for refining an existing, sometimes-correct behavior. GRPO’s realistic ceiling here was +6 to +8 points.
- Check for reward headroom before spending GPU-hours. If most groups are all-correct (GSM8K 90.5 percent base), the group-relative advantage collapses to zero and GRPO gets no gradient. Verify there is headroom (pass@k >> pass@1) before starting a GRPO run.
Clean up resources
To avoid ongoing charges, delete the workload resources and then the underlying infrastructure:
- Delete the training and inference pods and jobs:
- Scale down or delete the Amazon SageMaker HyperPod cluster or its node groups.
- Delete the Amazon FSx for Lustre file system once you have exported any checkpoints you want to keep.
- Delete any Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) buckets or objects used for training data or checkpoint archives.
Conclusion
We showed how to fine-tune GPT-OSS-20B for multilingual reasoning on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, and how to decide between SFT and GRPO. SFT did most of the work: reasoning-language went from 22 percent to 100 percent. GRPO added a real, modest refinement on top (answer 62 percent to 70 percent) where headroom existed. A parallel Qwen2.5-7B control confirmed the pattern. GRPO added +6 percent on multilingual reasoning, where there was room to improve. It added no gain on GSM8K, where the model was already at peak accuracy (90.5 percent).
Decision framework:
- Behavior the model can’t do at all: use SFT.
- Behavior it does sometimes, with headroom: use SFT then GRPO for a few points more.
- Model already at peak accuracy, or target has zero base probability: GRPO won’t help.
To try this yourself, walk through the test cases in the awsome-distributed-ai repository. For more on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, see the service detail page and the Amazon SageMaker HyperPod documentation. For a walkthrough of Ray on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, see the related post Running distributed training on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod with Ray and Amazon SageMaker Studio. The link will be added after that post is published. Share your results in the comments.

articles.title: Ya en Lidl (y rebajada a 88,99 euros) esta hidrolimpiadora Kärcher original con manguera de alta presión y 120 bares
articles.text:
Tener a punto el patio, la terraza o dejar el coche impecable sin necesidad de dejarse la espalda suele requerir una herramienta eficaz. Para facilitar estas tareas de exterior sin realizar una gran inversión, Lidl ha rebajado la hidrolimpiadora de alta presión Kärcher KHD 3 por solo 88,99 euros (frente a su PVP recomendado de 129,95 euros).
Limpiadora de alta presión Kärcher KHD 3
Si no llegas a tiempo a conseguir esta hidrolimpiadora en Lidl, en Amazon tienes una alternativa de la firma Cecotec que te puede interesar. Se trata de la HydroBoost 1600 Car&Garden, disponible por 79,90 euros y que tiene una potencia de 1.600 W, 135 bares y un caudal de 468 litros por hora.
Cecotec Hidrolimpiadora de Alta Presión HydroBoost 1600 Car&Garden
Una hidrolimpiadora de calidad a precio imbatible
Este modelo de la icónica marca alemana está diseñado para ofrecer un equilibrio perfecto entre compacidad, potencia y maniobrabilidad en entornos domésticos. Con sus 120 bares de presión máxima y un caudal de hasta 380 litros por hora, es capaz de arrancar la suciedad acumulada en baldosas, muebles de jardín, bicicletas, motocicletas y vehículos de forma rápida.
Incorpora la lanza pulverizadora Vario Power (VPS), que permite regular la presión del agua fácilmente con un simple giro, adaptando el chorro o la delicadeza o resistencia del material que vayas a limpiar.
También incorpora una boquilla con chorro puntual rotativo diseñada para desincrustar el barro o la suciedad más rebelde en piedra y hormigón. Asimismo, destaca su manguera de alta presión de cuatro metros, un rango de acción cómodo para trabajar sin necesidad de mover constantemente el cuerpo principal de la máquina.

articles.title: Trésor, Justice, État : l'IA chinoise DeepSeek doit disparaître des ordinateurs de l'administration américaine — Frandroid
articles.text:
Le Trésor, le département d’État et celui de la Justice ne peuvent plus utiliser DeepSeek, l’IA de la start-up chinoise du même nom. Le ministère américain de la Sécurité intérieure (DHS) a ordonné à toutes les agences fédérales civiles d’arrêter d’acheter ses produits et de les retirer de leurs systèmes informatiques. Le ministre Markwayne Mullin a signé l’ordre le 24 juillet, mais il n’a été rendu public que ce lundi 19 octobre, selon Reuters. Surtout, le texte vise aussi les logiciels d’autres éditeurs construits sur la technologie DeepSeek, y compris quand le nom n’apparaît nulle part.
Le DHS s’appuie sur le Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act, une loi de 2018 qui permet d’écarter un fournisseur jugé risqué des achats et des systèmes de l’État fédéral. Il a suivi une recommandation du Federal Acquisition Security Council, le comité chargé d’évaluer ces risques. L’ordre, publié ce mardi au Federal Register (le journal officiel américain), s’impose donc aux agences. Elles peuvent quand même demander des exceptions.
Le motif officiel est la sécurité nationale. Le DHS craint que les données sensibles des agents fédéraux deviennent accessibles aux autorités chinoises, puisque les serveurs de DeepSeek sont en Chine. Le ministère évoque aussi le risque de logiciels malveillants ou de failles dans les modèles.
Le Pentagone et le renseignement ne sont pas concernés, car le DHS n’a pas autorité sur eux. Ils avaient de toute façon pris de l’avance. Une loi adoptée en décembre 2025 visait déjà DeepSeek dans les systèmes de sécurité nationale du renseignement. Washington accuse aussi DeepSeek de distillation, une technique qui consiste à entraîner un modèle sur les réponses d’un autre. Anthropic, qui documente régulièrement les détournements de Claude, dit avoir repéré ce genre de tentatives de la part de DeepSeek.
Un modèle open source difficile à chasser
DeepSeek publie les poids de ses modèles V3 et R1 (les paramètres qui font tourner l’IA) sur Hugging Face et GitHub. N’importe qui peut donc les installer sur ses propres serveurs, sans envoyer une seule donnée en Chine. Sur le papier, l’ordre en tient compte, puisqu’il couvre les produits tiers « développés à partir d’implémentations DeepSeek ».
Le texte reste assez flou, il peut viser seulement les logiciels qui appellent DeepSeek par son API (l’interface qui permet de brancher le modèle dans un autre service). Il peut aussi viser une application dont les développeurs se sont servis de DeepSeek pour coder. La notice publiée ne dit pas non plus clairement si un modèle installé en local est concerné.
Sans oublier les passerelles d’IA comme OpenRouter. Ces services envoient chaque requête vers le modèle le moins cher ou le plus performant du moment. Une agence qui ne limite pas la liste des fournisseurs peut donc interroger DeepSeek sans le savoir.
Avec TikTok, la tâche était plus simple : l’administration visait une seule application, éditée par une seule entreprise, qu’il suffisait de retirer des téléphones de service. Un modèle ouvert, lui, peut être modifié, renommé et intégré dans n’importe quel produit. L’ordre demande d’ailleurs aux agences de surveiller les données qui sortent de leurs réseaux et de renforcer leurs journaux d’activité.
Pékin proteste et commande des cartes Nvidia par millions
La Chine n’a pas apprécié. Ce mardi, Mao Ning, porte-parole du ministère chinois des Affaires étrangères, a dénoncé une utilisation abusive du concept de sécurité nationale, comme le rélève TechCrunch.
Côté matériel, la Chine s’adapte aux règles américaines. Reuters a révélé ce mardi que ByteDance, Alibaba et Tencent avaient commandé plus de 3 millions de RTX Pro 5500 pour plus de 35 milliards de dollars (environ 31 milliards d’euros). Cette carte pour station de travail peut être exportée vers la Chine, alors que les H200 et B300 de Nvidia, plus puissantes, y sont interdites ou soumises à licence. Elle a autant de cœurs CUDA qu’une RTX 5090 et 84 Go de mémoire, de quoi faire tourner des modèles d’IA. Nvidia aurait prévenu ses clients qu’il ne pourrait livrer que 5 à 10 % des quantités demandées.
En France, l’ordre ne change rien sur le plan légal : il ne s’applique ni aux entreprises privées ni aux autres gouvernements. La CNIL avait d’ailleurs annoncé le 30 janvier 2025 qu’elle allait interroger DeepSeek, qui stocke les données de ses utilisateurs en Chine.

articles.text:
Good morning. ☀️ ️️️

M&A
Nedbank clears the final hurdle to take control of NCBA
Nine months after putting R13.9 billion ($855.5 million) on the table, Nedbank is finally at the end of its NCBA takeover.
The South African lender’s offer to acquire 66% of NCBA Group, one of East Africa’s largest banking groups, is now unconditional after clearing the remaining regulatory approvals.
Settlement begins this week, with the transfer of shares to Nedbank expected from early November. NCBA will become a Nedbank subsidiary, but keep its name, Nairobi headquarters, management, and Nairobi Securities Exchange (NSE) listing, according to its Monday filings.
Catch up: Nedbank first announced the deal in January. In February, Kenya’s capital markets regulator allowed it to buy 66% without making an offer for the entire company. The tender opened in May, and by July, shareholders had offered 79.9% of NCBA’s shares, more than Nedbank wanted. Those offers had to be scaled back to 66%.
Shareholders who sell will receive 80% of their payment in newly issued Nedbank shares and 20% in cash. The remaining 34% of NCBA will stay in public hands.
Between the lines: Nedbank is buying more than a Kenyan bank. NCBA already operates across Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania and Rwanda, with digital businesses in Ghana and Côte d’Ivoire. Its digital business accounted for 32% of group profit in 2025, and it disbursed KES 1.4 trillion ($10.8 billion) in digital loans.
The deal also shows how Nedbank’s Africa strategy has changed. In 2025, it sold its 21% stake in Ecobank and shifted towards markets where it can control the banking operation rather than remain a minority investor. NCBA gives it that control, plus customers, licences, and infrastructure across East Africa, without building them country by country.
What to watch: Nedbank has previously talked about using NCBA as a springboard into Ethiopia and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). Now it has the platform to try.
Happy customer service week.
Your success and ours are the same story. Happy Customer Service Week. This year’s theme is The Extra Mile, and it’s the only way we know how to do this. Visit: fincra.com.
Fintech
Why Onafriq shut down its Nigerian agent banking business
In hindsight, it is not hard to see the play Onafriq, the pan-African payments company, was making when it expanded into Nigeria by acquiring Baxi in 2021.
Nigeria still relied heavily on cash, and Baxi already had more than 90,000 agents. Onafriq could enter with a ready-made distribution network instead of spending years building one.
The timing looked good, too. OPay and Moniepoint had begun building large agent networks in 2019, while PalmPay entered agent banking later. In 2021, Baxi was already one of Nigeria’s biggest independent agent networks, giving Onafriq an early lead over some newer competitors.
But the lead did not hold. By the end of 2024, PalmPay reportedly had more than 700,000 agents, while Moniepoint had over 800,000 point-of-sale (PoS) terminals. But as of 2025, Baxi had just over 460,000 agents, paling in comparison. In October, it finally decided to shut down the business, months after trying to sell Baxi.
Between the lines: Agent banking became a scale game. Rivals poured money into terminals, agent recruitment, and incentives, making it easier to close the distribution gap. At the same time, agents could work with several providers, making a large network less defensible than it first appeared.
The economics also changed. More terminals entered the market much faster than transaction volumes grew, so providers competed over the same payments.
Meanwhile, account-to-account (A2A) transfers—direct bank payments—gave customers another way to move money without visiting an agent.
Onafriq’s attempt to sell Baxi before shutting it down shows that the problem was bigger than one bad year. The company had already decided the agent business no longer fit where it wanted to put capital.
Zoom out: Onafriq bought Baxi partly because physical distribution was scarce. Five years later, the market had plenty. Being early gave Baxi a head start, but it did not stop competitors from catching up and, eventually, passing it.
Ten years of telling African tech stories.
Class of 2016, stand up! Meet the storytellers behind a decade of storytelling for African tech. 230+ startups, VCs, and more. From first cheques to unicorns. Have a story to tell? Let’s make it count. #TheWimbarts
Ecommerce
South African union want Shein and Temu banned to protect local jobs
Behind the low-cost tops you see on Shein and Temu is a dispute over how foreign shopping platforms compete with local businesses, and what that means for the people who make and sell clothes in South Africa.
What happened? The Congress of South African Trade Unions (COSATU), the country’s largest trade union federation, wants South Africa to ban Shein and Temu. It backed a proposal from the Southern African Clothing and Textile Workers’ Union (SACTWU), which says the platforms hurt local jobs by undercutting domestic retailers and manufacturers.
Explain like I’m new here: Shein entered South Africa in 2020, while Temu followed in 2024. Both sell directly to consumers online, offering a wide range of clothing and other goods at prices that traditional retailers can find hard to match. A 2025 study by the Localisation Support Fund (LSF), a South African organisation focused on strengthening local production, estimated that Shein and Temu generated R7.3 billion ($444 million) in South African sales in 2024, equivalent to roughly 3.6% of the country’s retail market.
Can South Africa ban them? South Africa has already taken steps to narrow the tax advantage to benefit some low-value imports. Previously, goods worth less than R500 ($30.41) were cheaper to bring into the country. In 2024, the South African Revenue Service (SARS), the country’s taxman, introduced value-added tax (VAT) on low-value imports and subsequently ended their special customs-duty treatment.
However, COSATU’s proposal goes further than changing tax rules. If both platforms are banned, some consumers could pay more without automatically creating new jobs in local factories. South Africa still has to work out how to protect local jobs while allowing competition and preserving affordable choices for shoppers. Closing tax loopholes is one part of that effort; making local manufacturers more competitive is another.
Don’t miss Moonshot 2026 for anything in the world!
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. We’ve filtered the noise out of Moonshot 2026, optimising the conference strictly for high-calibre connections between startup founders, global financial operators, enterprise leaders and individuals rewiring Africa’s technical frameworks. Join us on October 28 & 29, 2026. Get your ticket.
Telecoms
Cameroon wants to put more Internet on its electricity poles
Building a fibre-optic network requires a place to lay the fibre, permission to use the land, and a lot of money. But what if the poles that already carry electricity could also help carry the Internet? Cameroon is exploring that option.
What happened? On October 16, Camtel, Cameroon’s state-owned telecoms operator, and Socadel, the country’s electricity provider, signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to explore sharing infrastructure for fibre deployment.
How would it work? Camtel has the fibre network and telecoms expertise, and Socadel has electricity infrastructure, such as utility poles and rights-of-way. Instead of Camtel building entirely new infrastructure to carry fibre cables, it could attach overhead cables to suitable electricity poles and use existing routes to reach more locations. The two companies will now study whether they can combine those assets for faster Internet access.
Cameroon has tried this before: In 2023, the government transferred about 812 kilometres (km) of overhead fibre that Eneo, Socadel’s predecessor, had installed on electricity poles along Cameroon’s southern interconnected grid to Camtel.
That network served major cities including Douala and Yaoundé, its capital, and added to Camtel’s fibre infrastructure, which stood at about 12,000km. The latest agreement focuses on closer infrastructure sharing, including the possibility of incorporating fibre into future electricity infrastructure projects.
What happens next? The companies have not yet announced a nationwide rollout or a specific number of new kilometres. Their immediate job is to determine where the arrangement makes sense and identify pilot sites. If the model works, Camtel could expand fibre routes without building every supporting telecom structure from scratch, reducing deployment costs.

articles.title: Visiting Slate’s first showroom as its $25,000 electric truck nears production
articles.text:
As I sat in the cab of the pickup truck and manually rolled down the windows, I closed my eyes and, for the briefest moment, flashed back to opening the windows on a cold, winter day in my dad’s 1975 Ford Ranger to let more cigarette smoke escape. I opened my eyes and looked through the windshield at a wall in the Slate Customer Experience Center studded with bright color chips.
Last week, in a former Tesla store staffed by some former Tesla employees, Slate opened its first showroom. Located in the Fulton Market District just northwest of the Chicago Loop, the Slate Experience Center is a place for would-be buyers to poke around a prototype, check out customization options, buy some Slate merch, and even preorder a new Slate Truck with a $300 deposit.
Designed for the American obsession with pickup trucks, the Slate Truck is a bare-bones electric pickup truck retailing for $24,950. It sports plastic panels, a minimalist interior design sensibility, actual window winders, and a projected range of 205 miles. Ars went for a ride in a Slate Truck over the summer, but we haven’t had a chance to shop for one. So I stopped by the Slate Experience Center so I could, er, experience the Slate.
The Slate Customer Experience Center in Chicago on a bright autumn day.
Eric Bangeman/Ars Technica
The Slate Customer Experience Center in Chicago on a bright autumn day.
Eric Bangeman/Ars Technica
Customers can wrap their Slate Truck with all the colors of the spectrum.
Eric Bangeman/Ars Technica
Customers can wrap their Slate Truck with all the colors of the spectrum.
Eric Bangeman/Ars Technica
The Slate Customer Experience Center in Chicago on a bright autumn day.
Eric Bangeman/Ars Technica
Customers can wrap their Slate Truck with all the colors of the spectrum.
Eric Bangeman/Ars Technica
Upon walking into the showroom on a Monday morning, the first thing I noticed was a marquee-style sign on the wall boldly and brightly serving as a price tag for the black truck parked in the middle of the showroom. The vibe was industrial-barn-chic-meets-SoHo-loft. Three other people were there, and another shopper entered as I left. One man alternated between sitting in the cab, peering at the truck as he walked around it, and peppering Manager of Customer Experience Steve Purdy with questions.
The showroom has been open since October 15, launching with a three-day event that offered ridealongs. Interest has been strong, Purdy told me, and while he couldn’t provide sales numbers, he said the response has been “incredible.”
“We’re really happy with the number of [$300] deposits we’ve gotten since we opened,” Purdy said.
I was hoping there would be at least two Slate Trucks on site so I could compare build quality between trucks and check things like panel gaps, window operation, and chassis creaks. But only one truck was on display. And it wasn’t close to a production model; rather, the black Slate Truck was a hand-built older prototype with a black wrap (the Slate Truck base color is gray). The bed and passenger sides were cordoned off, but the driver-side door was open so shoppers could hop in and check out the interior.
It was bigger than I expected—to my eye, roughly the size of a Hyundai Santa Cruz. The tailgate was down, and it felt reassuringly sturdy when I pressed down on it. The 5-foot-long (152.4 cm) bed floor looked and felt durable, not much different from any other pickup on the market.
I really wanted to jump up and down on the tailgate. But I couldn’t even sit on it.
Eric Bangeman/Ars Technica
I really wanted to jump up and down on the tailgate. But I couldn’t even sit on it.
Eric Bangeman/Ars Technica
You roll down the windows the old way.
Eric Bangeman/Ars Technica
You roll down the windows the old way.
Eric Bangeman/Ars Technica
The early prototype on display in the showroom.
Eric Bangeman/Ars Technica
The early prototype on display in the showroom.
Eric Bangeman/Ars Technica
You roll down the windows the old way.
Eric Bangeman/Ars Technica
The early prototype on display in the showroom.
Eric Bangeman/Ars Technica
The exterior passed the eye test, with the panels appearing well-fitted. The doors sat flush with the surrounding body panels when closed. Of course, I was looking at a prototype carefully built to be poked and prodded by automotive reporters and the general public, so the level of fit and finish was no surprise. The challenge for Slate will be getting consistent build quality with minimal panel gaps, watertight seals, consistent door-to-fender transitions, and hood/frunk alignment. The Slate assembly line in Warsaw, Indiana, is still making prototyping runs at this point, Purdy told me, and the company is hoping to start on production models “soon.”
I hopped inside the cab once I got the opportunity, and the door closed with a solid-sounding “thunk.” It’s spartan inside, with a small screen for the instrument panel, a phone holder, physical climate controls, and window winders. The seats were both supportive and comfortable, and, after moving my seat, I had ample legroom. While the seat slid back and forth smoothly, the seatback recline lever on the side didn’t work.
The shopping experience
Beyond the default Blank Slate body style, Slate offers two SUV options—the Squareback SUV and Fastback SUV—and an open-air kit. I asked Purdy if they were selling any of the SUVs. “Most customers are going with the truck configuration,” he said. “And then they’re customizing their trucks in the Slate Garage.”
Being able to order online and have the truck delivered is a major attraction for those who can’t stand “the kabuki dance of f***ery at a dealership,” as one of my colleagues put it. But if you want to do all that at the Slate Experience Center, staffers will sit down and help you configure your customized Slate. There is a wall with removable dashboard panels across the color spectrum and a couple of miniature models of the cab with tiny, colored panels to help customers decide on the details.
All the headlight and taillight options for the Slate Truck are on display.
Eric Bangeman/Ars Technica
All the headlight and taillight options for the Slate Truck are on display.
Eric Bangeman/Ars Technica
Miniature interior models help customers visualize what their Slate Truck will look like.
Eric Bangeman/Ars Technica
Miniature interior models help customers visualize what their Slate Truck will look like.
Eric Bangeman/Ars Technica
All the headlight and taillight options for the Slate Truck are on display.
Eric Bangeman/Ars Technica
Miniature interior models help customers visualize what their Slate Truck will look like.
Eric Bangeman/Ars Technica
Purdy told me that Slate is staying the course with the $24,950 sticker price. But will customers actually get their Slate Trucks this year as the company promised? “We will ship some trucks by the end of the year,” Purdy said. “Those will go to investors and employees, with early orderers receiving their Slate Trucks in early 2027.
For service, Slate will be using RepairPal. Owners will be able to choose from 4,000 shops, some of which can service the high-voltage electrical systems and others limited to body damage, Purdy said. For scratches or minor dings from fender benders, owners can replace the exterior body panels themselves. Pricing for replacement parts has yet to be finalized. And Slate is confident the plastic body panels will weather climate extremes without a hitch. “We’re a Michigan company,” Purdy reminded me.
Monday morning is not exactly prime time for dealership traffic, but a handful of prospective customers were in the showroom, which is a promising sign. While there is no shortage of electrified pickup trucks on the market, there is a shortage of affordable ones. At $25,000, the Slate Truck costs far less than a Rivian R1T, Tesla Cybertruck, Chevy Silverado EV, or any currently shipping battery-electric truck. It could be a breakout hit—especially if Slate can beat Ford’s sub-$30,000 Fathom pickup to market.
But the sleek-looking showroom and an attractive prototype still face a production reality check. Tesla had significant quality-control problems with early Model Ys, with customers receiving cars with loose seats and broken seatbelts, and some Cybertrucks have shipped with misaligned panel gaps. A new player is entering the game, but production is still on the (near) horizon, and no one knows if the Slate Trucks delivered to customers will live up to the promise of the carefully hand-built prototypes. People are definitely very interested in Slate. Now it’s time to deliver.
Eric Bangeman is the Managing Editor of Ars Technica. He lives in the northwest suburbs of Chicago, where he enjoys road cycling and plays bass in a band.
The black truck featured in this article was one of their earlier prototypes. The Slate guy I talked to at the event indicated that the other vehicles there were more recent. In addition to the roped off one, there was a grey truck (which I believe was the true base model) as well as an SUV configuration with a wrap. The SUV you could get in and sit and adjust the seats and look all over. I found the legroom quite good front and rear even with the seat fully retracted. Back seat access is only available from the passenger side. Seats are limited manually adjusted and acceptable moderately firm.
I did a ride-along, I’d compare the ride quality to a classic Ford Ranger. It handled the uneven Chicago road fine. No complaints. There wasn’t any opportunity to test its acceleration really due to lunch hour traffic.
The crowd did skew older, probably on account of it being a Thursday.
Regarding the manual windows, I tried them in the SUV and honestly the mechanism felt really good. Better than my old Rangers I’ve had.
The frunk is spacious, I think probably an entire shopping cart full of groceries can fit easily. Not quite Costco sized but not far off. The truck config has very little space behind the seats so I think the frunk will actually be used.
The SUV config is literally a roll cage and capper stuck in between the truck rear glass panel, with the bolster removed. Slate Guy told me it is possible to buy the SUV config and convert it to truck again if you buy the bolster, but final details on that aren’t finished.
Fasteners, at least on the outside, are generally exposed Torx T30 and imo panels look easy to swap. The actual panels seem really sturdy, more so than the super thin aluminum/steel common to normal cars. It’s like a composite and Slate Guy said the grey color is the actual material color all the way through.
The only downside I found is the heat is resistive, not a heat pump.
If I can I’ll try to post pictures I took.
(Edited for formatting and pictures)

articles.title: Gemini de Google logra terminar Minecraft después de 27 horas y sin ayuda humana
articles.text:
Cuatro agentes de inteligencia artificial lograron lo que hasta ahora parecía reservado a los jugadores humanos: terminar Minecraft de principio a fin sin ninguna ayuda externa. La hazaña la realizó Gemini 4 Argon, el modelo de Google DeepMind, que después de 27 horas y 14 minutos de juego consiguió derrotar al Ender Dragon, el jefe final del videojuego.
El experimento, descrito en un documento publicado por Google DeepMind y firmado por los investigadores Maxence Faldor, Satinder Singh y Roberta Raileanu, consistió en soltar a cuatro agentes dentro de un mundo de supervivencia generado al azar, en dificultad fácil.
La única instrucción fue clara: vencer al dragón. Nadie les dio un mapa, una estrategia ni herramientas diseñadas especialmente para el juego.
Cómo juega Minecraft una IA sin manos ni ojos
A diferencia de un jugador humano, los agentes no ven la pantalla ni usan teclado. Cada uno controla a su personaje a través de Mineflayer, una biblioteca de código abierto que les permite escribir programas en JavaScript para moverse, construir o pelear.
El proceso funciona así: el agente escribe un programa corto, por ejemplo, caminar hasta determinadas coordenadas y extraer todo el mineral de hierro cercano. Luego lee el resultado (su posición, su salud, lo que encontró o el error que tuvo) y, con esa información, escribe el siguiente programa.
En total, los cuatro agentes redactaron 2.783 programas distintos, que sumaron 63.313 líneas de código. Cada programa duró en promedio 33,5 segundos, y los agentes tuvieron código corriendo apenas el 40% del tiempo: el resto lo usaron para leer resultados y pensar el siguiente paso.
Completar Minecraft desde cero exige pasar por tres mundos distintos: conseguir herramientas en la superficie, obtener varas de blaze y perlas de Ender en el Nether, y finalmente localizar una fortaleza subterránea para entrar al End, donde vive el dragón.
Cómo surgió la división del trabajo
Nadie asignó roles a los agentes. Aun así, cada uno terminó especializándose en una tarea distinta a medida que avanzaba la partida.
Janesick fabricó herramientas, encontró la fortaleza del Nether y calculó la ubicación de la guarida subterránea. Gyldenia se encargó de reunir comida y suministros, y más tarde destruyó seis de los diez cristales que protegían al dragón. Auratian encendió el portal y descubrió cómo llegar a esos cristales sin necesidad de un pico. Bulicame ayudó a construir refugios para defenderse de los Endermen y asestó el golpe final.
Se coordinaron entre ellos mediante el chat del juego, donde intercambiaron 229 mensajes: avisos de peligro, coordenadas exactas, consejos sobre errores del sistema y rescates de objetos cuando alguno moría. También llevaron una memoria compartida con notas sobre trucos y fallos del propio Mineflayer, para no repetir los mismos errores dos veces.
El equipo murió 605 veces antes de ganar. La mayoría de esas muertes, 351, las causaron monstruos comunes. El dragón mató a los agentes 69 veces, el ahogamiento 67, las caídas al vacío 57 y la lava 47.
El experimento avanzó con dificultad durante la batalla final contra el dragón, que llegó a extenderse por casi 14 horas. El problema era que diez cristales ubicados sobre pilares de obsidiana le devolvían salud constantemente al monstruo.
Cerca de la hora 21, el agente auratian descubrió que esos cristales podían destruirse a golpes sin necesidad de un pico: bastaba apilar bloques de tierra para subir junto a cada pilar, golpear el cristal y bajar de nuevo. En las cuatro horas y cuarenta minutos siguientes, el equipo destruyó los diez cristales. Treinta y nueve minutos después, el dragón cayó derrotado.
Qué significa este resultado y qué limitaciones tiene
Los investigadores destacan que es la primera vez que agentes de inteligencia artificial completan Minecraft de principio a fin sin rutas prefijadas ni programas diseñados por humanos para el juego. El reto evaluó la capacidad de un equipo para sostener un plan durante miles de pasos a lo largo de más de un día, habilidad útil también en ingeniería de software real.
El propio estudio admite límites: jugaron en dificultad fácil, Mineflayer les reveló información invisible para un humano, el 22% de los programas falló y fue una sola partida, sin garantía de repetirse.
Como referencia, los humanos tardan en promedio 45 horas en completar la historia principal, aunque el récord de speedrun baja de siete minutos.

articles.title: Espoo's Coherence Quantum raises €2.78 million to build infrastructure for larger quantum computers | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Coherence Quantum, an Espoo-based quantum hardware company developing an integrated cryogenic signalling and control platform for future quantum computers, has raised €2.78 million in Seed funding to develop a new approach to the cryogenic infrastructure surrounding solid-state quantum processors.
The round was led by Helsinki-based early-stage investor Lifeline Ventures, with participation from technology entrepreneur Mårten Mickos.
Petteri Koponen of Lifeline Ventures said, “The quantum industry has proved that increasingly capable processors can be built. The next challenge is building the infrastructure that allows them to scale. Coherence Quantum is going after a fundamental part of that problem.
“They have an exceptional technical team with a clear view of where the industry is heading and the ambition to build far more than a single component. If quantum computers are going to scale, the architecture around the qubits has to scale with them, and we’re backing them to become a key part of how larger quantum computers are built.”
Coherence Quantum was founded in 2026 by Aashish Sah (CEO), Suman Kundu (CTO), and Erkki Soininen (CPO), and originated from research at Aalto University’s Quantum Computing and Devices group. The company is also supported by founding advisor Mikko Möttönen, a professor of quantum technology at Aalto University.
Sah is a quantum physicist specialising in superconducting qubits and their interaction with the electromagnetic environment. Kundu is an experimental quantum physicist who played a key role in building and setting up Aalto University’s 20-qubit Q20 quantum computer. Soininen holds a PhD in Physics and previously held a product leadership role at the cryogenics company Bluefors.
Coherence Quantum is developing an integrated cryogenic signalling and control platform for solid-state quantum computers, including superconducting and spin-qubit systems. 
According to the company, its goal is to help quantum systems scale, enabling more qubits while maintaining the low-noise, high-coherence environment needed for reliable operation.
But it says that scaling quantum computers by adding more qubits creates another scaling problem: everything needed to control them must scale as well. “As quantum processors grow, more control and readout signals need to reach the quantum processing unit (QPU). Conventional approaches require more wiring and signal-conditioning hardware inside a system with very limited space and cooling power. At the same time, the qubit environment has to remain protected from thermal noise and other disturbances that can affect performance,” the Finnish startup explained.
Coherence Quantum claims to be developing an integrated cryogenic signalling and control platform to address this scaling challenge. It notes that its first technologies focus on cryogenic signal conditioning, helping protect the environment around the qubit. From there, the company is developing higher-density signal interfaces and working towards bringing more control functionality inside the cryostat and closer to the quantum processing unit.
Sah said, “Quantum computers won’t scale by adding qubits alone. The infrastructure around them has to scale too. We’re starting with signal conditioning and building towards higher-density interfaces and, ultimately, more integrated cryogenic control. Our aim is to give quantum-computer builders an architecture that can support larger systems without wiring, cooling requirements, and complexity growing at the same rate.”
The company is building dedicated R&D, testing and manufacturing capabilities in Espoo, Finland, close to Aalto University and Finland’s growing quantum technology ecosystem. It plans to use the fresh capital to establish its lab in Espoo, build its first product prototypes and manufacturing process, continue R&D, and grow the team.
Starting with cryogenic signal-conditioning technologies, Coherence Quantum is working towards higher-density interfaces and increasingly integrated control inside the fridge. Its long-term ambition is to help establish a standardised blueprint for the cryogenic signalling and control stack, bringing its own technologies together with complementary technologies from across the quantum ecosystem.

articles.title: Ahold Delhaize Restoring Services Disrupted by Cyberattack
articles.text:
Dutch-Belgian grocery giant Ahold Delhaize has restored some of the services impacted by last week’s cyberattack and expects more to come back online within days.
On October 12, the company took its systems offline in response to “a security issue” within its network, which impacted its online services, including orders and deliveries across Europe and the US.
Without providing details on the incident, Ahold Delhaize confirmed last week that its local brands were affected, but said stores have remained open.
On Monday, the company confirmed that a cyberattack disrupted its services, which are now coming back online. Many of its European websites and applications are now restored, and Albert Heijn, its Dutch brand, is expected to resume home deliveries by Friday.
E-commerce services at Ahold Delhaize’s US brands are expected to be restored within days, but the company has not provided a specific timeframe.
“All stores across all brands have remained open throughout the incident, while we have continued the phased restoration of our systems and services to support the distribution of groceries to our brands’ customers as quickly as possible,” the grocery giant said.
While it refrained from sharing information on the type of cyberattack it fell victim to, Ahold Delhaize said it has no evidence that customer, associate, or partner data was stolen in the incident.
The company says it notified the Dutch National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) and relevant authorities shortly after discovering the attack and filed a formal police report this week.
“Taking systems offline to help protect them was a precautionary measure that affected most of our brands across Europe and the United States. Although this incident was caused by the malicious actions of others, we apologize for the inconvenience this has caused – especially to our customers,” Ahold Delhaize president and CEO Frans Muller said.

articles.title: SpaceX tentará capturar Starship e seu propulsor em pleno voo pela primeira vez
articles.text:
A SpaceX tentará capturar a nave Starship e seu propulsor Super Heavy durante o próximo voo de teste do sistema, previsto para novembro. O objetivo é recuperar as duas partes do veículo espacial com os braços mecânicos da torre de lançamento, em operação que, se bem-sucedida, será a primeira recuperação completa de um veículo lançador orbital da história.
O plano foi anunciado por Elon Musk, diretor-executivo da empresa, durante a apresentação dos resultados financeiros do terceiro trimestre, na terça-feira (20). Segundo o empresário, a próxima missão será a 15ª tentativa de voo da Starship em escala real.
“Se tivermos sucesso, será a primeira vez que um veículo lançador orbital terá sido totalmente recuperado”, afirmou Musk. Ele classificou a possível conquista como um marco tecnológico na história da civilização.
O executivo, porém, reconheceu que não há garantia de sucesso. Apesar disso, disse acreditar que a tentativa tem mais chances de dar certo do que de fracassar. Caso a operação não funcione, a SpaceX pretende continuar realizando testes até o fim do ano e aumentar a frequência dos voos em 2027.
Como funciona a tentativa de captura da Starship?
A Starship é um sistema de lançamento de dois estágios: o propulsor Super Heavy, responsável pela primeira etapa da subida, e a nave Starship, que constitui o segundo estágio. Juntos, eles formam um veículo com aproximadamente 120 metros de altura e nove metros de diâmetro.
O sistema utiliza motores Raptor, que queimam metano líquido e oxigênio líquido. Desde sua apresentação, em 2018, a Starship foi projetada para retornar ao local de lançamento e ser reutilizada.
Para isso, a SpaceX desenvolveu torres equipadas com braços mecânicos apelidados de “hashis” (chopsticks, em inglês). A estrutura pode agarrar o veículo durante o retorno, dispensando a necessidade de uma recuperação convencional no oceano.
A estratégia é importante porque a reutilização das duas partes permitiria à empresa recuperar componentes de um sistema orbital completo, em vez de perder o hardware a cada missão. O objetivo de longo prazo é tornar os lançamentos mais frequentes e ampliar a capacidade de transporte de cargas para o espaço.
Leia mais:
- Musk promete dar ações da SpaceX a todas as crianças dos EUA
- Dependência da Starlink preocupa governos e expõe poder de Elon Musk
- Elon Musk estuda fusão entre Tesla e SpaceX; negócio pode criar gigante de R$ 19,4 trilhões
Último voo da Starship chegou à órbita, mas terminou sem recuperação
- A tentativa anterior ocorreu em 28 de setembro, quando a Starship realizou seu 14º voo de teste e alcançou a órbita terrestre pela primeira vez. A missão também marcou a estreia do transporte de uma carga operacional: 26 satélites Starlink de terceira geração (V3);
- Apesar dos avanços, o voo apresentou problemas. Um dos motores Raptor do propulsor desligou prematuramente durante a subida, obrigando a equipe de controle da missão a adaptar o procedimento para continuar o lançamento;
- A SpaceX também encerrou a missão antes do previsto. O plano original previa aproximadamente dez horas de duração e seis voltas ao redor da Terra, mas o voo terminou após cerca de três horas e duas órbitas;
- Ao final, o Super Heavy caiu no Golfo do México. A nave Starship realizou uma queima para sair de órbita e retornou à atmosfera, terminando em pouso vertical no oceano Pacífico, ao norte do Havaí. Nenhuma das duas partes foi recuperada;
- A missão, portanto, demonstrou que a Starship pode alcançar a órbita e transportar satélites, mas a recuperação integral do sistema continua sendo um desafio.
SpaceX quer acelerar os testes
Musk afirmou que a empresa manterá sequência de tentativas caso a captura não funcione no próximo voo. A expectativa é ampliar o ritmo dos testes ao longo de 2027.
A recuperação das duas partes é uma etapa importante para os planos da SpaceX de desenvolver um sistema orbital totalmente reutilizável. A tecnologia também está ligada à ambição de transportar grandes quantidades de carga para o espaço e, futuramente, apoiar missões de exploração além da Terra.
Por enquanto, a captura simultânea da nave e do propulsor permanece como um objetivo de teste. O resultado da próxima missão mostrará se a empresa está pronta para avançar nessa etapa da reutilização da Starship.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: SmartBear’s BearQ adds Sources to find coverage gaps and Workflows to automate test runs - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
SmartBear’s BearQ adds Sources to find coverage gaps and Workflows to automate test runs
Software testing company SmartBear Software Inc. is pushing its BearQ agentic quality assurance system beyond test automation with two new capabilities released today.
Both additions target the part of quality assurance that artificial intelligence has made more difficult by speeding up coding. SmartBear calls them Sources and Workflows.
Automating individual tests is no longer the bottleneck, in the company’s telling. The tougher job now is working out what still needs testing across sprawling systems, much of it already covered by tests sitting in other tools.
Sources widens BearQ’s view past the application itself. Requirements and bug reports now flow in from Atlassian Corp.’s Jira so the agent knows what ought to be tested. SmartBear’s own Reflect and Zephyr testing tools show what existing tests already cover. BearQ draws on that context to find gaps in coverage before it writes anything new, so teams end up with fewer duplicate tests.
Workflows picks up from there, letting a team chain jobs together behind a single trigger. Once a build lands in the continuous integration and delivery pipeline, for example, BearQ can spin up a test environment and run regression tests against it. Whatever the run turns up goes back into the team’s connected systems, and anyone who would rather not tie testing to builds can put the same sequence on a schedule. How much of a workflow runs without human review is up to the team.
Progressive autonomy is SmartBear’s name for that arrangement. Teams begin with people signing off on what BearQ does, then hand over more of the process as their confidence grows. Trust was the top barrier to adopting or scaling autonomous testing, named by 23% of the 1,436 U.S. and U.K. respondents in a survey SmartBear released Sept. 30.
Bridges Smith, vice president of product management for AI at SmartBear, called autonomous testing “the first step.” By Smith’s account, the bigger opportunity is connecting how an application actually behaves with what a team intends it to do and the test suite it has built up. People would still set the guardrails, Smith said, describing the shift as a move “beyond autonomous testing toward autonomous quality.”
SmartBear has been building BearQ out since it first appeared in March, when the company opened early access for web applications built by midmarket software-as-a-service providers. A September update made it an assignable agent inside Jira. SmartBear’s older lineup includes the Swagger tools for designing application programming interfaces, and about 32,000 organizations use its software, by the company’s count.
More Sources connections are due before the quarter ends. Both features get a public demonstration Thursday in a livestream with “Project Hail Mary” author Andy Weir.

articles.title: UniUni go-public deal falls through as SPAC terminates agreement | BetaKit
articles.text:
Richmond, BC-based last-mile delivery company UniUni will need to find a new path to the public markets after its deal with a special purpose acquisition company (SPAC) was terminated.
The news: MAK Acquisition, a Toronto Stock Exchange (TSX)-listed SPAC led by ex-Dye & Durham CEO Matthew Proud, announced on Tuesday morning that it terminated its merger agreement with UniUni. Earlier this year, UniUni signed the deal to merge with MAK and trade on the TSX; a deal that would’ve valued the combined entity at more than $1 billion USD ($1.4 billion CAD).
The termination followed MAK warning UniUni nearly one month ago that it was in breach of its interim covenant, meaning UniUni wasn’t meeting a certain standard in the lead-up to the deal closing, as its business and financial performance had deteriorated. BetaKit has reached out to UniUni for comment.
From the source: “Under the Purchase Agreement, UniUni had 15 business days following receipt of the notice of breach to cure the breach, however the breach was incurable as UniUni exceeded its maximum cumulative pre-tax loss,” MAK said in its release. “As a result, MAK has exercised its right to terminate the Purchase Agreement, and the Proposed Transaction will not proceed.”
The context: The day after MAK warned UniUni of the breach, UniUni announced it was entering into a term sheet for a private funding round led by an undisclosed existing investor. It’s unclear if this funding was intended to improve its fiscal position for the SPAC deal, or as an alternative source of liquidity in preparation for the deal to fall through. UniUni said at the time that the funding was meant to support its continued growth across North America and strengthen its financial position heading into peak delivery season.
Final thought: Based out of Richmond, BC, UniUni uses gig workers and passenger vehicles to deliver goods to consumers. It has partnered with outlets like Temu, Shein, and AliExpress, and in 2025 claimed a network of more than 100,000 registered drivers across Canada and the US. While the company has raised multiple large funding rounds, recent reporting has suggested the company is “deeply unprofitable” as it faces several lawsuits, including class action allegations of unfair labour practices.

articles.title: Robotic therapy for stroke patients
articles.text:
Robotic therapy for stroke patients
An adaptive physical rehab system uses generative AI to learn from physical therapists and offer personalized support.
Strokes leave 5 million people with long-term impairments each year, and a growing shortage of physical therapists makes it hard for them to get the care they need. A new approach tries to solve that problem by combining artificial intelligence and human therapy.
Johannes Lachner, a former MIT postdoc who is now an assistant professor at Purdue University, and Noah Geiger, a former visiting student at MIT, developed a robotic system that uses generative AI and real-time force feedback to learn from real therapists. Drawing on what it’s learned, it gives patients just the right amount of assistance during physical rehabilitation exercises like reaching, lifting their arms, and performing tasks of daily living.
The goal is “not to replace therapists, but to extend their reach,” Lachner says.
“Initial robotic experiments have already demonstrated the feasibility of this approach,” he reports. “The next phase of the project aims to develop therapist-specific models and evaluate them in a long-term clinical study with the same patients who previously received manual therapy.” Beyond that, he envisions possible applications in contact-rich industrial settings or collaborative workspaces.

articles.title: Exclusive: Plants can speak using electricity, so this startup built an AI model to decipher their language | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Justin Mast’s life was changed by a cyborg plant.
A few years ago, Mast was reading through some scientific literature when he stumbled upon research about a houseplant wired to a motorized stand. When the plant wanted more light, electrical signals flowed through the living tissues. A control board sensed the current and wheeled the plant closer to the light source.
“I’m like, what the heck?” Mast told TechCrunch. “That was the entry to the rabbit hole for me.”
Mast wound up partnering with Lee von Kraus, a neuroscientist who has worked with DARPA, to found Electric Plant, which has been spending the past three years collecting data to build a large language model, Bombadil, capable of interpreting the subtle electrical signals coursing through a plant’s stem and relaying details about the plant’s needs to growers.
The founders believe their model could one day lead to a tool that would let people “speak” to plants. “We’re listening more than we’re speaking, but listening’s the first step,” said Mast, co-founder and CEO of Electric Plant.
To bring its sensors and Bombadil to market, Electric Plant recently raised an $11.2 million seed round led by Onto Ventures and Climactic, with participation from Ponderosa, Endeavor Catalyst, Ludlow, Michigan Rise, The Fund, Schox VC, and Dug Song.
Even in the most controlled greenhouses, farmers and growers don’t have full visibility of what their plants require, Mast said. Traditionally, farmers, growers, and foresters have relied on coarse tools that react to plants’ demands for water, nutrients, or light. And tools like soil probes, handheld spectroscopes, and satellite imagery work well enough, but they leave much to be desired, Mast said.
“That technology is sophisticated, but its ability to get at the inside of the plant isn’t very sophisticated. Most of that stuff still lags quite a bit behind the real-time needs of the plant,” he said.
Electric Plant had to start somewhere, though, so it used those devices to train its Bombadil model, which is capable of interpreting electrical signals in about 125 different species. “We know the model will surpass a lot of that equipment,” Mast said.
The startup’s sensors are also significantly cheaper than existing tools, which generally cost thousands of dollars. “This is tens of dollars,” he said.
The sensors, about the size of a regular iPhone folded lengthwise, are attached to a plant using stainless steel screws. The screws must penetrate the cambium — the layer of living tissue just under the bark — to connect to the microvolt changes occurring within the plant. Data collected from these sensors is sent to a base station via a low-power wireless network.
Electric Plant only needs a couple sensors per acre for accurate results, Mast said. The data gets interpreted by Bombadil in the cloud, and the results are sent back to the customer, who can use it to, for example, adjust their watering or fertilizer schedules. Mast claims such a system can boost yields while reducing water use by 20% or more.
Mast wouldn’t disclose who Electric Plant’s initial customers are, but it’s easy to imagine applications in agriculture and forestry.
Bombadil’s first hundred-plus species runs the gamut of plant forms, from ferns, redwoods, and tomatoes to dahlias, Mast said.
“This is the most diverse model ever created on biological electrical signals,” he said. “No one’s ever done anything equivalent to this in the animal world.”

articles.title: Hidden code suggests location sharing in Google Messages is about to get a major upgrade — which will make it easier to find people
articles.text:
This leaked Google Messages location-sharing upgrade might actually make it worth using over WhatsApp
More map styles and details
- A new location-sharing upgrade for Google Messages has been spotted
- You'll be able to add different map layers, including live traffic
- It's not clear how long it will be before the feature is enabled for everyone
While Google has added plenty of new features and refinements to its Google Messages app in recent months and years, it still lags behind competitors such as WhatsApp when it comes to certain facets of the app — like sharing your location with other people.
This is something that's essential for social meet-ups, keeping tabs on the kids, planning journey times, and more besides, and hidden code spotted by Android Authority suggests that location sharing in Google Messages is about to get a significant upgrade.
This is code that's present but not yet enabled in the latest beta version of Google Messages for Android, but the Android Authority team was able to get it working. It adds several map types and a map details option, when you choose to share your location.
Currently, you can only show a map in the default Google Maps style when location sharing in Google Messages, but the new options would let you switch to satellite or terrain views instead, as well as overlaying live traffic information on top.
Benefits to users
The satellite view would make it easier to find someone in relation to a landmark or a feature or the landscape, for example, while the terrain view would give you a better idea of how simple (or otherwise) it might be to reach someone in a remote area.
Then there's the traffic view — say if the roads were blocked up around a person you're trying to pick up in a car, you could get them to walk and come and meet you, rather than getting stuck in a traffic jam unnecessarily.
Most of the time I do tend to default to WhatsApp when it comes to letting people know where I am, because everyone's got the app and it's straightforward to use. You can also set time limits on location sharing, something which Google Messages doesn't have.

If improvements like this continue, I might switch to Google Messages for locations instead — at least for those people on Android. There's still work to do, but the feature only arrived earlier this year, so it's encouraging to see upgrades on the way already.

While Wi-Fi 7 support is the big deal here, the wired connections aren't bad, either. You get a 10Gb WAN port to hook this router up to your super-fast modem, giving you max speeds. You also get four 2.5Gb Ethernet ports for your home devices, including your PC, laptop, NAS drives, game consoles, and more.
Aside from the speeds, you get a USB 3.0 port on the side, which you could use to hook up a printer or external hard drive as a basic NAS. EasyMesh support, meanwhile, means you can use this as a wireless node in a mesh network. It also has Quality of Service controls to help you prioritize traffic for your core devices, such as your gaming PC, so you don't lose out when you're gaming.
The $189.98 sale price for this TP-Link Archer BE9700 router is a good one, even if it has yo-yo'd in price over recent months. That said, this is a solid discount off the $249.99 list price that it was at a few weeks ago, and one that'll give you an ultra-fast upgrade to your local network.

articles.title: Revolut sufre una caída masiva y no se puede ni usar la app ni pagar... o acceder a tu dinero
articles.text:
Revolut ha confirmado una caída masiva de sus sistemas que está impidiendo a los usuarios poder acceder a la app (y por tanto a sus cuentas) o poder pagar. Desde esta mañana, múltiples usuarios han reportado que no podían pagar con las tarjetas de Revolut, ni tampoco a través de sistemas de pago de terceros.
Ahora la compañía ha confirmado que ha sufrido una caída generalizada de sus sistemas que afecta a varios de sus servicios, aunque están trabajando en ello. Se desconoce cuándo volverán a estar operativos o qué nivel de disrupción está experimentando la compañía, así como las causas de la misma:
Actualmente estamos experimentando una interrupción en el servicio que afecta a varias funcionalidades, lo que podría hacer que algunos servicios no estén disponibles. Nuestro equipo de ingeniería está trabajando activamente para restablecer el servicio por completo a la mayor brevedad posible. Agradecemos su paciencia y pedimos disculpas por cualquier inconveniente que esto haya podido causar.
Actualmente, la web de servicio de la compañía confirma que 31 de sus instancias están afectadas o no disponibles, incluyendo los sistemas de registro, inicio de sesión, transferencias o pagos con tarjeta, sin que haya trascendido cuándo volverán a estar disponibles.
Si eres usuario de Revolut, te recomendamos estar atento al estado del sistema de la compañía y, mientras tanto, usar otros servicios bancarios alternativos.
