articles.title: London-based “Surgical Intelligence” company XRlabs raises €7.48 million to bring AI into the operating room | EU-Startups
articles.text:
XRlabs, the London-based Surgical Intelligence company built by surgeons for surgeons, has raised €7.48 million ($8.4 million) in Seed funding.
The round was led by Playground Global, the DeepTech-focused venture firm based in Palo Alto, with participation from London-based HealthTech investor Eka Ventures. Alongside the fundraise, XRlabs also announced that Omar Ishrak, who led Medtronic as Chairman and CEO from 2011 to 2020 and previously served as chairman of Intel’s board, has joined as Chair of its Board of Directors.
“The best physical AI companies come from people who’ve experienced a problem in their field firsthand and have the deep expertise to know how to fix it,” said Bruce Leak, General Partner at Playground Global.
Founded by practising neurosurgeon Dr. Ali Haddad in 2024, XRlabs is headquartered in London at the London Institute for Healthcare Engineering, with a second office in Palo Alto, California. The company develops modular, device-agnostic software that sits as an external AI layer across the surgical systems hospitals already own.
Its platform uses computer vision and deep learning to transform live video from surgical scopes, navigation telemetry, and pre-operative CT and MRI imaging into a single real-time, anatomy-aware view of each procedure. XRlabs says its platform has been deployed across more than 100 surgical cases on three continents.
The company offers two core products: XRlabs SIM and SurgicalOS. The XRlabs SIM is a patient-specific planning and rehearsal tool that transforms standard CT and MRI scans into interactive 3D reality models or digital twins, while SurgicalOS is an intraoperative intelligence layer that brings the digital twin created in SIM into the live operative view.
The XRlabs SIM and SurgicalOS together form what the company describes as “Pyramid of Surgical Intelligence,” a layered approach to building AI surgical understanding that mirrors how surgeons are trained, starting from anatomy and building toward real-time operative skill.
“Our conviction is that the operating room is the next frontier for physical AI. Surgery generates extraordinary data, yet almost none of it becomes intelligence in the moments that matter most. This financing lets us change that at scale, moving Surgical Intelligence from landmark first cases to foundational infrastructure in every operating room,” said Dr. Haddad, founder and CEO of XRlabs.
The funding comes on the back of major clinical achievements, including first-in-human use of physical AI in cranial neurosurgery, integrated with an ORBEYE 4K 3D exoscope under research conditions and a world-first in AI-designed patient-specific implants, used in the successful separation of craniopagus twins.
XRlabs says it will use the Seed funding to support the buildout of its engineering and clinical teams, advance its products through regulatory pathways in the UK, Europe, and the US, while extending the clinical evidence base at partner institutions globally. The company has also been awarded a compute allocation on the UK AI Research Resource (AIRR), the UK’s national AI compute infrastructure, which supports the development and scaling of its AI capabilities.

articles.title: Introducing tsrs: a Port of TypeScript to Rust
articles.text:
Introducing tsrs: A port of TypeScript to Rust
Cloudflare and VoidZero are now working with Max Schwenk of Owner.com on tsrs, a Rust port of the TypeScript compiler. We are doing this work in close collaboration with the TypeScript team, and incubating tsrs as part of the Oxc JavaScript compiler toolchain.
Our goal is to help developers spend less time waiting for their code to be checked and more time building. Making TypeScript faster and more memory-efficient also helps bring complete development environments to more places, including right in your browser.
To be clear, we are not forking TypeScript. We believe the TypeScript team should remain in full control of the language’s design and direction. They have maintained a long-term vision while guiding TypeScript’s adoption across the JavaScript community. We do not want to change that.
The TypeScript team can move quite fast on many things, but for some features they may spend years intentionally exploring options and making prototypes before picking the right implementation. A Rust port has to follow those decisions closely, or it will eventually fall apart and become incompatible. We have to preserve the TypeScript language strictly based on its original implementation – and the TypeScript team should remain solely responsible for deciding what that looks like.
Performance and memory improvements
Early benchmarks of our Rust port of TypeScript are promising: tsrs is up to 8x faster and uses ~70% less memory compared to TypeScript 7.0 when using the same number of type check workers:
As you can see, the next version of TypeScript already brings many performance improvements, making TypeScript 7.1 beta up to 2.5x faster than TypeScript 7.0. Some of these optimizations were upstreamed from tsrs, and we’re hoping to find more.
You may have seen recent benchmarks of different TypeScript ports with various performance claims, often due to using larger machine types and different options compared to TypeScript’s defaults. We worked with the TypeScript team to ensure the above benchmarks are comparing the same configuration.
By default, tsrs ships with an adaptive configuration dependent on the machine type that uses more memory but is even faster:
Try tsrs
TypeScript in Rust aims to be a faithful port of TypeScript. You can try an experimental release by installing the tsrs package from npm:
npm install tsrs
npx tsrs
Why now?
We’ve seen many attempts at porting TypeScript to other languages over the years. Because of the complexity involved, only one of the ports succeeded: the TypeScript team’s port of TypeScript from JavaScript to Go.
However, frontier AI models can now do large-scale ports almost independently in a matter of days. We have now seen slopforks, faithful ports, and completely re-architected versions of TypeScript in Rust or C++. There is clearly a demand for even faster TypeScript.
Why Rust?
You might be thinking: “TypeScript’s Go port already made TypeScript 10x faster and far more memory efficient than the previous version written in TypeScript. Why isn’t that enough?”
However, it’s not just about speed. Rust offers some unique advantages: running in WebAssembly. The Rust + Wasm story has always been strong, and one of the reasons comes down to the fundamentals of Rust’s language design. When you compile a Go program to Wasm, you have to compile Go’s garbage collector along with it. But Rust’s memory management model enables straightforward memory interactions between a WebAssembly guest and host. This is one of the key things that makes Rust a much better fit for the WebAssembly use-case: memory efficiency.
Cloudflare Workers have supported Wasm for a long time. Just a few weeks ago we announced supporting native Rust in Workers with the new Emscripten target for wasm-bindgen. When you run entire software build and deployment systems in tight loops on Workers, the benefits of a small memory footprint pay off quickly. It means you can run these workloads so efficiently that it’s now possible to run fully encapsulated development systems in places where they couldn’t have been run before.
This enables new possibilities when combined with agents: You are now able to run a development toolchain end-to-end in a fully sandboxed environment on Cloudflare. But with Wasm, you can also run those environments safely client-side in your browser, or on an embedded device, or an IoT application.
How will the tsrs port be maintained?
First, we are working with Theo Browne to merge tsc-rs and tsrs into a single package that supports all of TypeScript’s features including Language Server Protocol (LSP) and content mappers. Second, we’ve seen a lot of success with how we maintain Vinext in sync with its upstream, Next.js. We explained how we do this in a recent blog post:
Each morning, an agent reviews the changes, fetches diffs, and opens tracking issues for anything that could affect Vinext. Every night, the compatibility matrix is regenerated as we run the Next.js test suite against Vinext. When one of these tests or issues reveals a gap, agents are now in the position where they can identify the change across both codebases, build a reproduction, port any relevant tests, and propose a fix.
We will apply the same process to TypeScript, taking extreme care that we don’t introduce diverging behaviors from upstream TypeScript. When we come across performance improvements, we’ll attempt to contribute them back to the TypeScript Go codebase so everyone wins.
Finally, we recognize that there are some differences to the upstream version of TypeScript right now, like for example the order in which diagnostics are printed. We aim to reduce those differences to a minimum by the time we publish a stable release.
What’s next?
Cloudflare is already the home of many free and open source Rust tools that power the JavaScript ecosystem, such as Vite, Rolldown, Oxlint, and Oxfmt. With more than 10 million developers building on Cloudflare, we care a lot about making the underlying developer toolchain faster, more portable, and easier to run in more places. We are excited to experiment with deeper tsrs integrations into our stack, for example for type-aware lint rules in Oxlint.
Like with Vinext, our goal is to run tsrs as a well-maintained healthy open source project — without getting in the way of TypeScript itself. The Oxc team has already begun refactoring the codebase to make it faster, use less memory, and make it maintainable. We know the TypeScript team is taking this seriously – they are experimenting with memory and performance improvements for tsc. We are excited to collaborate with the TypeScript team and the JavaScript community to build the best and fastest implementations of TypeScript together.

articles.title: Microsoft admits 'frontier models can't be trusted', unveils new security tools to treat AI agents as insider threats
articles.text:
Microsoft admits 'frontier models can't be trusted', unveils new security tools to treat AI agents as insider threats
Say hi to your new Guardian Agent
- Microsoft unveils Guardian Agents to monitor, constrain, and manage risks posed by autonomous AI agents
- New controls dynamically adjust agent permissions, behavior, and access based on changing risk levels
- Company warns “agentic insiders” require continuous AI-driven oversight beyond traditional security controls
AI fans, your vocabulary is about to become two phrases richer: Agentic Insider, and Guardian Agent. These are the two phrases Microsoft used while announcing a swathe of new tools and features to help businesses secure their operations running AI agents.
A new Microsoft blog, published by Microsoft's Corporate VP for Identity and Network Access, Nadim Abdo, argues that agents, while not inherently malicious, can make mistakes or be manipulated and compromised.
Since they need to be granted relatively extensive permissions in order to be able to work properly, it creates the sort of risk that can prove disastrous if not properly handled.
Agentic Overwatch
Abdo also added that AI agents doing their master's bidding cannot be trusted with their own security.
"Satya Nadella, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Microsoft, recently described the trust architecture this new era requires: we must separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it," Abdo writes.
"We should not ask a model to be its own security authority. The controls that determine what it can access, what actions it can take, and whether it should continue operating must sit outside the model, where the model cannot bypass or tamper with them."
So, oversight is the keyword here. But AI agents move at machine speed, something no human can match, and therefore humans are not properly equipped for the job. Instead, separate AI agents need to be introduced to keep their juniors in check. Earlier, Microsoft introduced Project Perception and the Microsoft cyber stack, to help organizations defend with agents.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Project Perception is an AI-powered cybersecurity system designed to coordinate specialized AI agents that analyze security data, identify vulnerabilities, and investigate different threats. The system uses three types of agents: red agents that probe for weaknesses, blue agents that investigate potential threats, and green agents that implement corrections and fixes.
Now, Microsoft says it is extending the project to secure “the agentic insider”. They’re calling it - Guardian Agent.
“Guardian Agents help security teams operate continuously, at machine speed and scale, while sensors, context, and actuators across the cyber stack help understand changing agent risk and continuously adapt protection in response,” Abdo explained. “Project Perception and Microsoft Agent 365 share signals, context, and a unified registry giving IT and security teams a consistent view of agents and risk, with the controls each needs.”
Drill sergeant
Abdo says Guardian Agents build on a security principle where non-deterministic intelligence needs to be surrounded with deterministic controls, independent evidence, and containment boundaries.
These controls are divided into seven aspects - identity, permissions, data, endpoints, network, cloud, and runtime - and these have four responsibilities: to know which agent exists, who owns them and why, and what they’re doing; to contain what each agents can access and do before it acts; to protect the data, tools, runtime, resources, and systems the agent uses; and to adapt protection continuously as behavior, context, and risk change.
In other words, the AI needs to be the drill sergeant for the drones, adapting to changes in real-time to make sure they’re doing good work and not going rogue.
Microsoft also said it is expanding discovery to 35 additional types of local agents, including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and GitHub Copilot. It also announced extending Microsoft Entra Agent ID with identity types for additional agent patterns, including both local and previously unknown agents discovered through security sensors.
With “Dynamic Permissions” and “Dynamic Agent Risk”, Microsoft wants to give businesses tighter control over what AI agents can access and do, while keeping tabs on their behavior and risk levels. Dynamic Permissions limit agents to the access they need for a specific task, while Dynamic Agent Risk checks for potential threats.
Dynamic Conditional Access can then respond to rising risks by restricting permissions, blocking certain operations, or asking for human approval. In more extreme scenarios, an agent can be stopped and isolated.

articles.title: Reaction Dynamics plans rapid expansion to launch new medium-lift rocket by 2031
articles.text:
Reaction Dynamics is looking to raise hundreds of millions in funding and add nearly 300 employees over the next five years to send a new, more powerful rocket toward the stars.
At the SpaceBound Conference in Ottawa on Tuesday morning, the Longueuil, Que.-based rocket maker revealed its plans to develop and send a new medium-lift rocket to space by 2031. Dubbed Borealis, the medium-lift rocket is the larger sibling of Reaction Dynamics’ light-lift Aurora rocket. While Aurora is meant for payloads below half a tonne, Borealis is designed to haul a six-tonne payload to low Earth orbit for larger spacecraft deployments, satellite constellation launches, and other large space missions, similar to SpaceX’s Falcon 9 rocket.
“We founded Reaction Dynamics because we believe Canada should be able to reach orbit on its own terms.”
SpaceX’s rocket is so popular for shipping satellites to space that it’s started turning away customers past 2028. This has opened the door for Canada’s burgeoning space industry, including Reaction Dynamics. The company said it’s already signed 10 agreements and letters of intent with undisclosed prospective launch customers across Canada, the United States, and Europe.
“We see an opportunity to serve Canadian demand while providing additional dedicated launch capacity for customers in the United States, Europe, and allied countries,” Jesse Mikelberg, Reaction Dynamics’ director of business development and strategy, said in an email to BetaKit. “As a result, customers would have greater control over their launch schedule and destination orbit.”
To give those prospective customers a ride to space, Reaction Dynamics has set some big-time goals. First, the company wants to launch Aurora into orbit from Canadian soil by 2028. The company will then build on that base of manufacturing investments, equipment, processes, and expertise to get Borealis into space by 2031, Mikelberg explained.
“Aurora will give us flight experience and practical knowledge of manufacturing, transporting, integrating, and launching an orbital vehicle,” Mikelberg said. “It will also help us establish customer relationships, spaceport operations, and credibility through execution.”
While Mikelberg makes it sound simple, it is literally rocket science. This requires a lot of manpower and capital. Reaction Dynamics is planning for a large influx of both.
Over the next five years, the company aims to increase its headcount from 68 employees to 350. To accommodate all the new staff, Reaction Dynamics is also looking to increase its manufacturing and testing footprint from 60,000 square feet to 375,000 square feet. The company sees a “strong foundation” for this expansion in Québec, Mikelberg said, but it’s also eyeing land in Ontario or Nova Scotia.
RELATED: First Canada, then the world: nation’s rocket builders see a bigger opening in space
Expanding a business like this, let alone one that builds rockets, isn’t cheap. Reaction Dynamics is planning to raise around $350 million CAD in new private investment across two rounds over the next five years: a Series B targeting between $70 million and 100 million CAD to support Aurora’s first orbital launch in 2028, and then a Series C, or a similar funding instrument, targeting between $200 million and 250 million CAD to aid development for Borealis’ first launch in 2031.
This funding would come in addition to the $50 million Reaction Dynamics has already raised to date from private investors and non-dilutive government funding sources.
“Our approach is to broaden the investor base as we demonstrate propulsion performance, establish manufacturing capacity, secure customers, and gain flight experience,” Mikelberg said.
Founded in 2017, Reaction Dynamics has been building rocket propulsion systems since long before space became one of the “key sovereign capabilities” in the federal government’s Defence Industrial Strategy. Under the DIS, the 2025 federal budget committed $182.6 million over three years to the Department of National Defence (DND) to establish a sovereign space launch capability.
Reaction Dynamics benefitted from Canada’s renewed focus on space earlier this year when the company was awarded an $8.3 million grant under the first round of the DND’s Innovation for Defence Excellence and Security (IDEaS) Launch the North contest to build out its rocket launch capabilities. Reaction’s younger Canadian rocket-building peers, Canada Rocket Company and NordSpace, also received that funding.
The IDEaS funding was announced alongside the federal government signing a $200 million lease with Maritime Launch Services to establish a government spaceport in Nova Scotia. Reaction Dynamics has also invested in MLS, and its spaceport just outside Canso, NS, is the planned location for Aurora’s first orbital launch.
“We founded Reaction Dynamics because we believe Canada should be able to reach orbit on its own terms,” Reaction Dynamics founder and CEO Bachar Elzein said in a statement. “Aurora is how we get there in 2028. Borealis is how we build on that foundation to deliver medium lift by 2031. Nearly a decade of propulsion development and engineering, right here in Quebec, has brought us to this point.”
CLARIFICATION (10/20/2026): This story has been updated to note Jesse Mikelberg’s current title.
Feature image courtesy Reaction Dynamics.

articles.title: Exclusive: Kantata's Expertise Insights answers services firms' business questions in plain English - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Exclusive: Kantata’s Expertise Insights answers services firms’ business questions in plain English
Professional services automation software company Kantata Inc. today added generative business intelligence to its Expertise Engine platform with the launch of Expertise Insights.
Users ask about the business in plain English, as in where margin pressure is showing up, and the software answers with an interactive chart, a calculation or an executive summary.
Kantata’s pitch rests on how long it takes services firms to get answers out of their own data. The company says a request often has to go through a business intelligence analyst or a services engagement, and the wait can run to a week.
Sarah Edwards, Kantata’s chief product and strategy officer, said the value of an insight in professional services “depends on how quickly you can act on it.” Reports often show up after the moment has passed, she said.
Expertise Insights runs on Amazon Web Services Inc.’s Amazon Quick. On top of it Kantata has added a semantic layer that translates database field names into the vocabulary staff at a particular firm use every day. Firm-specific terms are covered, down to distinctions such as “chargeable utilization” versus “billable utilization.”
Kantata ships the product with four ready-made dashboards. Finance teams get margin, revenue per head and cost leakage trends in one of them, and the rest are given over to delivery, time and resourcing. On the delivery dashboard, project health is broken out by schedule, scope, budget and client health.
Users who need something the stock dashboards don’t show can turn to Ask Insights for new analysis on demand. Kantata says a complete board deck can be assembled in minutes. Saved work goes into Bookmarks and Pinboards, so a filtered view or a one-off analysis can be kept without spawning another copy of a master dashboard. Kantata is pitching that as a cure for dashboard sprawl.
The software can also link capacity, margin, delivery risk and financial performance. Piecing those relationships together might otherwise take several reports, or a seasoned operator who knows where to look.
Vikas Nehru, Kantata’s chief technology officer, said artificial intelligence in professional services should make a firm’s “collective expertise available at the moment a decision needs to be made.” That requires clean data and context, he said, plus AI that understands how a business works.
Life sciences consultancy Lumanity Inc. is among the customers already running the product. Andy Newbill, its senior manager of professional services automation, recently put together a complex report using calculated fields in an hour, and by his estimate the job would have taken hours before. Most striking to him was the chance to describe what he needs “in natural language and have the system help me build it.”
Kantata announced Expertise Insights at the Technology & Services World conference in Las Vegas, and it is available now. The company’s previous launch, Agent Studio, came a month ago and lets firms build custom AI agents by describing them in plain language.

articles.title: SpaceX alum's aviation startup, Reliable Robotics, lands $115M, topping $1B valuation | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Reliable Robotics has been working for nearly a decade to commercialize autonomous flying technology that can be installed on existing aircraft. Now, with a $115 million funding boost, the Mountain View, California-based startup has a longer runway as it pushes to get its autonomous flight system certified by the Federal Aviation Administration — a critical milestone that co-founder and CEO Robert Rose said the startup is inching toward.
The financing is an extension of its Series D round and includes $90 million in equity funding led by Nimble Partners and $25 million in debt from Silicon Valley Bank. The Series D round, which now totals $275 million, has pushed the startup’s valuation beyond the $1 billion mark. Other investors include Gideon Strategic Partners, RockCreek, Geek Ventures, Gold Hill Capital, Sparkwave Capital, and others. Reliable has raised $380 million to date.
“We continue to make steady progress and deliver evidence to the FAA and every day, we inch closer and closer,” said Rose, a former director of flight software at SpaceX who has also had stints at Tesla and Google. Reliable co-founder and CTO Juerg Frefel is also a SpaceX veteran who spent nearly a decade there as an engineer.
And in aviation — one of the most regulated industries in the world — moving toward certification of new technology is progress.
Reliable Robotics is working to gain FAA certification on four fronts, all of which are linked to its goal of autonomous flight.
Its first product, called continuous autopilot engagement, handles the engine startup, taxiing, takeoff, and landing for the pilot, who remains in the aircraft and interacts with the autonomous flight system through a touchscreen. Rose expects to receive certification for this critical first system in 18 to 24 months.
The second certification, which Rose says is at least three years away, removes the pilot from the cockpit and moves them to a ground-control station.
Reliable is also working toward certification of a collision-avoidance radar, which the company has developed in-house after failing to attract legacy suppliers to take on the project. Most conventional radar systems use an antenna that moves to scan the surrounding airspace. Reliable has developed a solid-state radar that has no moving parts and scans the sky at a longer range and at much higher resolution, according to Rose. It’s also easier to maintain because there are no moving parts and it costs less, he added.
“This is of great interest to operators these days, given the collisions that we’ve had recently in commercial aviation,” he said, adding that the radar also works on the ground to prevent collisions with other aircraft or infrastructure. Rose expects the solid-state radar to be certified by the end of 2027.
The final certification is for its airline, called Reliable Airlines, which will be the first airline certified to use the autonomous flying technology. The airline is based in Albuquerque and uses six Cessna Caravans — workhorses of the aviation industry — to fly cargo six days a week. (The FAA certifies equipment, but the agency also must certify the airline operations under a separate set of regulations.)
While the certification process is lengthy, Nimble Partners founder John Burbank said the benefits will be broad and significant.
“It’s a much bigger effort and much bigger opportunity than to just build one plane,” Burbank said, noting that Reliable is building a system that can be adopted by any airframe. “They had a really big vision nine years ago, and saw this as something needed and essential. Once they get the first one approved, then everyone will realize this is going to be the path for the industry, just as we’re seeing the path for the auto industry being autonomous.”

articles.title: Nebraska native explores galaxies far, far away
articles.text:
Nebraska native explores galaxies far, far away
Megan Donahue ’85
Growing up on a small farm in Nebraska, Megan Donahue ’85 discovered the wider world by reading her way through her local library. Today, she is learning how the wider universe works by studying galaxy clusters.
Donahue discovered her passion for physics in that library at age 12 and started her path into astronomy thanks to “a providential interaction.” Through MIT’s Undergraduate Research Opportunities Program, she got introduced to cutting-edge x-ray imaging—work she found “really cool.”
Now a professor of physics and astronomy at Michigan State University, she researches galaxy clusters and baryonic matter (matter made of protons and neutrons, as opposed to dark matter) in an effort to learn more about the composition of the universe and its evolution.
“Clusters of galaxies are very large scoops of the universe,” says Donahue, who served as president of the American Astronomical Society from 2018 to 2020. “It’s like taking a sample from the ocean. If you’re trying to find out the average composition of the ocean’s water, you’d want to study as big a scoop as possible.”

articles.title: Netflix is telling investors not to worry, even though you’re watching less and less
articles.text:
Netflix is making monetization a top priority amid reports of falling viewing time. As part of its third-quarter earnings report on Tuesday, Netflix lists improvements to monetization as one of its main focuses going forward, alongside efforts to boost entertainment value and leverage new technology.
Netflix is telling investors not to worry, even though you’re watching less and less
Improving monetization is one of Netflix’s top priorities.
The streaming giant doesn’t say exactly how it plans to improve its monetization, but the company notes that these goals will help Netflix “create member value that lets us occasionally raise prices, and increase advertiser demand.” Netflix also highlighted plans to push further into original titles, live events, and third-party programming as it faces an “intense competition and an explosion of content competing for consumer attention.”
An analysis from financial firm Jefferies estimated that Netflix’s monthly viewing time per member dropped to 49 hours in the first half of this year, down from 66 hours in the first half of 2023, according to a report from Reuters. At the same time, Netflix made up 7.8 percent of US viewing time in the US in July, a one-percentage-point dip from the same time last year, The New York Times reports.
During an earnings call, Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos pointed to success abroad when answering a question about the company’s content strategy. “We see titles across Latin America, EMEA (Europe, the Middle East and Africa), APAC (Asia-Pacific), driving engagement, subscriber growth, revenue, and profit,” Sarandos said. “Now, the US is also working. It’s just not growing as fast as it could or as fast as we’d like.”
Last week, Netflix laid off around 1,000 employees, while replacing key executives, including chief content officer Bela Bajaria and film head Dan Lin. Former Disney executive Peter Rice is taking over as chief content officer on October 26th. The Wall Street Journal recently reported that Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos complained internally that US-based users have been spending less time on the service, and that it’s “short on new hit shows.”
In its letter to investors, Netflix mentions its upcoming lineup of NFL games, its Grand Theft Auto VI preview, and its partnership with French TV station TF1 as evidence of opening its platform to a wider breadth of content. The company reported earning $12.9 billion over the past few months, marking a 12 percent year-over-year increase. It also plans to bring its ad-supported tier — which raked in $1.5 billion last year — to 15 new countries in 2027.
In the coming months, Netflix may be facing tougher competition from HBO Max and Paramount Plus following the Skydance megamerger, as co-CEO David Ellison has said that he plans to combine the two apps into a single service. The streamer struck deals with several creators as it competes with YouTube, which has reportedly offered channels “millions of dollars” not to post their videos on Netflix.
Netflix has also weighed making even bigger changes to its app, including integrating other third-party streamers, such as Peacock and Fox One, as well as adding always-on channels, according to reports from The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal.
Update, October 20th: Added a quote from Sarandos.

articles.title: Ukraine rescues wounded soldier using drone in daring 'world's first' UAV evacuation of a human — heavy-lift hexacopter carried injured 176-pound soldier 11 miles back to safety from minefield
articles.text:
Ukraine rescues wounded soldier using drone in daring 'world's first' UAV evacuation of a human — heavy-lift hexacopter carried injured 176-pound soldier 11 miles back to safety from minefield
In heavily mined terrain and surrounded by Russian kamikaze drones, 'Kostya' was hoisted by a Gurzuf Defence heavy UAV and guarded to safety by a fleet of smaller drones.
The Ukrainian military is claiming a world’s first after using an unmanned drone to rescue an injured soldier on the eastern Kharkiv front. Ukraine’s United24 news shared a video of the historic first. It also explained that the wounded infantryman was stuck in a heavily mined area, guarded by Russian kamikaze drones.
The above video starts with the Ukrainian drone locating the soldier, callsign ‘Kostya,’ in enemy territory. Various media reports suggest he was 11 miles (18km) behind enemy lines, at the mercy of Russian kamikaze drones, and perilously located in a minefield. Traditional land-based rescue was therefore not possible, but Kostya bravely agreed to be part of the first-ever human drone-lift rescue plan.
After being located, the injured infantryman clipped himself into a harness. He said, “That’s it, we can take off,” when he was fully buckled into the rudimentary-looking harness. UAV operator, callsign ‘Black’ from the 20th Mechanized Battalion, 30th Infantry Brigade, then appeared in the video and explained: “We were constantly in touch with him."
Ukrainian drone rescue key facts:
- Drone used: Gurzuf Defense hexacopter
- Drone capable of carrying 130kg (~287 pounds)
- Drone’s known range: it has previously transported 90kg (~198 pounds) loads up to 25km (16 miles)
- Infantryman weight: 80kg (~176 pounds)
- Rescue distance: 8km (11 miles)
- Hazards: enemy kamikaze drones, mines, gravity, many more
Being in constant touch with the operations HQ would have been reassuring. However, the surrounding presence of a fleet of Ukrainian support drones, both kamikaze devices and UAVs with anti-drone nets, was probably most comforting.
Eventually dropping back into safe(r) territory, after what must have been an arduous, nerve-wracking journey, control said, “Congratulations, you’re on the ground,” to Kostya, as he touched down in a field. Then the control room erupted into applause. They got their man back safely, and he is now being treated and is in recovery.
UAV operator ‘Black’ was delighted with the concerted efforts that brought back this wounded soldier. “A lot of people were involved, and everything worked out for us,” he said. Importantly, this may be the start of a whole new system of personnel evacuations for wounded and/or stranded soldiers using drone technology, indicated brigade leader ‘Napalm’ toward the end of the video.
