articles.title: US orders federal agencies to remove China’s DeepSeek AI from their systems | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The U.S. has ordered federal civilian agencies to stop purchasing services and products developed by Chinese AI startup DeepSeek and remove them from government IT systems over national security concerns tied to the Chinese AI startup’s operations in China, according to the Department of Homeland Security. The order goes beyond banning DeepSeek’s own product, and covers third-party products and services built using DeepSeek technology, though agencies can request exceptions.
The DHS raised concerns about DeepSeek’s handling of user data, warning that sensitive information from U.S. government users could potentially be accessible to Chinese authorities under Chinese law, the order said.
The move comes amid intensifying tech competition in AI between the U.S. and China. The Chinese AI model challenges its U.S. rivals, including OpenAI and Meta, with low-cost open-weight models.
China pushed back against the U.S.’s move. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Tuesday that Beijing opposes “overstretching the concept of national security and politicizing technology and trade issues,” according to an official briefing. “We will resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese enterprises,” the spokesperson added.
The U.S. has already taken steps to limit DeepSeek’s use in government. A law passed in December 2025 targeted its use in intelligence’s national security systems. The latest order extends the restrictions to federal civilian agencies, covering both new purchases and existing IT systems.
Meanwhile, China is reportedly considering export restrictions on 23 AI-related technologies, including chip designs and certain advanced AI models, to address security and misuse risks, Bloomberg reported last week.
The Chinese AI lab has faced scrutiny from governments and regulators across the globe since its R1 reasoning model shook the AI industry in January 2025, triggering a sharp sell-off of Nvidia shares.
The U.S. accused DeepSeek and five other Chinese AI companies, including Alibaba and Moonshot AI, of using large-scale model distillation to extract information from American AI systems, according to a September report.
In addition, OpenAI and Anthropic have separately raised concerns about DeepSeek’s alleged use of model distillation, a technique that uses outputs from one AI model to train another. Earlier this year, OpenAI told U.S. lawmakers it had observed suspected attempts by DeepSeek to distill its models, while Anthropic said it had identified unauthorized attempts by DeepSeek and other Chinese AI labs to collect outputs from Claude.

articles.title: Elon Musk estuda fusão entre Tesla e SpaceX; negócio pode criar gigante de R$ 19,4 trilhões
articles.text:
Elon Musk confirmou que uma fusão entre a Tesla e a SpaceX está sendo considerada pelas duas empresas. O empresário afirmou que vê vantagens na combinação dos negócios, mas ressaltou que ainda não existe um acordo sobre os termos da operação e que sua concretização está longe de ser garantida.
A possibilidade foi discutida nesta terça-feira (20), durante teleconferência sobre os resultados financeiros do terceiro trimestre da SpaceX. Segundo Musk, comitês especiais foram formados nas duas companhias para analisar a proposta. Os grupos são compostos por conselheiros independentes e foram criados a pedido de acionistas, de acordo com o executivo.
“Você acha que seria uma boa ideia? Sim”, declarou Musk ao comentar a possibilidade de unir as empresas. O empresário, que ocupa o cargo de diretor-executivo das duas companhias, afirmou que não participa das discussões por ser uma parte com interesses conflitantes. Os comitês ainda não chegaram a um acordo sobre os termos de uma eventual transação.
“Os comitês especiais não chegaram a um acordo sobre os termos de qualquer transação, e não há garantia de que chegarão”, disse Musk. Apesar das incertezas, ele afirmou acreditar que há vantagens significativas na combinação dos negócios.
Fusão pode criar empresa avaliada em mais de R$ 19,4 trilhões
- Uma união entre Tesla e SpaceX daria origem a uma das maiores operações corporativas da história. De acordo com os valores apresentados pelo The Verge, a empresa combinada poderia superar US$ 3,6 trilhões (cerca de R$ 19,4 trilhões) em valor de mercado;
- A Tesla está avaliada em aproximadamente US$ 1,5 trilhão (cerca de R$ 8,1 trilhões), enquanto a SpaceX alcançou US$ 2 trilhões (cerca de R$ 10,8 trilhões);
- Musk argumenta que a integração permitiria ampliar a colaboração em áreas, como inteligência artificial (IA), desenvolvimento de chips, software, robótica e conectividade. O empresário também citou a TeraFab, iniciativa conjunta das duas companhias voltada à fabricação de semicondutores;
- “Há muito a ganhar com a cooperação no desenvolvimento de software de superinteligência, design de chips, a TeraFab, obviamente robótica, transporte de massa para a órbita com a constelação Starmind e conectividade”, afirmou Musk;
- A aproximação entre as empresas já vinha sendo demonstrada por iniciativas compartilhadas. A TeraFab é um dos exemplos mais recentes de colaboração entre Tesla e SpaceX;
- No último ano, Musk também reuniu outras companhias sob estruturas corporativas mais amplas. Antes de abrir capital neste ano, a SpaceX adquiriu a xAI e o X, ambos controlados pelo empresário.
Acionistas terão a palavra final
Apesar do interesse de Musk, a fusão depende da aprovação dos acionistas. No caso da Tesla, o empresário afirmou que será necessário o apoio de pelo menos 50% de todas as ações, e não apenas da maioria dos votos efetivamente registrados. “Esse é um obstáculo bastante alto a superar”, declarou.
Musk também comparou a discussão sobre a fusão a uma situação delicada, devido ao seu papel de liderança nas duas companhias. Por isso, segundo ele, os comitês independentes precisam elaborar uma proposta que posteriormente será submetida aos investidores.
O histórico recente mostra que os acionistas da Tesla já apoiaram decisões importantes envolvendo o empresário. No ano passado, investidores aprovaram um pacote de remuneração para Musk avaliado em aproximadamente US$ 1 trilhão (cerca de R$ 5,4 trilhões).
Ainda assim, uma eventual combinação com a SpaceX pode provocar resistência entre parte dos investidores da montadora.
Leia mais:
- Tesla revela Roadster que “voa” e dirige de ponta-cabeça com tecnologia da SpaceX
- Musk promete dar ações da SpaceX a todas as crianças dos EUA
- Dependência da Starlink preocupa governos e expõe poder de Elon Musk
Quem assumiria o controle da empresa combinada?
Um dos principais pontos em aberto é a estrutura da operação. Segundo o The Verge, analistas de Wall Street e especialistas jurídicos citados pelo veículo consideram mais provável que a SpaceX adquira a Tesla — ou incorpore a empresa por meio de uma troca de ações — do que o caminho inverso.
Desde sua estreia no mercado de ações, a SpaceX mantém avaliação superior à da Tesla. Uma operação nessa direção permitiria que os acionistas da empresa espacial detivessem a maior parte do controle da companhia combinada.
Se a Tesla assumisse a aquisição da SpaceX, precisaria emitir milhões de novas ações. Isso reduziria proporcionalmente a participação dos atuais acionistas da montadora na empresa resultante da operação.
Há também diferenças importantes nas necessidades financeiras dos negócios. Os objetivos de lançamento da SpaceX exigem dezenas de bilhões de dólares por ano, gastos que poderiam limitar a capacidade da Tesla de investir na construção de novas fábricas de automóveis e baterias.
Por outro lado, a união criaria uma única companhia para investidores interessados na visão de futuro de Musk, que inclui carros robóticos, robôs humanoides, IA avançada e habitats humanos em Marte.
SpaceX supera Tesla em valor de mercado
Embora a Tesla seja conhecida principalmente pelos carros elétricos, Musk vem direcionando recursos da empresa para a robótica. A SpaceX, por sua vez, constrói foguetes e satélites de internet Starlink e está expandindo sua atuação para o fornecimento de capacidade computacional em nuvem a outras empresas de tecnologia, incluindo Anthropic e Google.
Segundo os resultados trimestrais mais recentes, essa atividade de computação em nuvem tornou-se a parte mais lucrativa da SpaceX, gerando US$ 7,5 bilhões (cerca de R$ 40,5 bilhões). Apesar disso, a companhia acumulou perdas de US$ 1,1 bilhão (cerca de R$ 5,9 bilhões) neste ano.
A possível fusão também entrou no radar de investidores antes do anúncio de Musk. No início de outubro, o Barclays publicou uma nota a clientes sugerindo que uma combinação entre Tesla e SpaceX poderia ser anunciada antes da assembleia anual de acionistas da montadora, marcada para 3 de dezembro de 2026.
Até o momento, porém, não há confirmação de que a operação será realizada. A decisão depende do trabalho dos comitês independentes e, posteriormente, do apoio dos acionistas das empresas.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Spain-Based Startups Advance Regional Innovation With Barcelona Supercomputing Center
articles.text:
The Barcelona Supercomputing Center (BSC)’s AI Factory Accelerator Programme, now in full operation following a pilot initiative, gives startups access to sovereign compute, technical support and training to support innovation across industries.
Many of these companies are also members of the NVIDIA Inception program for cutting-edge startups — and as of today, access to some of the BSC AI Factory services are available through the NVIDIA Inception portal.
NVIDIA Inception complements the BSC AI Factory Accelerator Programme by providing members with training through NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute open courses, business mentoring, venture capital connections and other resources.
An upcoming extension of MareNostrum 5 — BSC’s public infrastructure serving scientific and technological innovation, powered by NVIDIA accelerated computing — will deliver supercomputing access through the BSC AI Factory and other AI Factories across Europe. BSC AI Factory is among Europe’s first AI factories and the first in Spain, and has delivered more than 800 services to private and public-sector clients since its April 2025 launch.
Three Inception members were recently named the BSC AI Factory Accelerator Programme’s AI Champions at the pilot initiative’s demo day:
Qatium’s water-network platform — already used by more than 250 utilities in 16 countries — is now in early production with its Neural Water Intelligence technology, powered by proprietary AI models trained on MareNostrum 5. Built on NVIDIA accelerated computing, the NVIDIA cuGraph library, the NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo framework and NVIDIA Nemotron open models, the technology helps water utilities make better operational decisions every day.
OneCareAI, a research spin-off from BSC, used NVIDIA NIM microservices to develop technology designed to identify signs of hidden atrial fibrillation — an irregular heart rhythm — in seemingly normal ECGs, helping clinicians identify patients who may be at risk of stroke before one occurs.
Avatia built a voice-first, multi-agent system that provides pharmaceutical companies with agentic coworkers that support sales representatives and give doctors transparent, curated information about medicines, ultimately helping the right treatment reach the right patient sooner. The system taps into NVIDIA NIM microservices, the NVIDIA Nemotron 3 open model family and the open source NVIDIA NeMo Curator library.
Other BSC AI Factory startups — Agrikola AI, Elna Health, Lokutor, Montevive AI, Oppy, Pack2Earth and Up2Smart — span precision agriculture, medical imaging and knowledge access, speech services, enterprise security, sales intelligence and sustainable packaging.
The cohort reflects the breadth of what advanced intelligence can now unlock: preventing strokes, detecting breast cancer subtypes before biopsy, putting medical knowledge at doctors’ fingertips faster, replacing petroleum-based plastic with biobased compostable materials, protecting crops with robots instead of chemicals and more.
Learn more about NVIDIA Inception and the BSC AI Factory Accelerator Programme.

articles.title: A champion for brain injury patients
articles.text:
A champion for brain injury patients
Alissa Totman ’13
Alissa Totman ’13 was a sophomore when she joined MIT BrainTrust, a student-run organization that connects Institute undergraduates and people with brain injuries for support and socializing. “That group was a great way to learn about the human experience of what people go through when they experience a brain injury,” she says. And it laid the foundation for her life’s work.
Today, Totman is a physician specializing in brain injury medicine at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center, where she treats adults with head trauma, stroke, brain tumors, and more.
She is also the founder of Synapse, a nonprofit focused on providing support for such individuals. The organization grew out of a group she started with Jaclyn Konopka ’14 during medical school at Stanford, and Totman launched it as a national service organization in 2016, while pursuing her master’s degree in public health at Harvard.
There are now chapters at 28 universities across the country—and Totman still runs the organization. “There’s a big need for more resources like this,” she says.

articles.title: SpaceX says big AI growth fueled revenue jump
articles.text:
SpaceX announced revenues of $14.6 billion in its Q3 earnings on Tuesday, which it says was a growth of 161 percent year-over-year “fueled by our Super Intelligence (SI) segment and accelerated growth in Connectivity.” While its Space division posted a $7 million loss in income from operations, its Connectivity group posted income from operations $2.4 billion and its SI group posted $431 million.
SpaceX says big AI growth fueled revenue jump
SpaceX announced revenues of $7.6 billion for its ‘SI’ business in its Q3 2026 earnings.
The company’s so-called “SI” business saw revenues of $7.6 billion, which were up 830 percent year-over-year, “primarily driven” by “the activation of new cloud services agreements, the acquisition of Cursor, and increased Grok adoption across enterprise customers and consumers.” For its Connectivity business, SpaceX reported revenues of $5.2 billion and 13.6 million Starlink consumer subscribers. Space business revenues were $1.8 billion, up six percent year-over-year.
SpaceX is livestreamed a video of its earnings call on X, where Elon Musk said that SpaceX will try catching Starship and its booster next month, that Tesla and SpaceX are discussing a possible merger, and that its Starlink connectivity business could generate “several hundred billion dollars a year.”
This is the second earnings report from SpaceX after the company’s IPO in June. The earnings follow a busy Q3 for Elon Musk’s rocket, AI, and social media company, which included the official closing of its $60 billion deal to acquire AI coding tool Cursor, the 13th launch of SpaceX’s Starship, and the launch of a new V5 Starlink residential dish.
During the Q2 earnings call, president Gwynne Shotwell described plans to build out a terrestrial mobile network to compete with T-Mobile, AT&T and Verizon. In SpaceX’s Q2 earnings, the company also noted that its “connectivity” business, which encompasses Starlink, didn’t have a loss from operations, while its AI and space businesses did.
Tesla, where Musk is also CEO, reports earnings on Wednesday.
Update, October 20th: Added details from the Q3 earnings call.

articles.title: Build a semantic layer for agentic AI on AWS with AtScale and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Build a semantic layer for agentic AI on AWS with AtScale and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
In the first post in this series, we built a semantic layer on AWS using Stardog’s knowledge graph over Amazon Aurora and Amazon Redshift. We ran a Strands agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore against that layer. The second post kept the same customer 360 (C360) pattern and swapped in Denodo’s data virtualization platform, extending the source mix to include an on-premises PostgreSQL cluster. This post uses the same C360 pattern again, with AtScale as the semantic layer.
AtScale takes a different shape from the first two. The semantic model is dimensional (dimensions, hierarchies, and measures) rather than a graph of triples or a set of views. AtScale authors the model in the Semantic Modeling Language, an open, YAML-based specification versioned in Git, and exposes it simultaneously, from a single deployed model, over three protocols: SQL, XML for Analysis (XMLA), and the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The Strands agent and the business intelligence (BI) tools the enterprise already uses get the same computed answer from the same definitions.
The rest of the pattern carries over from the earlier posts. A foundation model on Amazon Bedrock (Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 for the walkthrough) plans and writes queries. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore hosts the Strands agent and manages the outbound credential the agent presents to AtScale. The joins, metric definitions, and row and column filters that apply to the caller live inside the semantic layer rather than the prompt.
We assume you’re familiar with the semantic-layer architecture from the first post in the series: what a semantic layer is, what it’s for, and why the model plans queries without owning the joins. If any of that is new, the first post covers the ground.
By the end of this post, you will know:
- How to model a C360 domain in the Semantic Modeling Language (SML): datasets, dimensions and hierarchies, facts, measures, calculated measures, and perspectives, versioned in Git.
- How AtScale plans a dimensional query against Amazon Redshift, and how AtScale’s autonomous aggregate management accelerates the query patterns an agent generates.
- How to expose the model to an AgentCore-hosted Strands agent through the AtScale MCP server, and how to register that MCP server with AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
- How the human user’s identity propagates from the enterprise identity provider through AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to AtScale, and how AtScale enforces role-based access control (RBAC), row security, and perspectives at query time.
- How to deploy AtScale on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) using the AtScale Helm chart and the AtScale K8S Blueprints repository.
The source of truth for the walkthrough is the AtScale C2026.7 release. Where a specific tool name or endpoint applies, we cite the AtScale documentation.
The example: Customer 360 on Amazon Redshift
The customer 360 pattern from the first two posts stays in place. A retail enterprise has customer records, orders, products, and rewards enrollments spread across systems, and business users want to ask cross-cutting questions without knowing which system holds which fact. The Stardog C360 Knowledge Kit we adapted for the first post in the series models this scenario with Customer, Order, Product, and Address entities joined on an integer cid that appears as a primary key in the customer table and as a plain column in the purchase table.
Where this post differs from the first two is where the data physically sits. Stardog and Denodo federate at query time across two engines. AtScale plans a dimensional query as native warehouse SQL and pushes it to one engine per query, so cross-engine data is consolidated upstream. For this walkthrough, all analytical C360 data lives in Amazon Redshift Serverless. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL remains the operational system of record, and a replication path (AWS Database Migration Service or Amazon Aurora zero-ETL to Amazon Redshift) keeps the analytical copy current. The agent queries a single AtScale model that maps to the Amazon Redshift tables.
The schema in Amazon Redshift:
| Table | Key columns | 
| customer | cid (PK), first_name, last_name, email, ssn, phone, location | 
| address | id (PK), city, state, zip, street_name | 
| credit_card | id (PK), cid, card_num, card_type | 
| rewards_account | id (PK), cid, account_id, create_date | 
| purchase | id (PK), pid, purchase_date, quantity, price, cid, card | 
| product | id (PK), name, brand, price, dept | 
| category | id (PK), dept_name, parent | 
| vendor | id (PK), vendor_name, industry | 
Nine columns of interest across eight tables. cid links customer records to purchases. pid links purchases to products. dept links products to categories. Everything analytical is in Amazon Redshift, so joins push down to native SQL rather than being resolved in the semantic layer or in an extract, transform, and load (ETL) pipeline.
A representative question that exercises the whole model: Which of our top 20 customers by lifetime spend haven’t enrolled in the rewards program yet? This is the auto-enrollment question from the Denodo post, carried over so a reader following the series can see the same request answered by a different semantic layer. It touches customer profile, address, purchase history, and enrollment status: one row per customer across four logical entities.
AtScale terms used in this post
AtScale implements the semantic layer as a dimensional model over a warehouse. The AtScale documentation and the SML specification use a specific set of primitives that come up throughout this post. A short reference is useful before we get to the walkthrough.
- Semantic Modeling Language (SML) – An open, YAML-based specification for describing semantic models. Every SML object (model, dataset, dimension, hierarchy, metric, calculation, perspective, row security) is a YAML file. The specification lives at github.com/semanticdatalayer/SML.
- Model – The top-level artifact. A model references datasets, dimensions, facts, and metrics, and exposes them through the AtScale query engine.
- Dimension and hierarchy – A dimension groups related attributes (customer, product, date). A hierarchy inside a dimension organizes those attributes into levels (product → category → department, or year → quarter → month → day).
- Fact and measure – A fact is a dataset that holds measurable events joined to dimensions on key columns. A measure is a quantity aggregated from a fact column, for example SUM(price * quantity) for revenue.
- Calculation – A derived measure expressed as a formula against other measures.
- Perspective – A publishable subset of the model exposed to a specific role or group. Perspectives are how AtScale controls which dimensions and measures a caller can see.
- Row security – A model object that filters rows returned to the caller based on the caller’s identity or attributes.
- Autonomous aggregate management – AtScale watches query patterns across consumers and materializes summary tables in the warehouse when a pattern is expensive enough to justify one. Subsequent queries that match the pattern route to the aggregate transparently.
- Design Center – The AtScale authoring surface. A modeler edits SML through a visual canvas or a text editor. Either way the artifact on disk is SML YAML in Git.
- AtScale MCP server – The in-product MCP endpoint at <atscale-host>/mcp that exposes the semantic model to any MCP client.
Where more detail is useful, the AtScale documentation and the SML specification are the authoritative references.
Reference architecture
The runtime splits into an inbound path and an outbound path, following the same shape as the Stardog and Denodo posts.
Inbound. A client sends the user’s question to the Strands agent through AgentCore Gateway. Gateway validates the JSON Web Token (JWT) that identifies the human user against the enterprise identity provider (IdP), then routes the request to AgentCore runtime (a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore), which hosts the agent process. The agent invokes Claude Sonnet 4.6 on Amazon Bedrock to interpret the prompt and plan the query.
Outbound. When the agent decides to query the semantic model, it invokes a tool call to the AtScale MCP server. AgentCore Gateway serves as the outbound proxy: the AtScale MCP server is registered as an MCP target on Gateway, so tool calls route through Gateway and AgentCore Identity injects the credential at that hop. AtScale’s MCP endpoint accepts either a bearer token (for development and single-identity scenarios) or an OAuth 2.0 access token issued by AtScale’s bundled Keycloak instance (the production path). The AtScale engine validates the token, resolves the caller to an AtScale role, and plans the query against the deployed C360 model.
The query request travels down through the AtScale engine, and the results travel back up. There’s no ETL job that pre-materializes cross-database joins. The analytical copy in Amazon Redshift is the source of truth for the semantic model, kept fresh from Aurora by the upstream replication path.
The architecture is deliberately opinionated on identity. Gateway and Identity hold the tokens at the runtime edges. The agent doesn’t see them and only orchestrates the conversation and the tool calls.
Build the semantic layer
AtScale’s semantic model is a collection of SML objects (datasets, dimensions, facts, measures, calculations, perspectives, row security) versioned in Git. A working model has a shape a data engineer will recognize from a star schema, but every object is expressed as YAML rather than data definition language (DDL), and every object is a separate file. Building the C360 model happens in three passes: datasets over the Amazon Redshift tables, dimensions and hierarchies with the joins between them, and measures and calculations that express the business logic.
Datasets. Each Amazon Redshift table becomes an SML dataset. A dataset declares the physical connection, the schema, the table, and the columns AtScale will surface. Datasets can be authored visually in Design Center or edited directly as YAML. Either surface writes the same SML file to Git.
Dimensions and hierarchies. The C360 model has seven dimensions. dim_customer holds customer profile attributes and joins to dim_address through the location key and to dim_rewards through cid. dim_product holds product attributes and organizes them into a hierarchy through dim_category. dim_date supports date-based analysis. dim_vendor groups products by supplier. dim_rewards holds one row per enrolled customer with account_id and create_date, and snowflakes off dim_customer so that never-enrolled customers surface as null in the enrollment attributes.
AtScale’s hierarchy primitive is the concise expression of the product-to-category relationship. A query against the model can navigate product → category → parent category without a recursive SQL common table expression, and the large language model (LLM) sees a single dimensional path rather than a join graph.
A representative SML fragment for the product hierarchy:
Facts and measures. The fact table for C360 is fact_purchase, mapped to the Amazon Redshift purchase table. It joins to dim_customer on cid, to dim_product on pid, and to dim_date on purchase_date. Measures come off the fact: total_revenue as SUM(price * quantity), order_count as COUNT(id), and units_sold as SUM(quantity).
Calculated measures. Business logic that lives in the model rather than in the query. customer_lifetime_value is total_revenue evaluated at customer grain, the same formula applied to a coarser slice of the fact. Segments like big_spender and spend_tier are calculated measures with conditional expressions:
The expression is evaluated at query time. A column would hold one answer at one grain. The expression recomputes for whatever slice the query asks about, by customer, by customer and year, or by region. When the definition changes (the threshold moves from $10,000 to $15,000), the update happens in one YAML file, gets reviewed as a pull request, and deploys through the AtScale CI hook. Each consumer picks up the new definition on the next query, whether that is the agent, Excel over XMLA, or Tableau over Multidimensional Expressions (MDX).
The artifact on the right of Figure 3 is not a description of the model. It is the model. Design Center’s visual canvas and the YAML editor are two views of the same file, and the Git diff is the authoritative record of every change. The files conform to the open-source SML specification, so the repository can be read without the engine.
After it’s deployed, the model is simultaneously reachable over SQL (for JDBC-based BI tools and notebooks), XMLA (for Excel and Power BI), and MCP (for the agent). The total_revenue calculation returns the same number to Claude Sonnet 4.6 as it does to an Excel PivotTable pointed at the same XMLA endpoint. We confirm this match in Verification.
How AtScale plans and pushes down queries
When the agent asks a question against the semantic model, AtScale’s AI Computation Engine (ACE) does the planning. The steps a query goes through are the same for a dimensional SQL request from the MCP run_query tool and for an XMLA request from Excel. Only the parser at the front differs.
Take the auto-enrollment question: Which of our top 20 customers by lifetime spend haven’t enrolled in the rewards program yet? The agent, prompted with the model context returned by describe_model, composes a dimensional SQL query against the C360 model. ACE parses that query into a logical plan, resolves the dimensional references to the underlying fact_purchase, dim_customer, dim_address, and dim_rewards datasets, applies any row security the caller is subject to, and then plans the physical query against Amazon Redshift.
Two things happen at the physical-planning stage that separate AtScale from a hand-written pipeline. First, the join is pushed to Amazon Redshift as a native SQL join rather than materialized in the semantic layer. The Amazon Redshift optimizer sees a single SQL statement with a filter and an aggregate, and executes it accordingly. Second, AtScale’s aggregate manager checks its registry for a pre-built aggregate that matches the query pattern. If a summary table exists that groups purchases by customer at the right grain, AtScale rewrites the query to hit the aggregate instead of scanning fact_purchase. The query returns in a fraction of the time it would take against the raw fact table, without the agent or the modeler doing any manual work to route it.
The aggregate manager is what makes an agent-driven workload economically feasible. LLM-driven analysis fires more queries than a human analyst would, and open-ended prompts like Tell me something interesting about our sales can spawn a dozen. AtScale watches the query pattern, materializes aggregates in the warehouse itself (not a separate cache), and routes matching queries transparently. Aggregate creation is demand-defined against observed traffic across consumers, not only the agent.
The audit record for the query captures both the dimensional SQL the LLM wrote and the warehouse-native SQL AtScale rewrote it into, along with whether an aggregate served the query. That record is available to an operator through the AtScale Queries page in Design Center, and it’s what the following governance section builds on.
A note on multi-source and interoperability
AtScale connects to warehouses over JDBC. The C360 walkthrough targets Amazon Redshift Serverless. The same SML model works over Snowflake, Databricks, and Google BigQuery, and AtScale documents the connection pattern for each. What changes when you swap the connection is the SQL dialect AtScale emits, not the SML in Git.
One architectural property is worth stating explicitly because it differs from the first two posts in this series. A single AtScale query resolves in one warehouse engine. If the C360 model spans two warehouses (dimensions on Snowflake, facts on Amazon Redshift, say), a query that touches both must be reconciled in one of two ways. The first is upstream, by consolidating an analytical copy in one warehouse through a replication path. The second is by the warehouse itself, using engine-level federation such as Amazon Redshift Spectrum for querying Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), or Apache Iceberg tables that both engines can read. AtScale plans a dimensional query and pushes it to one engine. The cross-engine story lives one layer down.
That choice cuts both ways. It rules out the live cross-engine federation Stardog and Denodo perform at query time, but it lets AtScale’s planner and aggregate manager work against a single-engine execution model, which is what makes the aggregate story load-bearing at scale. Enterprises that already run a warehouse-centric analytical architecture with change data capture (CDC) pipelines from operational systems reuse that architecture. Enterprises whose answers require live federation across engines are better served by the semantic layers in the first two posts.
Governed access: Identity propagation and runtime enforcement
Customer 360 data is regulated. Some users (HR, fraud) need to see personally identifiable information such as Social Security numbers and card numbers. Most users (marketing, analytics) must not. Row-level filters restrict analysts by geography, and a per-user audit trail must survive from the human’s browser through to the warehouse.
AtScale enforces these requirements at the semantic layer, before any query reaches the warehouse. Enforcement happens identically whether the caller is the Strands agent over MCP, an analyst in Excel over XMLA, or a notebook over JDBC. One row-security object in SML, one perspective, one set of role bindings, applied to each consumer of the model.
Identity propagation from the user to AtScale
The chain follows the same shape as the one in the Denodo post, with the terminal hop landing at the AtScale engine rather than continuing to the warehouse.
- The human authenticates to the application against the enterprise IdP and receives a JWT.
- The application forwards the JWT as a bearer token to the Strands agent through AgentCore Gateway, which validates it (issuer, audience, signature) and routes the request to AgentCore runtime.
- When the agent invokes a tool call to the AtScale MCP server, AgentCore Identity supplies the OAuth 2.0 access token issued by AtScale’s bundled Keycloak, mapped to the human user’s identity. The AtScale credential does not enter agent code.
- The AtScale MCP server accepts the OAuth token. The AtScale engine validates it against Keycloak, resolves the caller to an AtScale role, and plans the query with the caller’s row-security constraints and perspective bindings applied. The warehouse is reached with the AtScale connection identity from AWS Secrets Manager.
RBAC, row security, and perspectives
AtScale expresses access control as three composable primitives. RBAC assigns roles to callers based on Keycloak claims. Row security is a model object that filters rows returned to the caller based on the caller’s identity or attributes. A perspective is a publishable subset of the model exposed to a specific role or group.
For the C360 walkthrough, we define two roles.
- hr_user: sees the full C360 model, including ssn and card_num.
- marketing_user: sees the Marketing perspective, which hides ssn and card_num at the model layer.
When marketing_user asks a question that references ssn, the agent’s describe_model call returns the Marketing perspective, one that does not include ssn. The agent has no attribute to project. Row-level filters compose the same way: an SML row-security object that scopes customers by state restricts a caller to a specific set of rows without any change to the agent’s prompt.
Audit fidelity
Queries through the AtScale engine are logged with the caller’s identity, the model, the LLM-generated dimensional SQL, the AtScale-translated pushdown SQL that Amazon Redshift saw, the security policies applied, whether an aggregate served the query, and the row count returned. Because the record captures both the query the model wrote and the query the warehouse executed, an auditor can trace an answer from the human question to the SQL that produced the number. Neither the first nor the second post in this series captures both forms of the query in one record.
An audit record for a governed query looks like this:
The generated_sql and translated_pushdown_sql fields are the ones that make the trail complete: an auditor sees both the query the LLM composed against the semantic model and the query the warehouse actually ran.
Expose the layer through the AtScale MCP server
The AtScale MCP server is a component of the AtScale distribution, exposed at <atscale-host>/mcp. It’s generally available in the AtScale C2026.7 release and speaks the standard Model Context Protocol. Any MCP-compatible client (the Strands agent in AgentCore runtime, Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, VS Code) can connect to the same endpoint against the same deployed model.
The server exposes a set of tools scoped to querying the semantic model. The AtScale documentation publishes a tools reference per release. The tools that matter for an agent-driven workload are:
- list_models: Enumerate the models the caller can see, along with the column groups that describe how dimensions map to facts.
- describe_model: Return the dimensions, hierarchies, measures, calculations, and business descriptions for a chosen model. This is the payload the agent’s system prompt is loaded with before it starts composing queries.
- search_columns: Keyword search over the model’s columns. Useful when a full describe_model payload would use too much of the LLM’s context window.
- validate_query: Check that a dimensional SQL statement is compatible with the model without executing it against the warehouse. This lets the agent iterate on its query cheaply before firing anything Amazon Redshift will bill for.
- run_query: Execute a dimensional SQL statement against the model and return the rows.
- run_queries: Run multiple statements in a batch, useful for open-ended prompts where the agent fires several exploratory queries in parallel.
- get_version: Report the MCP server version, so a client can decide whether to cache the model schema.
The AtScale MCP endpoint accepts two authentication modes. The bearer-token path uses an API token minted from Design Center. Every request runs as the token owner, and this path suits a proof-of-concept or a single-identity service. The OAuth 2.0 path uses AtScale’s bundled Keycloak with a pre-provisioned client whose ID is exactly atscale-mcp, documented on the AtScale Connecting with Claude page. AgentCore Gateway presents the access token on the agent’s behalf, the AtScale engine validates it against Keycloak, and downstream policy evaluation uses the human user’s identity.
Registering the AtScale MCP server as an AgentCore Gateway target follows the standard Gateway MCP target flow. The tools listed earlier appear to the agent as ordinary tools, with AgentCore Identity handling the credential at the Gateway hop.
Sidebar: Extending the model with AI-assisted modeling
The AtScale MCP server exposes tools scoped to querying, and AtScale has been extending the MCP surface with author-side tools that let an agent introspect a warehouse schema, generate a candidate SML model from source metadata, validate the SML against the specification, and commit the result to Git. This pattern, in which an agent shapes the semantic model rather than only reading from it, is a natural fit for Claude Code and Cursor workflows. In those workflows, a data engineer collaborates with the LLM to bootstrap a model over a new dataset.
AtScale groups this direction into three capabilities. A Semantic Discovery Engine scans warehouse schemas, query history, and lineage to infer candidate joins, hierarchies, and metric definitions. A Model Recommendation System suggests dimensions, measures, and relationships based on observed query patterns. A Governed Feedback Loop keeps human review of AI suggestions in the SML-and-Git workflow, so changes are versioned and auditable.
The specific tools available at the time of publication are documented in the AtScale MCP tools reference. Check the current release notes for what is generally available and what is still in preview. The rest of this post covers the consumer path, an agent querying a deployed model, which is what a production C360 workflow relies on today.
Deploy and run the agent
Strands Agents is a small framework for building agents. A short Python entry point wires Claude Sonnet 4.6 on Amazon Bedrock to the AtScale MCP server as a tool source. AgentCore runtime hosts the process. AgentCore Gateway terminates inbound requests and holds the outbound AtScale credential through AgentCore Identity. Foundation model availability on Amazon Bedrock varies by AWS Region. For the current list, see Regional availability by models.
The system prompt matters. The AtScale documentation and the reference demos in the AtScale corpus consistently recommend a three-step call pattern for the agent: list_models to see what is available, then describe_model on the target model to load the dimensions and measures into context, and only then run_query (or validate_query first, if the query is expensive to iterate on). The reasoning is that the LLM should not fabricate column names or metric names. It should reference only what describe_model returned. The system prompt should say so explicitly, and it should include a short section on the business terminology in the target model (total_revenue means sales dollars, not units) so the agent maps user questions to the right measure.
Turn on Amazon Bedrock prompt caching for the reused portion of the system prompt. The describe_model payload runs to a few thousand tokens and does not change within a model version, so caching it drops the input-token cost per query on repeated calls. The cache-point configuration is a request parameter on the BedrockModel object. See the Strands documentation for the current parameter name.
Verification
To confirm the semantic layer, the agent, and the identity flow work as intended, we ran three queries through the agent and then a governance rerun of one of them under a different role. The following behavior is what should reproduce in a working deployment.
Query 1, single dimension
List our customers in Wisconsin, with their city.
The agent generates a dimensional SQL query against the C360 model that selects first_name, last_name, and city from dim_customer and dim_address where state = 'WI'. AtScale’s planner resolves the dimensional path to the customer and address tables in Amazon Redshift, pushes a single SQL statement down, and returns the rows.
Query 2, aggregation with aggregate hit
What are our top 10 products by units sold?
The agent aggregates units_sold by product and orders descending. AtScale’s aggregate manager finds a matching demand-defined aggregate and rewrites the query to hit the summary table in Amazon Redshift rather than scanning fact_purchase. The Queries page shows both the LLM-generated dimensional SQL and the aggregate-routed warehouse SQL side by side.
Query 3, cross-domain
Which of our top 20 customers by lifetime spend haven’t enrolled in the rewards program yet?
The agent generates a query that joins dim_customer, dim_address, dim_rewards, and fact_purchase, and aggregates customer_lifetime_value by customer. The query restricts to customers where dim_rewards.account_id is null. The left join to dim_customer on cid keeps never-enrolled customers, who surface with a null enrollment record. The agent returns the top 20 by lifetime spend. AtScale’s planner resolves the joins to native SQL against Amazon Redshift and returns the ranked list. The customer_lifetime_value formula is not something the LLM had to invent. It’s a calculated measure defined once in customer_lifetime_value.yml and referenced by name in the query.
Governance rerun
We run a variant of Query 1 that adds ssn to the projection (Show me our customers in Wisconsin, with their SSN) as two different callers. As hr_user, describe_model returns the full C360 model, the agent composes the query, and the result set includes the SSN values. As marketing_user, describe_model returns the Marketing perspective, which does not expose ssn. The agent has no attribute to project, so it returns an answer without SSN. Nothing changes between the two runs except the caller’s identity. The query text, the agent code, the MCP server, the AtScale engine, and Amazon Redshift are all untouched.
Cross-consumer confirmation
We opened the same C360 model in Excel through the AtScale XMLA endpoint and dragged Customer.State and Total Revenue onto a PivotTable. The state-level totals match the ones the agent returned for equivalent questions, to the exact number.
Extending across data sources
Adding a new data source to the C360 model is a modeling exercise, not an integration one. Suppose the customer support team asks that the model include ticket volumes so an agent can answer Which of our top spenders opened a support ticket in the last 30 days? The steps are:
- Land the support-ticket data in Amazon Redshift alongside the other C360 tables, using the same replication pattern used for the operational tables.
- Add an SML dataset that maps the new table to a logical object.
- Add or extend a dimension (dim_ticket) and add the join to dim_customer on cid.
- Add any new measures the model needs (open_ticket_count, avg_resolution_time).
- Commit the SML changes, review them as a pull request, and deploy through the AtScale CI hook.
Nothing changes in the agent code or the AgentCore configuration. The next time the agent calls describe_model, it sees the new dimension and measures, and it can compose questions against them. The same pattern applies to a different warehouse. If a source lands in Snowflake or Databricks rather than Amazon Redshift, the connection is a new SML dataset with a Snowflake or Databricks connection, and queries resolve in that engine per the earlier multi-source note.
Deployment: AtScale on Amazon EKS
AtScale runs on Kubernetes, and the reference deployment on AWS is Amazon EKS. AtScale ships an official Helm chart at oci://docker.io/atscaleinc/atscale, and the AtScale K8S Blueprints repository provides infrastructure as code (IaC) scaffolding for standing up an EKS cluster with the components AtScale expects: an ingress controller, a persistent store for the AtScale metadata database, a Redis instance for query caching, and an AtScale-configured Keycloak instance for identity federation.
The AtScale deployment on EKS runs across a small set of Kubernetes pods. atscale-engine is the core query planner and executor. atscale-mcp-server is the MCP endpoint the agent talks to. atscale-keycloak is the bundled identity provider that federates to Amazon Cognito, Okta, Azure Active Directory, and other OpenID Connect (OIDC)-compliant IdPs. Supporting pods handle the SML API and the Design Center UI (atscale-sml-api, atscale-sml-web), PostgreSQL metadata storage (atscale-db), the query cache (atscale-redis), and ingress (atscale-ingress, typically fronted by an AWS Network Load Balancer).
The C360 application (a chat UI or a client library that calls the agent) can run in the same EKS cluster in its own namespace. It uses an IAM role for service account (IRSA) to reach Bedrock and AWS Secrets Manager without embedding credentials.
Networking is standard: AtScale reaches Amazon Redshift through the virtual private cloud (VPC) endpoint or a security-group rule that permits the AtScale namespace’s egress to Amazon Redshift, and the human user reaches the application through the ingress load balancer.
AtScale offers cloud deployment options beyond self-managed EKS. Check the AtScale website for current offerings and AWS availability. The rest of this post assumes the self-managed pattern described earlier.
Conclusion
Agentic access to enterprise data needs three things working together: a foundation model that can plan and generate queries, a semantic layer that computes governed, business-meaningful answers over the live warehouse, and a runtime that hosts the agent and manages the identity flow. Amazon Bedrock, AtScale, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore each play one of those roles.
The agent talks to the semantic layer, not directly to the warehouse. Dimensions, hierarchies, measures, perspectives, and row security live in SML in Git. When a schema drifts or a governance rule changes, the update happens in one file, and each consumer (the agent, Excel, Tableau, Power BI) picks it up on the next query.
Where to start
Most teams that get this working start narrow and expand.
- Pick one workflow that spans two or three data sources and takes longer than it should to answer today.
- Write 3–5 questions the workflow needs to answer. These are the queries the semantic layer has to support on day one.
- Consolidate the analytical data into Amazon Redshift (or the warehouse of your choice), using AWS Database Migration Service or Amazon Aurora zero-ETL for operational data.
- Bootstrap the SML from the warehouse schema in Design Center, then refine it against the competency questions.
- Deploy AtScale on Amazon EKS with the AtScale Helm chart and the AtScale K8S Blueprints, register the AtScale MCP server as an AgentCore Gateway target, and wire a Strands agent through it.
Further reading
- AtScale MCP server documentation: Connect to AtScale with AI
- AtScale C2026.7 release notes: documentation.atscale.com
- AtScale MCP tools reference (published per release with the AtScale documentation)
- AtScale K8S Blueprints: github.com/AtScaleInc/atscale-k8s-blueprints
- Semantic Modeling Language specification: github.com/semanticdatalayer/SML
- Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide
- Amazon Bedrock prompt caching

- Build a semantic layer for agentic AI on AWS with Denodo and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (second post in this series)

articles.title: AI can act exactly like a human, but we still don't think it's conscious
articles.text:
AI can act exactly like a human, but we still don't think it's conscious
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München
- Summary:
- A new study reveals that people draw a surprisingly sharp line between human consciousness and artificial intelligence, even when both behave identically. Researchers found that participants considered even the most responsive AI less conscious than the least responsive human. Yet when asked about "awareness" instead, people judged humans and AI much more similarly.
- Share:
Even when artificial intelligence behaves exactly like a human, people are reluctant to consider it conscious, according to a new study from Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU).
As artificial intelligence becomes more advanced, reports of AI systems misleading users, working together, or appearing to pursue independent goals are becoming increasingly common. These behaviors often lead people to describe AI as though it can think, feel, or make decisions for itself. But does behaving like a human actually convince people that a machine has consciousness?
New research from LMU suggests that people make a clear distinction between displaying intelligent behavior and possessing a conscious mind, even when humans and AI act in precisely the same way.
How Scientists Tested Perceptions of AI Consciousness
Published in the journal Cognition, the study was led by Dr. Louis Longin of LMU's Chair of Philosophy of Mind, working alongside Dr. Bahador Bahrami, Professor Ophelia Deroy, and other researchers.
"Whereas previous studies have typically asked general questions about whether AI actually has mental states, our study is the first to directly compare how people attribute the same mental states to AI and humans behaving in exactly the same way, under identical circumstances," says Longin.
"We may be using mental terms to refer to AI, but this may only be because we lack better words," says Ophelia Deroy, philosopher and a senior author of the study. "After all, AI is trained to act and speak like a human, so these descriptions seem natural."
To investigate how people judge consciousness, the researchers conducted experiments involving nearly 1,100 participants. One group read brief descriptions of artificial agents that showed different levels of responsiveness to their environments. For example, some agents reacted to sounds or recognized the emotional states of others.
Another group encountered the same situations, except the characters were described as humans rather than AI systems. Participants then evaluated how conscious or aware each character seemed to be of its surroundings.
A Surprising Gap Between Human and AI Consciousness
The experiments revealed that responsiveness influenced how participants judged both humans and artificial intelligence. Characters that reacted more actively to their surroundings were generally considered more conscious and more aware.
However, a striking difference emerged when participants evaluated consciousness specifically. Even the most responsive AI was rated as less conscious than the least responsive human. In other words, identical behavior did not lead people to assign the same level of consciousness to humans and machines.
The results changed considerably when participants were asked about awareness instead. For this characteristic, judgments of humans and AI followed largely similar patterns, suggesting that people interpret awareness and consciousness in fundamentally different ways.
"There is a growing worry in public discussion that people will see AI behaving in a human-like way and start treating these systems as if they had human-like mental states," says Longin, lead author of the study. "We found something much more nuanced: People are quite willing to say that an AI notices things and is aware of its surroundings. But they clearly draw a line when it comes to the term 'consciousness'. People consistently attribute less consciousness to AI than humans -- even when their behavior is identical."
Although people sometimes describe AI as conscious when discussing its actions, the findings indicate that they still distinguish between artificial systems and human minds.
Why One Word Changes How We Perceive AI
The researchers believe the difference between consciousness and awareness offers an important insight into how people understand artificial intelligence.
Awareness is a relatively neutral term that can describe an agent's ability to detect and respond to information in its environment. Consciousness, however, carries deeper implications about subjective experience and what it means to have an inner mental life.
Because awareness focuses more directly on observable behavior, people appear comfortable applying it to both humans and AI. Consciousness carries a different meaning, leading people to judge the two much less similarly.
The findings also highlight why the language used to discuss artificial intelligence matters, particularly as AI systems become increasingly capable of producing convincing human behavior.
"Our study teaches us lessons for how we communicate about AI," says Bahador Bahrami, who is also a senior author of the study and an expert in social neuroscience. "Companies and journalists often reach for hyped descriptions of AI models, and credit them with intentions, plans, or even moral conscience and hesitation. What our study shows is that everyday judgments are much more discriminating: People do not simply put AI and humans on the same mental scale. But the boundary also depends on which terms we use. For more neutral descriptors such as 'awareness', the distinction can largely disappear. That makes our choice of language important."
Story Source:
Materials provided by Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Louis Longin, Jurgis Karpus, Nadine Meertens, Bahador Bahrami, Ophelia Deroy. AI is not as conscious as humans: Essentialism in mental state attributions to artificial systems. Cognition, 2027; 278: 106733 DOI: 10.1016/j.cognition.2026.106733

articles.title: Oura adds two new cardiovascular health tracking features to its smart rings
articles.text:
Oura is introducing two new cardiovascular-focused health tracking features to its smart rings designed to help users better understand the effect regular workouts and exercise are having on their long-term health, and whether they need to ramp it up or dial things down. Cardio Effort and automatic VO2 Max (previously known as Cardio Capacity) are available for the Oura Ring Gen 3 and later models, but only to users with an active Oura membership.
Oura adds two new cardiovascular health tracking features to its smart rings
The new features help users better understand how the intensity of regular workouts will affect their long-term health.
Instead of measuring how fast or far a user went during a run or bike ride, or metrics like calories burned, Cardio Effort measures how hard their cardiovascular system was working during exercise and how long that effort was sustained. Cardio Effort is calculated for individual workouts taking into account both intensity and duration but provides a plain language evaluation that compares a user’s cumulative weekly effort against a personalized baseline.
One one end of the scale is a Light rating that’s described as being a “substantially lower cardiovascular strain than your usual baseline.” The rating scale progresses through Fair, Maintaining, Building, and Reaching at the other end which means your weekly Cardio Effort had a “markedly higher exposure relative to your baseline, signaling that it may be time to prioritize recovery.” So instead of always pushing a user to increase their efforts, the feature does make recommendations for rest when it may be more beneficial.
Oura Rings already support VO2 Max readings that are used to track aerobic capacity, but the previous Cardio Capacity feature was somewhat cumbersome because estimating a user’s maximum oxygen uptake required a six-minute walking test for calibration. The new version, automatic VO2 Max, currently available as a beta feature through Oura Labs, automatically activates after users complete five “qualifying GPS-enabled activities” that include walks, runs, and hikes.
Once activated VO2 Max readings will be available in the Oura app’s My Health Heart Hub section with a user’s current estimate, their capacity rated as low, fair, high, or peak, how their aerobic capacity has changed over time, and personalized insights for when VO2 Max “meaningfully shifts or stays consistent.”

articles.title: A cleaner path to rare earth metals
articles.text:
A cleaner path to rare earth metals
Tomás Villalón Jr. ’14
Tomás Villalón Jr. ’14 was raised in San Antonio, Texas, but vividly remembers smog hanging over the city his family came from—Monterrey, Mexico, a steel manufacturing and metal fabrication hub. Even as a child, he realized it was problematic to breathe that air.
“I’m motivated because I’ve seen what metal-making does,” says Villalón, who majored in materials science and engineering. He started thinking about sustainable metallurgy senior year while working at Boston Metal, an MIT spinoff focused on decarbonizing steelmaking. In 2019 he cofounded Phoenix Tailings, which has developed an efficient process for extracting rare earth metals from mining waste.
“The mining ecosystem by itself makes over several billion tons of waste,” says Villalón, who serves as chief technology officer. (Others on the founding team are Michelle Chao ’17, Nick Myers, and Anthony Balladon.) “We have to get rid of this pollution.”
The company asserts that its proprietary electrochemical technique for processing rare earths generates no toxins and is carbon-free when fueled by renewables.

articles.title: « Une crise » : le nouveau patron d’Apple accorde sa première grande interview et évoque la pénurie de mémoire
articles.text:
John Ternus a accordé sa première grande interview au magazine américain TIME, qui le place en couverture de son numéro consacré aux inventions de l’année, en kiosque le 26 octobre. Le successeur de Tim Cook, en poste depuis le 1er septembre, y revient sur ses débuts éclairs, lui qui a dévoilé l’iPhone Duo huit jours seulement après sa prise de fonction. Interrogé sur la flambée des prix de la mémoire, il répond sans détour : « les contraintes qui pèsent sur la mémoire sont absolument une crise ».
Une crise assumée jusque devant Washington
La phrase répond à la lettre d’un groupe bipartisan de sénateurs, opposés au test de puces mémoire issues d’un fournisseur chinois, une piste explorée pour élargir un approvisionnement devenu critique. Ternus ne cède rien : « notre conviction profonde est que toutes les options doivent être sur la table ».
Le fournisseur en question serait CXMT, le champion chinois de la DRAM, dont des échantillons seraient déjà en cours d’évaluation à Cupertino. Le secrétaire américain au Commerce s’était pourtant opposé publiquement, dès le mois d’août, à l’idée de voir de la mémoire chinoise équiper les produits des grands groupes du pays. La mémoire pèse environ 10 % du coût des composants d’un iPhone, et les calculs de la banque JPMorgan la voient grimper jusqu’à 45 % d’ici 2027. Les prix de la RAM avaient déjà quadruplé au printemps, avant même les records battus cet été.
L’iPhone ne fait plus exception
Fin juin, Apple relevait de plusieurs dizaines à plusieurs centaines d’euros les tarifs des Mac, des iPad et de nombreux accessoires, en épargnant soigneusement l’iPhone. La digue a tenu trois mois. Les iPhone 18 Pro et 18 Pro Max présentés en septembre coûtent chacun 150 euros de plus que leurs prédécesseurs, à 1 479 et 1 629 euros. Les iPhone 17 restés au catalogue ont subi la même hausse, et l’iPhone Duo s’affiche à 2 339 euros.
Le keynote de rentrée a surtout confirmé une absence : aucun iPhone 18 classique n’accompagnait les modèles Pro et le pliable, une première pour la gamme. Le modèle qui porte traditionnellement les volumes de la marque n’arriverait qu’au printemps 2027, accompagné d’un iPhone 18e et d’un nouvel iPhone Air. La pénurie de mémoire est citée parmi les causes de ce décalage, Apple préférant réserver ses stocks de composants aux appareils les plus rentables.
Repousser le modèle le plus vendu, c’est aussi retarder le moment de fixer son prix en pleine tempête. Une hausse de 150 euros passe sur un téléphone à plus de 1 400 euros, beaucoup moins sur celui qui sert de porte d’entrée à l’écosystème.Tim Cook, devenu président exécutif du conseil d’administration, assure de son côté qu’il ne « se mêle pas » de la gestion quotidienne. Cette crise sera donc le premier vrai test de son successeur. Réponse au printemps, lorsque l’on saura si les iPhone grand public échappent encore à l’inflation qui a rattrapé tout le reste du catalogue.

Source : Time

articles.title: NVIDIA BlueField-4 STX Server for CMX at OCP 2026
articles.text:
At OCP 2026, we saw the new NVIDIA BlueField-4 STX Server for Context Memory (CMX). Partners had been asking for this, and NVIDIA delivered. Onboard, we have a lower-cost design than the dual-Vera setup we saw previously. Let us take a look at the new board.
NVIDIA BlueField-4 STX Server for CMX at OCP 2026
For context, this is the previously shown BlueField-4 DPU. That one, pictured below, is a dual Vera CPU setup, each with SOCAMM memory, plus four ConnectX-9 SuperNICs. NVIDIA calls this a DPU, but it is clearly more costly than a BlueField-1 or BlueField-3, which are much smaller and lower-power devices. For partners looking at building storage platforms, the below is more akin to a dual CPU server than a traditional DPU.
At OCP 2026, multiple partners showed off the BlueField-4 STX server for context memory (CMX). Here is the much smaller card, which still uses high-density connectors for PCIe and system connectivity.
NVIDIA BlueField-4 DPUs encompass both NVIDIA Grace and Vera CPU cores, but this one looks like a Vera package. That is a very substantial CPU. To be clear, this is not like the embedded-class CPUs that we typically have seen in DPUs previously. This is more like having a high-end single-socket server platform.
Another interesting feature is that the boards at OCP 2026 are using SOCAMM memory, so these should be relatively easy to put either a heatsink or a liquid cooling block on top of it.
Onboard, there is an M.2 slot. Usually these are for OS drives, but if you saw our recent Inside the Secretive AWS Networking Lab, the M.2 SSDs there are being used for log devices.
This may seem like a small feature, but it means NVIDIA designed this less like a traditional motherboard replacement and more like something that is easy to assemble automatically.
Something that may not immediately hit you if you are looking at photos is just the size of this board. A soldered CPU and LPDDR5X here, over traditional DDR5 DIMM slots, give NVIDIA a platform where the “motherboard” is roughly the size of an Intel DMR 16-channel socket or a 16-channel AMD EPYC Venice platform.
Final Words
This is just a neat platform. It almost feels like NVIDIA needs some brand between the Vera server line and the traditional BlueField DPU line. Something notable that we did not see on the boards shown at OCP 2026, or at least in our photos of them from various booths, is an NVIDIA ConnectX-9 SuperNIC. We expected that, but did not see it on this board. For context memory platforms, a single Vera versus a dual Vera makes this a lower-cost platform, and that will likely help the STX/ CMX systems come to market as the price of NAND has been rising meaningfully over the past year.

articles.title: Scientists recreate a bizarre quantum effect that stops a particle cold
articles.text:
Scientists recreate a bizarre quantum effect that stops a particle cold
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- University of Oxford
- Summary:
- Oxford physicists have recreated a bizarre quantum effect in which a particle responds to a magnetic field without ever traveling through it. Using a hybrid quantum computer, they demonstrated how introducing a simulated magnetic flux could completely halt a particle's movement through quantum interference. The experiment brings a decades-old prediction into a new setting where matter and quantum fields influence one another.
- Share:
A particle does not have to pass through a magnetic field to be influenced by it. That surprising feature of quantum physics has now been recreated by researchers at the University of Oxford, who used a hybrid quantum computer to demonstrate how an invisible magnetic influence can bring a simulated particle's movement to a complete stop.
The experiment reproduced a phenomenon known as the Aharonov-Bohm effect, in which a charged particle traveling around a region containing magnetic flux experiences a measurable change in its quantum state, even though its path never takes it through the magnetic field itself.
The Oxford team achieved this using a quantum system that combines qubits, the basic units of quantum information, with quantum oscillators, which represent vibrating motion. Their findings, published in Nature Physics, demonstrate how this combination could help scientists investigate fundamental interactions between matter and fields that are increasingly difficult to simulate using conventional computers.
A Strange Quantum Effect Predicted in 1959
In everyday physics, a charged particle responds to the electric and magnetic fields it encounters. Quantum mechanics, however, reveals that particles can behave in ways that have no straightforward counterpart in our ordinary experience.
In 1959, physicists Yakir Aharonov and David Bohm predicted that a charged particle could be affected by magnetic flux even if it traveled entirely outside the region containing the magnetic field. Rather than experiencing a conventional magnetic force along its path, the particle would undergo a change in its quantum phase.
Quantum phase describes an aspect of a particle's wave behavior that influences how different possible paths interfere with one another. Although the phase itself is not directly visible, differences in phase can produce measurable effects.
The prediction became known as the Aharonov-Bohm effect and was eventually verified in experiments involving real electrons. It remains one of the clearest demonstrations that the quantum world operates according to rules that go beyond the familiar laws of classical physics.
Researchers are now exploring how this phenomenon behaves in more complex theoretical systems known as lattice gauge theories.
These theories describe how matter interacts with fields associated with fundamental forces. They represent space as a grid, with matter located at individual points and fields associated with the connections between them. Such models are particularly important in particle physics and high-energy physics, where scientists study the basic particles and interactions that make up the universe.
The challenge is that the mathematics becomes extraordinarily demanding as these systems grow more complicated. Even powerful conventional computers can struggle to calculate how all the interacting components evolve.
Quantum computers offer a different approach. Instead of attempting to calculate every aspect of a quantum system using classical computing methods, scientists can construct another quantum system that follows the same underlying rules. They can then observe its behavior directly, an approach known as quantum simulation.
How Scientists Built the Quantum Experiment
The Oxford project began in 2022, when lead author Dr. Sebastian Saner, Dr. Oana Bazavan, and their colleagues started developing a way to simulate lattice gauge theories using a hybrid quantum system. They collaborated with Dr. Alejandro Bermudez of the Instituto de Física Teórica in Madrid.
Their experimental design relied on two different quantum components that performed separate functions.
The first consisted of qubits encoded in the internal states of trapped ions, which are electrically charged atoms held in place using electromagnetic fields. These qubits represented the gauge fields in the theoretical model.
The second component used quantum oscillators, created by the vibrations of those same trapped ions. These oscillators represented matter.
By combining the two, the researchers constructed a simple loop that served as a basic building block of a lattice gauge theory. Two oscillators represented matter at two different locations, while two qubits represented the fields connecting those locations.
Although the arrangement was small, it was sufficient to reproduce an important interaction between matter and magnetic flux.
Quantum Entanglement Creates a Surprising Solution
The researchers next placed the two qubits into an entangled quantum state. Entanglement is a phenomenon in which quantum systems become linked in ways that cannot be fully explained by classical physics.
Within the team's simulated lattice gauge theory, this entangled state represented magnetic flux passing through the center of the loop.
Initially, the researchers had planned to introduce the magnetic flux as a fixed background condition. However, creating the necessary interaction would have required capabilities that their quantum hardware did not possess.
Encoding the flux directly into the qubits provided a practical alternative. More importantly, it allowed the magnetic flux to become part of the evolving quantum system rather than remaining an unchanging external influence.
"For us, the exciting step was to encode the magnetic flux in a gauge field that was itself dynamical," says Dr. Saner. "Rather than having matter evolve in a fixed background, the matter and gauge field become part of the same quantum dynamics."
What began as a technical workaround ultimately enabled the researchers to explore a more interesting version of the phenomenon, one in which matter and the field could participate together in the quantum dynamics.
A Quantum Effect That Stops Particle Motion
With their simulated loop in place, the scientists examined how a matter particle moved between locations through a process known as quantum tunneling.
Quantum tunneling allows particles to move between states in ways that would not be possible under ordinary classical rules.
When the researchers ran their simulation without magnetic flux, the particle could tunnel freely around the loop.
Introducing the simulated flux produced a strikingly different result.
The particle had two possible paths around the loop, but the magnetic flux changed their relative quantum phases. As a result, the two paths interfered destructively, meaning their quantum contributions canceled each other out.
This interference completely suppressed the tunneling, leaving the simulated particle frozen in its original state.
The outcome demonstrated the Aharonov-Bohm effect within a lattice gauge theory containing a dynamical field. Rather than simply reproducing the familiar behavior of a particle moving around a fixed magnetic influence, the experiment showed how the phenomenon can emerge when matter and the field are both represented by interacting quantum components.
A New Tool for Exploring Fundamental Physics
The Oxford findings were published alongside a related study by researchers at the University of Maryland, led by Professor Norbert Linke.
The Maryland team also used a hybrid quantum system, but their experiment focused on simulating the Yukawa potential, a mathematical description of an interaction relevant to nuclear and particle physics.
Although the two research groups developed their methods independently, they later coordinated the submission of their studies to Nature Physics.
Together, the experiments demonstrate how hybrid quantum computers could become valuable tools for investigating fundamental interactions that are difficult to reproduce using classical simulations.
By combining different types of quantum components, researchers can build systems in which matter and fields are represented in ways that more closely reflect the physics they want to study.
The Oxford experiment provides an example of that potential. A phenomenon first predicted in 1959 and later observed with electrons has now been recreated in a quantum simulator where the field itself participates in the dynamics, offering scientists another way to explore the unusual rules governing the quantum world.

articles.title: 970,000 Medi-Cal Members Affected by Paradigm Healthcare Data Breach
articles.text:
Paradigm Healthcare Services has told the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) that a data breach discovered last year affected more than 970,000 people.
San Francisco-based Paradigm processes billing for Medi-Cal, California’s Medicaid program, under a data use agreement with the California Department of Health Care Services (DHCS). It also maintains Medi-Cal member identification numbers on the department’s behalf.
The company says it became aware of unauthorized access to its local network on October 13, 2025. “On August 18, 2026, we determined that certain files containing select individuals’ protected health information may have been accessed by an unauthorized party between October 8, 2025, and October 15, 2025,” Paradigm said.
The compromised files contained names, dates of birth, gender, and Medi-Cal member identification numbers. Paradigm says its online service documentation and billing platform, Student Health Network (SHN), was not impacted.
Paradigm’s notification letters are dated September 14, 2026, roughly 11 months after the intrusion was detected. “We have no evidence that any of your information has been used to commit fraud or identity theft as a result of this incident,” the company said.
The notice doesn’t name the threat actor, explain how the attackers gained access, or say whether data was exfiltrated. Paradigm says it took certain systems offline, notified law enforcement, and brought in outside incident response experts.
No known cybercrime group appears to have taken credit for an attack on Paradigm.
Tarter Krinsky & Drogin and Ridgeway Pharmacy data breaches
The HHS healthcare data breach tracker has been updated to show that a significant number of individuals were affected by separate incidents disclosed recently by the law firm Tarter Krinsky & Drogin (TKD) and Ridgeway Pharmacy Ltd.
TKD, which serves healthcare providers, started notifying individuals in early September that it had detected suspicious activity on its network in September 2025.
The company completed its investigation one year later and determined that attackers accessed certain servers between July 9 and September 9, 2025.
TKD told the HHS that the incident affected more than 196,000 individuals.
Ridgeway Pharmacy, which started sending out data breach notices on September 21, discovered unauthorized access to personal information on August 21, 2026.
The company discovered that its website was hacked and the attacker may have gained access to information such as name, address, date of birth, health and insurance information, prescription information, and payment card information.
Ridgeway Pharmacy informed the HHS that more than 258,000 individuals are affected.
Related: Healthcare data breaches
